Content: The unified namespace is the foundation of the business -- it is a the digital representation of all data, context and information... it is designed to treat all connected points as a node in an ecosystem -- so a PLC and a software application both consume data and produce information... and they consume from the unified namespace and publish back into it. Author: walker.reynolds
Content:
> @Walker Reynolds a unified namespace seems like a really concept but also seems like a single common of failure. Or rather a perfect point for a ransomware attack. 
> 
> Does a unified namespace usually come with redundancy? 
> 
> Admittedly I am unfamiliar with the concept.
@the-link A unified namespace is a single source of truth for the business -- we generally use MQTT brokers, which are redundant, we can make as many copies of the broker as we want -- simply by having a new instance of a broker install subscribe to all of the topics in another install.  So -- the unified namespace is a distributed single source of truth, with redundancy.

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: Remember, a unified namespace is the layer that all nodes in the ecosystem use to connect to one another, consume data from each other and publish information back.  All the namespace does is give the applications and hardware a place to plug into and talk to everything else.  It contains the structure, a list of all the nodes connected, and what each node is subscribing to.  When a node publishes back into the namespace, it notifies to the nodes that are subscribed to those topics what the new update is.

Author: vaughnturner8478
Content: @Walker Reynolds is an abstraction layer for disparagent systems to interface, or send and consume data to much of a generalization?

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: Abstraction happens before the data gets to the unified namespace in most instances -- however, there are scenarios where raw data (like process data from the edge) is published into the namespace to be consumed and abstracted by the node that organizes all of the unified data and information prior to publishing back to the namespace.

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: A single data point could be published and consumed from a namespace multiple times -- each time it may be abstracted in some way -- perhaps to add context.  However, each time it is published back, it goes to a new, unique location in the namespace.  Each topic in the namespace is controlled by a single node in the ecosystem -- if another node does something with it, then what is published goes into that nodes location.

Author: walker.reynolds
Content:
> Today I had a conversation with a person from industry regarding Unified  Name Space concept. I work in a company called Nexiona Connectocrats and we have a solution (MIIMETIQ) that could be used as UNS. The person told me that he's planning to do it with Osisoft PI, for my surprise as I was assuming it was just a process date historian solution. Could anybody confirm that it could be used as UNS. If not, what argumentation could be used to clarify it?
@Deleted User The answer is yes -- it could be used as a UNS as long as your are using MQTT and OPC for data transfer.  The Asset Frames in OSI give you the ability to abstract the edge data into the UNS structure and OSI can consume the structure from other MQTT client nodes.  That being said, NO, YOU SHOULD NOT USE OSI PI FOR YOUR UNS -- you should treat it as a node that provides historian functionality and has asset modeling available to convert edge data into the correct structure for publishing into the UNS.  Using OSI Pi as your UNS is like building  a wall on top of couch, the couch (OSI Pi or another application) will get changed out for another couch sometime down the road, so it shouldn't become critical to the foundation of your house (your digital architecture).

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: The answer is yes -- it should be decoupled.  I want to clarify something -- you can use a platform like Ignition for your unified namespace and have SCADA and UNS under the same platform for one reason -- Ignition is modular, it is a platform first and an application second.  I can use Ignition just as my UNS or I can add in other modules that provide node functionality of specific applications, like SCADA or MES, I can also pull the namespace out of Ignition and move it to a standalone UNS without any real work at all.  The same cannot be said for OSI-Pi, it is an application first, a historian application, it is not a platform at all.  It is an application that has some of the features of a platform but that doesn't make it a platform.  Moreover, putting the UNS in OSI-Pi is a strategic decision to paint yourself into a corner -- because decoupling from OSI means removing the couch from under the wall -- it breaks everything until you rebuild the UNS as stand alone.

We have also been discussing the efforts around embedding a Sparkplug conformant broker right into the hub. This would minimize one less component to manage and would also allow to auto-clean the Sparkplug namespace based on any configuration changes made to the product (for example, a user deletes an attribute on a model, but it has recently been published). Author: walker.reynolds
Content: OPC-UA has a place in the future, but its not with enterprise IIoT.  Even with the pub/sub standard, the standard is far too verbose to scale.  MQTT with Sparkplug is 1/25 the size of OPC-UA.  OPC-UA will live on the edge and MQTT or DNP3 or (insert other IIoT protocol) will handle the UNS.  I have several benchmarking examples that I use to demonstrate why OPC-UA does not scale at the enterprise level and why MQTT does.  I was an OPC-UA guy and all of my first attempts to digitally transform leveraged OPC-DA and UA, at first.  They hit critical mass and then you either drop data from the architecture or you take the network down.  This is an absolute empirical certainty.  RE: PackML is adopted with OPC-UA because of OMACs origins and their existing relationships with OPC Foundation, CSIA et al.  Their adoption is a function of the existing relationship, not the merits of the solution.  USCARS adopted OBD2, and so Ford, Chevy and Chrysler all use the standard, Tesla isn't part of the group and adopted a different standard -- just because the legacy players use existing relationships to leverage partnerships and strategic decisions, doesn't make them innovative or right.  OPC-UA is the choice of the legacy players because they are already invested in the standard AND they have existing partnerships that guarantee they will leverage the standard.  Their track record in Digital Transformation speaks for itself.  I don't have an allegiance to any standard -- except the best one.  Which is why we don't enter into strategic partnerships with vendors or organizations if the partnership requires we use their technology no matter the consequences to the success of the solution.  The industry is run like the mafia -- and it hurts consumers.  That has to change.  (OMACS partner list)

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: @Mario Ishikawa the answer is two-fold.  A. OPC-UA contains tags and elements in the standard that are appropriate for process control but not necessary outside of the edge.  It is very good at handling elements for PID, VFD et al as well as standard process control data types.  However, it was written for interoperability of Operations tools, and did not take into consideration interoperability with Business tools.  It is constrained by the era in which the standard was written.  MQTT was the response to those constraints.  B. MQTT was written for slow networks -- IBM, Phillips 66 and Arlen et all were trying to solve the problem of retrieving high speed process data over slow distributed networks at a resolution you could expect with fast networks.  The result was edge driven, report by exception and light weight.  Open architecture came along later -- and we're thankful for it.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
This is funny you mention this.  I ran into John at an OPC Foundation event last year.  A few weeks later we met up to discuss the disconnect between OPC Foundation initiatives and the end-user experience trying to adopt the tech.

Setting aside the distinctions of transport (e.g., TCP, MQTT, AMQP) and payload (OPC-UA, Sparkplug B), let's discuss broad adoption.  Theoretically, it's not an either/or thing.  But, in practice, it absolutely is.  If there aren't any devices or apps adopting this stuff, it's not particularly useful.  As John said, "..the best technology doesn't necessarily win."

When I first learned of OPC-UA, I was really impressed by the information modeling capabilities.  My org has struggled so much trying to get data out of our assets and normalize it into something useful.  I remember, at another OPC event, I asked Stefan and Uwe about the realities of implementing the technology on some of the high-profile use cases.  They kind of shrugged it off as if it was a trivial thing to do.  For anyone other than an OEM that knows their own product inside and out, I'm not so sure about that.  Even then, it's probably still really hard.  We Germans have a tendency to overlook adoption and focus on the tech.  Technical solutions to political problems. 
 Evidence:  First, count the number of OPC companion specs and working groups.  Now, count the number of [successful] commercial products adopting them.

I've yet to hear of industrial assets shipping with full-fledged OPC-UA servers with an information model.  I've yet to hear of leading apps/platforms (e.g., Ignition, ThingWorx, C3, Azure, AWS) that can consume these.  I've yet to hear of any one building modules or extensions to consume these.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
As John mentioned, Sparkplug B makes MQTT viable.  It defines the payload, structure, state, etc.  But, if there is one thing I wish it did, it would be to have something like the companion specs (e.g., VDMA, MTConnect, PackML, Euromap).  There is a great need for standardized namespaces and mappings.  There is still a big "basket full of remotes" problem (see Jean-Louis Gassée).  In discrete manufacturing, it can be truly a nightmare figuring out the memory tables of all the different assets.  Go spend some time with CNC machines.

Anyways, I hope that something like HighByte might allow for the exchange of information models in the future.  Imagine a git hub community in which people exchange mappings and information models.  Otherwise, widescale adoption of I4.0 / IIoT tech will be a large challenge.  We need to figure out a way to stop redoing the same one-off engineering projects to acquire data locked up in the field.

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: They generally need to be connected to the UNS to get updates, you can use QoS = 2 and Retain = 1 on the publish to make sure that any client that connects after the change gets the value published while they were gone. Author: laik6560
Content: @Walker Reynolds Hello Walker. Thank you for all the great content you and your team produce. In your opinion does HTTP protocol have a place in an IIoT Industry 4.0 environment? Would it be better to have everything over a protocol such as MQTT?

Author: walker.reynolds
Content:
> @Walker Reynolds Hello Walker. Thank you for all the great content you and your team produce. In your opinion does HTTP protocol have a place in an IIoT Industry 4.0 environment? Would it be better to have everything over a protocol such as MQTT?
@laik the short answer is yes -- HTTP has a place in IIoT.  However, not as the backbone of the IIoT infrastructure, but as a peer to peer connection between nodes.  The backbone of the architecture needs to meet these minimum requirements:

1. Report by exception (only values that change get pushed)
2. Edge driven (nodes push into the namespace, a server doesn't poll)
3. Open Architecture (there are no data points that are locked away and inaccessible, plays nice with other software)
4. Lightweight (conserves bandwidth, not overly verbose)

Content: OPC Foundation is working hard to maintain their place in the market and the future.  The issue is the verbosity of the standard.  Until they modify the standard to pair down the overhead required for an OPC-UA payload, it is a moot point. Author: walker.reynolds
Content: We have a standard for Machine and Line State -- and then we extend for machine/line/area/plant specific attributes.  In a nutshell, the namespace contains 'State' tag which is an INT.  It contains a 'State Definition' tag which is a dataset with the lookups (pulled from the MES back-end), these exist at cell and line levels in the namespace.  All process specific tags are modeled in a namespace called 'Edge' which is specific to the PLC or controller the tag comes from.  Edge is the raw connection then we have siblings of Edge that abstract for modeling/objects etc.

Content:
I'm not a Sparkplug B expert, but I can attest to the importance of payloads and data modeling.  Vague, inconsistent payloads have been plaguing industrial automation and its end users for decades.  They are a very real technical inhibitor.

If you can guarantee that your environment will never change (e.g., producers, consumers, content), perhaps it's not useful.

On the other hand, it can be shortsighted.  It's a missed opportunity not to organize and self-describe data sources.  While it's initially more work on the first step, it almost always pays off.

Do you care about connection state?  Do you want to assume context?  Do you want to manually "map" or contextualize data?  Will anyone other than you need to work on this? Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
HighByte is probably a beneficial tool to avoid vendor lock-in with IoT / SCADA platforms (e.g., Azure, AWS).  It decouples the data model and connections from the platforms themselves.  It serves as infrastructure for platforms to "plug into" and consume data.  This provides the benefit of relative portability between platforms without having to worry about data modeling.  While it's not a full on commoditization of platforms, it lowers the cost of switching.  It overcomes the problem of rebuilding data models / re-contextualizing.  This, especially with industrial data, is what consumes significant engineering resources.

If you're concerned about lock-in with HighByte itself, if I recall correctly, the models and config in HighByte are saved in a JSON file.  This allows for raw, en masse editing and imports/exports.  I suppose there is no reason why one couldn't rework the file to port their UNS models into a new a solution.  So, in this case, it's not like the model definitions are going into a black box and are lost.  Beyond this, all the connections would have to be migrated and reestablished.

Author: benveenema
Content:
The hierarchy refers to equipment, so even in discrete manufacturing this makes sense. Inventory/material need to be put in a separate space. ISA-95 defines a separate model for equipment, material and personnel. All of which are under a larger process model. 

ISA-95 equipment hierarchy (enterprise, site, area, process cell, line) doesn't define a UNS, a UNS uses the ISA-95 model. It will have to be adapted a bit. Perhaps there is a warehouse area in which inventory is stored. Or a line has a location where inventory can be temporarily associated with it. This will depend on the individual manufacturers implementation.

The UNS is more of an event based structure. A line will have an event where it produces a part. A database or historian subscribed to the UNS will capture these events. Inventory is a static object. Events like material handlers and production lines affect inventory. The current state of inventory may be in the UNS as many end nodes (DB, ERP, AI) may need access to it. In this case, the UNS is acting as a transport layer.

Content:
*As I see it*, the UNS is a common structure that takes care of all events from all nodes in the organization. The fact that UNS is structured (ISA-95) and that it reflects the organization in real time is the difference from a digital twin, as this does not have to be structured - but only represents an organization from any perspective without the information following a specific standard. . A digital twin is also not necessarily real-time dynamic.

When I have had to explain to explain it to people outside the tech community what the UNS is, I have used the Norwegian word "Felles NavneStruktur" ("gemeinsame Namensstruktur"?) And compared it with web addresses and explained that it gives machines and programs the opportunity to each has its own unique identity, which in addition tells where in the system the node is located. It is of course very simplified and not even completely correct, but it provides a starting point for understanding the concept.

You could probably also describe it as a "structured, real time digital twin" if you wanted.

Author: mparris
Content:
I'm starting evaluations myself, so I don't know the space yet.

My top questions to any IIoT platform would be:

1) If you provide the spinal cord, how do I integrate an external application?

2) If I replaced your spinal cord with an external commercial of the shelf product, what effort is required to integrate your platform?

The best architecture would be to list all the desired software on each functional box, and if the software you list allows you to mix and match because they use transparent and standard interfaces, then keep them on the list and pick what works best.  If the software you list requires proprietary interfaces or forces you to bundle multiple boxes together (either through licensing or for technical reasons), mark them off the list.

I could see a company selecting Platform A, which provides the data gateway, data spinal cord, modeling and visualization. Then the another company develops the Whizbang Platform and you want to switch.  What does that look like?  Can you keep some of it (like the gateways and the modeling) or is it an all or nothing choice?  Do you have to re-engineer connections to ERP, MES, and SCADA?  Or would your only choice be to force WizBang to develop a custom interface to your Platform A.

The Ignition Platform is a good example of what to look for... they have a menu of modules, where you use what you like. You don't want to use their Historian, plug in a different one.    Don't like to use their MQTT Distributor module, use EMQx, RabbitMQ, or HiveMQ.

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: They are not synonymous, no... but they are linked.  A tag provider in ignition is a master data model for a group of tags.  The UNS is the structure and events of a layer of the business or the business as a whole.  Tags in Ignition have structure (tagPath) and events (values with timestamps) but they are not a UNS UNLESS they are inclusive of all structure and events for a layer of the business OR the entire business.  In nearly all cases, we build the UNS in an MQTT broker -- Ignition is a node that consumes the topic namespace in the broker and converts that namespace into tags in Ignition.  So... while they are related, they are not the same.

Content: Yes... Example.. I have a paper company ingesting nearly 1000 edge nodes using TeliTs devices over kinesis into a S3 datalake. Author: michael.brown
Content:
I have an opinion that I'll share based on working with customers....plant data laying around in all its different data stores I'll catagorize as 3 types realtime/streaming (plc, SCADA, io servers) 
transactions, (mes systems, maintance, quality systems, sql servers) 
static (meta data, serial numbers, warranty info etc...)

UNS  accomplishes a few major things mainly but not exclusive to the realtime data and some transaction and static data as required. 
1. organizes and formats data to the same model
2. It provides a single source of truth for what's going on right now.
3. Provides effective pub/sub comms for efficient data communication. 

A Datalake is a repository for all data.. Period... My experience is the datalake requires the heirachy of the UNS to work effectively.

They are 2 sides of the same coin in my opinion... You need both. One for realtime and one for historical

Whats interesting to me is how the datalake platforms are evolving so quickly... I think it's a day soon that the UNS and datalake will be the same repository with 2 different interfaces.

Author: marioishikawa
Content: The term is new for me but it is certainly a very interesting concept. I'm not saying I'm right but this is my opinion by looking at a glance. It is about breaking data silos by connecting APIs in a central hub, the iPaas. I think Enterprise can take advantage of it on CRMs, ERPs, MES and historian but I would not see it as the UNS because it does not seem to be the ideal model for the stream of real-time/time-series data. MQTT is lightweight and if you have a REST API to send and receive data, you can receive data by exception by HTTP POST but it needed to be polled to send data, unless you use some websocket. But, the UNS could also have an API to be plugged on the iPaas. And if I understood it correct, it is more about connecting APIs than transforming data. With HighByte, you can transform you data in real time, applying formulas an calculations like you could do on a PLC and data gets out of there already normalized. For an iPaas, I believe you would need to send the data to another API to be normalized.

Author: michael.brown
Content:
OK, some thoughts  ....the iPaaS platforms are new and improved versions of the "Enterprise Service Bus" from the 90's (see IBM Websphere..) They are essentially still and effectively great tools for the Point to Point integration problem. I.E. I have multiple systems and need to "share messages/ transactions" between them. So I build an integration (point to point, I'm deciding how the data will be used here...) then throw the messages on the bus. Cool. but they are not a replacement for UNS platform or Datalake - they are ancillary toolsets - not platforms. 

The data strategy we are all chasing now is a hub and spoke. Not point to point. The hub being a UNS platform and Datalake 

So, from that perspective - a modern iPaaS solution (like Mulesoft or Tibco) might be a great tool to create the pseudo-point to point integration from the source data to the hub.. I am a big fan of "start where you are" so if you have access to these tools and know how to use them, I'd get the data pumping. However I'm not going to invest in them net new today without a significant driver that overcomes their cost and maintenance.

Edited: additional thoughts....building a hub and spoke data strategy requires requires integrating the silo'd sources into the hub...My personal preference is to get realtime data into the "Model" at the edge and get the not-realtime data into the lake in its rawest form (don't assume its future use by changing the format) I think products like HighByte are the next generation tools to enable the hub n spoke - specifically, if starting from scratch I'd choose a HighByte over Mulesoft every day of the week.

Author: michael.brown
Content:
One of the cultural leadership principles we use here at Amazon is identifying "if decisions are 1-way or 2 way doors." A 1-way door is a decision once made cannot be undone - you must live with it for a long time or forever based on commitment, cost, etc.... A 2-way door decision is easily modified. Many times if a 2-way decision has multiple options - we do all of them and let the data drive the best decision. .

I share this anecdote because I'd like everyone to Look at the players in this field.... Boomi, Informatica, Oracle, Mulesoft, etc... From my perspective I don't think anyone here is saying don't use these platforms. They are extremely powerful....and expensive....and heavy...and expensive...and complex..and require long term investments in training and support....did I mention expensive?

A fully implemented enterprise version of any of the leader quadrant can easily reach the millions of USD.
They are 1-way door decisions for most organizations.

Vs a 2-way door decision for products like Ignition/Highbyte/etc for UNS modeling and pay as you go for Cloud based data lakes - you can easily try, iterate, and experiment to build solutions.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
When someone asks "what data?" or "how much data?", simply nod your head and respond "yes".  Don't make assumptions about how data will be consumed.  Be prepared to simultaneously use none of it, some of it, and all of it.

First off, it's a good idea to always use VFDs.  They have so many benefits that justify the cost (e.g., flexibility, power management, filtering, integrated safety, diagnostics, control, regenerative braking).  It baffles me how low the adoption is.  Apparently every asset operates at 100% OEE, energy is free, the grid has infinite capacity, geopolitics don't exist, and the environment is doing just fine.

You're right.  Those VFDs generate huge amounts of data.  Staggering amounts of data.  I recently requested a UDT interface to pull data off an asset with several PowerFlex 527 drives.  I was blown away how much information they provide.  It was more than what I believe most could begin to think to model or make use of.  And that's totally okay.

Everything can be brought into the UNS.  What is known, goes into a logical model of the asset.  What is not known, is grouped as "other" within the logical model.  As knowledge expands and needs arise, the logical model can be tweaked.  Either way, the data is still accessible for consumption.

If the PLC lacks an embedded MQTT client, a gateway interfacing with the native communication protocol will be required.  Creating a sub routine to organize the data collection into a structure or contiguous block within the memory can make the native communications more efficient.  Additionally, this organization can provide the UNS somewhat of a head start.  This will contain all your VFD data.  If there are performance concerns, there's no harm being selective.  For example, a drive might have optional parameters unrelated to the application it was deployed in (e.g., encoder value).

Basically, try to avoid creating barriers to entry of data that you or anyone else may consume in the future.

Author: michael.brown
Content:
Using a historian is a common flawed approach that I have seen backed up many times in production. Historians - like PI interpolate the data captured into their own binary format for storage. When you want to send that data to the cloud in a ad-hoc casual way - its no problem, works great. BUT what many customers have experienced when they want a true data hub is the interpolated data has to be RECALCULATED in order to be sent to the cloud. This puts a huge load on the server and the replication job get pushed further and further down the priority list....ending up in the data replication to the cloud getting days to literally MONTHS behind. OSI literally told one customer that was trying to replicate 80K tags to the cloud that was 8 weeks behind  "Thats not what PI Integrator was made to do."

I love historians, use them where they provide the most value - in the plant looking at data right now and trends - due to their nature they are not central point for UNS.

Author: michael.brown
Content:
Oh, and OSI's solution to the above customer? Sell them more PI servers to put in the cloud - and replicate the binary format using Pi 2 Pi replication - but the data is still locked in the historian.

Now - don't get me wrong - if this architecture fits the customer's needs and they can act quickly to get going - its an awesome solution...but it is NOT a UNS strategy.

Author: jon.forbord
Content: My understanding researching into this is: Kafka is a distributed (for reliability) event streaming platform, it is not built to do modeling, and it uses a client/broker structure, and clients can subscribe to topics, similar to mqtt. The idea is that all (really ALL) data can be treated as a series of events. Including transactional data in a relational database. It can store all events in the cluster as long as the user wants. New York Times apparently has their entire publishing record in a Kafka cluster going back to 19th century. Kafka has more in common with mqtt than with highbyte, although the similarities between Kafka and mqtt are limited. Kafka can do some processing in incoming events. I have not seen anywhere that Kafka comes with connectors (edit: there’s a Kafka connect API, to build connectors to read write from systems to a Kafka cluster, and there are plenty available in the community for most common data sources) It’s heavy on the client side, meaning it probably won’t be an edge deployed system. Mqtt can handle millions of clients and topics, but Kafka struggles if you have a lot of clients publishing to many topics. Mqtt struggles with so called firehose subscribers. Mqtt and Kafka are commonly used together to complement each other’s shortcomings.

Author: jon.forbord

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
I'm not a PI user, but I believe it might be worthwhile exploring the Asset Framework (AF) functionality.  This can provide labeling and hierarchy to get the context you're after. 

If there is nothing else to key on, you could join on the tag name or the datetime column.  If you know what the time series is, you could arbitrarily add columns to it.

Here's some MS SQL style pseudo code to illustrate a simple join or overlaying extra columns for context.   The second example centers around the idea of providing a tag name to return context.   Consider this as an example to further guide the conversation and definitely not as prudent architecture.  There are lot of smart people here that can provide the latter.

Is this conceptually closer to what you're after?

```
--First crude example. DateTime join to a linked external server.
SELECT *
FROM LinkedPiServer.PiDB.dbo.PiTable as PI
JOIN RelationalDB.dbo.RelationalTable AS RT
  ON RT.DateTime = PI.DateTime
WHERE PI.DateBetween @Begin_DateTime AND @End_DateTime
  AND PI.Tag_Name = @Tag_Name

--Second crude example. Extracting a row of context from a relational db into a temp table and then adding one column of context into separate time series query.
SELECT
  RT.Context_Column_1
  RT.Context_Column_2
INTO #TempContext
FROM RelationalDB.dbo.RelationalTable AS RT
WHERE RT.Related_Column = @Tag_Name  --Or some sort of input parameter

SELECT
  PI.DateTime,
  PI.TagName,
  PI.Value,
  (
   SELECT
     TC.Context_Column_1
   FROM #TempContext AS TC
  ) AS 'Context'
FROM LinkedPiServer.PiDB.dbo.PiTable as PI
WHERE PI.DateBetween @Begin_DateTime AND @End_DateTime
  AND PI.Tag_Name = @Tag_Name
```

Author: mparris
Content:
Interoperability is the reason.

If you go vanilla MQTT to connect systems, then you have to do the work to define how the data should be formatted between those systems.

To get a bit technical, if a system sends "57" through an MQTT topic, what does this mean? Is it a number (integer)? Is it an ASCII code (string) representing the number 9?

So one could do the work to define the payload format, but then you have to do the work to translate to ask the devices that talk SparkplugB on the plant floor, for example.

This is all extra integration/engineering work that has plagued Industry 3.0 systems. The purpose of IIoT is to have a common language between systems so that this extra engineering is recouped for other more advanced initiatives.

Author: mparris
Content:
A point if clarification, when starting along the SparkplugB route, the topic space is more restricted.  This was out of scope for the tutorial you posted, but I want to give a heads up for those starting in SparkplugB.

The topic path is the following:
SpBv1.0/<groupID>/NDATA/<nodeID>

In your example, the nodeID is PLC.

Regarding the groupID, there are a couple options. Based on your example, you could use "Area" where the Enterprise is implied by the top level spBv1.0 topic, or you could use "Enterprise-Area" which is more explicit.

So, the topic path itself is flat, but applications can parse the groupID to filter on the topics it cares about.

Author: mparris
Content:
The group ID will be a single string representing anywhere in the enterprise.  With hierarchical systems, you will concatenate the names of different levels of the business to create the unique groupID for all nodes in that area to live.  For example:

spBv1.0/Plant1/DDATA/EdgeGateway/PLCnotIIoTready
or
spBv1.0/Plant1Line5/NDATA/AnotherGateway
or
spBv1.0/Plant3Line2Cell6/NDATA/IIoTReadyPLC

For those interested in a specific part of the business, they would subscribe to the relevant GroupIDs to get the relevant data:
spBv1.0/Plant1/#
spBv1.0/Plant1Line2/#
etc

Author: walker.reynolds
Content:
Rob,
   We use ISA-95 part 2 for constructing the namespace, the image @lenzo dropped is from ISA-95 part 1, which we believe will ultimately deprecate.  Part 2 == enterprise/site/area/line/cell. What we generally do is map the ERP data to an ERP namespace at the appropriate level in the namespace — think of it as a functional namespace within the ISA-95 part 2 standard.  You will see many ‘ERP’ namespaces within your unified namespace... a specific line will have an ERP namespace that contains parameters from the ERP like ‘assetID’, ‘workcenter’ etc.

Author: lenzo202
Content: Thanks for the clarification @Walker Reynolds. Would you ever have a subtopic under one of the higher level topics that is not one of the lower tier topics as you described. A topic under Enterprise that is not a Site. Maybe your CMMS has done some calculations about the failure rate of a common limit switch found on many cells across many plants. It seems to me that this would be a topic in the CMMS namespace under enterprise?

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: Lenzo -- yes... we might... but that is driven by the Master Data model in the ERP.  We use ISA95 part 2 because that is how the master data models in most ERP systems are designed and we want our OT master data to line up with the IT master data models.  In your example, we do add additional master levels (enterprise/site/area/line/cell) if the ERP contains them (enterprise/business unit/site/area/line/cell) but that is not typical.  It is much more common for us do something like this (enterprise/business unit_site/area/line/cell).  Architecting the namespace is a very important job in DT -- and it is driven from the master data model of the authority in the organization (most of the time this is ERP).  That being said, we don't copy the MDM of ERP but we do use it, generally, to drive the design of the UNS.

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: Yes... you will have many sub topics and you may have many instances or just one instance of a specific sub topic.

Author: mparris
Content:
This is one of the biggest weaknesses of SparkplugB: it requires the controls engineer to assume how people and applications will use the data, and so he must create logical groups of the data to optimize those use cases. I think that is too much to ask of a controls engineer.

It really should leverage the power of MQTT where clients can subscribe at a metric level as they need, not at a logical device level.

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: Agreed — but this is a limitation in brownfield implementations only... which are really designed to integrate legacy infrastructure.  In greenfield implementations, the logical namespace of the native device is published over SPb and then the metric subscription is handled at the broker level for most nodes... and at the metric level (via the native device) for specific nodes.  Legacy integrations are via a gateway which adds a layer of abstraction (and limits the elements or parameters available) but in greenfield implementations, that abstraction layer disappears and assuming the devices meet minimum technical requirements, your challenge is overcome.

In this config, the device becomes a landing place to know allow quick parsing of what metrics are available and allow clients to pick and choose what they want to get.

Content: WOW! what a pain!

So... we stopped dropping the vanilla transmitter once the FAT was completed and we kept it in for practical purposes.  But... initially, we had both connections to make browsing the namespace with non SPb clients easier (to speed up the dev process during de-bug).

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: If your IIoT platform doesn’t parse the SPb DDATA namespace so that the individual metrics within the SPb JSON are accessible individually, then you are stuck wading through a large payload for a single event.  However, that is a design decision that gets you there.

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: I do believe the ‘device centric’ approach to SPb is going to evolve into a ‘parameter centric’ approach with the ability to group parameters into devices.

Author: mparris
Content:
I think that is exactly my point, how to improve SparkplugB so clients don't have to parse the whole device namespace.

Although, I suppose there's is still the hurdle of clients understanding the Protobuf encoding also...

Publishing spB and vanilla about doubles the bandwidth, right? (Just to make sure I understand your setup)

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: In an SPb and Vanilla architecture, we publish SPb super slow (every minute, every 10 mins, maybe once per hour) since we are likely only using it for structure... and we publish vanilla at 1000ms or faster.

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: It varies on the individual architecture... but no, we do not double bandwidth even if we set the connections up with the same update rate... SPb connections in our architectures are compressed, so they are smaller than a comparable Vanilla connection.

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: These discussions right here are what drive the standard forward — the beauty of SPb though is that we have options to create an unlimited number of architectures because we haven’t been painted into a corner with a standard that tries to be everything to everyone.

Author: mparris
Content:
Yup, all that makes sense.

I think the whole protocol makes sense when viewed as a single primary scada application working in isolation with nodes/devices.

Its topic structures don't enable to easily scale up the Enterprise or work in distributed systems. And my primary interest in SpB is so other things like Canary just need to know Sparkplug and will be getting the data at the maximum rate possible.

I'm really hoping the Working Group will take this on as a major improvement in there next revision.

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: Got it — we achieve that now based on the level of the infrastructure the app resides... part of our technical specification is that we define the maximum rate of update for data based on each layer of the infrastructure — the SLA for data at each layer of the infrastructure.  This is a topic for Mastermind we will be going over this year.

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: If we want a single SLA for all data then we architect with S&F on the edge nodes and use SPb only

100%. I see SpB as the Agile version of IIoT vs the "waterfall" approach of OPC-UA.

Let the market adopt the standard then drive what is needed. Rather that developing everything that engineers think they market needs and then the market is presented with a albatross of a spec to implement.

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: This is a great point -- one thing I would like to clarify... ERP back-ends really act as an ORM where you can create any type of master data model structure.  While ISA-95 part 2 is the most common standard used, it isn't all-inclusive for all business structures.  We see many hybrid models out there -- some standardized, some not, some are extensions of existing standards.  The point I'd like to drive home -- we leverage MQTT and SPb because it meets our minimum technical requirements for IIoT (edge-driven, report by exception, lightweight, open architecture) AND it is flexible enough to work for all of the types of data models we run into.

Author: mparris
Content:
You can only have one piece of software that is representing a node, which can then have devices underneath the node.  The reason is that the seq metric in the SparkplugB payload is shared between NDATA and DDATA packets, and the only way to guarantee that the order of these packets matches the sequence value in the payload is to have one piece of software/hardware where all that information passes before going to the broker.

So back to your setup, if you have two different hardwares with the same nodeID, then they will be conflicting with each other: the sequence numbers won't be synchronized and you will have two things publishing two different birth certificates to represent all the data to be found for NDATA.

Author: mparris
Content:
Regarding having a device be in a different part of the UNS hierarchy, that's where you would append onto the groupID a certain amount of characters to represent the line underneath the area.

This is another weakness if SparkplugB: you can configure a bridging broker to mount its entire Namespace into a different MQTT topic path in the upstream broker, but since SpBv1.0 only uses a single topic for the groupID, the only choice is to have some very complicated scripting that takes the local groupID and prepends the higher-level hierarchy (Enterprise-Site) all through string parsing, which is ugly.

Also, you can't have the area/line/cell broker subscribe to a single topic in the higher level one, you would have to enumerate every possible combination of area/line/cell that it cares about, rather than a single subscription of "area/#" for example

Author: mparris
Content:
The groupID is very limiting when you are trying to federate with 2-way bridges over MQTT.

The lower level broker needs to know what level of nodes/devices it will ever work with, it also needs to know how high up the Enterprise it's data will ever go. Then based on that information is what you have to program ALL devices connected to that broker to use as a groupID scheme.

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: I'll shoot a video on this -- the answer is far too long.  In a nutshell, as @SherylM points out, Kafka solves a completely different set of problems.  Namely, how can we optimize the streaming of time series data from databases into data lakes (this is the most common use case in I 4.0).  Kafka is often part of our IIoT infrastructure (to get data into the dl efficiently) but to compare it to HighByte or a UNS isn't even an apples to orange comparison -- its apples to rocks.  The UNS serves many purposes, data unification, data normalization, information structure, node management... Kafka simply optimizes (mostly time-series) data for streaming (mostly to data-lakes).  The former is the foundation a house is built on, the latter is simply 1 leg on a table in the house built on top of the foundation.

This doesn't look to conform to Sparkplug topic path standards. In your setup, I'm curious what your DBIRTH packets look like.

Author: mparris
Content:
If talking sparkplug, the lowest-level of an MQTT packet/topic is NDATA or DDATA.  The payload of these topics contain multiple metrics.

To @Paulo Vitor point, if a fast changing analog value is a metric and also a slow-changing Discrete input, those could both be bundled in the same NDATA or DDATA packet.  For a low-powered device that only cares about the slow-changing Discrete, it has to wade through all the DDATA packets sent for the sake of the fast-changing analog just to see the 1 time that the discrete changes.  This is a weakness of Sparkplug.   I have the ability to segment data into different logical devices (fast and slow), but don't know how I can get an application like Ignition in a scalable way to ignore the fast devices and use the slow devices for its subscriptions.

I'm considering the use-case at how to reduce the publish rate of packets while moving up the enterprise in sparkplug.  For example, at a lower-level broker, you publish at 10ms rates, but when bridging to a higher-level broker, it only publishes at 1000ms. Thinking there could be some MQTT mechanism that a client specifies the maximum message rate per topic that it is able to handle.  I don't think this will help sparkplug, though, because if the broker that is throttling the data by dropping packets, then an application like Ignition will see the sparkplug sequence number is not congruent and will likely request a rebirth.

Author: patanj2
Content: I think if you want to publish locally at 10 ms  and then only publish at a slow rate (5s) to an enterprise broker or the cloud, this is a use case for an edge stream processing engine, where you could use built in functions to either filter, sample or aggregate the high speed data, or choose to ignore it.  I view this different than a simple bridge, and am not sure if that functionality needs to be built into the sparkplug standard.

There aren’t a lot of apps in the MES and ERP layers with native SpB connectivity. SpB is a very much a device-centric protocol and most of the initial applications have focused there. Content:
I spoke with Ian a couple weeks ago. Your observations are likely spot on to the target market (large corporations). They are working on a model that works better for typical industrial customer.

You are experiencing the convergence of IT and OT. MQTT is likely the best concrete example of that. It started in the late 90's as a protocol for operational data. Then IT got a hold of it and they proliferated it through cloud services.

Then SparkplugB came around and is starting to popularize MQTT for operational data.  If I'm not mistaken, HiveMQ is a recent member of the Sparkplug working group, then they are getting press through this channel and their published educational material, and Integrators are starting to present use-cases that that hasn't faced and that their business model isn't tailored for. I think they need to catch up to make themselves more accessable to small deployments.

I suggested a pricing model based on bandwidth throughout, where there would even be a free level with their GUI and bridge functions if the number of connections and amount is data was low enough. It could help protect their pricing model to large cloud customers, but grab a sector of the market that will never scale to that size.

Content:
Has anyone looked into project CHIP (Connected Home over IP)
https://buildwithmatter.com/
https://github.com/project-chip/connectedhomeip#readme

It looks to be the home/consumer version of the MQTT/UNS concept:

"Project Connected Home over IP is developed with the following goals and principles in mind:
- **Unifying**: Project CHIP will produce a new specification, building with and on top of market-tested, existing technologies.
- **Interoperable**: The specification permits communication between any Project CHIP-certified device, subject to users’ permission.
- **Secure**: The specification leverages modern security practices and protocols.
- **User Control**: The end user is in control of authorization for interaction with devices.
- **Federated**: No single entity serves as a throttle or a single-point-of-failure for root of trust.
- **Robust**: The set of protocols specify a complete lifecycle of a device — starting with the seamless out-of-box experience, through operational protocols, to device and system management specifications required for proper function in the presence of change.
- **Low Overhead**: The protocols are practically implementable on low compute-resource devices, such as MCUs.
- **Pervasive**: The protocols are broadly deployable and accessible, thanks to leveraging IP and being implementable on low-capability devices.
- **Ecosystem-Flexible**: The protocol must be flexible enough to accommodate deployment in ecosystems with differing policies.
- **Easy to Use**: The protocol should aim to provide smooth, cohesive, integrated provisioning and out-of-box experience.
- **Open**: The Project’s design and technical processes should be open and transparent to the general public, including to non-members wherever possible."

Content: There are certainly some limitations, as it's obvious spBv1.0 was designed with edge gateways/devices in mind vs application nodes.  However, the stateful nature for use in mission critical settings is very valuable vs plain mqtt.  @MParris  has a post from 5/21 in #reference-architectures that does a great job at compensating for this while accounting for the ISA95 hierarchy.   We are using spB for edge gateways as intended, and implementing Ignition application nodes as GroupID = Ent-Site-Area or Ent-Site-App, Edge Node = Asset Type, DeviceID = Asset Instance. A similar consumer, in cloud or on prem, could republish payloads into a flat structure, using comparable/additional conversion rules.  This has been the best path for us to take advantage of the Ignition/Operational benefits of spB, while also appeasing clients in business/IT domains who aren't going to be using spB anytime soon.

Author: mparris
Content:
I'm the world of sparkplug, every hardware or application that is publishing to a broker is considered a "node." You shouldn't have a configuration where two nodes have the same nodeID and they have the same groupID. They will be stepping on each other.

Another way to think of it: home addresses. deviceID is a room in a house, the nodeID it's the number on the street, and the groupID is the combination of street, city, state, etc. Start your journey through court if two people claim the same nodeID and groupID!  :laughing: 

The nodeID it's typically the name or id of the equipment directly publishing to the broker. The groupID is where you can create a naming scheme to match ISA-95 structures.

If you have two nodes publishing to a broker, configure then with different nodeIDs and then they can publish to the same groupID, such as "plant-line-cell"

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
I'm still learning about Sparkplug.  I'll yield to others on the specifics.  I can share how I've approached this with other technology.

I've encountered similar applications involving quality labs.  For example, product is sampled from a specific line or cell and brought to a lab for inspection (e.g., CMM, tracing, hardness testing).  The instruments in the lab were not associated with a specific line or cell in the namespace.  They had their own section of namespace.  When inspection was ran, the setup would prompt for parameters to indicate what is being inspected and what cell/line it's for.  These parameters would get passed in and the integration would route the data accordingly.  Sometimes this involved writing the data to other tags associated with line/cell.  Any apps and devices associated with the line/cell could consume the data as if the quality instruments "lived" in the line/cell.

So, if we were to extend to this approach to your environment, we would organize your mobile inspection units under some sort of pseudo line (e.g., "mobile inspection").  This would be the group.  Within this group, the namespace should contain parameters that identify the current location (i.e., line) and anything else the mobile inspection unit is doing.  The UNS or integration platform (e.g., HB, Ignition) would be configured to watch these parameters, copy the values, and write to the appropriate tags elsewhere in the namespace (e.g., Line 1).  This is how the mobile inspection units could have a fixed namespace path but their data could be routed dynamically based on where they are deployed.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
S/4HANA is just SAP's latest ERP running on SAP's latest database.  HANA is their database with in-memory and columnar storage technology.  This technology enables their traditional transactional database product to also function as a data warehouse for analytical workloads.  It's more like a historian for ERP apps than a UNS.

Integration Suite would be their closest thing to resembling a UNS.  It's a service bus with support for message queueing (i.e., pub/sub).  It's typical use case is to stich together enterprise applications.  The ideal use case is to do what's referred to as "service-oriented architecture" in which all the apps and processes are exposed as micro-services and intelligently orchestrated.  Most apps in this space are still fairly monolithic and costly to rearchitect.  It's not widely adopted.

I don't believe Integration Suite has support for industrial protocols to extend down the stack.  Most of their work down the stack has involved their MES product with OPC-UA client/server (i.e., point-to-point connections).  Invoking OPC-UA methods have been emphasized in their demos.  Their approach has the ERP layer consuming this data indirectly through the MES layer.

As I read the comments it appears there is a misunderstanding of the UNS. As defined in the community it is the single source of truth for data and events, as well as the structure of your business. It is not a database or data lake. It connects nodes from other systems so when events occur, other systems can consume the information. It is not store the data.

In your application you mention you want to keep track of alarm history. I would use a historian for that. Canary Labs has the ability to create Virtual Views which can organize the alarms into a UNS architecture so that alarms for a particular piece of equipment are groups together. I can then publish this structure to the UNS so that other systems can consume the data in context.

I hope this helps. And apologies if I am not understanding the question.

Author: markpitout
Content:
One topic that is common in the OT world, but not so much in the IT world is redundancy. For example, PLCs often have Hot-Standby variants and SCADA systems can often be configured with redundant servers. How can redundancy be implemented for MQTT brokers and the Unified Namespace, while still ensuring data consistency between redundant pairs of MQTT brokers / Unified Namespaces?
Or to word it differently, how should an edge device behave when an MQTT broker or Unified Namespace goes down? Is the only option store and forward, or are there solutions that can provide higher availability?

Author: thedavidschultz
Content:
MQTT brokers support clustering, which serves the purpose of redundancy. If one of the brokers goes down, other brokers in the cluster will be used. One of the advantages of HiveMQ is how it manages redundancy and failover. The failover is usually undetectable by other systems. 

There are also several ways to manage store-and-forward. One is on the device itself. Opto22 provide options for how this is managed in the EPIC and RIO. A Canary Labs collector can be used for this purpose, as well.

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content: It's also pretty cool that HiveMQ supports rolling upgrades for "minor" versions. As they use semantic versioning, "minor" just means no breaking changes. For example the last major version 4 was released in December 2018 which brought MQTT 5 and a new extension system. All upgrades since then were "minor" upgrades without breaking changes, although they added a lot of features.

Author: jon.forbord
Content:
Here’s a few notes on the UNS: 
- UNS is the single source of truth and is the structure and events of a business.
- UNS is not a relational database
- You can have layers of UNS throughout the layers of the organization. UNS is omnipresent.
- UNS contains current states. 
- UNS is not a time series database
- The most common implementation of a UNS uses one or more MQTT brokers to “host” the UNS. 
- UNS is in essence a concept, and can be implemented in a number of ways. UNS is not a software, neither Ignition nor Highbyte IS the UNS, but there are software tools that can be used to build and manage a UNS (or parts of it). 
- in a UNS, all your smart assets and business applications are nodes in the ecosystem publishing and subscribing to the UNS.
- UNS is built on a technology stack that meets the minimum technical requirements of Report by exception, open architecture, edge driven and lightweight.
- UNS is THE integration layer.
- UNS is constantly evolving and evolves as the business evolves or new nodes are added to the ecosystem. 
- the UNS structure can in theory be built on any structure as long as it is applied consistently throughout. It is, however, usually based on ISA 95 part 2.

Author: jon.forbord
Content: I’m struggling to get to grasps with how his original understanding was any less correct than his new interpretation. It was perhaps not wide enough in scope, but as I see it they’re all manifestations of digital twins, with different degrees of complexity or areas of application. A 3D model of an asset to which you can either feed data or connect live to the assets is a digital twin, the same can be said about a mathematical model of the asset, or logic simulating parts of the functionality of the asset. The digital twin can get as complex as you’d like. It can be as simple as a pressure output from a pump as a linear function of the pump speed, or as complex as a multitude of PLC simulations interacting with a 3D model of the plant complete with widgets flowing through the production lines giving feedback to the plc simulations in a closed loop, complete with operator stations and SCADA. It’s a digital copy of something, and the accuracy of the copy depends on the complexity of its implementation. You can use it for pretty much whatever you can imagine using the real asset to do, as long as the complexity of the model is appropriate for each use case. E.g. remote operation, software development, product development, troubleshooting. Software developers have as usual hijacked a term and bastardized it for their own use cases, just as they did with my job title (automation engineer, and I’ve gotten more than a few contacting me about software testing jobs in IT) 😅

Author: sherylmccrary
Content:
In the context of things and machines, I agree that all of these examples *could be* called digital twins. And in @ZackWooten  Zack's example, it's worth noting that the data model is adequate for a robot to play chess; it's only us humans that need a (human) visualization. 

But philosophically, I hesitate to call every digital representation of any measurement in real time a digital twin. A sonogram of an unborn infant is by that definition a digital twin, but it is not a "copy" of the baby. Given enough data at high resolution, however, we can perform surgery in the womb now. You could say that's a digital twin for the purpose of an intervening procedure. What I'm saying is, I think the concept behind the phrase "digital twin" implies a certain level of complexity as to enable ---or give preference to---  live interaction with the system being twinned in ways not previously possible via direct physical interaction.

Author: jon.forbord

There is a lot of data that is stranded on the factory floor due to these limitations. Industry 4.0 seeks to extract it through the use of protocols like MQTT.

Content: Hi @zackscriven, still cannot figure out, why you are considering the way of receiving data from the OPC UA server by a client using subscriptions and monitored items (that is not Part 14 PubSub) as Poll/Response. Maybe the existence of Publish request and Publish response makes you think that way? If so, how it works is the client sends more than one Publish request after creating a subscription, but multiple, there is a queue of Publish requests on the server-side. Whenever data value is sampled, and this new value is changed (in case of using deadband, if the change is greater than absolute or percent threshold), then this value is sent to the client-side as a Publish response, in the next publishing cycle. If there are more changes, they do not wait until the last Publish response is received by the client and the client sends a new Publish request. It is important to note that there are already more Publish requests in the queue. So if there are more changes detected shortly after, they are sent to the client within the publishing interval. In other words, if you set the Publishing interval let say to 1 ms, then the new value will be sent to the client within this 1 ms, even if the round trip over the network is let say 5 ms. Could I explain?

Author: ravil1
Content:
Yes, a Secure channel and Session should be established. They are created once and kept open, if the network connection is good, can be continuously used for days or months. No need to create a session every time you need to get new value from the server.
BTW, MQTT brokers communicate with publishers/subscribers very similar way. MQTT brokers have the option to keep the session open, so after re-connection subscribers don't need to subscribe to topics again. Similar to OPC UA Server, MQTT broker needs to maintain, for what topics, what data values to send to what subscriber, etc., depending on QoS and retention policy. As I wrote in another post before, the communication nature between  MQTT publishers/subscribers and the Broker is client-server, similar to OPC UA client-server. Just in the case of OPC UA, you have one session in the server for a given client connection required to convey data from the producer to the consumer. In the case of MQTT, the session lives in the MQTT broker (which also acts as a server), but in the end, you have even more sessions than in OPC UA: 2 sessions in the MQTT broker - one for a publisher, and the second for the subscriber. Just the load is moved from the publishers/subscribers to the broker. Yes, this makes publishers lighter, but that weight does not magically disappear, it moves to the broker side. But because the broker runs in the server-grade machine, moreover, can be implemented as a cluster of such servers, the load is manageable.

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content:
I think it's great that the OPC UA client subscriptions exist and they are often the better choice then to keep polling all the time but they still suffer from many limitations that the OPC foundation is trying to address with OPC UA Pub/Sub. For example:
- Client subcriptions still build on the client server notion with the publish requests / responds and it is relatively complex.
- You still specifically need to know the object structure that you want to monitor and the client has to actively request it directly from the server instead of „just“ subscribing to a topic on a central broker. The whole approach with the publish requests and responds is just weird in my opinion (just a personal impression).
- The client needs to initiate the connection „from the outside“ which means potentially firwall ports must be opened. One thing that I’m not sure about: Does the mechanism keep a standing tcp connection open between client and server or does it work with a return address / callback? 
- For each client a subscription and monitored items including queues for the monitored items need to be created on the server. This is different from a pub sup implementation in which you have a dedicated scaleble broker where creating sessions per client is not a big thing.
- There are no OPC UA servers that I know of that make the client subscriptions highly available / scalable through clustering & replication.
In summary it totally makes sense that the OPC foundation added OPC UA Pub / Sub because the client subscriptions were just a „crutch“ (helpful but not what you really want).

Author: ravil1
Content:
Hi @SherylM,
I have looked at the original report published by Johnathan-Hottell. It does not have a description of the methodology, so it is not possible to reproduce it exactly. But anyway I tried to do some observations on OPC UA packets captured by Wireshark, and they differ. 
For example, the reading a single value reported as taking 510 bytes. In my case read request is 140 bytes, the response is 118 bytes. I suspect maybe he used UaExpert as a client, which reads 19 attributes for a variable, not only value attribute. It is not known too, how a single value for a variable is read in MQTT. You need first to subscribe to that single topic, right. Otherwise, if the subscription is not for this exact topic, but for a parent, for example, you will get data published for lot more topics and the bandwidth will be much higher. And then you will need to un-subscribe, to stop receiving more data values. I doubt those packets are counted.
But single read is not so important anyway, because in real case OPC UA client would create a subscription and get values only when they are changed, or, using terminology here, reported by exception. The same with UNS I believe.
For data values for 24 tags (the same data types as in the report), received over OPC UA subscription, for 5 minutes, I got a total size of packets 422 Kb. This includes everything, establishing a connection too. If remove connection creation packets, and eliminate reporting of server timestamps (by default both source and server timestamps are published), it is reduced to 340 Kb.

Author: mparris
Content:
Some quick notes on Sparkplug: many times, the payload contents will be written as JSON to help people understand it, but the specification actually has the software encode the payload using ProtoBuf, a very efficient binary encoding.

Also, the alias field in sparkplug allows further payload compression by providing a lookup between the metric name (type string) name and an ID (integer)

Author: ravil1
Content:
Yes, with ProtoBuf payload should be smaller. My gut tells me that payload ProtoBuf encoded SparkPlug payload size is comparable with OPC UA messages,  which are in most cases binary encoded too. I think SparkPlug messages can be significantly smaller if compression is used. In OPC UA, eliminating timestamps can reduce the payload (if precise timestamps are not required, that is one timestamp for all values is enough). 
Anyhow, I don't think that OPC UA network bandwidth would be a major obstacle to use it. If there are such cases, I would like to learn more. 
OPC UA might be heavier, but that does not mean it is not lightweight at all. 

I think you need also take into consideration, that if your implementation of the UNS is done following the way how Walker describes, you might end up having much higher traffic, due to publishing all tags at the highest rate. And subscribers will get much more data than required for them. So this might diminish your gains on bandwidth.

Author: mparris
Content:
The idea that the client has to continuously feed the server with publish requests and that the server responds with PublishResponses is a Poll/Response design pattern.

The spec could have been developed to allow a client to state its required publish interval (and desired sampling interval with all the filtering requirements) up front upon initializing the connection/subscription, which would have aligned with a Pub/Sub design pattern.

Author: ravil1
Content:
@MParris,
No, it is not really Poll/Response pattern. I explained that in another thread, and can repeat it here one more time.
The point is, yes, the client should send Publish request and receives data in a Publish response.  And for that reason, you might think, OK, this is polling. 
And actually, it can be polling, if the client sends one Publish request, waits until the response is received, and then sends the next Publish request, and so on.
But in reality, after creating a subscription, the client sends multiple Publish requests, without waiting for the response. So on the server-side, there is a whole queue of Publish requests. 
Whenever data change is detected by the server, it is sent to the client, because there is a pending request. Therefore, it is "Report by Exception", not polling.
Also, we need to keep in mind that Publish request has also another mission - it lets the server know that it did receive previous data changes, so they can be marked by the server as delivered. 
Publish responses have also sequence numbers, so if some data changes are lost in the transport layer, the client can ask to re-send that data.
Using this design also allows keeping the server and the client in sync - if the server has too many data changes that the client cannot handle, it will slow down reporting of data changes.
So, in fact, you have to consider Publish Response as the initial message where subscription data is delivered, and the next Publish Request sent after that as an asynchronous acknowledgement confirming that data was received. 
I guess in MQTT there should be also something similar to this, to guarantee message delivery.

Author: dundo6741
Content:
I guess whether OPC UA pub/sub (or anything else) should be considered as "report by exception" or not depends on  whether the "publisher" resides on the device (PLC) itself or not.
If I understand it correctly, the only two ways to detect the data change (exception) are:
1. in your program
2. by keeping last values latched and compare them with new values

1. has to be on the device itself, 2. could be done on, say, PC, but that means polling all of the data frequently, keeping two sets of data (latched and new) locally, comparing them and raising exceptions on data change. While that limits potentially big data flow locally it still isn't optimal.

If 2. is done on device itself, that would be, in my opinion, true generic "report by exception".
Now, the question is: what is easier to implement on device of rather limited processing power: OPC UA pub/sub or MQTT (or similar lightweight protocol)?

Author: ravil1
Content:
@dundo
Yes, you are right, the new value must be compared with the previously reported value. OPC UA Servers do exactly that. 
Speaking of the "report by exception," BTW, it is not the feature belonging to MQTT. Nothing to do with MQTT at all even. I don't think that the MQTT broker compares the topic payload with the previously published value. It just delivers to the subscribers whatever was published by the publisher.
It is completely up to the Publisher application whether it will report by exception or keep publishing every predefined interval. If the data source is not in that application, then it has to pool the source, if the source itself does not support the report by exception.
When it comes to whatever is easier to implement, using available SDKs, for me as a Developer, there is no difference, OPC UA or MQTT with SparkPlugB. And in the majority of cases, I don't think that processing power is the limit. 
In the end, I think it all depends on the requirements. My opinion is that if you choose OPC UA as a common interface to access data **at the primary source**, it will meet a much wider set of requirements than MQTT. One example is modeling: if all you want is the ability to organize objects in a simple hierarchical view, then you don't need OPC UA  companion specs,  just simple MQTT topics are enough. Another is reporting data: if it is OK for all tags to be sampled and reported with the same interval to all consumers - again MQTT is enough. For more complex cases, OPC UA might be better. You can use a protocol converter at a higher layer if want to build UNS with MQTT Broker.

Author: ravil1
Content: In other words, I would say that OPC UA features are a superset of MQTT/SparkPlugB features, and in simple cases, MQTT might be more than enough. If you don't need those extra features, no point to spend resources on them. In any particular case, you select the one which better suited for your project, not the absolute best one. Like when you select a car, you don't select the one which can carry the most load. Otherwise, everybody would drive tracks.

Author: thedavidschultz
Content:
The goal of the UNS architecture is that every node/system will publish and subscribe to relevant data as defined by the node. Since few system currently support MQTT, the ERP will either publish purchase order data to a SQL table (this is the case in my example) or through a business connector as Walker mentioned. Ideally, the ERP would automatically publish the order to the broker, assigning the production based on AI/ML results through criteria like product code, availability, location, performance, etc.

How the MES detects the new work order depends on the MES. This is why the minimum technical requirement (MTR) is important. The simplest way is through a tag event script. Because the UNS uses report by exception, the new order would be an exception. The resulting tag change would facilitate the events by every system subscribing to that topic (not just the MES).

The broker does not store data, other than retained flags. There are underlying SQL databases/tables that store this data. The MES will receive this data in real time.

When the work order is complete, that event data is written to the broker which, again is consumed by every system that is subscribing to that topic. The end of a batch triggers another script which generates the trace data. This same publish can easily create a material movement in the WMS.

@MParris, Re: *Even if the network is ok and there is no reason to stop the session or subscription, if the client doesn't ever send a request packet, then no data will be sent.*
If the application behaves this way, I think it is a security vulnerability. If the client is inactive for a certain time, the connection must be closed.
In MQTT there are also keep-alive messages, acknowledge messages, so the communication is never only one way.
In Poll/Response, you cannot get data with a rate faster than request/response round trip time. 
OPC UA subscriptions mechanism allows for example get data with 10 ms sampling rate even if your network round trip time is 200 ms.

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content:
MQTT does support queuing messages for a client. Even better, broker implementations that support clustering make sure that the data is replicated in your cluster, so it doesn't matter if a single node fails (actually # of replicas is configurable, typically you would use 3 replicas distributed over 3 availability zones). It also doesn't matter to which of the nodes in your cluster a client reconnects. In MQTT 5 all sessions are persistent (unless you set the session expiry interval to 0). If you want the session to be cleaned on reconnect you can use the Clean Start flag. In MQTT 3.1.1 you have to use the Clean Session flag when connecting to indicate if you want a persistent session (clean session false) or not. 

Now a great features for brokers would be if they would support setting a node into a maintenance mode that would take that node out of the replication and would start draining the connected clients so they would not all reconnect at once and overload the cluster (as they often do not implement a reconnect backoff). And even better would be, if the broker's Kubernetes Operator would support this feature when replacing nodes. Wouldn't it, @Huber? 🙂 Ok, admittedly this is not so important for IIoT where you don't have as many clients compared to other IoT scenarios in which you might have millions of clients.

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content: If you use QoS Level 1 (at least once) or 2 (exactly once) for your messages and the client connected with a persistent session then the broker will store all messages for the topics a client subscribed to in the client’s session while a client is disconnected. The client will then receive the messages when it reconnects. MQTT 5 also supports client side load balancing aka shared subscriptions for messages. Shared subscription means that you can have multiple instances of a service that form a subscription group and the MQTT broker makes sure that each message is only received by one client instance. This lets you scale the amount of instances on the consuming side. HiveMQ already supported this for MQTT 3.1.1. QoS 0 (at most once) messages will be dropped while a client is disconnected.

If the spirit of the sparkplug standard was based on the notion of edge nodes publishing data from many devices group under that node, then I am more comfortable defining application spB publishers as a collection of edge nodes per application entity type, which each "device" being an instance of the entity.  At least if you wanted to flatten out, with consistent naming of edge nodes, you can subscribe, rearrange, and republish flat and retained with a simple paho client app.  The pictures here are an example of how we are modeling our Ignition tags, with the flattened/republished model as a custom namespace.
