Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
The Asset Administrative Shell (AAS) is another RAMI 4.0 concept that has been kicked around for years.  For me personally, it's a thought experiment if manufacturing had unlimited time and resources.  It’s what I look forward to learning about when I attend a presentation by someone smart like Martin Hankel (Bosch-Rexroth).  It’s a very interesting stuff.  Unfortunately, while much newer, AAS suffers from the same market adoption issues as OPC-UA.

Some of the European automation companies affiliated with Plattform Industrie 4.0 have created AAS proof-of-concepts for their products (e.g., panels, drives, pneumatic valves).  Microsoft has incorporated aspects of AAS into their Azure Digital Twin product.  But, these are not products one simply acquires and plug-and-plays.  They’re incomplete and they require a ton of engineering effort.  No one is building automation products or architecting factories around this technology.

Outside of a testbed affiliated with one of the major research institutes (e.g., Fraunhofer, RWTH Aachen), the AAS is purely theoretical.  This stuff requires more brain power to understand than it does to build the very products it's designed to accompany.  I can't see machine builders or end-users adopting technology like this for at least another decade or two.  When PLC programmers start resembling full-stack engineers and the investment mindset in industrial technology has transformed, something like this could potentially see the light of day.  It would also require automation and technology companies to be more “Switzerland-like” about data and interoperability.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
I think of AAS as the language of the "cyber" component of the "cyber-physical system" concept.  You might even call it an interface for the digital twin of an asset.  It's basically a layer of intelligence on an edge node.  It exposes an asset as a service for the IIoT ecosystem to consume and interact with in a standardized way.  It's a very rich API that exposes more than just controller memory tags, but all underlying engineering information about an asset.  An asset might contain components (e.g., hydraulics, drives, pneumatics, robotics, sensors).  Each of these components can have models that define what they are logically and physically.  These models are user-defined or manufacturer-defined according to industry standards (e.g., EPLAN, ecl@ss, PLCOpen, PackML, OPC-UA Companion Specs, CAEX, VDMA).  These models, in turn, are rolled up into one central ontological model and exposed as an OPC-UA server.  The central model defined by AutomationML or the OPC-UA I4AAS Information Model.

AAS, in practice, is a unification standard of everything OPC-UA attempts to unify and more.  Imagine building an extensive edge server that contains all information (e.g., physical, electrical, logical) about an asset.  This asset has exhaustive engineering models for everything.  Every sensor, every actuator, every cable, every mechanical component, etc is completely documented and modeled.  These models would take the form of standard libraries embedded into the server.  

AAS, in a way, is a like a “micro” UNS for an asset.  But, AAS sets out to “boil the ocean” as it is very much a synthesis of everything OPC-UA attempts to model.  It operates under the assumption that assets and apps have already been modeled according to standards and it’s simply a matter of organizing them into another standard to enable interoperability and Industry 4.0 outcomes.  It prescribes the impossible.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
UNS, as I interpret it, is a much more practical approach to modeling and distributing the intelligence of a business.  It basically accepts the premise that most namespaces of available intelligence (e.g., devices, apps) will be useless as-is for enabling Industry 4.0 outcomes.  It acknowledges the human nature of programmers and realities of programming.  Unless required and cost-effective to do so, data models are rarely standardized.  More often, they're improvised.  UNS prescribes building one model for a business largely based on hierarchy (i.e., ISA-95 structure) and reusable logical structure (e.g., UDTs) of what is available.  This enables a business to invest, innovate and iterate on its own achievable standard rather than waiting around for the market to adopt an unachievable one.  This enables a self-aware IIoT ecosystem sooner rather than later.  This is the requisite foundation to enable so-called “holy grail” outcomes through advance technology such as machining learning and artificial intelligence.

AAS and UNS are not really an either/or discussion per se.  They have similarities and overlap.  AAS and UNS could be used in the same architecture.  A UNS could contain asset data exchanged through an asset’s AAS.  The biggest difference is that the AAS typically prescribes assets be an OPC-UA server.  This means the IIoT ecosystem must consist of clients to request and consume the asset’s intelligence.  This is a fundamental difference from the UNS concept.  The UNS concept prescribes that an asset be a client that publishes its intelligence into the IIoT ecosystem.

My advice:  Don’t build product strategy or investment theses around AAS.  Like OPC-UA, you’ll be waiting forever for begin digital transformation. 

If assets were unicorns, AAS would be a universal saddle compatible with every unicorn.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
My apologies.  I was not clear on that statement.  I was not questioning the possibility of mapping one standard to another standard.  I was questioning the assumption that assets have been modeled to a standard at all.

Let's use MTConnect as an example.  I say this not as a critique of MTConnect, but the I4.0 and industrial automation space in general.  The standard itself is great.  Will Sobel and your org have done fantastic work building and maintaining the model.  If my assessment of the realities are off, please chime in.  I'm only speaking from experience.

When machine tool builders have a relatively vanilla implementation of a major control platform (e.g., Fanuc, Siemens, Mitsubishi), a generic adapter can work reasonably well.  But, when they don't have a vanilla implementation and they didn't build out an adapter for their machine at all, it doesn't work.  When it gets to this point, it doesn't matter how great MTConnect is or what other standards it's been mapped to or interoperates with (e.g., OPC-UA, AAS).  Someone has to implement the standard.

When an organization (e.g., OPC Foundation, Plattform I4.0, IIC, Microsoft) pats themselves on the back for creating or supporting a standard, they're often overlooking the last mile that makes a standard valuable.  They've assumed someone has completed the last mile.  If a manufacturer must make extreme investments to adopt a standard, it erodes or even eliminates the value of that standard as well as anything tied to it.  Theoretical interoperability is not actual interoperability.

An AAS for a CNC machine is only as good as the implementation, provided it exists, of the underlying standard for the machine.  It can be a brand new machine with the latest controls technology from a reputable builder.  If no one has bothered to implement a standard (e.g., MTConnect) for that machine tool, all other standards tied to that standard cannot be utilized (e.g., OPC-UA, AAS) without a major engineering investment.

Content: Just to add a few words to what @js and @Jon Forbord replied regarding high availability: You can also distribute your broker nodes over multiple availability zones. Author: dep05d
Content: We are piloting Solace PubSub+ for the first phase of our IIOT implementation.  You are correct that internally the multi-protocol support converts into a Solace messaging format, but we haven't had any issues using MQTT, at least in terms of common QOS 0/1 usage, Sparkplug B and NDEATH messages (though I hadn't noticed some of the gotchas on LWT until you just mentioned they exist).  Despite a few of the lacking MQTT features such as QOS 2 or shared subscriptions, we felt there were much bigger gains in terms of the multi protocol support and ease of setting up a distributed "mesh" of brokers. As one moves up the manufacturing software stack, there just isn't a lot of MQTT yet, let alone sparkplug B, in the ERP, Logistics, EAM, etc space. Those IT groups aren't generally interested in building MQTT/spB interfaces, and using something like Ignition as the integration layer (as we have done the last 10 years) is still point to point and eventually becomes brittle.  However, those systems and IT groups likely have REST/JMS, which they are more willing to work with, and having the ability to deliver real time messages to them, as well as allow them to publish into the UNS using their existing tools, was a big selling point for us.

Author: dep05d
Content:
For guaranteed delivery, we use Solace queue objects and their API. Beyond Qos2, it gets us around some sparkplug issues too. Sparkplug/Ignition MQTT Transmission historical data buffers and does not transmit when the primary host isn't online.  This can cause an issue when the primary SCADA server is not the historian server. If you have a cloud-based historian as primary host, and the WAN goes down, the primary SCADA app loses live data. If the SCADA is primary host, we won't buffer historian data correctly during network drops. The workaround is creating dual transmitters, which 1) wastes resources and 2) violates the goal of not designing your publishers with consumers in mind. This, along with the presence of non sparkplug data, led us to decide to handle buffering ourselves. Each Solace broker can create guaranteed messaging queues that consist of multiple UNS topic subscriptions (in Solace format: basically MQTT with different wildcards). The queue can be then be consumed via REST delivery, an app using the Solace API, or a remote broker/cluster.

Our approach is to have brokers (each can be standalone or HA cluster) local at each factory, which then queues all data until they are delivered to a cloud broker/cluster that again queues all the data from the sites. From there a parallel set of queue consumer application can deliver all messages to the data lake, historian, stream processors, etc in our cloud environment.   Doing this allows every single sparkplug metric (application nodes and devices) to be automatically archived to the cloud.  The same applies for non-sparkplug messages, but you'll have to curate your queue subscriptions as the namespace will be custom. The end result is full archival of data and events from our sites, as well as access to live data (and queued delivery with API use) from all nodes using multiple protocols.  Subscriptions can be auto-routed amongst brokers.  So far we have been happy with it's performance.  Hope this helps!

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content: In most IoT projects we have a Kafka connected to the MQTT broker (e.g. via HiveMQ Kafka extension) for analytics and stream processing so I would probably connect those kind of IT applications via Kafka if the IT department does not feel comfortable with MQTT or if Kafka is a company standard. Alternatively you could also build some EoN gateway service for them which interacts with the other systems via REST. In the end it depends on the specific setup. Sometimes you have to build some service anyway to load data from some horrible file based interface or because they don't want to make changes to their applications for you or they take too long 🙂 Although I have to say that MQTT 5 with application specific headers, correlation data (for logging) & request response support also works pretty well as a service-2-service messaging solution. As a reason not to use MQTT directly, you often hear that IT would prefer something like RabbitMQ because it "supports transactions" which is actually just the same as manual acknowledgements in MQTT (and pretty much useless as it reduces message throughput considerably).

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content:
> With manual ACK's in MQTT, isn't that generally intended to be an ACK that the message was received, not so much that any processing of the message was valid?
Manual acknowledgements exist for a subscriber to tell a MQTT broker if a message that has been sent by the broker should be considered handled or at least received. In the end it’s up to you to define what received / handled means for you and when you send the manual acknowledgement. Could be after receiving the message. Could be after storing it e.g. in Kafka or a database.

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content:
> My understanding is that MQTT "transactions" should be asynchronous, and this is where in my experience, it gets harder to integrate with transactional systems as-is.
Using an async API is not really hard. The only thing that really changes is that you have to send the manual acknowledge after having successfully performed some operation (e.g. storing the message somewhere). Even when using an async API, this still reduces message throughput considerably but at least make sure that you increase the max. number of unacknowledged messages via MQTT 5 flow control. Using a reactive API, as the HiveMQ Client lib provides it on top of blocking and async APIs, might need a bit more time to get used to for developers that are not used to reactive programming. Anyhow, often the better way when using MQTT / an MQTT broker would be to use a native Kafka integration as HiveMQ provides it (I think EMQ X has something similar), if you really want to make sure you don’t lose anything at all for certain topics (e.g. for data analytics). The HiveMQ Kafka extension guarantees the delivery to Kafka so you can’t lose any messages and after a message has been stored in Kafka it is safe. Kafka is then perfect if you want to store the messages somewhere efficiently in batches (DB or file storage): A Persist Service connected to Kafka can collect a batch of messages in memory (amount depending on the type of data store) and write them in one batch. If the service instance fails before writing it, it can just reload the messages from Kafka. As you mentioned, apparently solace has something like it, which is great.

> REST consumers work by pointing a queue to a web endpoint
This sounds like you have to configure it in the solace Broker. Doesn’t it offer a way to register a REST subscriber through an API so services can subscribe to a topic via HTTP ?

I just listened to what @Walker Reynolds was saying about UNS in the live Q&A from 1/11/21. What I found notable is that, if you gather data for analytics, you basically arrive at a time series database of snapshots of the UNS (the part on how Kafka is used in these scenarios ~ at 1:10:30). Now, I'm thinking an event-sourced architecture basically recording events that change the UNS and using that to be able to compute the state of the UNS at any given point in time is an interesting angle to pursue. Question 2: Do you see benefit in distributing the UNS (again, using change events rather than copying snapshots) to be available to interacting parties (machine gateways, line controllers, mobile devices) _locally_? Author: marc.jaeckle
Content: Actually doing snapshots of the UNS for analytics seems a bit weird to me. For me the normal approach for data analytics would be to just store every single event first in Kafka and from there both in a timeseries DB (e.g. Elastic) and file storage like S3 for long term / raw storage. Based on the events / state updates in Kafka you can build business objects that represent either a machine or a process step (or whatever you need) in realtime using a streaming solution like Flink. If you like your OPC UA information model you could build an object hierarchy based on it. The stream would keep the current state of each object and update the objects with new data. With each change (or some other trigger like time) you can write out the current state of an object to a data store. I simplified the stream processing pipeline a bit. Of course it would also include steps like cleaning data, normalizing it, extending it (e.g. with master data, order data or whatever) etc.

As I would use Kafka together with the stream processing solution the data would be available through Kafka topics for real-time processing anyway as I would let the stream(s) write the data back to Kafka as well. But I guess there could be cases in which it  makes sense to write them back to the UNS as well although I haven't done that so far. I would try to avoid too much data duplication though. For visualisation e.g. via Grafana I would access the timeseries database directly to avoid data duplication. Beyond Grafana I would offer the data via a REST API / a service that "owns" the respective table / index / database. For example if you want to display some KPIs in a nice web frontend, the frontend would use that REST API.

Content: I really want to point out here, that except for Grafana, I would only let a single service access a specific table / index / database directly  so if I change the table / index / database the change only affects this one service (data ownership principle). All other services would have to use the APIs of the first service to access the data (of course unless the data is accessible via a broker / messaging).

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
Building upon the great responses here, I'd like to point out a technique to sort out OPC-UA support.  We often discuss the "parts" of the UA spec and how many are optional.  But, going deeper (and more absurd), it's possible to support a part of a part of the spec.  Yes, it's rather convoluted.  For these reasons, I believe it's helpful to break down OPC-UA support by what's known as profiles and facets.  

OPC-UA features formally defined in Part 7's Profiles:
https://profiles.opcfoundation.org/v104/reporting/

Why is this important?  OPC-UA has a messaging (or even a misinformation) problem.  When one consumes OPC-UA marketing or attends an OPC Foundation event, there is a message that OPC technology is the "UN of Automation."  Specific features regarding transport, security, modeling, discoverability, adoption, and regulatory compliance are emphasized to uniquely address the interoperability required of Industry 4.0.  One is given the impression that investing in OPC-UA yields these things.

When one is in the position to invest in OPC technology, whether to build a product or integrate products, the reality is much more complicated.  It's not simply a matter of heading online or to a trade show to gather a list of products (e.g., devices, apps, SDKs) with an OPC-UA logo.  One must exhaustively gather which profiles (and version) the products support and, due to variations in implementation, potentially test them.  They'll quickly find that most products will support very few profiles.  They'll conclude that OPC-UA, in practice, yields them what OPC Classic did but with TCP/IP and transport security.  It's a far cry from what the OPC Foundation claimed it was.  It definitely is not unlocking Industry 4.0.

Kepware's UA Server interface has implemented profiles for just the core, data access, tcp binary, and security facets.  Here are the support statements on the bottom of page 25:
https://www.kepware.com/en-us/products/kepserverex/documents/kepserverex-manual/

Author: mparris
Content:
Per the sparkplug specification, every sparkplug node publish with the following topic structure:
spBv1.0/<groupID>/N<msgType>/<nodeID>

Some nodes will include devices and will provide data on their behalf:
spBv1.0/<groupID>/D<msgType>/<nodeID>/<deviceID>

Applications wanting to consume sparkplug data will subscribe to these topic structures.

Author: rkwadd
Content: This is more or less the entire point of UNS. You will _always_ have more than one term for the same thing, and there is no single correct approach. If 90% of the devices in the system use PackML tags for example, then you have (theoretically) 90% parity at the device. If it’s all one-off PLCs each setup by a different person at a different time, then there’s no point unifying terms at the PLC. You have to find someplace in the system where abstraction and normalization has already been done, or plan on spending an extreme amount of money to do it now.

Author: rkwadd
Content: So the creation of a unified namespace is precisely to establish rules, make or refer to standard definitions, and formalize governance. Hopefully in as automatic and repeatable a way as possible.

Author: mparris
Content:
Some thoughts:

SpB devices will publish all their metrics once with the birth certificate. After that, every packet just contains the metrics that have changed since that birth certificate. This satisfies report by exception.

Yes, you are likely understanding SpB correctly. An application cannot subscribe to just one metric of a node; it must receive ALL metrics of a node and then parse the payload for the specific metric it cares about.

Author: mparris
Content:
So given this limitation of spB, the best thing to do is to slice up your nodes and devices to contain as many metrics as is reasonable for the majority of applications to receive, even if they are interested in a single metric.

This will likely mean changing how you have your groupID/nodeID/deviceID mappings.

Some ideas:
1) Parris method: Change the groupID to include a concatenation of ISA levels, such as Enterprise-Site-Line
2) Schultz method: have separate brokers for each line where the Enterprise and site is implied by the identification/instance of the broker. Then have the application only subscribe to the broker it is interested in. This should let you use names for groupID that aren't unwieldy. Or, put the brokers at the site level, depending on the application.

@Walker Reynolds  thought experiment for you:

Given there exists a single broker at the Enterprise level running UNS. Instead of a single broker, an architect decides to have segmented brokers, each at the Site level. Content:
Yes, what you are experiencing is my top criticism of SpB.  The fact that the groupID is statically limited to 1 level and the metrics are statically limited to be lumped together within a single payload.

Those limitations prevent very interesting use cases, such as a small application subscribing to all wattage values of all Sparkplug nodes (equipment), for example.

The SpB working group is tied up with scrubbing the existing spec to improve clarity and build automated test package.  Once that gets released, they will have bandwidth to brainstorm how to fix the limitations.

Regarding publishing to the UNS: I would write a gateway service that talks to SAP via HTTP/REST (or whatever interfaces it provides) and publishes the information to the UNS. You then still need a way to store the group and node ids that you are using for the SAP system (could be a ConfigMap under Kubernetes) or you store those in SAP as well.
Regarding the asset structure: You could use the structure as groupID (aka the @MParris method) but I would have a really bad feeling if changes to this would be triggered automatically when someone changes something in SAP. This dynamic would need to be considered for publishes and subscriptions. Another question is how your machines or EoN nodes find out about their identity (node and device ids) or find out about updates to their identity. I think this depends a lot on how you provision them (if you use Kubernetes you could use ConfigMaps but then some service would need to know about how to update those ConfigMaps).

Author: aronsemle
Content: @dan24bxtxtttfdfzgtxdxz I think your idea to use something to go SPB --> MQTT --> ERP is spot on. And @js your thoughts about making SPB Group/EoN IDs dynamic in HighByte is clever, and not something we support today, but we're always open to clever ideas that make things easier. As a quick background, SPB is fantastic, and I still get excited when I see tags auto appear in Ignition. That said, it doesn't do a great job abstracting away the Group/EON stuff from the topic for factory use cases. In my opinion, this is an artifact of the standard coming from O&G/SCADA. So for now, when you're at the MES/ERP layer I'd recommend trying to convert SPB to generic MQTT. This will help with topic hierarchy and make it more interoperable with cloud and other systems that don't support sparkplugs compressed protobuf format. In terms of MQTT topic hierarchy, in our (HighByte) latest release you can make MQTT topic outputs dynamic, so you could do something like \topics\{@this.siteid}\{@this.machineid}... and build the topic out using data from the payload.

Author: hanno23
Content:
We have a case where an industrial radio OEM has now implemented SpB on their devices. With a simple firmware update existing sites' radios all become SpB clients. One of these projects (water industry) has boreholes, pumpstations , reservoirs, wtw, wwtw, weather stations etc. Some share a radio due to being close to each other and thus being cost effective. and some larger sites, like wwtw only have 1 radio. Point is, if I wanted to build out a S95 UNS I would have SpB clients on so many different level of the structure. Forcing me to use multiple brokers or flat tagpath in the Group ID. The latter definitely being the easiest to implement. But I do agree with @DavidSchultz , the broker method would really be cleaner but at the cost of much more complexity and cost, especially in my case. I wouldn't be able to use commercial brokers and clients since it wouldn't justify the cost. I saw in an earlier post you shared a link o BalenaOS and IOFrog which looks like a free and open source way of  implementing IOT on the Edge (MQTT brokers and transmitters). But it would be nice if there was a user-friendly way of quickly implementing a mesh of brokers that is low cost, minimal setup and easy to use for SI's. Then we would get best of both worlds. As more and more devices become SpB compliant , especially if it is existing infrastructure, where an engineer can't dictate the Group/Node/Device levels this becomes a glaring issue.

But I 100% agree with you @MParris , if we could give the GroupID an extended path that would really be great.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
I think the operative word is marketing.  I would venture to say that "Business Management" is a way to differentiate or disassociate from "ERP" and its negative connotations (e.g., failed implementations, cost, inflexibility, missing functionality, illusory product roadmaps).

Unless ERPs have evolved their architecture beyond the traditional transactional database technology, it's probably not a UNS.  A system designed for general ledgers and purchase orders is generally not well suited for the data streams coming off industrial assets.  It's not that it's inferior technology, but that they were built for different purposes.  Most ERPs were initially architected in the past and under very limited assumptions.  iPhone, IoT, ML, AI, NoSQL, etc were not in anyone's vocabulary back then.

I believe that ERPs won't become a "hub" for all data, but rather evolve as a node that interacts with more kinds of data in a more intelligent way.  If not, it will "collapse" or become absorbed into other functional nodes.  The ERP market caters to CFOs and CHROs as the primary constituents.  Most of these leaders have not been at the heart of automating core business processes in an org (e.g., designing/developing, selling, producing, logistics, supply chain, servicing).

What I have observed is that some ERPs are evolving with better analytical and integration capabilities.  They're closing-the-loop and providing visibility better than they have in the past.  There is a bigger emphasis on reusable and customizable platform capabilities for the partners and end-users to extend.  But, they're still largely the same in their intended scope.  I'm not seeing them become a "home" for everything else in the business -- especially further down the automation stack.

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content: It's not just "Historian products" that offer these frontends. Just look at Elasticsearch/OpenSearch with OpenSearch Dashboards/Kibana or Grafana as frontend for many data stores including InfluxDB, TimescaleDB, Elastic, Prometheus and many others. It would say that Kibana/Grafana are even the most sophisticated frontends of this kind and in both cases you can also get technical support AND the data stores they support have been proven at internet scale. Of course a historian vendor might add some other features but at their core the tools are time series DBs with a frontend.

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content: Now regarding S3, you would not use object or file storage as a hot data store for accessing data more or less in real-time. Instead you would use something like S3 (the product, not the API) for storing terabytes or petabytes of data that you don't need to access in real-time. E.g. you might store all your raw data there and just put processed / pre-processed data into your time series DB to access it with a very low latency or you might also use it as backup for your pre-processed data. It serves as cheap storage for the large amount of data that you don't need to access constantly. This allows you to reduce the amount of data stored in your time series DB which typically reduces costs and improves performance of the time series DB. You would make this data available e.g. to data scientists through things like a notebook solution combined with e.g. Spark or Flink (or in the case of AWS S3 through Athena) and you would also use the raw data stored there if you have to re-process some data because some of your calculations changed (or you had a bug in a calculation) and you want to update your pre-processed data. If you have to handle a really large amount of data, it even makes sense to monitor the time frames that people search for in order to determine which data you can throw out of your time series DB.

As I see it:

We use Ignition, FactoryStudio, HighByte, or any other solution that is capable of modeling eg raw / flat / vanilla MQTT to the correct structure (ISA-95 part two)

It does not have to be a SCADA system that does this, it just so happens that Ignition and FS are now capable of it and also function as a problem-solving platform for engineers in the field.

Which solution you choose in your system will be an architectural choice that you make based on what you master, what other tools you have and what you consider to be important for this particular system in general.

I see that the comparisons between OPC-UA and MQTT can be a bit confusing at times, but the thing is that while OPC-UA is excellent for tasks on the edge, it is not suitable as a backbone in an IIoT structure.

Author: ravil1
Content:
@Richard Shaw ard, #1. My tests did show that OPC UA is lighter than vanilla MQTT. #2 Report by exception is the most used case on collecting data over OPC UA, while MQTT has nothing to do with it.

BTW, I would not use #1 and #2 as some significant advantages of OPC UA, because often these are not the most important criteria. 
Moreover, it is not correct to compare OPC UA and MQTT without context/project requirements. They are not mutually exclusive and can co-exist in big projects, each used to solve those tasks where it is the best suitable. 
Also, in OPC UA PubSub  the MQTT is used as a protocol, so no point to think about them as antogonists.

Author: ravil1
Content:
In my opinion, at the primary source, it is best to have your data available over OPC UA. Because in this case, it will be available for a wide range of applications - SCADA, HMI, up to the ERP level (some of them have connectors).
And then you can easily convert it to other protocols, including MQTT, there are many such converters available in the market.
Why I prefer OPC UA as a primary source because over OPC UA you can provide all data, information, services which vanilla MQTT can provide. But the opposite is not true - you cannot convert OPC UA to MQTT without losing anything. Examples: non-hierarchical relations, reading, and writing historical data, including processed data (like averages, min, max, etc.), calling methods.
Another story if your use case is very simple, you don't need those fancy features, and MQTT can carry all you need., today and tomorrow.

Author: ravil1
Content:
In reverse connections, yes, the server needs to be aware of the client, just like the MQTT publisher needs the broker's address.
On the client-side, it can be implemented in different ways. UA Expert, for example, requires explicitly add a reverse connection. But it is possible to design a client in such a way, that it will accept new connections from servers if some criteria/requirements meet. Simplest case - allow all connections, Then it will be similar to MQTT broker accepting all connections from publishers.
And then it is up to the client application to automatically discover the server's address space and subscribe to desired variables at desired sampling/publishing rates.

So, OPC UA allows implementing Edge Driven behavior with no problem. Most SDKs support reverse connection and implement all service calls to autodiscovery etc. 

As noted here, you might not be able to find complete solutions implementing all that yet. But let's keep things in separate boxes - OPC UA as a spec, and applications which implement desired by customers functionality.

In my company's product, auto-discovery described here is not implemented yet, among with reserve connection. Until I joined discussions here, I just did not realize how this is important. Just a few days ago I asked my customer, would the auto-discovery of the address space be useful. He said, yes, but not extremely, because he spent only a few minutes adding all his tags due to the existing feature to add all child nodes of a folder.

In regard to OPC UA PubSub: yes, can be confusing first. It just covers more use cases.
Using multiple protocols - with UDP, you will have broker-less communications, with minimal delivery time (below milliseconds).
I would also point to the security side: with OPC UA PubSub, you can encrypt messages in such a way, that the broker can not decrypt them, only certain subscribers can decrypt. And that is without sharing the secret key between the publisher and the subscriber. And the publisher can decide, what subscribers can decrypt the message.
Most likely you don't need these features though. As I wrote before - in simple cases MQTT is often enough, and the way to go.

Both source and server timestamps are reported, not optimized.

Perhaps you could reduce traffic during establishing a connection, by turning off un-used endpoints, because each endpoint description returns a server certificate, which can be 1 to 2 Kb, or even larger if the certificate is signed by CA and the server is configured to send the whole certificate chain. Author: rickbullotta
Content: While I'm not a fan of OPC UA, I think many lose sight of the fact that it was just as much an incremental evolution of the OPC* specs (DA, Alarms & Events, Historical Data, etc) as something new.  And OPC* was intended mostly to be a "driver" or "API" layer (initially on the same box and eventually networked).  The platform-specific aspects of OPC* and the complexity and questionable future of DCOM forced something else.  It never even really lived up to its promise as a universal protocol driver model much less as an IIoT protocol under OPCUA.  I gave up on OPC UA as "the answer" a long time ago.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
Here’s a gross oversimplification of ITAR and other compliance.  Chances are, you’re not going to find specific brokers with ITAR compliance.  Your compliance is going to be more of a function of how they are deployed and utilized.

ITAR usually impacts ERP and PLM the most.  These best define what a product is, what it's for, how to make it, etc.  I think it might be helpful to start with these to form a basis of how to achieve compliance.  ERP and PLM typically run on top of a relational database.  Their security models are role-based and column-oriented.  That is, certain users with certain roles are allowed access to certain fields.  For example, these fields could be social security number or pricing.  

ITAR is not just about controlling access to fields, but more specifically records all together.  For example, certain products might be subject to ITAR / EAR.  Anyone not cleared for ITAR (e.g., foreign nationals), and sometimes even specific programs, will not have access.  Think of this as row-level security.  If a product has ITAR or certain program attributes, they’re subjected to a specific access control policy.

Unfortunately, many conflate caution with compliance.  Yes, the risk of non-compliance is expensive, but so is inefficient compliance.

Take HIPAA.  Many HR professionals were trained to use a separate filing cabinet for medical records.  But, many aren’t aware that modern HCM software can employ security on not just each employee file, but on records within them.  When they digitize (i.e., not digitally transform) HR, they merely make an inefficient filing system paperless.  This same mindset can occur with ITAR and other compliance.  Some people believe it only means that new filing cabinets (and their digital equivalents) must be stood up.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
In a “zero trust” architecture (Yes, I’ve grown to hate the phrase. Marketers have made the phrase meaningless.), security is inherent.  Everything is granularly tied to policy and intent.  Whether data is resting or moving, it’s always governed.  In these scenarios, it’s possible to create compliance-level access control.  Ironically, cloud apps do this quite well.  They don’t assume everything resides behind a secure perimeter on-premise.  Without this architecture, one is stuck using a “filing cabinet” approach.  In practice, this means separate application instances or tenets get spun up to segment classified records.  For example, some firms will create another instance of the ERP for specific programs (e.g., Acme Main, Acme Defense Program A, Acme Defense Program B).  They’re treated like separate business units.

As with all compliance, work with a compliance officer to determine what’s in scope and what’s out of scope.  If they say everything, they’re probably not doing their job.  They’re being cautious; not compliant.  For example, it’s not a state secret that industrial assets producing products for the defense industry might run on 480 volts.  However, it’s probably an issue exposing quality control records that could reveal product data.  Someone who has served as an external auditor will know what is required and how to demonstrate it.

Author: jon.forbord
Content: Small question. If I want an OPC UA tag to report on change within 50ms accuracy, but the tag changes only once per minute on average, will there be no exchange of packets between the server and the client if I set sample interval to 50ms, and publishing interval of 100ms, between each time it changes?

Author: ravil1
Content:
Hi Jon, In this case, every new value will be reported, with a minimum interval between timestamps of 50 ms. Reporting will happen with a minimum interval of 100 ms. So if the value is changing every 50 ms, then in case if the queue size is 1, you will have only 1 value reported every 100 ms, so every second value will be lost due to insufficient queue size. If the queue size is 2 or greater, then nothing is lost, every 100 ms 2 values will be reported. 
If the value changes only once per minute or 2 minutes, then each value will be reported within 100 ms after it changes. Between changes, no values will be reported, but so-called KeepAlive messages can be sent by the server. The keepAlive message is in fact Publish response with no values, so it is small. It is intended to inform the client that the subscription is still active, just nothing is changing. Note that KeepAlive is sent not for each value, per subscription.
Interval of KeepAlive messages is negotiable between client and server. If you configure it to be longer than the longest interval between data changes, then there will be no KeepAlive messages at all.

Author: ravil1
Content:
Yes, I see that missed this question.

OPC UA has a discovery mechanism using GDS (Global Discovery Server) or broadcasting in the network mDNS messages.
I think also in some cases would be possible to use a Local Discovery server instead of the global one. If all servers register themselves at some single instance of the  Local discovery server, clients can detect that new servers are registered.
Another way is using the reverse connection feature - then it would be similar to MQTT, all servers would be pointing to the client application's endpoint. The client application this way will have all the required information to detect new servers. 
If there are multiple clients, then just like in the case of the MQTT broker, aggregating/federating/gateway OPC UA server can be used as a single point of access to data from all servers. 
This server could be configured to automatically accept server connections if they conform to certain criteria. The simplest case is to accept all server connections - then it will be similar to MQTT.
Then the gateway server can add nodes from new servers to its address space and make them available to all clients.
To detect changes, clients can implement various logic: can either subscribe to address space change event and then re-browse address space or just re-browse address space periodically.
All this might look complex at the first glance, but these are implementation details, for developers, not a big deal. Support for mDNS and reverse connections are already implemented by most SDK vendors, so at the application level, features are available just by calling SDK API. Detection of changes in the address is not hard to implement either.
When it is implemented, for the end-users it will look just like how address space is updated in Ignition via SparkPlug. Dealing with seeming complex stuff is developers' business.

Author: rickbullotta
Content:
You generally should think of "hot", "warm" and "cold" data.  Hot = most recent data, Warm = near term historical data that you want fast access to for operational performance or analytics calculations, Cold = long term storage for compliance or as a data lake for analytics, training models, etc.

Because "stuff happens" you probably want the hot data to be persisted/snapshotted so that it can be restored in the event of a system component outage.  This could happen in a number of places, depending on your architecture, from an MQTT broker, to an IIoT platform, and so on.

I also think of the UNS as more than just data - it's an organizational model - a "metadata lake" if you will - which has intrinsic value on its own.  One natural use cases for it is as the organizing namespace that can be used to lookup how to access historical data.  It's also a great place (if architected with an appropriate type system and metadata model) for enabling "population queries" that join metadata with data to filter and aggregate stuff - e.g. compare the average pump energy consumption segmented by pump size and material type.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
MQTT is bidirectional (i.e., publish and subscribe).  Its underlying transport is TCP.  The TCP sessions are instantiated by the client.  The client would both publish and subscribe to topics over outbound TCP 1883 (without TLS) or outbound TCP 8883 (with TLS).

Think of it, in a narrow sense, like a typical HTTP API for a cloud app.  Most of the time, the services will be exposed as "inbound" APIs.  Whether client intends to read from or write to a data source, it will be executing the call.  The client can GET or POST over outbound TCP 443.

TCP is like a tunnel.  It can be funded and built by one country on one side, but the traffic inside of it flows both ways.

Author: geoffnunan
Content:
There are very real cultural differences between Australia and the US, and I agree completely with @NickN that the 4.0 Solutions videos do not translate well.
There is also a very different business reality for manufacturing as there are no trade barriers or federal taxes that protect the local manufacturing industry, so manufacturers need to compete on a level playing field with Asia where labor costs are negligible. 
Digital transformation in manufacturing, regardless of culture or nation, must deliver real, tangible, quantifiable $$ benefits back to the bottom line or it will not be sustained. Pilots that aim to prove tech with a "build it and they will come" justification don't succeed in the long run. (The exception to this rule is if you're using SAP for your transformation, then it's game on!)
So where can the $$ come from, and how can you justify it to the CFO? You have to start looking at your business the way the CFO looks at it. 
Many types of manufacturing are suitable for a "Standard-Cost" based cost accounting method, but most business lack the data to achieve it and so resort to "Black-box" cost accounting where you track the cost of things that go into the factory, and the value of things that come out, subtract the difference in inventory and average. This approach, although by far the most common, provides almost no information that can help cost accountants identify and report on problems in the factory. 
If you can explain the digital transformation in terms of how it makes the CFO's life easier, and demonstrate with a small pilot, you are will on the way to getting proper funding.
Justifying a big spend initially does not happen, you need small wins to create credibility and trust.

@RickBullotta With our group having more than a decade of experience in PI AF, I can tell you that, in theory, AF is capable, via the PI Web API, of doing what TQS claims  but the problem is scaling. 

Getting the data into the system isn't particularly difficult...

But, in order to really do anything with the data set you need to make heavy use of PI Analyses and PI Event Frames. 

One of the primary driving forces behind what was to become Libre was that a guy named Jason Prosser (probably the world's foremost expert in the customization of the PI System and specifically PI AF), from Spruik Technologies, managed to collapse a PI Server under the weight of a broad OEE query that was using PI EF and Analyses. And - that was for a query that involved a single line.

As a result of that spectacular failure, we are deploying Libre into a an enterprise-class  PI AF customer for purposes of running a scalable Eventing and Analysis engine on a Kubernetes cluster that can actual perform for large scale Electronic Batch Records. Ironically, PI will still be the system of record, but all of the heavy lifting is being done by Libre and pushed back to PI AF so that the reporting structures and data lakes don't have to be changed.

For those that really want to know what PI AF is capable of and want to know the edge of it's limitations, maybe we can get Jason on here to answer some very pointed technical questions about how to kill a PI System.

Author: jon.forbord
Content: Here are my thoughts around this topic of digital threading, from reading a ton of stuff and research (watching YouTube). In short: yes, I believe digital threading is compatible with UNS, but with some tweaks to how you’d normally implement threading. It largely fails to achieve the goal of treating all projects as part of a bigger whole. It does not unlock the data for other systems to consume, and if all you collect are modeled machine data, you’ll potentially have data gaps from SCADA/MES/ERP etc. It’s also the approach that kept me in the camp of I4.0 skeptics for a long time. “You’re collecting machine data and doing stuff with it in decentralized compute (cloud) .. so what?!” “It doesn’t solve ANY of the problems I’m working , or make my life easier” But: UNS - collect all data, treat your business as an ecosystem rather than siloed solutions, make integrations easier, use the same source of information everywhere, make it easy to solve problems and do more with less, in real time, and add some ML-cherry on top! Now THAT’S exciting! What I’m trying to say is that digital threading is going to fail because it provides little value to the people working on the plant floor solving problems every day. It’s a one stop solution to solve one problem, and it doesn’t provide value to other solutions, it doesn’t gradually expand your business’ capabilities to solve problems. As a UNS matures each next step increases the collective knowledge in the business, as more nodes use data to create information and contributes back to the ecosystem.

Author: rickbullotta
Content: Digital thread and UNS and digital twins and dairy-as-a-service and so on are "AND" not "OR", IMO.

Author: rickbullotta
Content: I also think that UNS needs a complementary data model that is more "process-focused", since processes (and their steps and inputs and outputs) provide very meaningful context for stuff that spans many branches of a more asset-oriented UNS.

Author: jon.forbord
Content: Yes, if I didn't make it clear, it is an AND, not an OR. But digital thread as your "digital strategy" will not be a complete strategy, and will fail to achieve the fully connected business. Add to it if you implement it without it being a part of a sound overall architecture, you'll have some technical debt to bring with you.

Author: rickbullotta
Content:
What's interesting is that there are actually scenarios where higher OEE can lead to reduced profitability - the "costs" of losses quality, availability, and productivity are never identical.  And running your operations at the highest possible throughput and/or OEE can lead to safety issues in some cases.  Also, many processes are extremely energy or resource (water, etc) intensive, and optimizing for those can have a great impact on results also.   And if the production team makes the wrong orders but at high OEE, that's a giant fail too.  Ultimately a single metric like OEE is just a really, really bad idea.  The component metrics, in context, are fine.  And in quite a few cases, even the component metrics are garbage - quality is the most common one to be inaccurate (due to losses later in the production process as a result of upstream quality issues), and throughput metrics usually fail to account for continuous improvement efforts and ongoing equipment and process improvements that have "moved the goalposts" as to theoretical maximums.

All of these metrics need to be taken in the specific context of a specific manufacturing operation.

But please, don't drive your business by OEE.

Author: geoffnunan
Content:
Agreed, and for some businesses, a 1% hit on customer service level can easily trump a 10% hit in quality.
In general, there are a handful of different supply-chain strategies that can be used depending on what's most important to the customer. 
The CFO should have a crystal clear understanding of which strategy the business is trying to leverage. Often it's some version of "Good, Fast, Cheap or Dependable"
If your No1 KPI is Customer Service Level, you will definitely carry more production capacity than you need, and more inventory that you need in order to hit the CSL targets and so won't be too concerned with OEE improvement.
If your No1 KPI is Cheap, you will be completely focused on cost, will be running your equipment as hard as you can, and will be OK will missing a customer order every now and then when things go wrong.
This is a bit of an over-simplification, but you get the idea.
Knowing how the CFO views your business, and which KPI are important to his strategy tells you a lot about where your digital transformation efforts should be aimed. 
If the CFO does not give you the funding you need for your project, maybe it's just that your project is not that important to the business.

Author: brianpribe
Content:
I think to start if a business has no measurements on production then OEE is a good place to start. Having something point you in some direction is better than not getting any direction at all. That being said Rick is right in saying you shouldn’t run your business on it. Here’s an example: 
A CNC shop has an OEE of 70%. So they decide to speed up production and get to an OEE of 75%. Right now there is a tooling shortage and the cost of end-Mills have skyrocketed. Now for the CNC shop to maintain its 75% OEE they will need to buy more of these expensive end-mills. The accountant sends out the monthly earnings report and it shows a 5% decrease in earnings. 
Another scenario: Same CNC shop with 70% OEE. Management asks operators what they want, and they ask for more time off/shorter hours/ flexible hours. Management grants them shorter hours. OEE goes down to 60% OEE. Now the market goes onto a hiring frenzy and employers are jacking up hourly rates 25%. The CNC shop maintains its hourly salary and schedule and has no employee turn-over. Accountant comes back and says they had a 5% decrease in earnings. Productivity went down, but the business could have gotten a much worse decrease in earnings had they not shortened hours. 
Moral of the story is OEE should not drive your business, but it’s a tool to indicate where in your production you could improve for more throughput.

Author: rickbullotta
Content: Agents exist for common protocols (OPC, OPC UA, MQTT), data sources like RDBMSs, most major historians, some of the leading HMIs, and some MES products.  On the cloud side you model stuff in a manner not dissimilar to the UNS approach, and map properties/data into that model (can merge data from multiple sources of course).  If historical data is available, it'll get loaded so that it can be used to train model(s).  Generally, nothing needs to be added at the PLC level unless you're adding new sensors.  You can then apply any of about 20-25 ML applications (for energy, predictive quality, uptime optimization, failure detection, and so on) or you can build your own or bring your own using the curated datasets.  Also has an interface to Jupyter if you want to do some experimentation on those datasets.  Once the models are generated and trained it'll give you a fairly detailed description of the model(s) utilized and which inputs were most relevant.  You can then operationalize those models to notify people or to trigger events/actions.  There's also a UX for modeling and for operator usage, but you can also push back predictions and events into other systems if you prefer.

Content: Also there's a REST API for both the configuration/dev side and the runtime side.  One missing piece today is integration of outbound pub-sub for events and data originating from the app itself, but that's under construction.

Content:
While Kepware has interfaces for all sorts of device and application protocols, it's limited in it's ability to contextualize and model data in between connections.  It's more of a "raw" protocol converter.  Yes, it can relay the tag value of a PLC to an MES like one would to a historian.  But, it will quickly reach limitations when it needs to do more than this.  MES and ERP apps are not telemetry systems.  They're transactional systems.  They have methods that must be evoked dynamically.  For example, in most cases, Kepware is not going to facilitate the logic required to transact with an MES when a container has been filled to its standard pack.  It would need to know the a bunch of things about the production process (e.g., workcenter, job/part, container, inventory units, standard pack size) and employ logic to do something with it.  If all the context about the production process that an MES transaction would need to know is in the PLC, this might be possible.  In most environments, the PLC has little context beyond what is necessary to control the machine.

How does everyone approach "normalizing" relationships between objects in a UNS?  For example, when a topic name changes, how does all the logic tied to that keep up?  How does one avoid "breaking" relationships or structure as object names may need to change?

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
I've always had some reservations on how the term "ISA-95" is thrown around.  It can create confusion.  Colloquially, it's narrowly referring to the Equipment Hierarchy in the Object Model Attributes (ISA-95 Pt 2).  This is verbose.  But, it's only natural to shorten and imply meaning in conversation.

If one is familiar with ISA-95, they'll know it's much more than this.  It "boils the ocean" in terms of modeling a manufacturing enterprise.  If you're wondering if a MQTT-based UNS is an implementation of ISA-95 in the same way that B2MML or the OPC-UA ISA-95 companion spec is, it's not.  I wouldn't put much value in any implementation of ISA-95.  Market adoption is spotty.  In the real world, manufacturers don't explicitly architect their business according to ISA-95.  They generally procure or develop automation for specific purposes without a broader enterprise context.  In practice, ISA-95 is more like a frame of reference or a recommendation than a standard.  One is more likely to observe aspects that "rhyme" with the spec rather comply with it.  Even ERP and MES companies concede this.

May I ask how you're using ISA-95?  Do you have an MES with a B2MML support?

There's nothing stopping anyone from taking those ISA-95 models and serializing them as, say, JSON in an MQTT payload.  It would be cool to see.  ISA-95 does not prescribe anything about transport or exchange.  ISA-95 would certainly challenge the telemetry use-cases of MQTT.  It will be somewhat unintuitive with regards to request/response patterns.  MQTT, being a simple pub/sub message pattern, isn't method or transaction friendly.  It's not going to natively constrain responses to requests invoked.  The clients will need further definition on handling this.

SAP essentially expressing skepticism over using ISA-95 as a basis for integration:
https://blogs.sap.com/2013/12/06/sap-mii-and-b2mml/

HighByte demonstrating ISA-95 hierarchy as MQTT topic paths:
https://youtu.be/PWEyMLtKvXI?t=1230

Author: rickbullotta
Content:
As someone who attended ISA-95 meeting number one (and quite a few after that), I have to say that overall B2MML and ISA-95 have lost their luster for me. Broadly, they grew out of the batch/hybrid application area (it was mostly the same folks from the ISA-88 work, including me), and over time it was tried to be adapted to other production scenarios (process, discrete, etc), with very mixed success.  I also felt like it never really represented how real world factories were modeled, since the physical equipment was more graph-y than hierarchical.  Add to that the fact that it look an insanely long time to complete the spec work (heck, JSON support didn't even come until 25 years after the first meeting), and it just kind of faded to irrelevance for me.  

I also am not a fan of layer cake models for organizations and organizational functions - I see them more as a network/graph also, increasingly so in an era where contract manufacturing and more complex and interconnected value chains is more common.

Sam Castro's article (the SAP one) also makes a point I have always made about standards - there's not a lot of value in using a standard/intermediate format if you're doing a 1:1 mapping.  Different if the apps support the standard out of the box, but usually they don't, so a lot of companies end up doing twice the work for little value.

And then there's the myth of interoperability - the truth is that many, MANY implementations of standards like B2MML and BatchML heavily leverage the (permitted) capability of adding extensions and custom elements/attributes (the heinous xsd:any in schemas).  That basically leads to no interop.  It's silly.

Rant off.  Do what you must, but don't assume there's much incremental value in applying ISA-95 to your facilities.  It might just end up costing you time and money.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
The best one is the one that works for you.

I would say don't wait around and develop your own.  At the same time, be sensible about adaptability and portability to take advantage what may be available in future.  In general, there is nothing to "rule them all" and there is not indication there will be any time soon.  As Rick mentioned earlier, it's entirely possible for the cost of adopting a standard to exceed its benefit.  As someone who prefers semantic modeling and loves the idea of plug-n-play, I can even concede that rolling one's own is sensible.  These standards can be a losing proposition for many companies.  Companies can find themselves building Rube Goldberg machines with nothing to show for it.  Take a Metcalfe's Law approach and ask how valuable the standard's ecosystem is.  If you're building all the nodes in the ecosystem yourself and don't reasonable expect anyone else to, it's not unreasonable to question the value of utilizing a standard over your own.

There exist large platform players such as Microsoft that will claim that end-users will lose out on many fronts if they don't adopt this stuff.  Their motive is not necessarily your digital transformation success.  Their motive in advocating for interoperability is for their benefit.  They want others to build the last mile of an ecosystem that they can sell cloud computing services into.  Take these standards with a grain of salt.

In terms of standards , Factory+ is an honorable mention.  It's super new.  It's a much more practical approach to implementing the OPC-UA companion specifications.  There are implementation guides for popular platforms in the industrial space.

Factory+:
https://factoryplus.app.amrc.co.uk/
https://factoryplus.app.amrc.co.uk/docs/specification/messages-payload/common-data-structures/cds-overview

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
You probably won't find a torque tool natively supporting Sparkplug.  I'm not aware of any that support MQTT.  Most support some basic TCP/IP or potentially a fieldbus.  Select whatever torque tools fit your application and budget, but include a criteria in your RFP for protocol support.  200 is a sizable order and the supplier may just satisfy your protocol requirements to win it.  In the end, I suspect you'll be working with Atlas Copco units.  Kepware has a driver for these.

Given the number of devices and they're all on the same LAN, a central instance of Kepware is probably the most economical approach.  Pairing it with something like HighByte (or Ignition) to pull in additional context would be advisable.  One thing I find challenging with "smart" tools or instrumentation is that they're not actually that smart.  They can't pull in much data and they don't really know how they're being used.  As a result, it's possible to collect noisy data in non-production states (e.g., troubleshooting, maintenance, testing).  PLCs, especially if they're already available and utilized elsewhere in the process, could be an optimal gateway.

The good news is that there are options.  As your requirements become more precise, these options could be narrowed down.

[Torque Tool] <- Torque Tool Ethernet -> [Kepware w/ IoT Gateway] <- MQTT -> [Broker]
[Torque Tool] <- Torque Tool Ethernet -> [Kepware] <- OPC-UA -> [Ignition] <- MQTT SpB -> [Broker]
[Torque Tool] <- Torque Tool Ethernet -> [Kepware] <- OPC-UA -> [HighByte] <- MQTT SpB -> [Broker]
[Torque Tool] <- UCON TCP/IP -> [Kepware] <- OPC-UA -> [HighByte] <- MQTT SpB -> [Broker]
[Torque Tool] <- TCP/IP -> [RTA -or- Maple Systems Gateway] <- MQTT/SpB -> [Broker]
[Torque Tool] <- TCP/IP -> [Ignition Edge] <- MQTT SpB -> [Broker]
[Torque Tool] <- TCP/IP -or- Fieldbus -> [Opto22 / Siemens S7 / Beckhoff / Wago PLC] <- MQTT/SpB -> [Broker]
[Torque Tool] <- TCP/IP -or- Fieldbus -> [Beckhoff IoT Bus Coupler] <- MQTT -> [Broker]

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
**Torque Tool**
Ignition has a generic TCP/IP driver.  It will consume an ASCII payload from a TCP Server into a tag.  You would have to build a script to parse the ASCII payload generated by the Torque Tool.

Ignition TCP/IP and UDP/IP Driver:
https://docs.inductiveautomation.com/display/DOC79/UDP+and+TCP+Driver

**MTConnect**
Ignition does not have a native MTConnect driver.  If you're already using Kepware, they have a MTConnect driver available.  Additionally, if you're motivated, Ignition could parse the XML payload in HTTP responses from an MTConnect Adapter.

__Innorobix MTConnect Module__
[CNC] <- MTConnect -> [Innorobix Module | Ignition]
https://inductiveautomation.com/moduleshowcase/module/innorobix-automation-inc-mtconnect

__Kepware MTConnect Driver__
[CNC] <- MTConnect -> [Kepware] <- OPC-UA -> [Ignition]
[CNC] <- MTConnect -> [Kepware w/ IoT Gateway ] <- MQTT -> [Broker]
https://www.kepware.com/en-us/products/kepserverex/drivers/mtconnect/

__DIY MTConnect Interface__
[CNC] <- MTConnect -> [Web Services (HTTP) + XML Parse (Etree Library) Script |  Ignition]

Author: mparris
Content:
I don't know what the right limit is of frequency, but I would put 5ms publish rate in the box of too fast to publish. At some point, you have to consider the overhead that comes with each publish (Ethernet header, IP header, TCP header, MQTT header, etc). It very well could be that the overhead is larger than the data you are trying to send and levying a hefty requirement onto the clients to be able to process that data.

Likely the better approach is to publish in batches at a slower rate. Yes, it will add some latency to your data pipeline, but I think it will be a more stable config.

Content:
So i've done a bit more hacking on my POC of the "uber broker" and added a couple cool features:

- Sparkplug *DATA payload expansion: basically this automatically extracts metrics and re-publishes them with a "normal" MQTT topic name (groupid/edgenodeid/[deviceid]/metricname)

- More comprehensive historization (includes non-numeric types as well), which currently uses InfluxDB but could work with generally any historian

- Expanded the REST API to remove topics and retained messages

This is not something I'll likely ever publish or finish but it's something I'm using to hack ideas that might find their way into products like HighByte at some future point

Author: rickbullotta
Content: I use a separate metadata store + a REST API that uses a single topic namespace.  So if I want to get a current value or historical view of /MyHouse/Office/Temperature, I use the REST API, but if I want a subscription I use an MQTT subscription. Author: jon.forbord
Content: I read an interesting article on the next stage in data warehouse/data lake/all data in one place. The data mesh. Realizing that putting all the data in one place is just a means to an end, with the goal being to be able to analyze data from many different sources. The concept of the mesh is that it makes it all accessible in a unified way, such that it behaves as if it’s all in one place (at least that’s my understanding). So I’ve been thinking about the same concept around a UNS. As long as the data and information is accessible in a unified way and that everyone has access to it, it doesn’t matter where that data “lives” (in a zero-latency-infinite-bandwidth-world). So the UNS “lives” in a broker, but that doesn’t really matter, the broker is just the technology you use to make data accessible. So it is omnipresent and lives everywhere and nowhere.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
Theoretically, yes. A UNS is basically a brokered service bus mapping many disparate structures into one. Absent capabilities such as industrial interfaces (e.g., MQTT, OPC-UA, native gateways) and industrial data types (e.g., tags, UDTs), it can get clunky. A good UNS is one that connect to everything in the plant and in the office. Not only must it connect to everything, it also must be able to address the unfortunate reality that is industrial automation data.  

If an IT dept asks “Why do we need X (e.g., HighByte, Ignition, FS)? We already have Y (e.g., WebSphere, Tibco, Boomi).”, take a step back to make sure they have a full appreciation of how industrial automation is programmed and what its data looks like. When industrial automation is approached as just another data source, there is a higher risk of project delay or failure. Because most industrial automation is stood up under narrow assumptions, its data is as well. It’s definitely not another database or web service to connect. The problem space of industrial automation will change the scope of DataOps beyond consolidating licensing or aligning with personnel experience/familiarity.

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content: The concept of a UNS does not depend on a product like Highbyte. In the end a UNS is a combination of having a central pub/sub broker with a standardised topic structure, clearly defined data models / interfaces with (well documented) schemas and features like birth and death messages as found in Sparkplug for creating a dynamic system. Highbyte can help you when your PLCs send unreadable variables in a non-optimal structure with non-normalised units etc. but it's preferable if the the PLCs can already send defined data models that other systems / services can use directly without having to transform the data first.

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content: At least in the last draft version I read, they made some things worse with the clarification. For example now (unless they changed it again) Sparkplug requires QoS 0 to be used for any data messages. Explanation was that some SCADA systems have difficulties with handling duplicate messages. So much for the user / practitioner driven spec 🙂 Ignoring how much that reasoning annoys me, why not just make it configurable so if you have a shitty SCADA system you use QoS 0 and if you want to make sure not to lose any data you use QoS 1. The delivery guaranty of QoS 0 (at most once) isn't even the big problem regarding the risk of data loss but that a MQTT broker will not queue QoS 0 messages and messages will be dropped right away when there is no subscriber.

Author: mparris
Content: Isn't the QoS level driven by the client, so is it feasible to have the publisher connect via QoS1 and a subscriber connect via QoS0?

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content: The way I remember the MQTT spec, the QoS level you define in the subscription must be understood as a maximum QoS. So a QoS 0 publish would still not be stored in the persistent session if a client subscribed with a requested QoS level of 1 or 2. Also the publishing client would drop a QoS 0 message right away if it has no connection to the broker. A client might also drop QoS 0 messages if it uses MQTT 5 backpressure handling support (but I'm not sure if you can configure what your mqtt client lib does with QoS 0 messages in a backpressure situation). Anyone here who knows the MQTT spec better than I do who can confirm or deny this?

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content: Maybe a better solution for those SCADA systems would be to change the spec so the sequence number in the payload may use more than 1 byte (counting up to 255 and then start over again). This would even be possible without changing the current proto schema as the sequence number is defined as optional uint64.

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content: (Don't quote me on the Sparkplug spec only allowing the 256 values. I didn't check this again 🙂 )

Author: mparris
Content:
You are correct about 255 sequence numbers.

What about the case with a publisher sending QoS1 and a subscriber using QoS0?

I can't remember if subscribers can specify a qos

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content: As the requested QoS of the subscriber is to be treated as maximum QoS, the broker would "use" QoS 0. Again, that's what I think the MQTT spec says but I'm not reading it too often.

Author: mparris
Content: Then shouldn't a bad SCADA just do QoS0 as you say, and allow others to publish QoS1 in case others can benefit?

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content: Good point, that should actually also "fix" their problem. But then again, they should be able to handle duplicate and delayed / out-of-order messages. If they don't, they can't even use Shared Subscriptions to scale & and for high availability.

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content: Now that I thought about it again: This can still cause duplicates as the communication from the publisher to the broker is QoS 1 so duplicates might be created there. Only the communication from the broker to the subscriber would be QoS 0. So you would end up with a "never, once or more than once" QoS from an end-to-end perspective.

Content: Great question. There are some more questions you have to ask yourself to arrive to an answer that best applies to your application. Ideally, you publish directly to the broker, but you might have security concerns with flat MQTT or the data needs context for your ignition GW to understand it. If security is a concern an EON could convert flat MQTT to MQTT SpB. If security isn't a concern, but you want to contextualize it, I would still publish directly to the broker, but have an application like HighByte to contextualize/model the data and then put it back into the broker for your ignition GW to subscribe to. If both security and context is a concern, apply both methods. So my order of preference would be 3..2..1..IGNITION!

Content: It depends. Ideally you combine 3 and 2 (flat MQTT to MQTT SpB) so that the broker gets DBIRTH DDEATH certificates (This is assuming the EoN is in the machine). If your EoN is connected to 10 other flat MQTT devices, you might want to change how you go about it. QoS (quality of service) is another parameter you could utilize for monitoring connection status. Say you have your device pubs ever 5 seconds with a QoS 2. In your EoN MQTT SpB payload, you could have a topic on connection status.Your EoN can have a script where after 10 seconds with no pub, change the connection status to "buffering". After 20 seconds, pub a "disconnected" status.

Author: mdowdell
Content:
Part 1:

As the readers of this discord know, the UNS is the KEY element of a successful IIoT solution. We are currently using it and with great success! Having said that, we have run into an issue.

The issue is with SpB. SpB is an industrial implementation of the more generic MQTT 3.1.1 standard and provides specific functionality required in industrial applications. We try to use it whenever possible, but careful… all manufacturers do not implement the entire specification, nor do it well.  We discovered this during PoC and benchmarking. I recommend that all go through this process for product / software validation before selling or putting into production. 

Going back to the UNS. The power of the UNS lies in its hierarchy (see ISA 95) and the implicit contextualization that it provides. We typically use something like this:

ABInBev/Modelo/Hidalgo/Bottling/Line1/Filler/OeeRaw which is:

Enterprise/Business Unit/Site/Area/Line/Cell/UDTs

After going through and OEE engine the output is written to:

ABInBev/Modelo/Hidalgo/Bottling/Line1/Filler/OeeCalc

This information can then be used by any other node that is subscribed to the topic. Very powerful.

Author: mdowdell
Content:
Part 2:

But here is the issue. SpB has three parameters that we must define - group_id, edge_node_id, and device_id. And with respect to the group_id naming, the SpB specification states, “The format of the group_id element is not dictated in that it can be any valid UTF-8 alphanumeric string except for the reserved characters of ‘+’ (plus), ‘/’ (forward slash), and ‘#’ (number sign).” This requirement also extends to edge_node_id and device_id naming convention. So, we cannot define the UNS hierarchy when specifying the node names. 

We have been using ignition and Factory Studio (FS) to read the incoming messages and map them to the UNS, but it is an additional step that I would like to avoid. Also, we have been discussing this issue with HiveMQ (very helpful BTW), but their solution appears to be a remapping within the broker instead of using another application like Ignition or FS. Has its benefits, but still cludgey and with their “per-core” pricing can create additional costs seeing that user generally (>90%) wants a SCADA type interface so Ignition or FS would be used anyway.

My ask is to modify the SpB specification to allow for the full definition / declaration of topic at the edge to reduce additional work, possible errors, and compute load.
Any other ways that the community has worked around this issue or something that I am missing?

@Arlen Nipper @Walker Reynolds Your comments would be greatly appreciated.

Author: mdowdell
Content: @RickBullottaThanks. However, I am looking towards a more comprehensive solution (And something that would be adopted by manufacturers trying to comply with the SpB spec) that addresses the fundamental issue - my reason for tagging @Arlen Nipper

Author: rickbullotta

Author: rickbullotta
Content: My take is that ISA95/Purdue described a command-and-control model of operating a self-contained manufacturing business that was relevant until perhaps the mid-90's.  B2MML was fatally flawed with way extensions were implemented on most elements, which rendered interoperability nearly impossible. The result was many "flavors" of B2MML from different apps/vendors.

Author: rickbullotta
Content:
There was also a clear bias towards batch/hybrid manufacturing models (versus process/flow manufacturing or discrete manufacturing) due to the heritage of the team, most of whom (including me) had worked on ISA88.

I am not questioning whether there was/is some benefit to common terminology - that was most of what ISA88 actually accomplished, but I do question whether there is much benefit to going "all in" on ISA95 as your foundational approach for a UNS, integration models, and so on.
