Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
B2MML is basically a representation of ISA95 in XML form.  Basically, the vision was have a standard way of describing everything in a manufacturing environment and enable plug-n-play between systems.  You can go online and spend hours reading ISA95 specs.  You'll learn that very few businesses have adopted or embraced this.  That are operations and automation professionals with decades of experience that have never heard of ISA95.

In practice, B2MML is an interface you might occasionally show up on MES or ERP systems.  Think of it as some XML that HighByte might need to be able to parse from time-to-time when a customer has an app that uses it.

Another way to think of B2MML is like OPC-UA.  In the real world, most devices have native protocols and you end up using Kepware to access the tags.  Devices almost never have a full-blown OPC-UA server with all the features that would make them plug n play.  B2MML is like MES/ERP equivalent of this.  Plug-n-play MES doesn't exist.  More often than not, you'll use a native web services interface to connect to these systems.  If you ask the software vendor if you can use B2MML, they're more likely to say "lol why?" than "absolutely, we fully support it without any caveats".

This community throws around the term "ISA95" in the context of organizing a UNS using the terminology specifically from ISA 95 Pt 2 (e.g., Enterprise, Site, Area, Line).  This is not the same thing as building a business and modeling everything inside of it according to ISA95.

Author: geoffnunan
Content:
ISA 95 > B2MML
B2MML is just a suggested canonical model for passing data between the ERP and the MES. 
ISA95 covers an information model for what Manufacturing Operations across industry verticals should cover. 
ISA95 is not intended to be a Physical data model, It's a logical data model describing concepts. The huge value of a company adopting ISA95 into the Enterprise Information Architecture patterns is that it provides a common language. It allows ERP functional consultants to talk to MES application designers and Control Systems Engineers using terms that are vendor agnostic and common across the stack.
One of the things that I like about the ISA95 standard is that you don't have to implement all of it.(Unlike B2MML if you are integrating point-to-point between MES and ERP). You can start to publish parts of the model, and know that if you keep to the standard, you will be able to expand you scope into other areas without breaking the information model.
If you want to just start with Machine Status, you can publish that using the ISA95 model (With a little help from ISA88). Then when you're ready, you can add calendars to describe shift patterns, and publish shift change events into your model. That gives you the ability to understand machine state in the context of shift. Then you can add materials, and schedules and recipes and routings and ... all while sticking to the original schema. you never need to come back and change the schema when you add new functions into your system.
@Brian Pribe I've worked across a lot of companies and most have ISA95 in some form. @js is right when he mentioned that is normally only shows between MES and ERP, but this is because of legacy point-to-point architectures, and the ability to have a different schema for each interface.
A UNS has to consider the needs of all of the functions that will be published into it. Achieving that common, cross-domain agreement is hard without starting from ISA95.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
UNS' structure could be used as the basis for the structure/context in a data warehouse (or historian).  I don't think it's a hard-and-fast rule or the sole way.  Data warehouses are tricky because the structure to efficiently enable analytics can differ greatly from the structure for transactions (e.g., UNS, ERP, MES).  For example, a historical gross margin report might benefit from transforming general ledger data into star or cube schemas instead of raw rows from transaction tables.   

I think the power of the UNS is its ability to mesh together different systems and create context as it happens.  Provided it's planned, it's much easier to log this in-context that it is to ETL disparate historical data stores into something cohesive.  Where it gets challenging is dealing with modified or adjusted records.  Additionally, I find that there are a lot of points of inquiry that can completely challenge the way data is organized.  It's almost impossible to anticipate these.

BI can display data sets from a UNS like HMI/SCADA screen can, but not as sophisticated as it can from a "proper" data warehouse.  A data warehouse can be queried with more options and more efficiently.  I like to think of a UNS dataset as like a "flattened image" in photoshop.  It's easier to consume, it loads faster, and is more portable.  When it's not flattened and left in the native photoshop format, all the layers are exposed and there much more flexibility in how one consumes the image.

Another way is to think about it is by functional role.  The data science or process engineer investigating a specific issue may not necessarily find everything they're looking for in a UNS dataset or in a historical datastore with structure prescribed by a UNS.  They may need to mesh together different historical datastores in ways that were never imagined or architected in a UNS.  Operations personnel, consuming a routine KPI or measure, could very well consume this directly or indirectly through a UNS.

Author: brianpribe
Content: I think its a given that some of the data is not in the correct or optimized format that an analysts needs it in (and this is when the data has been contextualized and organized in the UNS). If he/she needs it reformatted for an analysis, then yes do so. At least you need to reformat it once to get all of the data arranged to your liking. But there's no benefit of pushing that into a UNS or data lake, cuz all it is is reformatted data, nothing new. I purpose to push this reformatted data into a playground DB that your application utilizes. Now once you perform your analysis and gather new data from it, THEN push it to the UNS.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
Random thoughts that came across the way having worked on a few BI projects lately.

-UNS can indirectly shape analytics because it can essentially propagate a master data model throughout various application nodes.  It's an effective messaging technique to keep context consistent.  So, while one may not be querying data store that is historizing a UNS, they may be querying an application node's historical data store that were the result of transactions through the UNS.

-Absent strong data governance policies (aka red tape that makes everyone scared to change anything), I'm not really a fan of the logging information in parallel to transactions just for purpose of reporting.  It creates secondary forms of truth.  This remind me of someone maintaining a spreadsheet and then one day realizing all the attributes they used have been modified elsewhere (e.g., renamed, split, consolidated).  It's not a very resilient approach to change.  It creates all these problems that a well-designed and fully normalized schema already solved.

-The scale/scope of context varies at different levels of the automation stack.  PLC/SCADA levels tend to be stood up for narrow purposes and context tends to be an afterthought.  Well-architected MES and ERP can be super contextual, but sometimes miss some operational context because it's too cumbersome to capture without the right automation.  I think UNS is a game changer for SCADA and historians because it brings a lot more context into these systems that is usually too challenging with legacy approaches to integration.  MES and ERP systems, by comparison, are much more transactional.  It's not a raw process historian.  It's set of records linked to other records that are modified constantly.  Additionally, those modifications are logged as records as well.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
In my experience, I find it much more likely to hit the reporting database of an MES or ERP than something that was logging UNS or middleware events as they happened.  Why?  The records may have been modified in the MES or ERP that were outside the scope of the integrations.  Or, there was context that was missing.  For example, the UNS may have been used to shuttle inventory transactions around but not necessarily how inventory history is captured.  But relying on what was historized for integration, one is essentially making assumptions on how data is consumed.

Where the UNS-driven-analytics approach can work out well is with data lakes or process historians focused on the (I hate saying this) IT-OT "splits" among application nodes.  There aren't as many natural "homes" for a lot of process or operational data up the stack (and vice versa).  They usually make their way into a historical data store at the SCADA level, but they're also missing context.  By providing more context than just timestamps or a basic asset model, this data can be meshed more easily and intelligently with other historical data stores.  For example, logging the key or identity of a production run (e.g., job no, work no) can make it easier to later "join" in other context that may be reclassified over time (e.g., employee name, part name, defect name, customer name).  I believe that it's more sustainable to capture the relationships as opposed to set of raw values as a point in time.  Otherwise, it's very easy to end up with discontinuities in historical data (e.g., classified as "X" until CY2020:Q3, but "Y" after).  This can, in-turn, drive all sorts of maintenance projects or, ironically, the need for a data warehouse.

Logging data for the short-term is easy and meets many needs, but how to make useful for long-term needs is much more challenging.

Author: jon.forbord
Content: This is where the life of the architect becomes interesting in my view. UNS does get rid of a lot of what would usually be done as discrete connections, particularly on the OT level or between OT and IT. UNS does not get rid of ALL discrete connections. I would definitely make a discrete connection between my SCADA application and my Historian, because it is a much more efficient connection. I would not try to connect powerBI to UNS directly, unless I had a really good reason to do so. I would pull a inventory table and publish it to UNS as a huge array, if I just needed the information as context for something. It's not super hard to filter or query that array for user applications. I would make a discrete connection to the same DB (or API) if I needed to do ad-hoc relational queries to multiple tables, but I would probably publish the result into the right place in the UNS as well, if that is what the architecture requires. UNS shouldn't be thought of as the ONLY connection you ever make between systems, but it is the single source of current state and events, and this can mean that a consuming application (could be cloud or whatever), will put this data into it's own database. It might be duplicating something living elsewhere, but if it makes sense, I see no problem in doing this. The events of a stop on the machine, will both live in the historian or alarm record, as well as in the MES stop reason table. I really don't think one should overthink this. Relax and do whatever makes sense and you think will make your life easier in the long run. Don't impose strict rules, keep an enablement mindset, just do it and cross your fingers it doesn't burn too much down the road. Next time you will know better what to do.

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content: The earlier you normalise your data the better/easier/less effort. Ideally you can already define what the data must look like that the machines send via OPC UA information models or some other form of schema (which of course might not be possible if you can't influence what the machines send). By introducing unit conventions, time format conventions, naming conventions, etc. as part of the machine interface definition, you can reduce you effort on the data analytics side considerably.  Even if you can't change the machine interface, you can do a good amount of normalisation on an edge of network node that gets the data from the machine.

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content: Another worst practise is that people are still trying to process all the data via ETL to press it some form of global database schema. The problem is that there is no globally optimal schema. Instead companies are ending up with a database schema that actually does not work well for anyone (and is usually very slow). Instead people should provide optimised views for different users / needs and only transform what they actually need. When you do real-time processing, it also helps if you publish cleaned, normalized (and maybe extended) data / business objects back to a Kafka so other streams can work with your results.

Author: rickbullotta
Content: Technically what we were using was a combo of Neo4J + Lucene (for the non-time series indexing), so there was a bit of extra overhead behind the scenes.  What's cool though is that these were fully ACID compliant transactions so we could design for (nearly) zero data loss.   Realize that our primary use case was not as a multi-tenant cloud time series store - rather, as an edge data store or single tenant data store.  We had a somewhat crude but effective scale-out model where different "classes" of things could store to different time series storage (and you could even mix and match, where some stored to Cassandra, some to Postgres, some to Neo4J, some to InfluxDB, etc).  It was a pluggable provider architecture for time series data, document data, textual data, and structured/tabular data.  Each could use a different type of DB as needed.

Author: rickbullotta
Content: Ah.  I see what the mixup is - you're talking about Azure IoT *Edge*, not *Hub*.  The MQTT broker in IoT Edge is indeed a generic enough one (unlike the one in IoT Hub) that you could use it for an *edge* UNS, but you'd need a different broker in the cloud to federate multiple IoT Edge(s) together.  The one in IoT Hub is not suitable for that use case.  Azure Digital Twins is a good option as the federation point, because it not only allows you to create a namespace and model of the entities/devices/assets/systems/machines you deal with, but it also allows you to flexibly define the relationship(s) between them.  Something that a generic MQTT broker cannot do easily or in a way that can be navigated.

Author: jon.forbord
Content: Neither Ignition, nor Highbyte or any of the usual suspects in this discord “are” a Unified Namespace, in that sense neither is Azure IoT edge. Unified namespace is an architecture, the structure and the events of the business. It can live in many places, and take on many forms. Generally you need some software to bridge the gap between the UNS and nodes that don’t support (MQTT) natively, and to build and maintain the namespace. This is where Highbyte or Ignition or I guess IoT edge comes in. This is sometimes referred to as a Data Hub or an IIoT platform. What makes or brakes a solutions ability to serve as the gatekeeper of a UNS is how open architecture it is. Most solutions makes it easy to get data into the solution, but then getting data back out of it, is a major pain.

Author: mparris
Content:
Likely the simplest definition of UNS I can come up with is:

UNS is the infrastructure to allow any employee or application consume the data they care about from any other employee or application within an Enterprise.



Any IIoT platform, historian, or data lake claiming to be or being considered as "the UNS" should be evaluated against this definition. And they are very likely wrong in their claims.

You'll find that one platform can't implement the UNS in its own; in reality, UNS is a platform of platforms.

The word "unified" conveys a central, common, or single infrastructure. Ethernet, TCP/IP, MQTT, SparkplugB, Kafka, DB, HTTPS, etc all play a role.

The word "namespace" conveys the need to organize data in a way that consumers can understand.  ISA 95 can be one way to organize it. I'm sure each company has their own way to organize the data.

The UNS concept isn't revolutionary in its own; anyone working on a computer in a company with many different applications has wondered (even if secretly) what it would need like if all the data would be available through a single interface and organized in a way that was easy to find and consume.

Instead, the revolutionary part of UNS is actually building one, and then enjoying the efficiencies brought to employees using it.

Author: rickbullotta
Content:
A few thoughts on flaws/challenges with the current approaches to a UNS:

- If the external system does not support event-driven or change-driven communications (such as an MES or ERP system), then polling that data with a query or API call and pushing that to the UNS can and will often be out of date.  For this reason, I propose solving this by exposing a "method" or "service" as a node/topic in the UNS so that it provides an invocation path for that service.  There still may be valid cases to expose a "cached" version of course.

- Sparkplug B is fine for shipping data back and forth in some cases, but mostly awful for the application level UNS.  We've gotta make this mapping easier.  Also, node/device constructs do not often map well to the semantic models in the UNS that we want to use to expose data and events.  Let's solve this universally.

- Data formats are not really normalized or standardized.  A sensor value might be exposed as a floating point number, an integer, a string, or a JSON object.  We should recommend a specific format for data to ensure interoperability.  This extends to complex data, such as the list of orders for plant area "A", as an example.  This is an area where some of SpB can be repurposed.  And of course, this needs topic metadata to help interpret the data type and other important aspects of the topic.

- As many of us know, the UNS is great for "current state" and events, but not great for accessing the historical exhaust that the UNS can generate.  We can come up with patterns and best practices for exposing historical data through a UNS (somewhat related to the first bullet above)

- Two giant flaws of using MQTT for the UNS are that topics are not queryable and that topics cannot have metadata attached to them.  SpB tries to handle these, but falls short IMO.  This will require functionality that goes beyond MQTT brokers as we know them today, but is essential.

Let's discuss.

Author: mkashwin
Content: In my mental model, the UNS needs to have the following capabilities 1. Ability to be event driven i.e. loosely coupled. 2. Merge / Consolidate messages on a topic 3. Historize the messages. Based on the various discussions here I  build this using #emq-x #timescaledb #python #K8s and #node4J ..  If Node4j has retained its support for historization that would have been a simpler setup. .   @RickBullotta  This approach I think should address most of the points you raised about the UNS except the primary one of publishing MQTT messages for systems which do not have this support, specially the IT behemoth systems like ERP, CRM etc. IMHO most of the systems are slowly beginning to support it e.g. SAP started support for an API to implement MQTT client. I need to check what we have on the CRM side but 3rd party solutions like Striim exist to seamlessly transfer data from CRM like Salesforce over MQTT.. Gradually the UNS will need to transform to be the source of truth of the organization and that transformation (like any) is not easy,

It's a good point that you raise. We use Quickbooks for financials, and Harvest for Timesheets and project status tracking, and these two have native integration between them so no need to build custom workflow.
If I was to try and build workflow integration, a UNS is not the right model for doing it. You have to keep in mind that a UNS is just Visibility of the current state of things. Workflow could be an app that subscribed to the current state of things to trigger a process, but workflow is task management, and that involves a bunch of concepts over and above visibility of things. Task Management really needs a queue, not just a topic.

Author: geoffnunan

Absolutely, common technology is a great approach. 
We are really taking about tge orchestration of actions in response to an event. Those actions may fire new events which go back to the UNS.
Consider for a moment a workflow that triggers two action in two different application in parrallel. Now consider one of those applications fails during the execution and never fires the resulting event.
Two questions arrise. 1-is the other action still valid, or does it need to be reversed? 
2- how do a re-try the failed event?

It may not be a popular opinion in this discord, but MQTT is not a good protocol for managing transactions across applications.

Author: geoffnunan
Content:
It's more than just an ack. There's a bunch of functionality that you have with message queues that is there to handle all the edge cases. Acks is one part, queues are another, retries are another. I'm not saying that MQTT does not have it's place, I'm just saying that MQTT's place is in publishing the current state of something. That's a different use-case to a work-queue.
It boils down to this:
- Events should be published using PubSub when they occur.
- If you're using the Orchestration pattern, your Orchestration service can subscribe to these events and manage the subsequent requests to other services.
- If your workflow runs across applications or networks there are a ton of failure scenarios to consider. A reliable messaging service provides functionality that an MQTT broker does not have which helps manage these failure scenarios.
- Your UNS (If you take that to mean your MQTT Broker) is not queryable other than with very restrictive wildcard filters, and only contains the current state of stuff unless you're doing something very special with topic naming. So your UNS data needs to go into a database, which will need to be exposed through an API if you want to access it.

We need to start to think about the UNS as much more than just a namespace in an MQTT broker if we ever want to consider use-cases outside of HMI and SCADA.

Author: akoscs
Content: This! Exactly! Sensor info and similar is very “pub-sub”-able. There are always some request reply type queries in a system which do not really fit a pub-sub type mechanism. You mentioned recipies, but there are a lot of other ones! Depending on how you structure you namespace you can do something like each product code is a topic and it has a sub-topic for its recipie, but then you boot up a new machine and need the recipie. You either configure your broker to retain that recipie for that topic (where you will eventually be keeping all your recipies in the broker memory) or you need a trigger to request that recipie to be published after your new machine (client) subscribed. This kind of query is just not well suited for pub sub type system. What you could do is have a recipie-request topic where anyone can request recipies. Now the trick is to provide a new UUID with the request along with an identifier which identifies the recipie, and have the client issueing the request subscribe the a topic with a topic name that UUID. The recipie publisher gets the request and publishes to that new UUID topic. This way, you can request something over a broker (not knowing whonpublishes the recipie) and can get a reply  in a topic to which only the client subscribes to.  Only that interested party gets the recipie and the while topic will never be used again. The topic can be abandoned right after the exchange.

Author: petersorowka
Content:
my 2 cents here: I think one very important distinction to make is if your product really acts as a data publisher (i.e. MQTT client) or as a data source that can be queried (i.e. OPC UA Server).

When you are a data source to be queried
=============================
you can develop your product mostly neglecting the context environment of your customer because you essentially don't care about which IT system will query the data. you can provide data in a structure that makes most sense from the perspective of your asset and leave it to the surrounding systems to define which data to read, write, subscribe and in which sampling intervals. You can (and should) implement a reasonable and configurable authentication system that clients will connect to in order to maintain a good security level. Let data come out of the assets mostly ready (without requiring additional software to be installed somewhere) and don't make too many assumptions about the use case the customer has (because they'll eventually be creative anyway).

When you are an active publisher
=======================
you will need to make many assumptions about the specific customers environment and these assumptions will with high likeliness not match all customers. customers are creative when it comes to:
- data models and semantics
- topic structures
- client authentication schemes

Your client needs to be extremely configurable (at least topics, sampling intervals, which signals to publish, what to subscribe to) and very likely needs to implement different authentication mechanisms (password, client certificates and very important an automatable certificate rotation scheme) in order to be implementable into enterprise factory environments.

When you ask what's the biggest thing OEMs miss, my answer is: they miss to plan with the customers IT security and policy agenda

Author: mparris
Content:
You're getting at one of my main complaints of today's systems...

To integrate a new sensor on the plant floor, how many network devices, gateway devices,  or applications must now be touched to integrate that new sensor?

In reality, the answer will likely be all applications will need to be modified in some way because the system may not know the ultimate purpose of the new sensor.

So given that, the question becomes: to what degree must everything be modified to make use of a new sensor? 

1) Do I have to enable network infrastructure to get the data?

2) Do I have to connect my application to some endpoint to access the data?

3) Do I have to load a special decoder to understand the data?

4) Do I have to manually parse the information to map to whatever native information model of the application?

5) And finally, do I have to tell the application what to do with the new information?


If we can achieve just needing to do #5 when something is added, then we are cooking with gas. Even in some limited use cases, #5 can be automated as well.

Author: rickbullotta
Content:
Core MQTT issues:
 
- Decision to use 4 bits for message type. Short sighted and now a major limitation
- Multi-publish is essential (publish more than one topic in a single message)
- Topics should have durable metadata (could be passed as headers in publish or as its own message type)
- Payloads should have a data type (mime type) to enable parsing/processing by subscribers or intermediaries
- Topic binding should be a built-in broker feature (like a symlink) - topic aliases are not this
- The lack of a capability to query topics is a huge flaw/gap. Ideally these queries should be able to include metadata filters as well
- MQTT's subscription patterns are hopeless limiting. They should support richer match expressions and also metadata filters
- MQTT should officially support a REST binding for request/response query/publish/read/subscribe/unsubscribe
- Handling of large payloads (e.g. file uploads, video content, firmware/software updates, method responses) needs a lot of work to improve reliability
- Handling of RPC/method invocations remains an awful hack. This MUST be addressed.

Author: rickbullotta
Content:
Core Sparkplug issues:
 
- The rigid Node/Device format does not fit real world models. Do away with one of them and allow more flexible topic hiearchies.
- The handling of *BIRTH messages and the intermingling of data and metadata in them is a poor design
- The process for requesting *BIRTH messages is terribly inefficient. Metadata should be retained, not requested each time by each client.
- There should be *METADATA messages to deal with metadata
- The opaque/multi-value nature of *DATA messages makes it impossible for client(s) to subscribe to individual metrics. Huge issue.
- The "primary client" stuff is unnecessary and should be removed
- Any device commands/methods should be fully declared (inputs and outputs fully typed)
- Naming of metrics/commands needs to be locked down to a more restricted character set
- Add a few more top level data types (Location, BLOB (w/mime type),
- Support other encodings besides Protobuf (e.g. plain JSON, zipped JSON, BSON, etc.)
- Millisecond resolution for timestamps is inadequate for modern systems where accurate event sequence is critical (e.g. power grid)

- Do you want to transfer large files via MQTT or just provide a standard way of interacting with file storage solutions incl. authentication so a client can easily download files via HTTPS (essentially by adding a best practice to the standard)?
- Do you have any concrete suggestion how RPC should look like? My first thought is that I don’t want to marry RPC functionality with MQTT as a lean messaging standard. RPC tends to make things a lot more complex. When I use MQTT I actually want to use messaging.

- Do you have some examples when you needed publishing to multiple topics with a single publish?

Author: dep05d
Content: I just want to step in amongst the sparkplug hate and show it some love, even though I share many of the frustrations with it, and would love to see all the described enhancements. A large segment of users here are coming from the SCADA world and are using Ignition. In that context, using sparkplug for large distributed systems has been a far better experience than using OPC or the Gateway Network.  Automatic discovery, edge driven, network resilient, lightweight, etc have made scaling up so much easier than manually maintaining point to point integrations like we have in the past. As Marc suggested, we generally relegate sparkplug to sharing tags in a publish subscribe manner, and use a simple subscriber to "flatten out" sparkplug metrics to open up our processing to the cloud streaming and analytics world.  We also selected a message broker with multi-protocol functionality beyond core MQTT to address some, but not all, of the other issues listed.  I just worry that most industrial software will remain hot garbage and 10 years behind the rest of the software world. Sparkplug, on the other hand, is IMHO the best/only first attempt towards a standard next generation pub/sub architecture for industry with any adoption or momentum, and I hate to outright discourage newcomers from pursuing sparkplug if it fits their use case because it's not perfect....especially with all these great minds collaborating on improved future iterations of it 😎

Author: akoscs
Content: Based on roles and-or atributes and/or claims.  When you enroll something to the system it has to identify itself and it gets a list of claims (i.e. What does it have access to). “Gets” a list of claims is tricky and the granularity has to be  matched with the application. I.e has readd access to all, has read access to all temperatures, has read access to the temp in room1. Security policiea tell you to make it as resteictes as possible. The granularity can be a topic mask (or more topic masks). Allow subscribe or allow publish for a list of topic masks. So you are whitelisting topics as access control. But the broker does not need to do this. It only must be able to verify the claims of the client based on a jwt token (or similar). If historical data is in a db and the db structre reflects somehow the topic structure then it can work, but i doubt that dbs let you set access control this granular (maybe only firestore) so you need a different service getting the queries checking the query against the claims and executing or denying the query. (I do not know how access control in GraphQL works, but that could be a start)

Author: jermuk
Content:
The correct IT terms are "event-driven architecture" (EDA), which uses "message broker" with "Apache Kafka" being a very popular one. 

Data warehouse is something where data is stored permanently for analytics purposes or for batch processing (e.g., providing movie recommendations in Netflix). 

EDA in comparison is used to process  incoming banking transactions, checking them for fraud in real-time, and executing the necessary steps to do actually transfer the money. 

Both types (warehouse and EDA) are often used together. EDA for real-time stream processing and warehouse for historical batch processing

Hope that is helpful. Might not be 100 percent correct, but provides a good entrypoint

Content:
So I went down this rabbit hole of EDA. I particularly liked this talk on EDA. It made a lot of sense to me, classifying EDA into categories of patterns. Event Notification, Event sourcing, Event-carried state transfer, command query responsibility segregation. Event notification pattern assumes the consumer of the event will query for the state, while state transfer includes the state change in the event and each consumer keeps a copy of the state within itself, and event sourcing requires the state to be deterministically derivable from the event log.

Author: mparris
Content:
My best advise with Sparkplug is to not use NodeId or DeviceId as parts of your ISA95 hierarchy...I think you'll get into trouble. Just use deviceID (name is a device) and nodeID as the name of the publisher.

In the Sparkplug ecosystem, the first principle is a node is the thing that actually publishes Sparkplug packets. You should not have the same nodeID shared between two things publishing that are in the same groupID. The primary reason is that the node must issue a birth certificate of its own to advertise what data it has available. There is a strong chance that two nodes don't share the same data structures. 

Consider the case where two nodes share the same nodeID , When nodeA publishes it's birth certificate and a client consumes it, then nodeB publishes data that doesn't match the structure of nodeA, the client will detect that and issue a command to rebirth to "nodeID". Since these two nodes share the same ID, they will both receive that command and both publish their birth certificates. The client will get both, and the second to be published will likely overwrite the first. (Undetermined which will win). Then when the client receives data from a node that doesn't match the structure of the other, it will issue a Rebirth command. Lather, rinse, repeat.

If it's working for you, I think the two nodes share the same data structure (maybe from the same vendor?) or they don't have any data structure at the node level. It's not by design that it's working correctly, but your particular configuration is just lucky to work that way. If you try to add a device from a different vendor using the same strategy (same nodeID but different deviceID), you'll have some fun trying to troubleshoot why the system suddenly broke. 😁

Content: I'm curious about this as well. In Simple IoT (still in the experimental phase), I've chosen to not represent structure in the message broker topics, but rather a graph of nodes (specifically a directed acyclic graph). One problem I ran into early on is that I need entities (like users) to live in multiple places in the graph, which does not work very well in a simple hierarchy. An application for this may be that a user needs to have access to several sites. So in this case, the message bus topics do not represent structure, but rather an API. In the node graph, I do use a concept of upstream/downstream instances where the downstream (edge) graph is a subset of the upstream (cloud) graph.

Content:
thanks for the "Using MQTT and UNS architectures at Enterprise level" video link -- watched both part1/2 -- very helpful. There seems to be two primary challenges brought up during the discussion:

2) challenge of developing a topic hierarchy that meets all needs. In SimpleIoT this problem is solved by storing granular nodes in a graph where the nodes can be aliased at multiple locations in the graph. Then the structure can change dynamically as the needs change. Data can also be aliased to any location where it is needed. This is a simple idea, but a challenge to implement and there are complexities such as AuthN.

Content: Have you checked out Solace PubSub+? Beyond MQTT, the AMQP/Webhook/JMS/Solace Messaging API's allow for more reliable guaranteed processing of queued data along the lines of RabbitMQ.  We mix and match these protocols with common namespace definitions to allow local factory business and SCADA systems to participate in a pub/sub architecture without managing a Kafka cluster, Kafka connect, and MQTT broker at each and every site.  There is also a REST microgateway mode that allows for events to be generated from existing synchronous web service integrations that pass through the broker proxy. Content:
nice, good to hear that you do not have to worry about that difficult database anymore 😄

I have heard now quite often the topic of "do not put too much stress on the hardware", "we have to think about the bandwith", etc. and mostly it is coming from old-school OT people. i really did not experience any limitations yet using MQTT or Kafka in terms of bandwith or anything like that. 

lets do a very basic calculation: if you have a one gigabit network cable (e.g., cat 7), then you should be able to push through at least 200 mb/s. assuming you have one 32bit integer + 32bit timestamp it would allow you to send that message 26 million times per second. 200mb/s is nothing for current SSDs, so a single disk / node kafka instance wil lalso not be a bottleneck.

of course there are bottlenecks along the entire way and some tuning (e.g., batching some messages), but in general you can assume that you can send all data through a UNS.

Author: dep05d
Content: Not just setup and config, also support and potential failure points, upgrades, patches etc. I agree Kafka is the de facto standard for stream processing and for analytics/AI use cases it is great. I do think there are some limitations as a messaging backbone (coarse topic names, in-order processing by partition only, heavy clients).  For background, we are end users that exist in an "IT within OT" group and have around a dozen people supporting over 100 Ignition gateways, numerous SQL db's, opc servers, cloud assets etc.  We also integrate with LIMS, MES, and other business apps.  We've found great value building out all of these systems over the last decade, but are simply surpassing the reasonable limit of scale with legacy integration methods. Thus our digital strategy regarding IIOT/UNS is to simplify integration and information sharing amongst industrial assets, while accelerating our ability to execute and scale new solutions. This includes live/retained MQTT tags but also the type of guaranteed messaging discussed earlier in the thread that MQTT isn't really fit for.  If our IIOT strategy doesn't enable local nodes to communicate with each other the same way cloud-native nodes do, we risk falling into a trap of the digital thread and maintaining redundant integrations. That's where Solace gave us the most robust distributed messaging features in the smallest footprint.  As our Kubernetes experiences grows, the number of microservice nodes start to dwarf infrastructure nodes, and business use cases evolve, perhaps localized Kafka will make sense, but for now it seems to be the best path forward for us. I will continue to follow your UMH learning content to help decide how and when 😎

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
@Jon Forbord is right.  Those companion specs attempt to "boil the ocean".  It should be apparent these are basically unusable for anyone who has ever been responsible for industrial automation technology in the real world.  It's like these were conceived under the assumption that machines and factories have been explicitly designed around these standards.  This might work in a strict "top-down" contract manufacturing ecosystem (e.g., Apple, Nike).  But even then, it's still probably lower cost to define "what" suppliers deliver rather than "how".

I recently met with the VDMA.  They're responsible for building and maintaining many of these models (e.g., UA for Machinery).  When asked about reference implementations for popular solutions on the market, they were confused.  I brought up a hypothetical:  Suppose we were to focus on market adoption for the 'UA for Machine Tools' model.  Let's implement a server for the top 5 machine tool builders.  Let's implement a client for a few of the top SCADA solutions.  Let's implement a open source dashboard in AWS and Azure to consume it.

4 in 5 individuals present had never heard of Ignition or even Wonderware, Iconics, WinCC.  They knew of big names like Siemens, SAP, Rockwell.  But, they weren't really knowledgeable about the product portfolios and what manufacturers use.  Additionally, regarding the UMATI initiative, none of them had any idea that most of their members had no real-world implementations.  They were like literally surprised.  It was particularly comical discussing one of the members, a machine tool builder, I met with on data acquisition issues not even two hours earlier.  If a machine builder's head of controls for an entire continent can't access registers over a native protocol, why would VDMA or anyone else be able to for an information model?

It's baffling to me how an organization can proudly put member logos on a wall while said members are actively undermining said organization's mission.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
Anyways, regarding SAP, this is tricky because the model will vary drastically based on your operation and implementation.  I find that ERP and MES will be governed more by the native interfaces and structure of your org.  For example, if your MES is a module in an ERP, you may not need to model as much about Work Orders.

Looking at your list, it looks like your focus is on CMMS.  I must commend you on having all those Asset BOM defined for spares and supplies.  Most orgs struggle to get that right in one node.  They don't even get to all nodes.  Out of curiosity, what is application node is consuming the inventory info?  Is it for purchasing?  If it were for BI or an Ignition screen, I'd probably opt to simply query the CMMS' database.  You could perhaps "feed" a stored procedure parameters (e.g., Asset ID, Line) to retrieve MRO inventory based on the user's role or interest (e.g., asset, line).

You could create some sort of CMMS structure under assets.  In it, there could be a structure for critical spares and inventory on hand.  Along side it, a structure for the recent maintenance activity.  I really like this maintenance activity use case for HMIs and dashboards.

Regarding PLC, I would consider a structure for availability/utilization, alarms and telemetry.  The telemetry can be broken down by sub systems (e.g., hydraulics, motion, lubrication, coolant) and then the component within (e.g., drive, motor, filter, tank).

Here's a paper I quite like on UDT and tag naming conventions.  If PLC programmers could follow this, we probably wouldn't have so many discussions about UNS, Asset Frames, Information Models, etc.  It's one thing to map, it's another to map garbage.
https://www.optimizedtechnicalsolutions.com/ReferenceDocuments/Naming%20Conventions%20and%20Data%20Structures%20for%20Industrial%20PLCs.pdf

Content: As in a - state of the "union"? What I'd like to see isn't another article on OPC UA. I'd like to see a demo-video, less than 15 minutes, that demonstrates why OPC UA and why I should care, the TRUE power of OPC UA and the information models superiority. I think OPC UA DA is great, and in combination with MQTT and sparkplug B, it's awesome. Author: dep05d
Content: The UMH architecture requires Kafka for messaging. Regarding the open source discussion, while a commercial product with it's own underlying binary protocol, Solace supports multiple open protocols (MQTT, REST, JMS, AMQP).  While there are also proprietary features, they are primarily there to save you from having to build, manage, and orchestrate those protocol and broker integrations yourself. Effectively, it allows for the flexible topic structure and routing we all like in MQTT, with support for more robust message exchange patterns across additional protocols. You are always free to build that out yourself if needing to change brokers. Our goal was a lean footprint at each factory to enable local event driven integrations, MQTT/Sparkplug for our ICS, and automatic subscription bridging across all brokers at sites and cloud, so a single broker solution was very appealing. But really, anytime you run Kafka or MQTT other than from scratch (Confluent, HiveMQ, EMQ etc), you are going to incur some vendor lock the instant you use any feature beyond the core spec. Not a huge deal, IMHO, just be mindful of not getting stuck. In order to avoid vendor lock completely, though, there may be other tradeoffs in maintenance and support of all those clusters and supporting services at each site.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
Most of the time, ERPs are going to have HTTP-based web services.  UNS will function as a client to consume these web services.  These will web services will have different APIs for retrieving and updating different records (e.g., Get Parts List, Get BOMs by Part, Add/Move Inventory).

First step is to figure out what use cases you'll be initially addressing.  This will dictate what data will be in and routed through the UNS.  Approach this holistically.  It will evolve over time.  Find some sort reusable structure to grow into.

This first step is particularly important because saying "we need everything" isn't really viable tactic.  It's not that an IT shouldn't be able to give you everything.  The issue is that it's a misunderstanding of how ERP systems work.  Data moves in and out of ERPs the following ways:  UIs, APIs, or database connectivity.  The database connectivity is generally only appropriate for mass updates for implementation work or for reporting.  It's not really advisable for transactions as it can circumvent business logic enforced in the application layers.  So, you're going to use APIs.  There isn't really one API for everything, but many.  They're typically conceived by copying or reusing code associated with a particular screen or action in the UI.  This code usually calls up procedure in the database to retrieve records.

I mention this because many APIs in ERPs are not necessarily intent-based.  They're usually derived from some functionality in the UI that users desired to automate.  This functionality might call up a sequence of APIs.  As a result, it can appear unintuitive.

The next step is to find someone fluent with the ERP's APIs.  They should be capable of replicating what's in the UIs.  A really practical approach is to use a API testing tool such as Postman or SOAP UI.  This individual should demonstrate retrieving and updating records for specific use cases.  The DataOps or IIoT platform would later replace this testing tool.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
_
Summary:

1)  Find out what it takes to get data in and out of the ERP.  Most of the time, it will be web services.

2)  Determine what data you plan to work with.

3)  Find someone who can demonstrate #1 with data from #2 using an API test tool or console app.  Validate this work.

4)  Transfer the results from #3 to an DataOps or IIoT platform to facilitate publishing and subscribing to the UNS.

Author: rehenley
Content: @akos as I see it - the UNS is a group of different namespaces brought together at an enterprise level.  There are edge namespaces, maybe even area namespaces, site namespaces but the top tier of the namespace hierarchy is the Unified namespace - within which top level data can be produced or consumed by any node in the hierarchy.   I believe you are thinking there is a single over reaching name space that holds everything or that there are multiples that hold the same data / information, that is not the case.   All information in an edge namespace doesn’t also reside in a UNS.  The data structure remains consistent throughout the various namespaces but the data itself is refined, contextualized, analyzed, etc. up thru the hierarchy.  I think of it as a file structure that doesn’t reside in a single location.  The data and or analytics used to create the data that resides in namespace 3C does NOT also necessarily reside in that 3C namespace. When I think of it as a file structure of addresses and data points it makes more sense to me.

“Unified Namespace -  [ ˈyü-nə-ˌfīd ˈnām-spās ] 1. A term coined by Walker D. Reynolds a thought leader in the fourth industrial revolution. Derived from the words unified and namespace. Unified - brought together as one, Namespace - a space of names,, i.e. the set of names, often referred to in programming as the set of signs (names) used to identify and refer to objects. Business applications in the third industrial revolution would have a namespace specific the the business application and only accessible to other business applications through the use of often expensive or proprietary APIs. The unified namespace is the architectural concept of bringing together all the application specific namespaces (local namespace) into ONE «Unified Namespace».

Author: zeratall
Content:
Question for those that have experience with UNS implementations. I really like and understand the use case behind a UNS, having a central data structure that all your tools integrates with really helps with scalability. However one thing I have been struggling with is the following: By creating and implementing a UNS in your architecture, you creating tight couplings between the UNS and the Integrated Tools. In Microservice Architecture most approaches try to turn tight couplings into loose couplings, they do this by reducing the number of shared databases between services, and when a service needs data it always calls out the service that owns that data. Similar to a 3.0 approach. In the Microservice Architecture world, that is the standard approach (aka not a shared data/UNS approach). Architecture is always about weighing the pros/cons and finding a solution that meets the requirements, so I could see arguments for both approaches.

My question, for those that have implemented UNS, do you have any lessons learned or ran into any issues due to tight coupling?

Author: thunt.career
Content:
I am not your target audience to answer this question as I'm also pretty new to this. I'm going to try to answer as it may help me understand further and I have struggled with a similar mindset as I think you have. 

The UNS isn't a centralized data store. It's not a database schema where all the applications are reading different rows and values. It is the common namespace (data model using ISA 95 enterprise-site-area-line-cell) built on top an event driven architecture. The event driven architecture comes from the pub/sub pattern. With the pub/sub pattern, the data is consumed as it is produced by whoever needs that data. Now a data store can be added on as a component consuming data from the produces as a system of record or other purpose but the UNS isn't itself that data store. 

I find myself falling back into the idea of data persistence and having all the data stored in some location that everything is accessing which is why I'm answering your question. That mental visual is easier for me to understand than data in motion. That is not what event driven architecture / UNS is about. 

An example might be that a new sales order has been entered into the ERP system. The ERP system does some workflow on the order and at the end publishes certain data on the Enterprise/ERP/SalesOrders topic. The MES system consumes from that topic and creates its own WorkOrder with production details in its system. MES might publish data to topics related to this. A scheduler (human or automated) then assigns that WorkOrder to be manufactured in a given production cell. The MES publishes that to Enterprise/Site/Area/Line/Cell topics with data such as WorkOrder number and recipe info and other. The SCADA/HMI might then consume that data and save it locally in tags (SQLTags in Ignition for example). This is then used by the operator or PLC at the machine to start production and build whatever widget.

Author: hutcheb
Content:
Having persistence within the UNS brings its own challenges. A lot of the clients in a typical SCADA/MES system only require real-time data, they would then have to confirm that the data they have is the latest and if not, consume until they reach the latest. Not a major issue, but if most of the clients don't need it, it just adds a layer of complexity.

There are other brokers that do have data persistence, Kafka would be my go to example. It has data persistence and you can integrate a schema registry into it.  It also has the most amount of infrastructure to support querying that data via KSQL. 

I would agree having the schema registry in most cases would be ideal to enforce the data structure, with the MQTT brokers though this is probably filed by relying on something like the SparkPlug B standard. 

Querying within a real time streaming platform is generally going to hard, they aren't great at storing historical data in an easily accessible format. This is where adding an external historical store comes in. You'd firstly have to identify what you want to store in it, historical topic data or your topic structure (what topics you have). Using a timeseries database for historical data is probably your best bet, and if you need, using a graph database for your topic structure makes sense.

MQTT, I believe gets used for it's simplicity (and comparability with constrained devices) adding these features is great, if you need them.

Author: rickbullotta
Content: "Standards", when most of your legacy stuff doesn't support it, and much of the best-of-breed stuff doesn't, can actually cost you MORE money and time.  Let's imagine you need to integrate systems X, Y, and Z.  Z supports the cool new MQOPC standard.  X and Y do not.  And let's say you need to integrate X to Y.  If you insist on using the "standard", you'll need to write two custom converters - one for X and one for Y (to and from the "standard").  If you do point-to-point interfaces you can get by with just one.  I saw this often with ISA95/B2MML.  Despite all the hoopla during the project spec and bid stage around standards, when project budgets and schedules got tight, most of that was abandoned.  "In theory" investing in the standards-based interface may someday, possibly, perhaps save you money in the long run, but usually doesn't, unless it's directly supported by the vendors.

Author: rickbullotta
Content: Sharing best practices and open source examples >>> standards almost all of the time.   Stated differently, "standards" don't need to be an approved international standard.  They just need to be a consistent and better way of doing things that might be "standard" just within your company, your industry, and so on.

Author: rickbullotta
Content:
Maybe a different spin makes sense: when you move out-of-process, out-of-box, and onto a network, you add points of failure, and exponentially increasing costs to mitigate those failures.  There's a reason you wouldn't link triple modular redundant PLCs together via a cloud proxy over the internet.  So when I look at some of these "eye chart" diagrams that the cloud vendors slap up there to show how you wire up 25 of their services to accomplish some task, I just shake my head.  Even if each of those services is highly available and reliable, using 25 of them increases your failure surface massively, and you still need to architect/design to deal with cross component failures.  "But we put in a durable queue" isn't an answer.  

If a Tweet doesn't get delivered, or a Hulu stream doesn't start the first try, no big deal.  If a surgical robot is requested to make a thoracic incision and carries it out zero or two times instead of one, that's a really big deal.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
In addition to work orders, I would recommend focusing on products, processes, and resources that produce them.  This should provide enough context to answer practical questions with enough detail (e.g., what is being produced, how/where is it being produced).

The point I was making about ERP APIs was not necessarily a political one for navigating IT turf wars.  This was more focused on the technical nuance and reality of integrating with ERPs.  There usually isn't one magical API that provides everything.  What is exposed and how it is exposed is not always necessarily based on some integration intent.  For example, it might just be some database procedure wrapped as an API.  It may not necessarily do what was configured in the UI that users are accustomed to.  You may have to devise some process or logic to recreate this (e.g., get A and B, use this to get C, and then post to D).  Much of this is due to the mess that ERP architectures can be, but also the variation in configuration across implementations.  There are some ERPs with literally hundreds of configurations for order management.  To assume that there is one clean interface that respects these configurations is not necessarily realistic.  Features often get developed to acquire customers or get through high-stakes implementations -- not seamless integration.  The consequences of this are technical debt.

So, the key here is to be specific.  Instead of asking "We want all the data.", "We're looking to retrieve records from the X module, Y screen, in Z form.  Which is the appropriate API?  Could we validate this together in the test environment?  Does this align with the config in the UI?"

Virtually no ERPs will support report-by-exception.  Generally, you'll be invoking an API from middleware.  You'll need to "pull" from the EPR periodically and employ logic to detect changes.  If there is a service bus involved, the ERP may be able to sophisticatedly "push" events.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
**List of connectors:**
AWS, Azure, Files, GCP, HTTP, Modbus, MQTT, OPC UA, SQL, InfluxDB, OSI PI
https://www.highbyte.com/intelligence-hub-connect.html

**Upgrade / Availability**
In my experience, upgrades require stopping the runtime.  There is a high availability option (i.e., Active/Standby), but I believe the pair must be the same versions.  If downtime is a concern, segmenting the deployment into multiple instances (e.g., by area, by line, by cell) could improve coordinating upgrades with other planned downtime events.

**Latency**
I can't speak to benchmarking.  But I will say HB seems within the norm as one would expect from the underlying protocols it supports.  When I think of OPC UA or MQTT, ignoring infrastructure constraints, 100ms is what I would consider normal for most use cases.  It's worth mentioning that the latest releases have included conditioning (e.g., deadbanding) and historian interfaces.  This can allow for efficient, high-resolution data capture at the edge.  By filtering out the noise, this can help alleviate infrastructure limitations or cost.  Performance is probably best considered in the context of the use case.

**MQTT Message Delivery**
Delivery can be managed with the QoS parameter (i.e., '1' = at least once).

**Container Support**
Can be deployed as a docker image
https://www.highbyte.com/blog/expanded-connectivity-highbyte-intelligence-hub-version-13-is-here

**Grafana**
Not a Grafana guru, but I would probably approach this by having Grafana subscribe to a broker or query a database that HB is publishing data into.  It's worth mentioning that, as of the latest release of HB, there is a native broker that could be connected to.

**Trial Program**
Request a trial here
https://www.highbyte.com/try-and-buy.html

Hopefully this helps.  @Richard Shaw or @kurt.peterson.highbyte can help expand or fill in the blanks.

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content:
The main thing that a UNS has in common with an event driven architecture is that it uses asynchronous messaging and in both cases events are being exchanged. A UNS is different from an event driven architecture or goes beyond it in the following regards, at least in the view of many here:
- A fully event driven architecture (from an academic point of view) would not include a UNS. Through a UNS, you exchange events AND the current state of things and not just events.
- The UNS defines a standardized topic structure that includes information on the locality / where data has been created. You can do that in an event driven architecture but it’s not a must.
- The UNS should always use a "report by exception" model. Other people would even use the term „must“ here.
- A UNS should be lightweight and use an open architecture approach. Not a necessity for an event driven architecture.
- A system based on a UNS should be self-aware meaning that you can easily add new communication participants (services, devices, sensors, PLCs…) and theri data will be directly integrated by the other communication participants.
- UNS always uses Pub/Sub. Also not a necessity for an event driven architecture (but of course it makes sense most of the times).

You can take a book on EDA MSA and apply it to IIoT, but that doesn't make it UNS. I would even go as far, as saying you will have a lot of trouble if you applied typical EDA for MSA-patterns in IIoT/manufacturing/industry. EDA MSA is designed to work in an environment where it's ALL build, nothing off the shelf.  The CLOSEST concept in traditional EDA to a UNS I've come across is a pattern known as event-driven-state-transfer. But if you look into the details of the pattern, there is mostly a conceptual commonality. A UNS is typically implemented with mostly off-the-shelf software, and the occasional build. The domain is completely different. an EDA MSA is an application architecture pattern, not a business architecture. You could also say the UNS is just the enterprise service bus with some variations, and find similarities there as well. but again, the devil really is in the details. And newness really doesn't matter. Agree 100% that looking at other similar work to learn, is always a good idea 🙂

Author: dvy___
Content:
I think the UNS concept is on to something, and people here have shown implementations that are very powerful. But I don't see how it is the full answer and solution for all architectures and industries. Yet is often presented as such.
For some background you can see some theoretical architecture iterations I make in #reference-architectures in the last three weeks.

Some key questions that I don't find a good answer to with the entire architecture built around a UNS, especially based on only an MQTT broker:
1. How do all the applications access the historical data? With MQTT they just have the latest values. But many use cases require queries for both historical timeseries and transaction data. We need all three kinds of data (latest, timeseries and transactions) to be easily accessible and be in the same namespace. Not just the latest.
2. How to handle the reverse data flow. For sure MQTT is powerful when capturing data from the factory floor to higher-level applications. But the drawing has arrows in two directions. For example how to give the 'open valve' command from an HMI or SCADA to the PLC? The recommendation is to pass it over MQTT? It obviously isn't. (or is it?) Also for an MES that needs to pass part of the production order to the PLC for execution. The PLC will subscribe to check for new production orders? Then how does that work? A PLC typically only has room for the current order that needs to be produced. Currently it's the MES or similar system that will make sure that the implementation on the PLC side is as simple as possible.
3. This doesn't apply to batch-based process industries like food, pharma, fine chemicals, ... right? If the answer here is 'yes' then really interested to discuss further.

Author: jon.forbord
Content: Except ERP i believe this architecture is technically possible with off the shelf software and hardware, But it would be a slightly limited selection of the software and hardware and very likely not the best architecture for most companies. I’m not sure I’d go as far as saying its misleading, but I’d agree on perhaps a simplification. I could show you our architecture diagram, but it would be wayyyyyyy to much detail for a blog post for a broad audience.. and these diagrams are from blogs or the likes for broader audiences.

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content:
Ad 1: Either domain driven services (see domain driven design) provide the historic data for their domain through REST APIs or a generic historic data service provides the data through a REST API. In both cases the services would typically store the historic data in a timeseries database if there is a lot of data. For more non-telemetry & operational data, the data would probably be stored in some SQL database. Typically some services will also provide some form of KPIs (including historic data) through higher level APIs. 
Ad 2: “Reverse data flow” is also sent through MQTT topics. You just need to define topics to which the PLCs are subscribed. Or you use Sparkplug that defines a standardized (but in some regards limited) topic structure for you. If your PLCs are limited as you describe them, the MES could send the data after the respective machine has finished the last order. So for example the PLC would publish the event that it has finished an order with “interesting” additional data and then the MES would send the next order. That’s just a very theoretic example to explain how this might work via MQTT. 
Ad 3: Can you elaborate the question a bit? I don’t understand why using MQTT and a UNS would not work in those industries.

Author: dvy___
Content:
1. Indeed so 3 types of data: latest, historic timeseries and non-telemetry/operational data. In the mentioned industries we need all three of them.  Only the latest data could be accessed by MQTT, but the timeseries and operational data need direct access to the systems, indeed for example with REST API's. And with 'Domain Driven Design' you refer to S95? For these industries there's also S88, which is at least as important as S95.
2. Yes I understand how that example might work over MQTT. But does it make sense to switch to MQTT if we're reaching this level of direct coordination between two systems? And as you say: it's theoretic. Who has this working in production?
3. I didn't say that MQTT and a UNS would not work. I don't see how a UNS built ** only around** MQTT would work. The historian probably at least needs to be added inside the UNS. Then we start approaching a good solution, and it's indeed an architecture many of these manufacturers are moving towards. But it's still mainly as a data-reporting platform. Then there's still the MES/Batch applications: where to fit them? S88 is the domain language in these industries, and a correct designed architecture will have S88 applied vertically over these systems. S88 is typically a lot of transactions. So what's the vision there? Recommend to keep a more classical architecture for that part? In that case the MQTT-centric architecture is not really the right representation.

Author: dvy___
Content:
By the way I agree there's need to improve on the architectures and solutions we have in these industries. But there's some other topics that are at least as important if we want to realize this and should be considered alongside the UNS approach:
- Decoupling of the OT hardware and software (See the OPAF initiative pushed by some big manufacturers in these fields: https://www.opengroup.org/forum/open-process-automation-forum) 
- Allowing Test Driven Development at OT-level. (Big part of the manual validation effort in pharma for example is because there's just no (easy) way to perform automated tests.)
- Moving to architectures that allows for devops-like deployment of systems and updates.
- Move towards more practical/lean S88/Batch/MES architectures in these fields.

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content:
1. By Domain Driven Design I was referring to the architecture approach that you design your services around business domains or business topics. It’s about what to put together into a service or a component of a service.

In my view the UNS is only about making the current state / events accessible. It’s not for accessing historic data. For that I would provide separate REST APIs. Just to mention it, often the same service that would provide an event or state through the UNS would also provide a REST API that also makes this current data / state available via HTTPS. 
2. The UNS approach has multiple advantages over doing lots of direct client server connections from reducing configuration overhead or doing report by exception instead of polling to being able to build more dynamic systems that can react on new / changed communication partners. Another big advantage of using a messaging solution is that the PLCs/edge devices connect to the outside so you don’t have to make the PLCs directly accessible on a TCP/IP level. Although, especially in brownfield scenarios it’s common to have extra edge devices in front of the PLCs and the PLCs might not even be connected directly to the production network for security reasons.

By „theoretic“ I only meant the example I gave. We already built such platforms for customers of ours. 
2. yes it often does for the mentioned reasons but also because others can consume these messages and do something with it. For example some other system might consume the OrderCompletedEvent from the example before and do something with it. Also maybe the same event is being consumed by some stream processing that calculates some KPIs for some dashboards and it would also be stored with all the other historic data in some data analytics systems. Of course sometimes it will still make sense to use a synchronous communication for some reason but then you should still publish relevant state changes and events to the UNS.

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content:
3. That depends on how you define a UNS. If your definition of the UNS includes historic data then a messaging protocol like MQTT alone doesn’t make sense. As I said, for me the UNS is about the current state and events.

About the process industry: I think you can’t give some general answer on how to implement a UNS but I don’t see any fundamental problem in using a UNS approach there. You would really have to look at how to solve specific problems. We did use a UNS approach in a project in the process industry but there it was only used for data analytics and production monitoring while we were still involved.

Sounds that MQTT has then just become a recommended technology to implement part of the UNS.
Limiting the UNS to the current state and events will not be enough to cover all applications in all industries.
It needs to at least include the historical data for many use cases.

Author: zeratall
Content: Your last statement is how most UNS are architected. Aka not EVERY interface is going through the UNS. Yes the majority of your EDA and Data are going through the interface but like you said you will still have some point to point interfaces, its a mix between a hub and spoke, and partial mesh. That's why I said UNS is more of a architecture design pattern then anything. Most people think of MQTT as being synonymous with UNS, but that's just because IIoT favors MQTT for being light weight, you could use any event streaming technology/protocol and still implement a UNS design pattern into your architecture if you wanted. a UNS just becomes a great way to break down data silos (allows more access to data without major refactoring or changing existing interfaces, and allows a centeral location in the architecture to visualize and formalize what some of the EDA relationships are to help understand dependencies).

Author: youri.regnaud
Content: In the representation of our architecture we decided to rename the UNS to "Event Hub" to indicate that it is only events,  current states. We name the data persistence « Industrial/IIoT DataHub » for access to the data history. IIoT DataHub is a node to the « Event Hub ». In terms of technologies, the Event Hub is composed of a network of Solace instances that are augmented by Highbyte for the Edge part and SAP Integration Suite for the Cloud/IT part. We want start soon an MVP with LibreMFG for the IIoT DataHub. Libre combines the storage of structured data in a graph database with the storage of time series. All this data is exposed by a single GraphQL API. Thus, it is possible to request or subscribe (with GraphQL subscription) to historical data. MQTT is use for telemetry only. The beauty of Solace is that it exposes several protocols (MQTT, AMQP, REST, …)

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content:
I'm not sure how useful this comparison is. The first thing I stumbled upon is that they seemed to have tested the OpenSource version of EMQX which I think only supports in-memory message persistence (can someone confirm this?) which might explain the message loss they were observing and at the same time make the results worthless if they tested against disk persistence. The second thing I noticed is that they did not seem to use any shared subscriptions which have a significant impact on message throughput. Too bad they didn't publish their test setup / test code on GitHub.

In general, such generic, artificial comparisons can only give a first impression as the performance of each broker can be different from use case to use case depending on your amount of client connections, amount of topics, amount of publishers/subscribers, usage of shared subscriptions etc. Also network optimizations have a further impact. So for larger installations it's advisable to do your own testing.

Disclaimer: I hope I didn't overlook anything, because I just skimmed over the text 🙂

Author: Deleted User
Content:
Hi, I am currently working on a Sparkplug B implementation and run into a question. The sparkplug specification defines, "Host applications" such as SCADA and MES systems. It  describes how these host systems communicate to Edge nodes, but does not specify how hosts could communicate with each other.

My question is about two host systems communicating between them. So, for example, a MES directly communicating to a SCADA system. In which topic should the MES system publish? According to the SPb specification, the “namespace/group_id/message_type/edge_node_id/[device_id]” topic structure is only meant for edge devices.

Author: mparris
Content:
Think of the network as a bubble, and devices or applications are either in the bubble or outside the bubble.

EoN Nodes are in the bubble and typically forward data from devices that are outside the bubble.

Anything can be a Node if it speaks Sparkplug. So applications can communicate by subscribing to the NDATA topics of another application.

The standard had in mind a SCADA application receiving ALL THE DATA from all devices, not well designed for many applications to receive some if the data.

The way things are named in the spec is confusing, until you start looking at it from this narrow perspective.

A graph database would add a couple of layers of complexity:
1. an extra database in the architectures (next to for example the timeseries and MES database)
2. graph-like data structures instead of table-based: more difficult to handle once data needs to be exchanged with other systems. (See our recent discussion in #reference-architectures )
3. unfamiliar type of database for most people

Just quickly scrolling through the use cases of neo4j (https://neo4j.com/case-studies/) people use it to enter known relationships, and then discover hidden ones. For example for transparency, compliance, knowledge, ... . UNS is a tree-graph, which is more simple to manage than a graph where you could add any relation.

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content: Storing the message with high ingest rates isn't really the issue. Especially with batching you can get most timeseries data into pretty much any database. It becomes interesting when you have to do analytics / KPI calculations on top of it. I think being able to filter and aggregate large amounts of data quickly is much more important than the ingest rates. This is the reason why for example a document store / search engine as Elasticsearch works so well for timeseries data even though it hasn't originally been built with timeseries data in mind. It's just extremely good at filtering and aggregating using the internal aggregation functions of Elastic. On the other hand it's not to most efficient data store when it comes to memory requirements 🙂

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content: Also, just because someone puts a "timeseries" label on top of a data store doesn't mean it fits the requirement of being able to do analytics / KPI calculations quickly on a large amount of data. For example Microsoft keeps telling people that Azure Data Explorer is also a timeseries database (because they don't have a proper timeseries database in their Azure portfolio) but it's really a distributed SQL Engine on top of object storage which lets it process a lot of data but just not quickly.

By default, the device will be treated as, 'offline' with 0 state.  We generally set historians up with QOS 2, retained, so on the trend it will just hold the last good value.  Depending on the data point, it may be necessary to show the outage and a -1 will be stored as soon as state switches to 0 or offline.

Author: walker.reynolds
Content:
This is a great point, JP.  Before, IA, it was impossible to put a platform to any kind of test without first making the business case to internal and external stakeholders, then go to the vendor and make your case to them, and then MAYBE you would get a shot at testing out an idea.  FactoryPMI (the original Ignition) wasn't built for anyone other than Steve's Integration team.  By an integrator, for an integrator.  Once other Integrators were exposed to their platform, by chance, then they realized they had an MVP on their hands.  They stuck to their pillars -- cross platform, unlimited, open, short time to value -- rebranded and then made it as easy as possible for the world to test.  Integrators sold for them.  

The simple fact of the matter is -- most platforms are built by software developers, acting on the guidance of business analysts, to build function to a specific market segment.  They generally have no idea what the actual problems are, what the realities are on the plant floor, how manufacturing actually works, how quickly it changes (see CI programs across all of Industry) and are simply not positioned to build a platform that is anything but niche.
