Author: tord4874
Content:
Anyone has any articles or thoughts around SparkplugB UNS, regarding using primary host ID.

We implement the UNS using high availability MQTT-Broker (clustered). So the "traversing" various brokers looking for online primary host is not the issue here.

We are implementing Historian, SCADA, MES as nodes. All of them kind of need to be prime applications:
* Historian needs to sample history
* SCADA needs to trigger alarms
* MES needs to track stuff
* ++

My impressions is when using primary host id, then all other systems will stop receiving data if primary host goes down. And as all systems are equally important i therefore conclude with not using primary host ID as the best solution.

Comments?

Author: mparris
Content:
I agree with your conclusion.

The Primary Host concept is an example of the thinking when designing Sparkplug. It clearly was intended for SCADA, where there would be a single, monolithic application receiving all the data, and if that application was down then all the devices should begin to store their data to then forward when the Primary Host comes back online.

I don't know ief a mechanism for two Primary Hosts, so best to not use that function.  But FYI, if not using it, then the store and forward concept won't be used either.  Maybe this is mitigated for you with the clustered broker, but won't protect from any one application missing out on data if the consuming application goes down.

Another idea is to create a tiered approach, where a single application (like your SCADA) is the primary host, then that application is a Node to another primary host (like historian)

Author: tord4874
Content: The idea about the tiered approach is interesting. I will keep that one in mind 🙂

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: We generally only use primary host for east/west high availability, primarily in SCADA applications where API1167 and similar standards apply.  Tiered (north/south) is the most common mitigation.

Author: donpancoe
Content: Okay. Bit intimidating to think that my newbie question kicked off such an active - but insightful, TBH - thread. There are points to be considered on the "tone" of community interaction that might relate to much larger issues in our country today, but I won't wade into those. I will share, FWIW, my own experience of the OT / IT split. Much of my early controls experience comes from passenger rail, where the OT side were part of the group responsible for delivering passengers to their destination *safely*, but also **on time**. The IT department typically grew out of the finance department, where they were originally called MIS. As tech usage grew outside of the mainframe room, IT became the de facto owner of most office tech, but the OT was different enough that it was largely left alone. Over time, though, the actual tech that both departments were using became almost indistinguishable, leading to turf battles. A theoretical ideal would be one unified department, or at least two *cooperative* departments, that combines the operational sensitivity and new-tech-skepticism (where appropriate) of the OT side with the business goal orientation and new-tech-openness of the IT side.

@Jon Forbord - I do understand what you're saying; however, this a two-part issue from our perspective as well...

It costs a lot of money to maintain a high-quality, secure codebase. It costs even more money to maintain that codebase for a platform-level product. It costs even MORE money when the code base is regulatory compliant. In the current labor market it's a really big number that we need to maintain the current codebase and continue to develop along our roadmap.

"Little guys" generally struggle with value proposition (as you pointed out in your real world example.) What that translates to is a much higher cost of customer acquisition for the vendor that is often coupled with a lower appetite for cost by the prospect (because of the poor understanding of value prop). That's the worst case scenario for an emerging tech product.

"The big guys" generally don't have that same problem. Even if they struggle with value prop in their leadership, they frequently don't have the issues with aversion to license pricing and are happy to run a paid PoC to establish value prop. What this means is that it is more cost effective for the emerging tech vendor to engage the bigger company.

Consequently - a company like Libre will often move in the direction of targeting bigger customers because it takes fewer customers of that size to underwrite the annual cost of the codebase and it often comes with a lower cost of customer acquisition (overhead). That creates a more rapid progression to a cash neutral or profitable company.

It isn't really a "choice" to move in this direction - it is a requirement for financial stability - especially for a platform product.

Author: thunt.career
Content:
A few more UNS questions:
> - Is it accurate to say a node should publish everything and consume only what the node needs for whatever node functions (e.g. HMI control) or dependent usage (e.g. PLC setpoints)? By publish everything I'm assuming the data is well structured/normalized and not constrained by either physical or arbitrary limits.
> - Is it typical to have a "big brother" node that consumes all topics to better manage and visualize the namespace? If not, how is that managed or documented to prevent uncontrolled growth of the namespace/topics? What kind of governance is used to maintain the UNS?
> - Does a proper UNS eliminate the need for a centralized monolith MES solution? It might not cover all the MES functions but I find it is generally a system that performs a lot of the integration between ERP, Warehouse, and Inventory Management systems. If those systems are connected to the UNS, the edge nodes will be reporting material movement, reporting consumptions and handling work order management. There is no need for an master system that integrates and orchestrates to all the edge nodes. Individual MES functions probably exist at a node that interfaces with one of those business systems unless it is open and can speak the protocol of the UNS.

Author: hobbes1069
Content:
My thoughts (in the same order)
- Pretty much, because a node like an edge device could be easily overwhelmed with data. As far as "everything" there's the ideal everything is well formed, but that's usually not reality so products like HighByte help model the "as is" data into something normalized/contextualized and then is republished into the UNS. Now that HB includes an internal broker, it would also give you the opportunity to clean up the data before publishing it to an Enterprise broker.

Author: hobbes1069
Content:
- In some way's "a node is a node", but yes, some are much larger than others. For instance a tiny node may be an IoT device that just publishes sensor readings, but large ones would be Ignition, Canary, HighByte, etc. Typically you would use a historian like Canary to visualize your data, but there seems to be a trend to move this functionality to data lakes / blob storage if they're performant enough. 

Governance is largely at the whim of the architect, but there are best practices, such as a topic naming scheme modeled after ISA 95 (Enterprise/Site/Area/Line/etc.) And then under those main topics, break up your data into organized types of namespaces. Maintaining that structure is key so you have a predictible pattern to your namespace. This is key because at some point you won't be able to subscribe to `#` in MQTT Explorer 🙂

Author: hobbes1069
Content: - There's a lot to unpack in your third point so I'll try to summarize. I would say that the UNS doesn't provide MES functions, but it makes those functions possible and scalable. A good MES will probably a custom MES because it's usually far more effective creating a solution that fits how your business is actually run than trying to fit how your business runs into an off-the-shelf solution. For that reason your MES's should probably live at the Site or Area level, which means you'll have multiple, but that doesn't mean they can't communicate to each other, that's the beauty of integrating into a UNS instead of point-to-point integrations!

Author: jon.forbord
Content: Only thing I’d add is that it is not uncommon to do both at the edge, and sometimes it makes sense to map the raw tags as is to a separate edge-namespace and start collecting this in order to learn and explore the data. Next to this you’ll gradually build the functional namespace for edge as you understand better how to map and model the data. This approach has a couple of benefits. 1. You can start collecting from day 1, 2. You don’t have to have the “perfect” hierarchy or models to get started. You can start with the easy stuff, and hold the hard stuff until you learn more about the data, while “everything” is still available in the UNS. I basically put everything in your list into the raw namespace as collecting literally everything kills the embedded OPC UA servers, so we had to make concessions. The functional namespace consists (currently) of around 20-30% of those tags again. The functional namespace is continuously expanded as we learn more.

Author: jon.forbord
Content: And just to be clear, all edge data modeling is still done at the edge gateway.

Author: dep05d
Content: We wrote a sparkplug discovery service that subscribes all birth messages from all brokers in our mesh, and merges them into a database of all known group/edgenode/deviceID's.  We also have some custom logic to parse out special naming conventions we use for group and edge node.  We also store the last known birth message.  The benefits go beyond querying for discovery purposes; it also provides all the data needed to build a front end to define a mapping layer to associate DDATA/NDATA metrics to a flattened MQTT/REST payload, or vice versa. I was able to build a parent-child virtual asset hierarchy table along with a Node-Red prototype (future python I think) to republish sparkplug messages into the virtual asset namespaces with very little code.  Also, this central repository of sparkplug devices also could serve as a handy way to automate the tag (re)build of your edge nodes during upgrades (let's assume Ignition here - fetch list of devices for a given edge node and rebuild your UDTs).  Another option would be to publish the full list of known assets, when changes are found, to a retained tag in a directory namespace

Author: akoscs
Content:
You are definetly on the right track goal wise! What you describe is a very plug and play approach to adding a production line. This requires that the data models piblished (the UDTs) are compatible with the running system, in your case the scheduler, but for sich a plug and play approach to work you need some kind of capability descripton. I am line 5 I can produce all products with the product code matching xyz-5-abcd. Or the sam thing, but not with product code, but product characteristics. The schedular needs to be able match these to workorders. So the workorders in the backgound need the product codes or product characteristics descriptions which it can match to the line. However the acheduler also needs to check inventory / materials needed and allocate it, but that is more product related then line related. The product might also require specific application programs (i.e. A g code) or recipies or a parameter set that needs to be activated on the line so the line needs to be able to recive these. (And the product specific parts might be also line specific, in other words when line 5 is making product A it has a different paramter set and line 4 making the product might have a different paramter set, if they are not built exactly the same way)

The UNS and the topic structre is just the means to achieve this. This functionality uses the UNS it is not the UNS itself.

Content:
Here's a thought - coming from a data perspective, analytics, ML/AI
- UNS is report by exception, so where do the conditions that these exceptions abide by live? (is it on the edge, on the device/control level, is it a threshold or something?)
- While reporting by exception is good, one of the tenets of analytics is to identify trends (up/down etc.) and identify potential issues before they happen, but if UNS is report by exception, then it will only tell you when something is wrong vs. being an indicator of analysis that something could go wrong, or is going in the wrong direction
- So from an analytics, AI/ML & data analysis perspective I feel the options are:
            * Have a means to persist data over a certain period of time, and have a topic that publishes the "last 10 cycle" aggregate, or something
            * Rely on databases and realtime analytics (potentially windowing of data), to analyze the trends over time

If the 2nd option is a better approach, then it furthers my understanding that the UNS is really designed as a data-broker for non mission critical data - while some sort of data persistence is needed to evaluate how the last 5 minutes look, the last hour, and evaluate the trends there - which COULD update the exceptions by which the UNS reports against?

Sorry if that's a little wordy....but hopefully it came across somewhat coherent

Tag Pacing Period

    The buffer period for outgoing Transmission messages in milliseconds.  The default is 1000ms.  This means when a tag change event is detected 1000ms will elapse before an MQTT message is sent. Author: douga.7429
Content:
The proposed MES system aims to provide a real-time, flexible, and scalable solution for manufacturing environments. It leverages edge PLC devices for data aggregation and MQTT messaging for transmitting data as event streams. This approach allows for dynamic line configurations, preceding and output workcenters, LOT information, and even the production of multiple items simultaneously.

The core components of the system include:

Edge PLC devices: These devices are responsible for aggregating item production and asset utilization data to the minute. The PLC program is designed to handle various scenarios, including dynamic line configurations, preceding and output workcenters, and simultaneous production of multiple items.

MQTT message broker: The aggregated data from PLC devices is transmitted as event streams using an MQTT message broker. This enables real-time data collection and decouples data producers (PLCs) from data consumers (data storage and analytics systems).

Data storage and analytics: The event-sourced data is stored in a data lake or equivalent storage system, which allows for scalable and cost-effective handling of diverse data. A star schema database is created in Power BI or an equivalent BI tool for efficient data analysis. Advanced analytics tools and data science techniques can be applied to gain valuable insights into the production processes.

Author: douga.7429
douga.7429
Content:
The code snippet demonstrates the core concepts of the proposed MES system. It includes the MinuteDataArray structure, which is used to store the aggregated data for each minute of the day. The AggregateData method contains the logic for computing and storing various data points, such as event ID, reason code, state, workcenter information, LOT, produced items, production percentages, and other metrics.

Additionally, the SendDataToMQTTBroker method is responsible for sending the aggregated data to the MQTT message broker. This method iterates through the MinuteDataArray and creates a message payload for each minute's data, which is then sent to the MQTT broker. The MQTT broker, in turn, handles the distribution of the messages to the appropriate data consumers, such as data storage and analytics systems.

In summary, this code snippet showcases the core concepts and functionality of the proposed MES system. It demonstrates how data is aggregated at the edge, using PLC devices, and transmitted as event streams via an MQTT message broker. This approach provides real-time data collection, flexibility in handling dynamic production scenarios, and decouples data producers from data consumers.

Author: asthomas
Content: @Aviator You can use Cogent DataHub in conjunction with Kepware to get SpB support.  Kepware provides the low-level fieldbus conversion to OPC, then DataHub reads that and converts it to SpB.  If you are working with MQTT equipment that only supports JSON, DataHub can convert that JSON data to SpB as well.  It has a built-in JSON parser that converts the JSON message into individual data points and then an SpB implementation that combines the data points into an SpB EoN device.  If your PLC supports OPC directly you may not need Kepware.  It is more processing steps, but that's what protocol conversion needs.

Author: asthomas
Content: In my experience there are a few challenges with passing machine instructions via an asynchronous router like MQTT. 1) The instructions are intended to be transactions, with certainty that they are delivered and that a result has been generated.  You likely need to use multiple topics to implement a handshake so the transmitter knows the machine has received the instructions, that the machine is busy, etc.  Similar to a command/confirm pattern using 2 registers in a PLC.  2) The broker needs to guarantee delivery, and delivery order, of at least the latest values for each topic in the handshake.  MQTT may not be suitable here since it guarantees neither. 3) If the instructions are passed in a single topic then you need an expressive, agreed-upon format. It's not so much a challenge as just a thing you need to do. JSON and XML strings work. 4) If the instructions or parameters arrive as individual topics then you need a slightly different handshake involving filling the individual topics and then sending a "GO" signal.  Topic ordering is crucial here. If this information arrives from OPC, for example, then you cannot rely on ordering, and you have to fall back on timing for the GO signal, which is fragile.  What you want can be done, but it does require some communication design, and preferably a broker that guarantees message order with an eventually-consistent QoS.

Content: I wouldn’t dismiss it so quickly. Ricks point about the shortcomings of SpB is about what could be better, doesn’t mean it’s useless. The question it boils down to me, is do you want autodiscovery of tags, UDTs, metadata etc from the edge? If you use flat mqtt, you need to define a json scheme yourself, you need to define a standard for metadata vs data etc. This is with OTS solutions and SpB pretty much a done deal. We take OPC UA tags and convert them to SpB and use Ignition as the IIoT platform. It has changed my life as an automation engineer. Could the spec be improved to cover a broader range of use-cases, absolutely. But I wouldn’t dismiss it so quickly, it really depends on what the rest of the architecture looks like and the use-cases.

Author: asthomas
Content: That was the original intent of MQTT - every metric in its own topic, retention of most recent value and report by exception only for those metrics you are interested in.  The downside is that relationships are implicit due to hierarchy, the payload format is undefined, there's a lot of wasted bandwidth re-transmitting the topic name, and LWT messages place a big information and configuration load on clients.  Sparkplug was intended to fix some of that, but as you point out, it introduces new problems.  Personally I think Sparkplug's problems are due to the desire to keep the broker uninvolved.  A broker that understands and manages the client connections could selectively synthesize and deliver birth messages only to clients that need them.  It's the blind broadcast cases in Sparkplug that generate the message storms.  The trouble is, if you put smarts into the broker, it is no longer strictly MQTT.

We are currently trying to stitch together a plan for a PoC, which would involve the following:

We would also save the data to our central database and we would provide API access to the CRM data for systems to be integrated later, and only publish the data to the MQTT broker that some system would like to access through this channel. We try to stay agile and build on the proper foundations with every iteration and ultimately replace all the Custom-ERP system's functions and implement the necessary new ones. In Phase 1 we also plan to deploy an Edge Node, with Node-red and start collecting machine data and transforming it into MQTT and Sparkplug B payloads.

Is it OK to write our own code or is there an open-source or cheaper alternative to Ignition to get started with? Our Phase 1 with CRM and fractional ERP integration would be pushed into a production environment and used in their day to day.

Do I miss some key understanding or am I overcomplicating it? 😀 Please shed some light on us.

Content: We are working on an easy solution that does away with the BIRTH dance altogether.  Solved by separating data and metadata, and leveraging MQTT’s retain flag.  Waaaaaay more efficient, plus allows offline development when the devices aren’t connected.

Content: I recall an earlier post you made, talking about splitting the metrics out to one per topic.  Won't that ultimately boil down to a naming convention for topics and a per-tag payload definition?  There's going to be a substantial bandwidth penalty for that. In theory you could drop the idea of separate metadata, though at the cost of even more bandwidth.  Is this something the Sparkplug working group is looking into?

Author: rickbullotta
Content: Yup, but the expansion happens on the broker side so you get the best of both worlds!  For now, I'm simply using the metric name(s) as the topic name(s), though I did build in support for aliasing as well.  So basically zero incremental bandwidth needed, and all the goodness!

Author: rickbullotta
Content: Also, in a single wildcard subscription you can get all of the metadata if you'd like, since it is required to be retained in my proposal.  No communications with the devices or nodes is required - just to the broker.  So ultimately it's MUCH more efficient.  And devices/nodes now only need to send metadata when it changes.

Author: asthomas
Content: Have you written down your proposal?  I'm curious to see if I can find any weaknesses in it.  On the surface it sounds more robust - the birth + changes model in Sparkplug is fragile.  The only thing that immediately comes to mind is that the payloads of most values (boolean, int or double) will be fairly small compared to the topic name and TCP packet header overhead, so I cannot see how it would be more bandwidth efficient than Sparkplug.  Having said that, only applications running on bandwidth-constrained networks would even notice.

Author: rickbullotta

Author: rickbullotta
Content: It is still Sparkplug/Protobuf on the wire.  The expansion to individual topics happens after the Sparkplug message is received.  I can’t find any downside.

Author: rickbullotta
Content: Additionally, I propose that clients request the Sparkplug version they want, and the broker can act as the arbiter. The idea that the MQTT broker should remain “pure” is so epically stupid. That’s what forces us to add another layer to the architecture.  Which adds cost, latency, and another point of failure.

Author: asthomas
Content: We do that with Cogent DataHub as well. The built-in broker decomposes Sparkplug into individual data points and republishes them as OPC, MQTT+JSON, Modbus, etc., and rebuilds the Sparkplug when necessary to close the loop.  That is the broker acting as a gateway to other protocols more than it is an evolution of Sparkplug.  I imagine there will be a Sparkplug 4.0, and it would be nice to see end-to-end fixes for issues like birth storms, ping/pong busy failures, message order inversion, QoS propagation, broker chaining, write confirmation and birth sequence nonsense.  Some of those appear unsolvable with a "pure" MQTT broker.  We deal with some of them in our broker, but others need to be resolved in the Sparkplug spec or in the MQTT spec.

Author: asthomas
Content: No question that it's possible - you've demonstrated it using two different methods in very little time, and we have done something similar ourselves.  If the Sparkplug working group were to adopt that idea into the specification, it would oblige every Sparkplug implementation to use HiveMQ (I'm sure they'd be happy) or every MQTT broker to implement deep knowledge of Sparkplug.  In addition the separation of data from metadata, while being a good idea, would break all hope of backward compatibility.  That idea has been floated here: https://github.com/eclipse-sparkplug/sparkplug/blob/develop/docs/roadmap.md  (https://github.com/eclipse-sparkplug/sparkplug/issues/96) but did not make it into Sparkplug 3.0.  Once a change of that magnitude is considered for the spec, a reference implementation needs to be created and the edge cases identified.  One example edge case that comes to mind:  MQTT does not guarantee message order, so consecutive birth and data messages can swap order.  If birth messages are persistent then a listener could get a data message relative to an old birth message.  If the data message uses aliases, those aliases could point to different PLC addresses, and that could result in controlling the wrong transducer.  The spec would need to ensure that does not happen.  The current spec handles this message order problem with message sequence numbers.  That would not work if birth messages are persistent.

Author: rickbullotta
Content: It adds a little value by reducing overhead when publishing relatively large amounts of data more frequently, but that could be solved trivially if the MQTT committee would simply add a multi-publish message type.

I'm not ready to give up 100% on Sparkplug yet, but it's severely broken at present.  We shall see if they have the willingness to fix its flaws.

Content: Hi everyone.. Considering what I see at Industry 3.0, lots of customers send all data they can to an Historian and there they make some calculations - let´s say OEE calculations. Some system integrators argue they prefer to send the data to the Historian and do the calculations (OEE, for exemple) at the Historian. But considering we can have all data from the edge into the UNS I also can do the calculations (in this example, the OEE calculations) at the UNS. So, what are the pros and cons of making the calculations at the historian or at the UNS? What are your suggestions?

Author: akoscs
Content: I do not thing this is a pure i4.0 question. The current trend in IT is a microservices based event driven archtirecture. Microservices are oposed to monolithic software, where the system consists of independtent runtimes usually packaged as containers. There are advantages and disadvantages to this is the current trend. Now using this logic, a modenr IT system would have microservices calculating the OEE and not a historian. Now keep in mind, that this refers to software development. If you are buying, not developing you may very well choose a more monolithical aproach and buy a historian. (I know that amazon recently stepped away from microservices, but that is not yet a trend)

Author: newtonfernandez

Author: akoscs
Content: To my knowledge the UNS does not “do” anything. It is the “glue” that holds everything together. If you want to run logic (code, nodered, whatever) the input comes from the UNS, output goes in the UNS, but the UNS is just the current state of everything with a well defined interface, it does not “do” calculations.

Author: jon.forbord
Content: The UNS doesnt do anything as @akos states. Any calculation or deduced information from the UNS would be performed at a node in the ecosystem (which is tied together by the UNS). Whether this node is a historian or some «microservice» or another OTS-solution would be highly dependent on many factors, but in general a historian lacks all the context necessary to actually calculate OEE, so I would not start there. And where you do the calculation doesn’t actually matter if all else is equal, and the information goes back into the UNS. In some scenarios the closer you can get to the source of the data the better.

Author: jon.forbord
Content: You still need a historian or other form of record of history as one of the nodes in your UNS ecosystem. I guess the difference in traditional architecture and a UNS architecture is that in the traditional architecture the historian is the single source of truth all consumers consume from, while a UNS, the historian is just a node in that ecosystem.

Author: rickbullotta
Content:
I tossed out a couple other scenarios why OEE sucks the other day, and would welcome everyone's feedback:

- Near the end of his/her shift, a worker drops their lunchbox into the packing machine.  They're only charged with 2 minutes of downtime, but the machine isn't repaired until halfway through the next shift.  The next crew is charged with a ton of downtime.  Is that fair?

- Crew "X" runs 10,000 units of product ABC, even though product DEF was also scheduled, because it's easier to run and they can maximum their shift bonus with higher OEE.  The next shift gets saddled with running DEF and their OEE and bonus suffer.  Is that fair?

- The night shift runs the machine "balls out" to maximize their OEE number, wearing the extruder dies.  Next shift quality goes to hell because the product is out of tolerance, and their OEE suffers.  Is that fair?

- An assembly tech making $30 an hour is running tests on $10,000 avionics systems, and while rushing to maximize OEE, scraps one of the 180 units they processed that shift.  While OEE shows higher, the net cost of scrap/rework GREATLY outweighs the incremental throughput.  Is that smart?

Author: sparkylarks
Content:
I think your examples are bordering on "Reductio ad absurdum". Of course if you blindly follow OEE and ignore all other factors your will get poor results.
Noone is suggesting that.

Those examples, in particular the first 3, do support a view that OEE is a metric that has low value over the short term. But if you consider two plants where OEE is not calculated on one where OEE is calculated the second has a much great chance of detecting the issues, identifying the route cause and taking steps to prevent them in the future.

The three examples do tend to assume a narrative I have seen where OEE can be used to drive gamifications where one shift will compete against the other. I've be working with operators for the past 20 years, IMHO that isn't how they tend to react that measure like that.

I certainly agree bonuses for OEE on shift is a bad idea. I have never seen it, but I have seen bonuses for Schedule adherence.

The 4th example only give support the a view that either OEE is not suitable for all companies, or that OEE is needs to be tempered with other procedures.

Author: sparkylarks
Content:
I think the key question that needs to be answered is
- Is it worth calculating OEE and I would argue yes becuause
a) It is simple

c) It can provide a simple first measure and can then be broken down for different Attributes

e) It is a useful tool that engineers can use to support their views when discussing with finance and management
f) There is a standard formula that allows some comparison across differnt companies( though this assumes that it is correctly applies)

Is it a magic metric that if you follow it and ignore the rest of the business is a guaranteed success, Of course not but I woudl sat that claim is as accurate as your claim that it is "junk"

Author: geoffnunan
Content:
There are a few types of production line for which OEE provides a reasonable measure or how things are going. 
There are many where it does not.
For example, A customer I've been working with has machines that run at 17% OEE when everything runs perfectly. In this example, there is a lot of setup time to process a widget, but actually processing the widget does not take that long. 
For this example, setting up is a manual task, and must be done for every widget.
Having a metric of 17% OEE causes managers in other departments of the business to draw the wrong conclusions about this particular factory.

I've seen this in other factories too that have a mix of manual and automated steps in the production process.

When I've looked deeper into who drives performance improvement and how do they do it, the common themes are:
- Have a standard
- Measure against the standard
- Identify, Investigate and take action on deviations from the standard
- Adjust the standard in small increments

These 4 steps are often applied to the whole production machine with OEE. For machines that run continually, there can be good information on the deviation ( Maybe there was a breakdown, or a quality issue ).
For machines that run intermittently, with a mix of manual and automated process steps, there is rarely enough information to identify the deviation and investigate. 

Driving improvement is about knowing where the opportunities are at a level where they can be actioned. If OEE provides this to your factory then it's doing what it needs to do.

Author: jermuk
Content:
oh, I read GigE Vision Camera and need to jump in. Too many wasted months (!) in the field of GenICam. It's been some time, so not everything might be correct or up-to-date. Also, it is very opinionated.

GenICam is not open at all. Not a single bit except the label. Entirely propriety and you cannot swap cameras out, as they are incompatible with each other. Essentially, every vendor is doing their own protocols and definitions. Similar to OPC-UA, but **much worse**. 

The core of GenICam is always the driver "GenTL producer". Even though the driver should in theory be compatible with all cameras, because they are all relying on the same protocols (GigE Vision), **they are in fact not compatible**. They might be speaking the same protocol, but because the protocol has so many capabilities, there are too many ways to do the same thing. Each driver only implements a sub-part of the entire standard. So it is gambling and trying out which driver works with which camera.

Also the underlying standard, GigEVision is not officially public. It is only available to members, and the last time I checked you needed to be voted in as well as pay around a million USD in yearly fees to be a member (source: https://www.automate.org/a3-content/gige-vision-license-product-registration)

The driver is always provided in a compiled form including sometimes hundreds of shared libraries (in case of Linux), which is a nightmare to install and maintain. Some drivers are incompatible with Docker and Kubernetes, because they use some very rare networking capabilities which are not included in Docker (I think it was UDP multicast or something). There are some very weird limitations as well and the entire standard does not harmonize with IT at all. They basically decided to re-invent the wheel

This is also the reason why most startups / companies use webcams instead of industrial cameras. If you want, I can hook you up with a company who already worked a lot with it.

Author: mparris
Content:
I suspect all those "IT" streaming technologies make heavy use of compression... Especially lossy compression.

When transferring a 5MP image exactly as acquired for measurement where every pixel is 12-bit up to 24-bit assigned to describe brightness and chroma, the payload size adds up quick, especially when trying to get faster framerates...

And so, to decrease latency, GigEVision cameras typically require a NIC dedicated just for it with jumbo packets enabled, to reduce the Ethernet overhead. And since the cameras are on a LAN directly connected to the computer, there is no need for IP and definitely no need for TCP or UDP when sending the image data, as that just adds payload overhead and processing latency on the computer.

Content:
I'm enjoying this detour discussion about vision technology.  As for the core discussion, you cited a great example of not having camera hardware "married" to software or other hardware like controllers.  I've seen entire vision systems replaced simply because a controller couldn't support a particular light accessory within the same brand / product line. The devices, especially line scan cameras and laser profilers, would need very specific network settings (e.g., jumbo frames).  Each device is its own network, basically.  I can imagine some applications where simple images sent across a network would suffice.  But others, not so much.

To @Jermuk's point about the standards, I've found the support to be inconsistent.  While it's not complete ecosystem or product line lock-in like much in the Cognex and Keyence portfolios, certain devices enjoy better support from certain apps.  The most frustrating thing was even once the right combination is selected, the versioning are never seamless like one would expect using a standard.  When one problem is solved by a firmware or software upgrade, it introduces many more problems or the whole thing stops working.  More often than not, interoperability was a function of asking vendors has "Has device {model, sdk} been tested with app {version, interface}?"

I am really trying to understand how far from the broker the UNS boundary actually is. i.e. what data which is not in my Broker is part of the UNS.

So I am trying to get away from the often said phrase "Publish data to the UNS" If we take a simple example. a temperature sensor. The 4-20mA signal from the PLC passing through a varying resistance. The PLC reads the current, and store the raw value as an Integer typically. The user writes a bit of code that will convert from a raw Integer to a meaningful measurement( maybe this is more configuration than coding depending on the device). Lets say the measured value is written to a modbus register 40001 as an integer, and 40002 is the scaling  of that measurement.

A gateway is used to read the two integers and convert to a Real/Float and it is published to a MQTT broker.
Often that process is written or said, to be "Publishing the value to the UNS". That statement clashes in my mind with the UNS<> Broker.
So I need to work it out.

One model in my head is that All data in the system is part of the UNS, even it it cannot be accessed, easily by other programs.
So the Integer for the Raw Value, and the variables used for the conversion and the Real value in the PLC and the Integer in the Modbus register and the scaling value are as much part of the UNS as the value published in the UNS.
This model is helpful to me when stating "All data matters".  If I think of the UNS as just the MQTT Broker, I think I start to create a hierarchy of data and leave lots of data behind.  

Limitation of existing equipment might force me to leave data behind, so I might not be able to make the variables used to convert the raw values in the PLC accessible to other users.

So is it ok to say that all data is part of the UNS even it it isn't all accessible yet.

Author: willemrs
Content:
In our case a production line is a PLC or a group of like PLC's that all perform a given function together.  I refer to the programs running on each of these lines as its own namespace as it defines its own functions and variables which are understood by the other devices on that line.   Then we are implementing the UNS which is a separate namespace and instead of living in the PLCs it exists inside MQTT.   
Since none of our PLC's can publish directly into the UNS as they don't have MQTT built in, we use ignition and their drivers to connect to the PLC's directly.  When things are published into the UNS they are now available for all other subscribers along with any context we added inside of Ignition.   
In a perfect world I would think that our PLCs would directly publish into the UNS, so a PLC programmer would write their logic knowing that their equipment was going to be published into a larger UNS.  If this were the case we could skip portions of the  data modeling step that we now do inside of Ignition.  

Lastly, this may not be the book definition of a UNS either... 😃

Author: sparkylarks
Content:
I worked in a plant, some Line had 1 PLC per line, some had 3 or 4 PLC's per line. and we had 4 Lines where
- 1 PLC (PLC A) controlled the 4 Hazardous Labeller
- 1 PLC (PLC B) controlled the rest of another Line( Line 1)
- 1 PLC (PLC C) controlled the functions on Line  2 and Line 3 and some of Line 4
- the last PLC controlled the remaining functions on Line 4

So the Idea of Simply mapping the PLC data into a central repository, based on device is one that I woudl be skeptical towards.
We didn't have a UNS as such but used a Semantic hierarchy where we focused on the Functional grouping and following ISA-95 so
Ent->Site->Area->Line->Cell->Device  where the Cell was functional so
Ent->Site->Filling hall->Line 1
                                   -> Filling
                                   -> Capping
                                   -> Checkweighing
                                   -> Product Labeller
                                   -> GHS Labeller
 If I was applying what I have learned since I would at the Line or Area Level have a PLC/Edge group
If a PLC is for a Line only I would  put it there If it covered a number of Lines I would have it in the Filling Area e.g. PLC A above

On that project I contextualised the data and in the PLC, and then formed the hierarchy in System Platform.
If I was starting again, I would.
1 - Publish the Raw data into a Edge namespace in the Broker
2- Use some Data Ops software e.g. high byte to map the data from the Device namespace to the Functional Namespace
3- That allows Nodes that are "higher in the perdue model" access the functional data

For a greenfield site I would 
1) Enforce 1 Line Per PLC as much as possible.
2) Contextualise the data in the PLC , so it can be published directly into the functional namespace
3)  Publish the raw data into the Edge namespace as above
4) IF needed to supplement the directly published data use some dataOps software to contextualise the raw data into functional data.

Content:
I don't think that is particularly Bad practice as you describe. 
My 2  tests area always, can you write a document explaining how it is structured and someone who understand the technology can follow and use it without you explain all the details to them. Can you add to your structure in the future, e.g. add new controller or HMI's , or add a PLC that suppor MQTT and publish directly. In both cases I think you can. 

I would not dump all the data from all the PLC's into a single space. I would split out the data as you describe.

I think you need to decide how and where you apply context to your Data. 
Normally that happen in the "Gateway". So If you are using Ignition to pull the data from the devices and publish to the Broker, then that is probably the best place.
If you have no Gateway and are publishing from the device to the Broker, then you might want to use a Data ops software. I might use Node Red for a hobby/Proof of concept and use Highbyte for scale

To me I would think that your HMI is your Gateway here but not sure that is is the best place to do the data Modelling. 
I would publish the Data to the Broker in the Device Format, and then use Node Red to map the data from the device name space to the relevant functional name space.

What helped me when in a similar place to you was to create by ISA-95 Hierarchy and  at every level there is a Functional, Informational , and device name space. The Device Name Space is where I publish the Raw MQTT from each Device. I then map the data from the Device into the correct Functional Topic, that should be where in the structure of the business should that data live,

If you can name the Tags in the PLC or the HMI according to their Function it can allow you to automatically map the data, e.g. Name your Tags A1L1C1.... so A1L1C2WT1
A1 ( Area1) Filling Hall
L1( Line 1) Multi Filler
C2(Checkweigher)
WT1( Gross Weight) WT2 might be Tare WT3 Net weight etc.

Author: sparkylarks
Content: That naming allow you to have a script that Automatically maps any data to the correct functional location int he UNS and you don't have to manually map it. But even if you are doing in Manually it make it much simpler and less error prone.

Author: walker.reynolds
Content:
I will not be commenting on this publicly unless directly asked.  I have read the intro and the first couple of sections.  Its clear he has scraped the internet for the high level overview, applied process integration steps and asked ChatGPT to write him a book.  I think its a good thing because it continues to raise the profile of UNS -- its a bad thing because Alex clearly doesn't understand what UNS is or what Digital Transformation is.  Following Corso's model, an org will create technical debt -- assuming becoming 'digital' is the goal.  There's no discussion of context/normalization or pattern matching on the back-end, no discussion of digital supply chain integration.  So -- on the one hand, its a good thing, on the other, its going to confuse people and muddy the waters on the definition of 'Unified Namespace'.  

At the end of the day -- Alex is about Alex and nothing more.  I can't fault him for trying to jump on the bandwagon but I do fault him for lying (been using UNS since 2007).

I'll read the whole thing -- and cross my fingers that he doesn't go too far out of the way.

Some points to keep in mind -- there can be no definitive guide for UNS because it is evolving.  The manual we drop on July 15 points this out.  Since UNS is the structure of a business and its events, in real time, it follows that not all enterprise UNS will look the same or even take the same form.  It is absolutely critical to start with Digital Strategy, Architecture and Minimum Technical Requirements -- anything else is just folly.

I will give Alex credit for finally using the term 'Semantic Hierarchy' -- but I do lament that it took 3 reaction videos to get him corrected.  It is a shame that he continues to take the approach he has -- but its not surprising.

UNS has been my baby since 2005, so I am a little protective of the term and its meaning -- but at the end of the day, whatever helps serve the mission of saving and creating Middle Class jobs in the U.S. (and UNS architectures do that) is a win in my book.

Would I recommend this book to someone?  Based on the preceding blog posts and Alex' conduct up this point, no.  But I will have to reserve judgement until I get all the way through it this week.

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: AMQP is the reason that [A very large Japanese Automaker's] first stab at Digital Transformation failed.  They hit critical mass with AMQP as transport and standard from edge through DMZ to Azure cloud and could not undo the technical debt.  We followed that team at Factory of the Future and deployed MQTT, and working with Omron were able to get them past critical mass.  AMQP is great tech but definitely more verbose across the wire.  I really struggle with AMQP and MQTT -- because MQTT is missing important elements needed for mature data-ops -- like methods and micro-service.  AMQP supports both in at least some capacity -- but for me, scale with short time to value is paramount for orgs and AMQP is second best in class there.

Author: rickbullotta
Content:
MQTT does not support either of those, but Sparkplug helps a little bit. 

The original version of ThingWorx was built fully on Neo4J graph database BTW.  Used it for metadata, data, modeling, and even human generated content.

Here's my MQTT/Sparkplug list of recommendations again:

Core MQTT issues:

- Decision to use 4 bits for message type. Short sighted and now a major limitation
- Multi-publish is essential (publish more than one topic in a single message)
- Topics should have durable metadata (could be passed as headers in publish or as its own message type)
- Payloads should have a data type (mime type) to enable parsing/processing by subscribers or intermediaries
- Topic binding should be a built-in broker feature (like a symlink) - topic aliases are not this
- The lack of a capability to query topics is a huge flaw/gap. Ideally these queries should be able to include metadata filters as well
- MQTT's subscription patterns are hopeless limiting. They should support richer match expressions and also metadata filters
- MQTT should officially support a REST binding for request/response query/publish/read/subscribe/unsubscribe
- Handling of large payloads (e.g. file uploads, video content, firmware/software updates, method responses) needs a lot of work to improve reliability
- Handling of RPC/method invocations remains an awful hack. This MUST be addressed.

Author: rickbullotta
Content:
Core Sparkplug issues:

- The rigid Node/Device format does not fit real world models. Do away with one of them and allow more flexible topic hiearchies.
- The handling of *BIRTH messages and the intermingling of data and metadata in them is a poor design
- The process for requesting *BIRTH messages is terribly inefficient. Metadata should be retained, not requested each time by each client.
- There should be *METADATA messages to deal with metadata
- The opaque/multi-value nature of *DATA messages makes it impossible for client(s) to subscribe to individual metrics. Huge issue.
- The "primary client" stuff is unnecessary and should be removed
- Any device commands/methods should be fully declared (inputs and outputs fully typed)
- Naming of metrics/commands needs to be locked down to a more restricted character set
- Add a few more top level data types (Location, BLOB (w/mime type), 
- Support other encodings besides Protobuf (e.g. plain JSON, zipped JSON, BSON, etc.)
- Millisecond resolution for timestamps is inadequate for modern systems where accurate event sequence is critical (e.g. power grid)

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: Doug -- this is a common question, so don't sweat it.  You should start by asking what a historian is and what function it serves.  It is nothing but a data store that stores history of events in a structured way.  Generally, aggregation tools and visualization for analysis sit on top.  The historian that stores the events (from the current state) consume from UNS as a subscriber and store using the semantic hierarchy structure (Historians generally call this 'asset model').  Aggregation and visualization remain unchanged.  That's your 10k view.  If you'd like, I can explain further if you want to know how historian interacts with UNS on the pub side.

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: The beauty of UNS with historian is that you can (and we do this frequently) store both raw events AND transactions from a single trigger.  For example, lets say I have a sensor that changes once per second and I have a PID loop that calculates once every 5 seconds.  I can store the raw changes from the sensor A (the one that changes every second) and trigger a store off the same event to store the pv, cv, sp of the pid controller -- even though they only change, at most, once every 5 seconds.  Why is this important?  For ML use cases -- what we've done is eliminate the acquisition, contextualizing, cleansing and normalization steps in ML by baking them into the architecture.

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: One last step with Historians and UNS -- we can also 'store' history in the UNS by having a topic whose payload is a JSON or DataSet that contains history for x variable over n time.  It is very common to have x variable as a topic in the namespace and right next to it x_history_lasthour from the historian.

Author: douglawrie
Content:
Another UNS Q because it seems there are lots of smart people here. 
We want structures and hierarchies of data to be defined at the edge, and to reflect equipment on the ground faithfully. We also want data coming from equipment that is essentially the same to look the same, even if it’s slightly different. To be concrete, if I have multiple battery energy storage systems from multiple manufacturers, I want to be able to compare them directly and have a unified concept of a BESS, but the systems from different manufacturers produce different sets of data. What is the approach here? Do I centrally define a structure (UDT) and overlay that at the edge onto all systems past present and future?

Author: rickbullotta
Content: I'm a fan of base type(s) + extend (basic OOP modeling).  So you'd have a "base" BESS type that included all of the telemetry and commands that are common to all BESS's.  You'd do engineering unit normalization at the edge (e.g. everything in a particular set of units).  You can have additional types or even individual metrics unique to a single unit or group of units (e.g. all of the BESS systems from Tesla also have a Tesla type that includes a unique set of capabilities).  It's the way we designed the type system in ThingWorx, so that you could look at a set of things polymorphically (and assign rules, visualizations, ML models, etc to them knowing that they implement a specific set of capabilities).

Author: mparris
Content:
Contrast OPC UA with Sparkplug, which is laser-focused, a clear, singularly-defined interface. It was able to break into the market fairly easily given it's definition was lightweight: (1) use an existing payload encoding (protobuf), (2) use an existing transport protocol (MQTT), (3) define a semantic structure, and (4) define how to use the transport protocol. Author: sparkylarks
Content:
Are UNS and Digital Threads really mutually exclusive? 
I think of a Unified Namespace (UNS) as the pattern used in creating a tapestry. Without this pattern, or design guide, the threads can become a tangled mess. This is especially true in a digital factory, where new threads  will continually be added by different people over time.

On the other hand, a Digital Thread could be seen as each individual strand woven into that tapestry. Each strand tells a part of the overall story, tracing the lifecycle of an asset, a process, or an item.

So, in our tapestry analogy, the UNS provides the framework (pattern) that guides how these Digital Threads are woven together. It allows all the different threads (data from different machines and systems) to interweave in a coherent, organized way, creating a complete and comprehensible picture. Without a clear pattern (UNS), it would be challenging to add new threads over time and maintain a cohesive and clear story (Digital Thread).

These concepts are not mutually exclusive, but rather work together to effectively manage and make sense of the diverse and evolving data within a digital factory.
that Pattern concept is a bit unfair to the UNS as a UNS is more that just a template, but it is the part that brings a structure as we break down silo's

But of course most people use Digital Thread to mean point to point linear systems integration to the exclusion of UNS and graphed association data infrastructures.

For interoperability to work within the OPC ecosystem, application developers are forced to downselect to a certain functional minimum of what is possible, simply because they don't have unlimited time and money to incorporate all the options for transport, encoding, companion spec, etc.

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: This could not be a more inappropriate metaphor. If, for any reason at all, to demonstrate to the MQTT and SPb working groups what is missing in their specs.  @Dylan DuFresne even you defaulted to GraphQL in your use case -- and its because it makes sense.  @GeoffNunan GraphQL isn't the api for an MQTT Broker -- its the API between the Broker Structure (semantic hierarchy), Payload Events, State History in some other back-end.  This spec is designed to use GraphQL for illustrative purposes -- to demonstrate what is missing and how to close the gap.

Author: akoscs
Content: So "This will provide clients with the ability to fetch exactly what they need in a single request and enable more efficient utilization of network resources." fetch means for me request-reply. I strongly agree that using pub-sub is not well suited for all types off comms which happen in an IoT or IIoT setting. I did request-reply over MQTT by sending a query and specifying a GUID (or UUID for the non .net fans) as a "return" topic in the message. So the entity getting the query by subscribing to the query topic knew it had to respond using the GUID topic. Obviously the entity sending the query subscribed to the GUID topic beforehand, so it was already listening to the responce. By implementing such an approach, if I understand the PDF correclty (which I am not sure I do) the specification could become GraphQL over MQTT, not extending MQTT which I think is way more productive and much better suited for such an application.

Database Specific Configurations: "database.hostname", "database.port", "database.user", "database.password", and "database.dbname" should be updated to match your SQL Server details.

Debezium Snapshot Mode: Microsoft SQL Server requires a snapshot mode. Add "snapshot.mode": "initial" to the config.

Change Data Capture (CDC): Microsoft SQL Server uses a system called Change Data Capture (CDC) to track changes, unlike PostgreSQL that uses Write-Ahead Logging (WAL). You need to enable CDC on the tables that Debezium will capture.

Here is how the revised ConfigMap would look:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: sqlserver-connector-config
  namespace: united-manufacturing-hub
data:
  connector.json: |-
    {
      "name": "sqlserver-connector",
      "config": {
        "connector.class": "io.debezium.connector.sqlserver.SqlServerConnector",
        "database.hostname": "your_sql_server",
        "database.port": "1433",
        "database.user": "debezium",
        "database.password": "changeme",
        "database.dbname": "your_database",
        "database.server.name": "ia.raw.sqlserver.your_database",
        "table.include.list": "public.assettable",
        "snapshot.mode": "initial"
      }
    }
```

As for preparing SQL Server, the steps are a little different. You need to:

Set up a user for Debezium with appropriate permissions.
Enable CDC on your database and the tables that you want to track. This usually involves running SQL commands like EXEC sys.sp_cdc_enable_db and EXEC sys.sp_cdc_enable_table.

Author: vaughnturner
Content:
Using the ISA-95 Part 2 standard in a UNS architecture can be a good idea for several reasons:
1.    Industry-Proven Standard: The ISA-95 standard is an internationally recognized.
2.    Consistent and Interoperable Data Models: ISA-95 Part 2 provides a standardized data model for manufacturing operations management (MOM) functions. 
3.    Seamless Data Integration: The Unified Namespace architecture aims to create a unified view of data from various sources, including disparate systems and devices. By utilizing the Part 2 standard, the integration of data becomes more straightforward and seamless.
4.    Reduced Integration Efforts: With a standardized data model, the effort required to integrate different systems and data sources is reduced. 
5.    Simplified Maintenance: Standardized data models make it easier to maintain the architecture over time. 
6.    Improved Data Quality and Accuracy: With a well-defined data model, the chances of data inconsistencies and errors are minimized.
7.    Enhanced Decision Making: A standardized data model allows for better data analytics and reporting capabilities. 
8.    Vendor-Neutral Approach: The standard is not tied to any specific vendor or technology, making it a vendor-neutral approach. 

Just my humble thoughts here, I'm definitely no Walker or Rick Bullotta.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
This is the problem that DataOps seeks to solve.

[Making sure data model is being followed]
Run everything through abstracted data models.  Even if some nodes require little-to-no transformations, this enforces that a data model is adhered to.

[Centralization]
Being able to centrally define data models independent of where data is produced or consumed is important.

[Version control]
In the absence of a data infrastructure, version control is more critical.  Compliance is voluntary or best effort.  One needs to make sure disparate nodes are configured to the right model as requirements evolve over time.  With DataOps, models are enforced and schema drift is addressed.  It's less critical to track versioning because it's not possible to have version conflicts.  That said, there are still opportunities to formally lifecycle data models.  One can create distinct models as versions of each other.  One can subject model definitions and associated configurations to a CI/CD process.

[Automated tests]
By running everything through abstracted data models, there is no variation.  This eliminates the need to test anything.  By modeling data before it lands, it prevents data issues.  Conventional ETL and data warehousing techniques focus on modeling data after it lands.  The problem with this approach is that it does not prevent the problem of creating data that is not modeled.  It requires some sort of ongoing maintenance to make sure all data is getting properly normalized.

Author: geoffnunan
Content:
This is a great topic of discussion.
We currently have a very strongly governed schema defined by ISA95 in our data hub (The database where all the messages get stored). 
We are now implementing a schema for each topic in the broker using AsyncAPI specifications.
The logic for this is that an event that occurs in the process creates a message that gets published to the broker. If I want to subscribe to that event, I need to know the schema of the information in that topic. Which fields can I rely on always being present, which are optional, what enumeration values can I expect to find, etc.
The schema for a topic in the broker may represent a sub-set of the schema of the database that stores all messages.
Example:
- I have a topic in my broker where Production Schedule updates are published by the ERP. That topic has a schema that defines the message payload.
- I subscribe to that message and when new messages are received, I need to query some other data before storing the schedule in the data hub.
The schema of the data hub is not the same as the schema of the message.

So I dont have anything I can quote if that's what you mean, that statement was my own. That being said my experience as an EA is around distributed architecture for the IT domain specifically MSA. So a lot of my design philosphy is around MSA (which actually has a lot of parallels to I4.0 Architecture). The main two references that have formed my ideas around data structure are these two books. That being said, to answer your question: The main difference between explicit, implict, and schemaless schemas is the following:

Explicit: The Structure of the Data is well Defined and Stricly enforced.
Implicit: Data is structured, however no structure is explicitly defined or enforced, however structure of the data can be inferred from the data itself. 
Schemaless: The Data is structured, however no structure is explicity defined or enforced, and structure of the data cannot be inferred from the data. 

A UNS does not have an explicit schema (I think we can all agree on that), however  it is not considered schemeless because the data is still structured in a hierarchical manner that allows machines to understand the relationships between entities and hierarchies. Based on the MQTT Topic Path.  This enables machines to autonomously find relevant information and act on it, which is not possible when schemaless.

Yeah absolutely, one thing that excites me with that design pattern as an architect is the ability to “visualize” architectures. What I mean is currently as an architect I model the architecture in a modeling tool like “cameo” which allows me to form graph like relationships to develop architecture and have different views of the architecture, physical, logical, permissions, etc. we then take that descriptive model and implement it. Problem is what happen if changes happen? With a model that is utilizing a graph backend with edges, we can let the the graph db tell us the current configuration of the architecture based on the relationships established in the meta data. Aka the descriptive model of the architecture is the architecture itself in real time.

Content: 2. We collect 1000hz data by sampling/buffering at the edge, and send every 1 second, through mqtt, sparkplug B. Rule of thumb for mqtt is 250ms publish interval is the fastest that is recommended, although nothing prevents you from publishing at higher frequencies. mqtt is a bit of fire-and-forget protocol. QoS only guarantees message delivery, not processing. We rely on redundancy and store and forward capability to ensure minimal loss of data. If you want 100% guaranteed processing, I’m not sure mqtt alone is the protocol you should rely on. There are ways to do transactions over mqtt, but that generally requires workarounds.

Author: jon.forbord
Content: Isn’t idempotency generally used for transactions? To in essence avoid duplicates? Eg you order a potato on Amazon Potato Service. The order is sent, the order processing microservice processes the order and sends the acknowledge, but the client doesn’t get the ack and believes the potato has not been processed completely, and sends another order request etc, and you all of a sudden have 2000 potatoes on your doorstep. Idempotency ensures the uniqueness of the initial order is preserved and the order processing microservice correctly recognizes the second duplicate order request and prevents more potatoes being ordered.

Author: akoscs

Author: ravil1
Content:
Hi,
I have a beginner's question about UNS in general. I can understand why all data should be published on UNS. In the end, why would you have that variable/tag in the first place, if it does not worth making it available on UNS?
What is not clear to me is about publishing data "when it is changed". 
For example, my home heating thermostat has low precision, just one decimal place.  So its values not changing often. Humidity is displayed just as an integer. With this level of precision, their values do not change often. But if I stay looking for a longer time, the humidity value can increase by 1 or  2 percent from my breath. But I would ignore that change and consider as a  valid only value displayed when I just came to check it. Because that change is at noise  level and I would just ignore it.
When I was doing lab workshops when I was a student, on physics, I remember that on some measurements of some properties we were receiving every time new value, just slightly different, maybe 0.00001 or so. Strictly speaking unless you round it, it would be always changed.
In terms of OPC UA, whenever I do a new measurement, that would be a "sampling". 
So the frequency of how often values are reported/published in such scenario would completely depend on the sampling interval. My question: how this interval is configured? I guess in the case of PLC that can be PLC's scan rate. But is that rate what you really want data to be published up to the cloud? And, is it easy to change that rate in PLC? 
And what if you want to change that rate? Or you want to apply some deadband? Or you want to change that deadband value? Or you want it to change those options only for subset of data sources? How do you do that when you have hundreds of such data sources?

Author: jermuk
Content: Why do more granular subscriptions sound painful? The more granular they are, the better you can control who receives what. Also it makes sense that every message type lands up in their own sub-topic (like /images), so that services can only subscribe to what they really need. Also it makes implementation and parsing easier if the service can already see from the topic what type of payload it can expect. In a future state, you could even enforce certain topic and payload structures, and therefore protecting that certain microservicrs don't crash / fail / or simply not work because of a malformatted message

Yeah I see your question, and why we use intelligence hub. Some producers we have no control over the structure of the payload. For us it’s a lot of the payloads from our machines, they might contain a bunch of tags in a single payload. We don’t want to propagate that single payload  and then require each consumer to parse the payload especially if they are only interested in one data point.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
"Yeah I see your question, and why we use intelligence hub. Some producers we have no control over the structure of the payload. For us it’s a lot of the payloads from our machines, they might contain a bunch of tags in a single payload. We don’t want to propagate that single payload  and then require each consumer to parse the payload especially if they are only interested in one data point."

This is so well put.  It seems there is a great challenge in industry grasping the concept of modeling to needs of the consumer and not the producer.  

Lately, I've been encountering the opposite problem in which people try to model an entire factory.  Think huge, monolithic payloads in pub/sub architecture with very few (sometimes one) topics, publishers, subscribers, etc.  It completely burdens the consumer with excessive parsing and transformations.

I feel there is this lingering "historian mindset" of just dumping tags into hierarchy.  This might be okay if the consumer is a process engineer concerned with instrumentation telemetry.  But, what about the broader context of that telemetry?

This is why I feel it's best to model according to use cases and needs of the consumer.  One can still have some canonical or base form to acquire and normalize data.  But, at the end of the day, consumers should be able to subscribe to data and quickly put it to use.

Author: douglasalbright
Content:
The ideal solution is an analytical tool capable of filtering OEE by any given dimension. This can be accomplished using applications like MS Tabular or implementing a Unified Star Schema. It requires real-time transformation in an operational data warehouse, enabled by Data Vault 2.0. Although creating a Data Vault and Unified Star Schema can be complex, better LLM models effectively handle it. The challenge lies in data accessibility and quality.

Data Vault 2.0 supports agile development and allows for Minimum Viable Product (MVP) building, provided clients understand the value of abstraction layers. Given the necessary source files and context, they can easily complete 80% of the task. The Unified Star Schema provides data story insights but tying events to it requires substantial effort.

The notion of effortlessly migrating current states to the cloud isn’t realistic. It disregards the necessary work to ensure data flow. In reality, one must account for scan times and the inner workings of the system. Identifying an event, confirming its completion, and avoiding duplicates may sound straightforward but is actually complicated by the speed of processing and distributed computing.

Author: suran23.
Content: @Dylan_IIoT if i may try to answer your qs. There're 2 main things before you get started with your UNS implementation: defining the data structure and choosing the right message broker technology. For the first, you want to design a hierarchy or framework that best suits your use case or organizational need. You could essentially choose ISA-95 or a custom one that meets your business needs. Following ISA-95 will simplify a ton of things such as compatibility and ease of integration with other systems complying to the same standard. An example structure can be: Enterprise > Site > Area> Line > Cell . ... Now for the message broker you could choose MQTT, Amqp and DNP3, as long as the message broker can support event driven architecture, enabling loosely coupled applications exchanging data through the broker. If you are using Sparkplug, you may be limited by the number of levels allowed in your hierarchy. But there are work arounds. Happy to get into that too if you need. But an example namespace would look like spBv/group_id/message_type/edge_nodeid_/device_id

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
Because most MQTT clients consume structured data (e.g., JSON payloads), UNS is not really a practical place for this IMO.  I would be curious to know if others have a found a way around this.  It's theoretical possible.

I think of this problem similar to images and databases.  While it's theoretically possible to publish the binary of an image in a database, it's more efficient to store the image outside the database and publish data on how to retrieve it.

I would opt to use the native data transport technology your image and video data sources support.  I would land the image/video in a file system or object store.  As the events are created, I would generate metadata about the image/video and publish them to a UNS or a database.  The UNS would serve more as a lookup function.  A subscriber could use the UNS to look up the location (e.g., URL, file name) of the image/video.

UNS is not just limited to structured data you can have unstructured data as well however, it is the structure of your business which means what is the input what is the output what is the function details etc. should be available in UNS
Ignition is great for several use cases but there are some cases where alternative technologies has more capabilities in terms of protocol conversion, normalizing, transformation

Author: eddiiee_
Content:
Yes they are in the same broker, but we seperated them under **Site** vs **Raw** as you wrote. Why we chose this was mainly because some PLC's and sensor data doesn't make sense to put under a specific workcell or a productionline. 
Examples:
Our PLC that controls the waterflow supply all production lines
The Print and apply system sends information for all printers in the whole factory in one JSON.
The data from MES also comes in a  big JSON-chunk for all production lines.

Therefore some PLC's could be allocated into the structure under the workcell. But many of them needed data transformation & Cleaning before it makes sense to put them into the structure. E.g. split up the MES & printer data to respective line. And it's not an option (system limitation) to make those systems to send small package of data in the topic structure. Therefore it made more sense for us to gather all "Raw" (Mixed)-data in once place.

Author: vatsalshah
Content:
1. If using 5G for factory floor, when we put in MQTT broker server in OT however this needs to be on IT corporate network due to traditional IT policies, so question is do we push machine data from 5G network to WiFi network as UNS is on IT network

- I assume you are on Private 5G nodes for the plant floor. 
- I would very much keep it isolated from OT network and IT network (5G network). 
- We did a project where 5G node was running K8S workload + 5G WAN services + LAN services via NFVs
- Depending on which vendor you are using, you might want to ask them if the correct firewall / networking policies are in place for strict WAN / LAN isolation
- For this project we did 
PLCs / SCADA / Historian -> *Existing Network* -> Litmus Edge deployed with K8S -> *5G private network*  -> Kafka broker ->  *5G WAN to cloud* -> Cloud

Well validated for security and limited network hops for better latecy controls. 

2. PLCs and machines directly connected only to SCADA? And publish to UNS? Is it good to have a industrial dataops Layer to handle the UNS broker setup?
-  As a security principal SCADA should not be exposed to your IT or cloud layer directly.
- Depending on the namespace you design, SCADA / PLCs / DCS -> Edge Product (Like Litmus Edge) -> UNS -> UNS Cloud or Central bridge 

3. Where OPC UA to MQTT conversion happens? As we need to support OPC UA as well
- OPCUA -> Edge Product (Like Litmus Edge) -> MQTT / Others

It's not a hard claim to make. 
On each of two sites I have  three nodes, a SCADA, a PLC and an Third Party Wind Turbine Controller. Each of theses is a namespaces.

2. The OPC UA spec it too big, too complicated, and much of it is optional so a device just saying it supports OPC UA doesn't really tell you much.
3. MQTT is payload agnostic. In order to transfer files in OPC UA you have to support Part 20 of the spec.

Content:
In the another, "general" topic, I just posted a message that the main advantage of MQTT is not RBE, it is PWWW (Publish Whatever and Whenever to Whoever".
I did post also my results of testing network data for MQTT vs OPC UA , which shows that OPC UA is much lighter than MQTT: https://onewayautomation.com/blog/53-opcua-mqtt
As it is noticed absolutely correctly, if there were some bottlenecks, for example crash of OPC UA application at 32 K tags - that is nothing todo with OPC UA, that is how the application was designed. BTW, I asked if possible how the team managed to build such application which crashes at 32 K tags - did not get answer yet. I think you have to put some efforts to create such a bad performant application. Maybe it was done by students, not sure.
In our product ogamma Visual Logger for OPC do you know what protocol is we get the lowest throughput? It is MQTT. While we easily can log 100K values per second to InfluxDB, we can log to MQTT only 3K/second with QoS 1, and with QoS 0 it is better, depends on the broker, can be 30K or 50K.  Total number of tags can be much higher, the main metric is values per second. If values change once in 10 seconds, then can be 1 mln. tags. And that is single instance of the application, not cluster.
I think often comparison is done apples vs oranges. It is obvious that if you add to the PLC additional load to handle 100 or 1000s of connections from OPC UA clients, it will not survive. 

I believe you can use OPC UA as a protocol to build UNS, but for that architecture should be designed in a similar way as in case of using MQTT broker the center. 
As correctly mentioned, OPC Servers like  PLCs should use reverse connection to publish data to the central piece - OPC UA federation server (FS). That OPC OPC UA FS shroud be implemented pretty much the same way as MQTT brokers - with horizontal scalability/clustering support etc.
