Author: ravil1
Content:
@Jeff@Flow, in my tests the conclusion was (https://onewayautomation.com/blog/53-opcua-mqtt): 
Total network traffic in the case of using MQTT protocol is multiple times (from 3.76 to 7.91 depending on the test case) higher than in OPC UA. Which does not correlate with results published by Johnathan Hottell.

Note that I did not test with Sparkplug, only plain MQTT.

Note that in scientific domain results are considered reliable if they can be reproduced by others. I tried to get better results in favor of MQTT to make them closer to what Johnathan claims he got, but could not. Isn't it obvious that while OPC UA by design packages values for multiple variables into one publish message, using integer identifiers, and transfers it in a binary format, in MQTT if you want each variable to be published on its own topic, you need to send separate message for each variable, and moreover need to repeat whole topic as a text in each publish message, OPC UA is naturally more efficient in terms of bytes transferred and number of messages?

Author: ravil1
Content:
For those for who number of transferred on the network bytes are so important to prove that MQTT is super-lightweight, I think the best would be to design test methodology, select products available in the market (trial versions, free versions, etc.), describe used configuration settings, data sources - so everybody can repeat the tests and agree with the results. 
I think this could be a good project for interns.

I wrote multiple times that attempts to represent value of the MQTT using misleading arguments that it is lightweight on the wire comparing to OPC UA and only it supports RBE because OPC UA uses request-responses are baseless, and can serve against MQTT. The MQTT does not need to use false claims to artificially exaggerate its importance, it has more important characteristics which makes it as the only suitable protocol in many use cases.

If you want to present it as lightweight, I think better to focus on size of C or C++ libraries for example - you can say that size of paho-mqtt library is more than 10 times smaller that open62541. As a result, the application publishing data over MQTT will require less memory than over OPC UA. I don't think you will find somebody who prove the opposite, because this is fact.

And even if you somehow convince somebody that MQTT is lighter (BTW, you always need to mention comparing to what), in order to have some advantage this criteria must be important enough in order to affect the final decision. For example it does not matter if your application requires  128 Kb or 256 Kb in RAM, if you have a device with 4 Gb RAM.

Author: john.harrington
Content: This deck is great but the bar charts don't have the same protocols.  Sometimes OPC is included, sometimes it is not, the same with Sparkplug.  I know you didn't write it, not bashing you.  This would be great if it was a bit more complete.  Comparing these protocols is not as straight forward.  OPC UA has a subscription capability where the client subscribes to tags on the OPC server.  The server typically polls the devices, because the devices do not support anything else but request response, but from server to client if the items were subscribed to then only changes are sent. OPC also typically batches publishes from multiple PLCs in a single packet, I believe MQTT does not do that, each individual topic payload is independently sent across the wire.  All that said, I am an advocate of MQTT with JSON payloads when publishing to the upper levels of the UNS.  HighByte Intelligence Hub make it possible for any protocol to be used when publishing, the target system typically has a preferred approach, IoT Core - MQTT, Tulip - REST, S3 - Files to their using their SDK, Kafka, and the list goes on.  The data structures and the protocols are more often than not defined by the software consuming the data.  Flexibility is required.

Author: suran23.
Content:
@aleem I would say the justification for UNS lies in enabling the autonomy and agility of individual plants without sacrificing larger enterprise initiatives. What does that mean? There are 3 key things that UNS will enable:
1. Drive corporate initiatives without interference: Feed data science and cloud initiatives without disrupting day-to-day workloads of the plant
2. Let Engineers be Engineers: Enable autonomy and agility in the plant to allow engineers to solve problems on their own terms.
3. Build a trustable data sources: Derive a single source of truth to feed shop floor agility and enable corporate initiatives.

Now onto contextualization. It's the What, When, How, Why that really makes the data insightful and actionable. This needs some amount of data correlation, joined analysis, and taking related aspects and data into consideration. You could do all of that in the cloud but it would also mean shooting your cloud cost out of the roof. Instead, contextualizing it and feeding contextualized data to applications and subscribers of your data can deliver faster time-to-value.

Data driven can be an after thought. Most plants need to know what's happening to my line right now. But even that needs more context and data trustability. Defining downtime differently across plants can have a big impact on overall OEE calculation. And that's only a simple example. Once again reiterating the importance of working from a single source of truth and a establishing a common namespace.

DataOps is a way to avoid opportunity cost. Piece meal approach could work but eventually fails to deliver on the autonomy and agility of plants. Afterall, if piecemeal would work, would Industry 4.0 or broader IIoT implementation remain such a challenge even after decades of these terms floating around? And if everything is hunky dory, why would anyone even be considering these solutions. Clearly, there is a need.

One thing I suspect is that it is just human nature, love of freedom of doing things in own way. I think it is always much harder to follow some standards and perform things in a specific way. Often standard requirements can be just not relevant to your specific use case. I think for that reason people is tend just to reject the whole standard specification, no matter how good it is or not so good. And I think that is completely valid and recpectable decision. Why you should follow some standard at the end. Do your own way, or invent another, supposedly better one. But this one can have the same result though. Very often new implementation can be free from disadvantages of the existing one, have new pros, but can have own cons too.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
Interesting quesiton.  I see Mulesoft now has a partner plugin for MQTT.  I'm curious how well this works.

iPaaS and IT-oriented middleware solutions work well as gateways and abstraction for IT applications.  They're not built for industrial data and the kinds of integration problems it poses.  The interfaces and scale are different in these worlds.  For these reasons, IT middleware can sometimes feel like a poor fit or incapable for use cases involving industrial data.

iPaaS might be used to synchronizing master data among ERP applications.  This might be integrating a few SaaS apps (HCM, FM, SCM, CRM).  Or, it might be integrating a few different business units.  This might be dozens of point to point connections.  Each node is sufficiently large and has an interface to encapsulate many dimensions (e.g., business units, customers, regions, cost centers, employees, products) of the enterprise.  To use an analogy, IT middleware is like translating vocabulary between two similar languages (e.g., Portuguese and Spanish).  It's for similar interfaces that were intended for a similar purpose.

A UNS may contain an abstraction of many hundreds or even thousands of nodes that may have data contextualized from other nodes.  The underlying interfaces in industrial data were not really designed for bulk data transactions or specific use cases beyond basic data acquisition or telemetry logging.  Invariably, OT data requires some sort of ETL.  UNS is great because it provides some level of abstraction, but an MQTT subscription is not really a method call and the IT middleware may need to do additional abstraction.  How well it can do this abstraction depends on the use case.  To use an analogy, industrial middleware is like interpreting a cave painting into a modern written language.  It's for dissimilar interfaces that were never intended to interoperate or even remotely aware each other's existence.

Author: rickbullotta
Content: ...except there's no easy or obvious way to allow your middleware stack to do on-demand reads of data from the UNS if it is MQTT based.  It will get a bit cumbersome if you end up having to deal with lots and lots of asynchronous stuff to interact with an MQTT broker.  It's fine for when a workflow or task is triggered by an MQTT subscription, but when you want to read data values from the UNS, it gets really awkward.  If you introduce a persistent datastore in the middle, then you introduce some more timing and async issues (e.g. the event was received by your middleware, but related data has not yet landed in the datastore).

Author: rickbullotta
Content: I'd like to see MQTT brokers offer a simple REST API for reading and writing/publishing topics.  As long as the topic is published from its source with the "retain" flag, this would be trivial.  I wrote a prototype of an extension for HiveMQ, for example, that can do that.  I assume the same could be possible with other brokers.  But I feel strongly that this should be built-in functionality.

Author: yasirtuncer
Content:
For the architects who are having a hard time convincing why we need broker technology, I will give you a real-life example from a technical point of view. 

There are a certain number of connections that Modbus TCP/IP or OPC UA etc. can support while several applications are trying to request information. Moreover, if you exceed this number then the applications will cannibalize the connection and you will get too many session errors. 

When we engaged this client their energy analyzers were already maxed out in terms of sessions due to several applications and slaves were connected. Another initiated session actually led to data loss for other applications, thus we transferred some of those connections to our broker and served to other applications. 
 
Always keep in mind the long game, nothing will remain as-is for manufacturers and the infrastructure, the architecture you select should support you throughout the journey.

Author: walker.reynolds
Content:
They do not understand UNS.

1. There is no integration strategy decision tree — that’s legacy thinking.  There is digital strategy, there is architecture, there are minimum technical requirements — there is an architect who ensures that all homogenous features are integrated in compliance with MTR.
2. UNS is single source of truth, semantic hierarchy, structure and events — it isn’t mutually exclusive to point to point integration — it engineers out p2p in most cases and augments in all others. 

Summary:

About 80% of all data operations use cases are covered with the native IIoT Protocol and infrastructure — about 20% are covered by point to point integrations using REST, HTTP, SQL et al.  The rule is — if any new data or information is generated with point to point then one or both of the nodes must publish the newly generated data/info to UNS.
Let me know if that clarifies — if not, I can shoot another video to cover this.  🙏

Author: akoscs
Content: It all comes down to semantics. Nowadays the protocols are not the biggest problem (if you do not have really old systems). Semantics is the bigger issue! After looking into HighByte and similar tools in detail, they are doing protocol conversion, yes, but there are many other solutions to that. They are, hovewer mixing in semantic mapping to the protocol conversion in an intuitive way. That bundle together brings the high (pun intended) added value. Standardization of data models are the only thing (currently) that helps with semantic interoperability and are extremly hard to standardize. The UNS takes "a leave it to the user" kind of stance, which will always rely on a user (programmer) implemented semantic mapping which will always fuel a need for HighByte like tools to increase productiivity and not make a SW dev project out of digitalisation on the side close to OT. OPC-UA has the companion spec (however good or bad, but at least is an effort in the right direction). STEP and STEP-NC did also take steps in this direction, but the underlying syntax is kind of confusing. Worked for STEP, kind of, did not work well for STEP-NC. AutomationML has (had?) no standardized semantics and...look how well that turned out... CanOpen has standardized semantics, Profinet also, Profibus also, EtherCAT borrows semantics from CANOpen and/or sercos, sercos has defined semantics, Modbus has no defined semantics (arguably it distinguishes I/Os and registers, but no application level semantics),. Protocols intended to be used by the manufacturere of the device (ie has control over both ends of the communication) like S7com and ADS have also no application level semantics. From the IT world, USB has defined semantics, RS-232 has not. If you take a look at how a browser displays information, the topmost layer which is interpreted, HTML, has defined semantics.

Author: marioishikawa
Content: I think the point is also that modeling is not easy, and if you do it wrong, you have a lot of technical debt. The same way for a standard. If you model in a way that will follow a standard, you do that at the risk of not being flexible for other or future approaches. And why does it matter? With the wrong model, all business rules get way more complicated than needed, and reports also become quite complex to do as the queries are no longer simple or intuitive as they could. In most cases, the simple queries are already hard to do from the perspective of the citizen developer. One thing I like about the UNS is that you can normalize information from different sources for the same asset with the same time. With that you are avoiding the trouble the citizen developers can have on their future dashboards. Also, ML and Data Scientist professionals usually spend a lot of time on data preparation. Some say 60%, some say more. One of the key reasons is that when it gets to this level, you are usually talking about someone that don't understand every single source of data and their data model. They don't know PLCs and their registers. So it is awesome for them if they can have a large table with not only production and state every minute (or less), but also even other information that will repeat a lot as they don't change so frequently, such as machine mode, if applicable, OEE, product family, machine type, operator, and so on. If you ever played with Power BI you can see how cool it is that the charts are interactive and their elements work as filters or path to drill down. If you have several different tables not properly linked such as with foreign keys, you will then spend a lot of time understanding how those tables can be linked, what exists in one and not in another and how to deal with it, etc etc.

Author: geoffnunan
Content:
ISA95 has low adoption because the original intent of the standard is solving a problem that few people or companies care deeply about. That is "Plug and Play" integration between COTS ERP and COTS MOM. Honestly who cares when in the 30 years of the standard, neither the ERP vendors or the MOM vendors have adopted the standard for integration.

ISA95 also has low adoption because Pub/Sub architectures are relatively new in Manufacturing, and DataHub architectures are even newer, but the standard schemas defined by Part 2 and 4 are well suited to defining the schemas that get published and subscribed, and even more suited to how you store all those messages in a data hub.

History should not be taken as an accurate prediction of the future

Author: walker.reynolds
Content:
Red models are the only models that need to be 'managed' and 'blue' models are tracked for quality and for potential promotion to red.  Lacking a schema registry is a problem, yes, but is currently managed with external services that monitor the broker namespaces and leverage regx for pattern matching.  This is why MQTT needs methods and or GraphQL plug in for querying the namespace without the need for external services.

It isn't difficult to manage if the external services are built correctly.  'Schema enforcement' outside of red models is completely unnecessary.  What matters is minimum technical requirements for OEMs and developers that enforce the rules for application.  It is imperative that citizen developers solve their problems in service of the orgs digital strategy, in the same infrastructure that the standardized business operates.  This is how digital infrastructure/solutions/applications remain agile and adjust with the business' needs.

Content:
We have a big but probably dumb question on the UNS:

With multiple systems feeding the UNS (ERP, MES, SCADA, CRM, etc) -> is the data typically segregated by ERP, MES, SCADA within the namespace, or does this defeat the "unified" part of the UNS?

We are discussing work orders for example, and some team members feel strongly that an update to a work order made by ERP would have to land in an ERP section, and a separate change made by MES must land in an MES section etc, and so we are unsure if they (ERP and MES etc) can safely independently update information about a work order in a single topic.

My feeling is that these separate systems would be feeding a single UNS, and the segregation of systems within the UNS is incorrect, but we're stuck on this.

I interpret a line in the HiveMQ UNS fundamentals book that a goal of the UNS is to: "..map namespaces from disparate industrial systems into one standardized topic structure."  as meaning not separate MES, SCADA, ERP topics, but a single company -> site -> area -> etc type structure, but could see the possibility of interpreting this differently due to the wording of "mapping namespace from disparate systems" possibly meaning separate MES, SCADA, ERP topics and so am seeking clarification.

It seems that the UNS should be broken down by an *enterprise* hiearchy, and as the various systems don't represent an enterprise structure, they don't belong in the UNS. And that the UNS is a single interface for the digital system - if any of the systems were completely removed or changed out, the UNS can continue completely independent.

Author: ricardo_maestas
Content:
@dave mays I'll take a crack at this... From my perspective (IT background, done Ignition implementations, new to MQTT/Sparkplug)...

A benefit of SparkplugB is simplification when it comes to connecting to devices at the edge. In my projects I am used to connecting to an edge device, usually with OPC UA (sometimes Modbus), and starting with dozens of  unlabeled "tags" or memory registers. With SpB, when connecting an Edge device, it will prompt for broker IP, some parameters for the topic namespace (Group ID, Edge Node ID), and boom — ~~values will start writing to the broker~~ (Kudzai's video shows this in action: https://youtu.be/eIp3FdQYFnQ?si=Mtfk75RaxlwjtDX4&t=1597). On the consuming side, if the subscriber supports SpB, it effectively "automatically" discovers all the values in the SpB message payload and displays them, eliminating the steps required with OPC UA and Modbus devices to label what the values are.

A DataOps intermediary can be fed with these values, and re-publish them into an ISA95 topic structure. This solves the issue of getting SpB to play nicely with UNS.

Speed is an interesting topic to bring up in the context of SpB. On the one hand, yes it does have lightweight packets and is efficient over the wire, but this is more of a side-effect than the intended-effect for the problem it is trying to solve. 

MQTT is already RBE, therefore SpB also is.

As of today, I don't think there is any replacement for the speed and logic provided by running programs natively on PLC's. Maybe there is a version of the future where edge programs/logic is executed on IT systems for time-sensitive operations, and maybe SpB will have a role in that, but I don't think it is the wisest way to go today.

Author: zeratall
Content:
Centeral or Master Data Models, are often amazing tools for homogenous architectures or architectures that are somewhat rigid and don't change often. But when you have a very dynamic architecture, or a very heterogenous one with lots of different domains, the data model becomes the botlteneck for scaling. With Distributed Domain Ownership, you are still enforcing understanding of the data (contextualization), but you are giving the freedom for the different domains to define their own data models, that get "mapped" back to an enterprise ontology. Thereby still providing the relationship/edges to map data between domain and enterprise, but giving the freedom to the manufacturing floor so the data meets their consumer needs. Additionally, decentralized data ownership pairs well with federated data governance which is often a requirement for many large  enterprise org structures.

The downside of the decenteralized domain data ownership approach is that it's often much more complex to implement, instead of a standard schema that must be enforced, now you need to establish and maintain all the relationships between domain models and the enterprise ontology. This often means more nodes in the architecture like a graphDB, etc. Which is more complexity to maintain long term.

Author: geoffnunan
Content:
This is a pipe-dream if your approach is to simply use an MQTT broker as your "UNS"
Mostly, that's because MQTT lacks a schema registry that defines the messages that you intend to publish and subscribe to, and because MQTT clients lack the ability to "Acknowledge after processing" rather than "Acknowledge on receipt"
The UNS is a SCADA centric architecture that is a good 1st step towards getting to the diagram you draw, but you will also require step 2,3,4 and 5.

Author: geoffnunan
Content:
Assuming Step 1 is publishing the current state of things to an MQTT broker
Step 2 would be publishing 'Events' rather than state.
Step 3 would be moving to an 'Orchestration' pattern rather than a 'Choreography' pattern, which will require schema enforcement and "Ack after processing"
Step 4 would be storing the events in a central repository and making it all available through a simple to use API
Step 5 would be to enable innovation to occur more rapidly by using low/no code solutions on top of that easy to use API.

Maybe your experience is different, but in my experience the actual ownership is with a few key people, experts in data modelling, who are closely colaborating on data use-cases with domain experts. Not all models have to follow a central meta-model or a central standard, but they have to be able to map certain elements of the data model to the enterprise use-cases. Especially this mapping is very problematic, in my experience, if you let the domain experts take ownership.  Furthermore, having similar models for the different domains if the use-cases allow it would be very benficial form a productivity poitn of view. Distributed ownership in many cases takes this advantage away.

Author: zeratall
Content: With your definition, "*Not all models have to follow a central meta-model or a central standard, but they have to be able to map certain elements of the data model*", that is the very definition of Decentralized Domain Data Ownership, aka Domain Models being defined by the domain. You are correct those models are a collaboration between data modeling experts, data governance experts, and domain mfg experts, but they are unique to the domain which is where the "Domain Ownership" comes in.

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content: It’s a bit hard to discuss this on a very generic level as certain things depend on your specific architecture. You can set up a UNS highly available and very secure. For example when we build an IIoT platform for our customers we typically have a MQTT broker cluster per plant and one in the (private) cloud. The plant clusters connect to cluster in the cloud from the inside to the outside via a MQTT bridge. PLCs are typically connected via a machine connectivity solution like litmus edge to the MQTT broker cluster in the plant. Both the clusters in the plants and the one in the cloud run on highly available Kubernetes clusters (which are fully automated based on a GitOps approach, and constantly monitored). If the costs are accepted we also distribute them over multiple availability zones. If the PLCs are on separate subnets in the production network than the Kubernetes cluster in the plant and the security department does not allow to open firewall ports between the Kubernetes plant cluster and the PLCs then we would put additional edge devices running single node Kubernetes (e.g. k3s) and the machine connectivity on the subnets of the PLCs. Then the machine connectivity solution connects to the PLC and connects from the inside to the outside via MQTT to the plant broker. Due to the costs of this I would advise against this approach as all these edge devices need to be bought, installed and managed. It’s always better to have just the central cluster and run the machine connectivity solution and the MQTT broker there. Alternatively you can also make the PLCs connect directly via MQTT to the plant cluster (has some disadvantages and is sometimes not even an option).

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content: And regarding security: When we build solutions like this they are typically more secure and highly available then anything else running on the shopfloor (where you can often find things like Windows XP IPCs with auto login with admin rights, operators watching YouTube via IE6, everything manually installed, software that never gets updated or in the best case via USB sticks, PLCs with well known critical vulnerabilities, no monitoring and alerting, no security scanning …).

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content: In the end the security level depends on how much effort and money you are willing to spend and what’s reasonable.

Content:
We use schema definitions for the payloads being published to topics to introduce some type-safety which helps a lot. We also use the "Orchestration" pattern rather than the "Choreography" pattern which provides a central place to check payload schema, trace the information flow, handle errors, etc.
Comparing to public and private variables in code, it's only the public variables that should be published to a broker, they are effectively your contract with other services. The AsyncAPI specification helps a lot with keeping things under control. https://www.asyncapi.com/

Ask first the question "Does this make sense outside my private context?" Often if the data is related to a business event, rather than an internal system event, the answer should be Yes.

Author: vaughnturner
Content:
Walker Reynolds
ACL, access control lists by functional namespace.  The data that is shared is mapped to a functional namespace -- it can either be broken now by topics or the endpoint can be a single topic with a JSON payload that they consume.  You use ACL to grant access to the topic or namespace, you give them a cert to access the broker.

I'll take a crack at answering your questions, but Walker may very well come in and correct me. At a High Level a UNS is a structure that is bringing everything to together but more importantly making it easier for humans to understand the context of the data, that is the semantic part of it. There are different approaches' for how you structure that data walker talks about ISA 95 a lot so Enterprise/Site/Area/Line/Cell, but within each of that physical representation(lets use Cell for example) we may have different "types" of data for that specific physical topic, and we may want to structure and organize the data within that physical topic so its easier to understand. Functional Namespace is typically going to be your actual functional data so things like OT Telemetry, etc. Definitional Namespace is typically things like a description of the machine, or where its located, etc. a Informative Namespace could contain things like OEE, and metrics, or a link to a dashboard. 
Be mindful a UNS is really drawing on the idea of distributed stucture, so you don't have to stop at this level you could keep drilling down, for example in functional namespace, you might have a OT Namespace, a MES Namespace, and a ERP Namespace, etc.

Content: From my point of view it's more of an ecosystem capability issue than anything else.  Bi-directional & request response can still be done over MQTT. When we execute an MES transaction in automation we don't stop the automation waiting for a response. We allow the process (sync) to carry on and allow for async processes (MES) to complete. If it's really bad then we knowingly break/stop things on the automation side to recover but at some point that is unavoidable depending on the issue.

Content:
This is exactly what I've been thinking about too, and having similar background in software engineering.
Asked this in the #mqtt channel the other week. https://discord.com/channels/738470295056416930/1166016853991235594/1179764480570298408

We have a local mqtt broker per edge pc that would have a part of the UNS related to the machine/cell it's serving. 
So far we've only done some basic data aq. from PLCs and by different means getting it through a middleware (PLC to MQTT integration) into a flat MQTT UNS structure, like `corp/site/area/machine/plc/measurement1` etc. These topics are the relayed upstream to an Azure EventHub.
Now, our next thing to tackle at the edge is to relay events to/from MES (actually ERP, which holds quite some MES functionality). These signals are delivered through other means up/down to the edge pc's MQTT broker. However the asynchronous nature of a pub/sub broker is a bit challenging as our first plan was to use the flat UNS topic structure such as  `corp/site/area/machine/erp/ordernumber`, `corp/site/area/machine/erp/orderlinenumber` etc.  and when the PLC reports the machine has started (boolean rising edge) we could see what the current order number it's working on. However, this won't work as there can be comm drops and what not causing these to be out of sync. One would also need to keep track of the state somewhere as the data is scattered among multiple topics. That's why we're now more looking into sending all data in a topic with a payload that contains all necessary information for the "transaction" and lift some of these bits to the UNS structure.

Any good advice along the way are more than welcome 🙂

Author: zeratall
Content:
Based on reading the comments above, I think the issue is everyone has differing ideas/definitions on what a UNS is. 

I agree with @GeoffNunan, with the considerations he brought up. Those things need to be in the architecture in one form or another, and @RickBullotta  I agree with your comments as well, there are many views of the data/events/functions, that we need to be able to represent.

However, that being said my interpretation of UNS differs slightly.__** I view it less as a standalone entity and more as an integral component within a larger ecosystem. **__

I view the UNS akin to something almost like an API Gateway in MSA - essential for organizing and structuring messages/events, but not the sole player. For example, in MSA, while the API Gateway receives and structures messages and events, it’s complemented by other services like orchestrators, databases, caching systems, and authentication services for a well-rounded architecture. 

Similarly, UNS provides the foundational framework, but it requires additional nodes/components, such as graph for diverse data representations and models, datahubs, different datastores, SCADA, IIoT Platform, etc. Embracing this approach of distributed architecture allows for a dynamic, scalable architecture where UNS is a key piece, but not the entire puzzle.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
Setting aside the limitations of UNS, this is where I think it's useful to have a more open-ended discussion about what kind of events one is looking to historize or store.

Historians, at least for me, generally conjure up a very "industry 3.0" way of thinking about data.  It's just name-value tags being logged from the SCADA.  It's a "dump" of telemetry data and not information.  Sometimes this is relevant if one is a process engineer or data scientist exploring data.  But often, it's generally not ready for mainstream operational use.  It's usually logged without much context.  It burdens the user with turning this data into information.  They're just as likely to export the data in a spreadsheet to do something useful with it.

I think it's more useful to think of persisting events as complex objects.  Imagine an executive summary of downtime or quality events with their potential contributing factors including more than PLC/SCADA data.  This is far more useful to a user than a bunch of alarms they must root cause in a sea of timeseries data.  Human beings like to manage-by-exception and solve problems.  They don't like to sift through data.

This is not a bash against a historians.  They have their place.  But, for many, historians have not delivered on the vision of transforming operations with data.  They have modeling issues, interface issues, cost issues, etc.  Most of all, I think their issues stem from a poor data strategy.  There's more to an industrial organization than just raw telemetry from instrumentation or PLCs.

Author: vaughnturner
Content:
Yes, a UNS is not MQTT protocol or Broker, It doesn't have to be built around that protocol, it could be others like AMQP, or DNP3 for example. 

The UNS isn't a piece of technology but a comprehensive architectural approach. That organizes your data into a semantic hierarchy following ISA95 pt. 2.  It focuses on how different components in your ecosystem interact and communicate. This architecture ensures that data  can flow seamlessly across various devices, systems, and platforms.

UNS serves as the backbone of IIoT ecosystems. It's the single source of truth for all data and information in your business that connects all the different elements of an industrial internet network, from sensors and machines to data analytics platforms and user interfaces.

Author: ravil1
Content:
I don't think getting historical data via MQTT subscription is good idea. For some predefined short period, with predefined resolution (so number of values is well known) - maybe. But usually I guess queries to historian can vary, for different time period, and probably raw data as well processed data, like minimum, maximum for period, with reduced interval (downsampled), or maybe interpolated, etc. Not easy to create topic structure for all combinations, and it could be too mush load for the broker as well as for some  subscribers to handle raw data.
Probably better to have historian separate, and in MQTT provide some metadata describing how to get history for that topic value. If this is SQL database, then ID of the variable, if it is InfluxDB, bucket, measurement, tags, and field, etc. And then the application should be smart enough to get this metadata , connect to the historian, and read historical data.

All of these problems that are mentioned are problems that I have not had. I mean not that they aren’t real, it’s just that I’m generally focused on what I can do TODAY with solutions (preferably open source or OTS) that are available NOW, that also doesn’t cost a gazillion dollars and doesn’t require me to go five years back on school to learn.

Author: jon.forbord
Content:
Now, understand I’m not saying UNS is perfect, what I’m saying is that it’s a meaningless statement. UNS is a strategic approach to architecture, data and information, with the elusive events at the center of the universe, for industry. 

I liken it to Test Driven Development. Take a team of developers and say that we are now going to change from designing software the old way, into doing Test Driven Development! Now to succeed with this, the shift in mindset and how you approach solving problems is MUCH MUCH MUCH more important than which framework you use to run your test driven development or which programming language you use. There’s probably specific frameworks that are better for big companies or big teams, and there’s probably features in those frameworks that are essential to some teams. But the true value of TDD is how this change in methodology changes the output. 

The same can be said for the UNS. The change in people’s mindset is much more important than anything technological.. 

 In its essence it’s an event driven approach, (although not to be confused with common EDA patterns for microservice archs). Would you ever say EDA is for SCADA systems only?! Would you say EDA is flawed because there’s no schema registry?! Now this starts getting ridiculous.. 

So to your question, if not mqtt, then what? I’m not aware of technology that offers all we could ever want from a central hub, but there sure is vendors ready to solve some of these problems with mqtt or tech in general, with their solution/stack of open source, which you can buy, usually at a gazillion dollars.. 

GraphQL-federation looks interesting (queryable and subscribable), but I don’t know much about it yet.

Author: jon.forbord
Content: And while I’m at it. I think Walker is also confusing people when he says, UNS is the single source of truth. This make people jump preemptively to the conclusion UNS is the single interface. This isn’t necesaarily the case. When he says UNS is the single source of truth, it really means the source of truth as much as the events in an Event-Driven-Architecture is the source of truth. Some consider the event log the source of truth, or the database in system of ownership for the event as the source of truth. But the UNS is the source of truth for all data, as any database, record of history etc is populated with the events from the UNS.

Author: jon.forbord
Content:
You can have Kafka in a UNS architecture. In fact we decided against adding Kafka, because we concluded we didn’t need another moving piece to the puzzle, yet. 

I really enjoy fireships YouTube videos. He has one that should be mandatory for developers:

https://youtu.be/Sxxw3qtb3_g?si=9xuaF9adNhnvYONj

I think most of us are prone to over-engineer rather than under-engineer. It feels much safer to over-engineer. It takes some guts and skill to aim for good enough, but to keep the door open for the future. 

One aspect I really like about the UNS is that it is a foundation to build upon. It can scale up and down. It doesn’t give you everything you need, but I truly believe it’s a foundation you can build upon and scale, regardless of your scale ( I mean there’s always a limit, but you get the idea). 

I’m actually 💯 % sure that my approach to UNS will not scale beyond a certain size in some dimension, but if we had needed that scale, I would’ve engineered it differently. And if we need that scale in the future, we hopefully can add elements to handle that scale and not have to clean up too much technical debt. 

Now, don’t think for a second this means that your original statement has any meaning. It’s nonsensical and meaningless, and to some extent ignorant and misleading. UNS ≠ MQTT.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
Model to the needs of the consumers (e.g., apps, services, users).  Industry 4.0 is not about building yet another SCADA or historian.  It's about more than process control.  Unless people have them memorized and know what they mean, leave the cryptic OT identifiers and naming conventions behind.  Consider creating complex objects with metadata that makes sense to someone other than the person who designed or programmed the production process.  It should be intuitive enough that someone can go into an application, understand what is happening, and make use of the data.

Also, consider that there are multiple layers of context in an enterprise.  If the context is not consumable by process control nodes, that context can be layered on above it.  Additionally, this will evolve over time as new use cases arise and the organization introduces more nodes.  It's best to do it a way such that it can be changed without significant resources.

I personally don't like verbose tag names.  It makes user experience in visualization and analytics awkward.  It can be hard to understand and burdens the consumer with parsing/sorting identifiers.  I'd rather have multiple attributes to use for filtering.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
I also endorse the view of trying to build some base context in the PLC.  Working with a raw PLC namespace can have a lot of uncontrolled dependencies.

Yeah, it's not not always possible to modify PLC code, but it reinforces to those working in the silo of process control that this just isn't "their" data, but data for the whole enterprise.  A UDT can function as not just a data structure, but as an interface for external consumers / data infrastructure.  It's valuable to have a well-defined interface for ingress and egress on an asset.  It prevents a programmer from introducing content that, at worst, makes sense to no one but themselves or, at best, requires an IDE open to read the descriptions.

For example, suppose tags are renamed or if another sensor or drive is added to an asset.  If they want to be lazy with their new logic and tags (e.g., autobit7, autobit8, autobit9), they can.  But, they must map in the new content into UDTs that external consumers rely on.  If it's a legacy PLC or specialized controller (e.g., cnc, robot, motion) with only registers, this work can be done in the dataops platform.  When it's clear what the end outcome is, it helps discourage practices that incur technical debt.  Introducing or modifying data and assuming it's someone else's problem is not sustainable.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
It depends on the interface of the PLC and if the data structure can be modified.  In many real world, there are practical limitations to be truly “edge driven” on all assets.  While it’s really cool to have stuff magically show up in a SCADA, it depends on PLC code being governed by a process and not a controls engineer improvising their way through an acceptance test or downtime event.  It assumes that it’s possible to acquire industrial assets that don’t deviate from a technology spec, the PLC program isn’t garbage (e.g., missing documentation, cryptic tag names, missing descriptions), and the program can be easily modified/maintained.  In reality, all greenfield is brownfield because machine builders recycle old designs and their engineering processes don’t efficiently manage change.

I suppose there are few ways of going about it:

A) Lazily publish the whole set or subset of raw PLC tags into an edge namespace
B) Use OPC UA to “cherry-pick” tags of interest
C)  Create a UDT or contiguous block of memory objects for aliasing or “mapping out” to the external consumer. Consume over OPC UA or MQTT.

I don’t believe that the PLC should be the source of truth for asset models.  I believe this is this the domain of DataOps.  Models need to be able to be created and modified quickly.  Their definitions will be influenced by applications, users, use cases, and evolving digital maturity.  The cost of changing them needs to be as close to zero as possible.  PLCs, at their core, are process control nodes.  They’re designed to reliably run a physical process for decades.  While there is exciting DevOps technology and methodologies slowly making its way to the PLC world, they’re still not easy to change.

I think the most important thing is that the data in PLCs, whether natively or externally (e.g., OPC UA Server, MQTT Broker), needs to be browsable and reasonably intuitive.  Garbage in, garbage out.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
I personally like a two-tier approach.

1) Ideally, a PLC programmer should “map out” data into a UDT or contiguous block.  It doesn’t necessarily have to follow a rigid structure or standard.  But, it should be labeled and documented.  Think of it as like an “OT” API for an asset.  It's not an asset model, but a basis for one.  This provides separation from process control but also indicates there are dependencies for external consumers.  It prevents someone from unknowingly creating a breaking change.  With native protocols, it can also be more performant reading from a condensed block of registers.

The best example I ever saw of this was by a machine builder that actually built out set of registers and a corresponding HMI sub-menu with a table defining the map.  It listed everything that was in an RFQ/spec as well as what they thought was useful (e.g., process values referenced in maintenance manual, other HMI menus).  Even though it had a native protocol that was not browsable, it was a breeze to load the registers into an OPC UA Server gateway and move on.

2) Use OPC UA subscriptions to consume the “map” associated with the PLC.  This allows for easy and flexible abstraction into asset models via DataOps.  This approach enables a balance of centrally-orchestrated data acquisition, report-by-exception, data governance, security, etc.  Everything beyond this is MQTT (e.g., UNS, events for cloud services), HTTP (e.g., apps, cloud services), and SQL (databases).  Above SCADA, most services don't really support OPC UA or Sparkplug.  In practice, more time is spent engineering around them than making use of them.

While this two-tier approach may seem redundant and may not possible in every environment, I think this approach is the most sustainable.  The first step decouples process control from data acquisition.  The second step decouples data acquisition from data modeling.  It reflects the reality of PLCs and that data consumed by users will evolve over time.

Content: Hi vikan, you're completely right. The technology is not yet ready for that, but on my opinion the work is almost done and there are a lot of advantages there. I've created a diagram to clarify my idea and to comment your points. (1) SCADA, PLC, and any other MQTT Ready device or system can publish easily since they do it on the broker, and any interested MQTT ready system can subscribe that topic. But, in addition, that topic is mapped to a semantic layer where a higher level of management, combination, adaptation and governance can be performed. Once there, that information can be explored, discovered or self-consumed or even shared through a data service. As you can see on my schema  (the right side has been added by me over a Denodo's architecture schema). Really Denodo has not a MQTT connector or mapper from topics to views and from views to topics as far as I know (I don't know if there is any other DV platform that includes it). (3) Good point. There will be much work here to auto-generate raw views on the semantic layer when new topics appear, but I find it relatively approachable. I think Data Virtualization approach brings some advantages catalyzing some UNS integration problems such as historical data access or giving to not MQTT ready systems an easier way to publish (through the data service as you can see in the example).  Data federation allows every system to keep its data, minimizing the information flow and bandwidth requirements. For sure, this approach is not completely tied and has its consistencies to work on but I think empowers the UNS concept and makes it more corporate.

Author: jpmoniz
Content: Well still evaluating what works the best.  Most would think a simple MQTT transmission client would work the best but there are issues even with that.  It all depends on what the structure look like that you are publishing.  For example if I try to publish a complex equipment namespace with Transmission you end up with a ton of overhead in Transmission tags.  This is due to the Group/Node/Device construct.  If you have Equipment structures with deep levels of nested UDT's  Then you can generate a lot of overhead tags due to transmission wanting to turn everything in the structure into a device and then creating transmission client tags for that device.  This is where I think HB may be better for this just pulling from Ignition OPC-UA but I haven't really given it too much time.    As an Example I have one asset being published right now that generates 12000 topics and growing as we continue to semantically model it. A Typical topic looks something like this. Area/Line/Functions/Mandrel Thrust Block 1/Motion/Axis/MotorOvertemperatureFLFault.  I replaced the area and line with generic terms for obvious reasons.  At scale I dont think the centralized ignition method is the way to go. depending on complexity of data structures transmission overhead can scale out of control. This is why I have a ton of interest in the Litmus edge and Hive MQ edge brokers. HB belongs in that conversation as well. The use case of processing and modeling at the source is growing stronger in my head. I just waiting for these edge products to mature a bit more so the needed functionality is there.

Author: tomashidalgo0847
Content:
This sounds good, but what is the technology behind the UNS balloon? Just a MQTT Broker? I think that should be much more than that. For sure, data federation and a pub/sub communication are fundamental pillars on this model, I’m OK with that, but, I find Data Governance and Data Integration lacks here. This cannot be an IT/OT real converged model and a real single source of truth without considering: 

DATA AWARENESS FEATURES
1)    Metadata Management: Provide information about the structure, format, location, and quality of data without having to access the actual datasets.
2)    Data Discovery: For allowing users to search and browse a data catalog to discover relevant datasets.
3)    Data Lineage: Provide information about the origin and transformation history of the data.
4)    Collaboration: Allow users to annotate and share insights about specific datasets.
5)    Access and Security: Provide information about data access permissions and security measures.

DATA OBSERVABILITY FEATURES, enforce data reiability.
1)    Monitoring and Logging: provide logging information about data errors, anomalies, and any issues that may arise.
2)    Quality Metrics: ensuring that data meets predefined standards (accuracy, completeness, consistency, …).
3)    Alerting and Notifications: provide alerting mechanisms that notify data teams when issues or anomalies are detected.
4)    Performance Monitoring: Ensure that data is processed within acceptable timeframes.

Author: tomashidalgo0847
Content:
DATA INTEGRATION FEATURES, assure open connectivity (open source is different from open architecture).
1)    Connectivity: easily connect to a wide range of data sources and enable publishing for easy sharing not only with an MQTT client also via standard interfaces like SQL, JSON, REST, and GraphQL APIs. 
2)    Flexibility: adapts to a wide range of use case requirements, from real-time federation to selective materialization.
3)    Data abstraction Ability to represents all data assets in an abstracted form (semantic model), decoupled from the source systems that store the data.
4)    Security: A fine-grained security policies that apply to any data and any access method.

DATA AVAILABILITY FEATURES, Ensure that data is accessible when needed. A “Single source of truth” is also a “Single point of failure”.
1)    Infrastructure Reliability: The reliability of the underlying IT infrastructure, including servers, storage systems, and networks has to be enforced.
2)    High Availability Architecture: This may involve using load balancing, clustering, and failover mechanisms to ensure that applications and services remain accessible even if one component fails.
3)    Monitoring and Alerting: Implementing monitoring tools allows organizations to track the health and performance of their systems in real-time.
4)    Scalability: Scalable architectures can handle increased workloads without sacrificing performance, ensuring that data remains available as the organization's needs evolve.

Author: sparkylarks
Content:
While I agree with @Jon Forbord , I do want to know what people are doing so here is how one unhinged community member is doing it.
For a system with and Existing ERP and Scheduler, Orders are created throughout the day and the schedule is updated  at the start of each day. and sometime more frequently. 

So when an order is changed in the ERP that Data is posted to a XML file that is read in and posted to the ERP with a Single payload with all the PO information.

When the Schedule is released, the Entire Schedule is published, to a XML file that read by Ignition Every 15 minutes

The data is then parrsed by the MES and consumed as needed.

When a Job is started on a machine, a subset of the Job and Schedule information is published to the Machine topic in the traditional Ent/Site/line/Unit hierarchy. so to is the information for Next Job. 

Initially we used a JDBC connector to query the ERP every 15 minutes to look for Jobs that had been modified in the last 15 minutes and return them, and then published each job as above.

WE also publish the Material dat from the ERP in a pauload per material, where a XML is cretated when the MAterial Master record is updated.

I'll answer slightly differently. No a full history does not belong in the UNS, as others have pointed out the historian should be a node in it. But if you have clients that want specific aggregated data, let's say a plot of production output over the last 30 days. That absolutely should be published into the UNS (in the correct location based on ISA 95 Part 2) so that all consumers get the same data.

Author: rickbullotta
Content: There is no "predefined schema for the necessary back and forth" in MQTT or Sparkplug.  None. Also, it requires some ugly hacks to (maybe) ensure that the response gets sent to the correct requestor, and even more hacks if you need to handle a multi-part response (which HTTP handles quite well).  I've actually coded something very much like this - and using topics for responses is NOT the way to go.  Request/response needs to be associated with the *connection* (socket, websocket, etc).  Also needs a formal pattern for error handling as well as successful responses.  Again, all dealt with via HTTP quite well.  I've built software routing to enable request/response over TCP, UDP, and websockets as part of the "Always On" protocol we had in ThingWorx.  And there's a whole other level of complexity when you want to scale this across multiple servers and route it across multiple tiers (e.g. a user at Site "A" wants to make a request/response call to Site "B", and there are brokers at each site and in the cloud/data center).

Author: sparkylarks
Content:
John, I do use Line and Cell, but sometimes I have small Machines there IT is a Line of 1 Cell so it can get a bit confusing.
I like  your  approach here and I do something very similar, 
Here are some of the differences, but not necessarily improvements

The Lines I tend to work with have 1 or 2 PLCs. so ERP and MES Data on a given line aren't different from Cell to Cell. 
On a automotive live or in a steel processing facility that might be different.
And that is important, the UNS structure should suit the business.

 I Do not have the MES and ERP namespaces at a Line Level, 
I normally have an ERP namespace  at the Plant Level( or Area in a larger Plant), and the ERP would publish the data there.
the MES would Publish most of the Data to the Line, into a MES namespace at line level, so Current Scheduled Job, Next Job, Avail, Quality.....
But some Aggregate Data might be published into a MES namespace at Plant or Area Level
When the MES is doing scheduling that tends to be a Plant MES level

I don't use Edge  as a description much, Edge Data( to me from the PLC SCAD or HMI) is published to the relevant Line or Cell level, most of it is is Cell but information about the Job Running or recipes is often Line.

But I would often also use a RAW name space( at Line or Cell Level) to publish all the data from the Edge, and keep the UNS for Contextualised Data.
So where I am counting pulses🙄 the pulse goes into the Raw namespace, but the Count goes into the Cell Name Space.

Author: ravil1
Content:
Familiar use case with querying of the historical data. 
This is well thought while ago in OPC UA. For example, given historical data can be huge, when data for a long range of time is requested. Option maxRows (numValuesPerNode in OPC UA) limits the number of returned values. If there is more data, then so so-called continuationPoint returned by the server allows us to continue getting the next portion of data. The same is used when browse results are returned. This allows to transfer of large data reliably, without overflowing transport protocol data buffers. 
I am not sure how this kind of task would be implemented over MQTT. The publisher should transfer some portion of the data, and then wait for the response from the subscriber when it has been received, and then continue the next portion, etc. MQTT was not originally designed for this kind of communication pattern. The publisher by design is not aware of who are the subscribers and what they want.  I don't think impossible, but not trivial.

Author: mparris
Content:
The Github issue #441 is to specify a generic method() capability.

Within this capability would allow a client to BROWSE a node for what commands it offers.  Within those commands, a client would also be able to inspect the number of parameters that should be included for that method, and the expected datatypes for each parameter, along with the name (and description?) of each of the input parameters.  A Sparkplug method function would also allow a client to know what datatype will be returned to it (if any).  This all pre-supposes a common command design pattern that was mentioned above by @RickBullotta.

Author: mparris
Content:
With Sparkplug today, a client cannot even determine which metrics are "commands/methods", which are read-only metrics, and which are read-write metrics.

Browsing a node is just a flat list of names.  And once the names are there, you only know the data type of the metric.  No return value is possible to acknowledge that the command was successful (received by the node, which is different than an MQTT ACK if considering QoS).

Simple example of a "method" is a reboot command.  An input parameter could be the number of seconds the node should wait to reboot.

(yuk)  Should it be a single string metric, but what's the basic syntax for this string to convey the structure of the parameters? 

ETC

Author: tomashidalgo0847
Content: I still don't understand what really strong data typing means. As I explained a few days ago, I've implemented a request/response fully typed mechanism using Sparkplug B 3.0. It's a matter of defining in the receiver node a CommandX Request Template (tCommandXRequest) containing as many metrics as parameters the command needs, and a CallbackID field (unique identifier) to be replicated later by the receiver node in the response message. An instance of the tCommandXRequest template will be published by the sender in the .../NCMD/CommandXRequest topic of the receiver node when launching a command. The response is also conceived as a template (tCommandXResponse) and contains a CallbackID metric and as many other metrics as needed in the response to a CommandX Request. You can include for example a result code, a result  message, and even a Dataset metric if you want to return structured data like as could be a database query result. The node which received the command, after processing it, generates an instance of the response template (tCommandXResponse) and publish it in the topic .../NDATA/CommandXResponse setting before the CallbackID metric value to the one the sender wrote in the command request. This will allow the sender, subscribed to that topic, to know that is a response for its command. That is. Is not an very ellegant or canonical solution but it works for synchronous and asynchronous commands, and It's fully typed. Every node in the network is aware of command request and response structure since are published  as templates in the .../NBIRD topic of the receiver. A problem with this approach  is that every sender receives allways any response generated by the receiver and has to use the CallbackID field to discard foreign responses. I look forward for a better solution or smarter  implementation on Sparkplug 4.0 but, by the moment, I'm using this technique and works fine enought.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
Yeah, Sparkplug doesn't aggregate well.  Its limitations lead to unwieldy metric payloads that burden the consumers with work to use the data.  It's easy to find oneself spending more time engineering around Sparkplug than using it.
 
Here’s a few observations how HighByte and Ignition users are addressing this:
 
**A) Use OPC UA instead**
Ignition can expose its namespace over OPC UA.  This works especially well if most of the data are tags coming from PLCs.  HighByte can connect to this as well as create subscriptions to enable a report-by-exception communication pattern.  Working with individual name-value pairs can be easier and more flexible than parsing through a SCADA namespace crammed into Sparkplug payloads.  It can also help improve scale and deployment through templating, parameterizing, and tying together inputs.  From there, they’ll leverage all the modeling and data engineering tooling in HighByte to govern the UNS.  Ignition, through the MQTT Engine module, can subscribe to this modeled and contextualized data.
**B) Transform Sparkplug**
Another option some take is to simply use the MQTT Transmission module to publish out via Sparkplug and transform it outside of Ignition.  This eliminates the need for tag change scripts.  HighByte users will subscribe to the topic and transform it to a usable namespace with a Pipeline transform.  This is the approach Walker took in one of his videos.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
**C) Move Ignition up in the architecture**
For users that already have connectivity sorted out (e.g., OPC server gateway, native IIoT support on devices) and they’re not doing “traditional” SCADA things (e.g., process control supervision, dedicated HMI), they may find Ignition might be more useful in a place higher up in the stack.  They may not want Sparkplug to be the core of their data infrastructure.  They find it imposes too many limitations on the interoperability with nodes outside of Ignition (e.g., PI, AWS, Azure, Influx, Snowflake, Databricks, SAP, Tulip).  They desire more architectural flexibility.  They’ll deploy HighByte at the edge to model  and enrich data going into the broker.  They’ll also deploy HighByte elsewhere, where necessary, to aid nodes consuming from the broker.  Some have gone as far to leverage config scripts, as a head start, to migrate all the OPC UA tags and UDTs.  They’ll use Ignition in the architecture for HMI, alarming, MES, custom frontline apps, etc.  This approach works well for multi-site architectures with many Ignition gateways.

Author: ravil1
Content:
Haha. "anti-UNS people", cool term!
To me this is just an architectural approach. Not something completely new and revolutionary.  Hub & Spoke term, like a synonim, for example used decades long. And as often it is associated with MQTT broker as a Hub, just broker technology by definiton assumes that it will be implemented this way, all your data being accessed by central access point - broker. And unifying, standartizing namespace is not brand new, for example it is defined by ISA95 taken by UNS concept as a base. 
I think it was marketed by Walker and become a buzzword in the Industry 4.0 domain now. And more and more vendors realize that actually what they do can fall into this term. Particularly, I think that ProsysOPC UA Forge actually easily can be considered as a UNS implementation, but not with MQTT as a single used protocol. Although it does use MQTT, main data collection channel is done via OPC UA .
So I don't think there are "anti-UNS people" here.
But, speaking of OPC UA, probably there are "anti-OPC UA people" here.

Author: sparkylarks
Content:
UNS is not the same as MTP and OPAF and OPC-UA and Profinet and Ethercat
OPC-UA Profinet and Ethercat are communication protocols.
With a UNS you use protocols within it but it is not a protocol. I maintain that you can use OPCUA as your technology for a UNs, others disagree but regardless, AMQP, MQTT and DNS all certainly can be used and they have documents that describe how to use them

MTP , is an approach to standardise the description of process equipment and modules would not be mutually exclusive to a UNS approach but I would not mandate it either. But as the UNS is combining, ERP, MES, CRM data, and I am even planning with one customer to included health and safety report data, and aptempt to classify such disparate domains would be Brobdingnagian in scope

OPAF, would be the most similar, but that is to me too big and too much reading, with very little gain , and while the UNS coud take such and approach I would not think it is a good idea. And I am very pro standards.

But a UNS is an architectural concept. It is an approach to how to develop solutions to,
         Allow companies to make data driven decisions in real time.
         And do so in a way that will allow them to meet the company needs now and in the future,
         and position companies in a good place to take advantage of digital supply chains.

If a standard will impose approaches, I do not know if that will help. If a standard is written will it enforce where ERP data is published to? How will that help?
Will a standard define what technologies can be used. Will that limit the adoption of new and better technologies?

I think that companies do need to develop their own standards and guidelines for their UNS, but I do not see much value in ensuring that the UNS in different organisation follow the same standard.

Content: The idea of a Single Source of Truth or Real-Time Snapshot can only be achieved if data is pushed from originating sources at the edge into a common data infrastructure. Not when data that is manipulated along some data pipeline, because then it ceases to be SSOT. This is also partly what "Edge Driven" means IMO. Content:
Best Practices for Backing Up MQTT Broker Data?

Hey folks,


I am reaching out to inquire about the most effective strategies for backing up data from an MQTT broker, specifically concerning the mosquito.db file. Our objective is to implement daily backups, but we've encountered a few challenges that I hope you can provide guidance on:

Broker Downtime for Consistency: We've found it necessary to temporarily halt the MQTT broker during backups to avoid data inconsistencies. Is this a common practice, or are there alternative methods that allow for live backups without risking data integrity?

Memory to Database Synchronization: To ensure all data in memory is accurately written to the mosquito.db file, stopping the broker seems mandatory. Are there strategies or configurations that facilitate this synchronization without needing to disrupt the broker service?

Subscriber Configuration Data: The mosquito.db file not only holds the current state of data but also the configurations for its subscribers, which are essential for smooth operation. This dual role makes the file a critical component for both operation and recovery.

Given these points, backing up the mosquito.db file directly appears to be a straightforward solution due to its ease of restoration, the inclusiveness of current data and subscriber information, albeit with the drawback of not being a continuous backup solution. However, the idea of integrating an external database for backup purposes raises concerns about the complexity of restoration and the exclusion of subscriber data.

Could you recommend best practices for backing up an MQTT broker, considering the need for both data integrity and minimal service interruption? Additionally, if leveraging an external database is advisable, how can we address the restoration process and the inclusion of subscriber data effectively?

Thank you for your guidance and expertise.

Author: johnmaldonado
Content:
I’ve kept track of some of the main points the keep being pointed out about SpB and MQTT and their deficiencies in regard to being a unified protocol for a unified namespace:

1. Protobuf in SpB obfuscates the payload and  it’s embedded metric structure from clients that don’t support SpB or protobuf. Protobuf is just another dependency that may not be available for all clients. Many feel the compression is not useful except for the bandwidth restricted scenario.

2. SpB topic structure is limited. Without creative node and device naming, little context can be attributed to the metrics that might be contained in the payload. This adds a layer of confusion to building a semantic hierarchy. Metrics names can be extended to contain full context but again that doesn’t help if you can’t read the message before subscribing to it.

3. MQTT’s pub sub architecture is not optimal for some clients use cases. They may not fit well in an event driven architecture. They may not need to listen for updated information at all times, they may instead need it at their leisure.

4. Clients cannot browse the topic structure. They must be programmed with prior knowledge about the topic structure or must discover it from messages on on topics reserved for publishing the data model like birth messages or a vanilla MQTT equivalent.

5. Due to points 3 and 4 data must be stored on the broker in the form of retained messages, which may lead to performance issues on the broker. And maybe a fragile method of data storage.

These points all make me wonder if a UNS broker needs to have a twin in the form of a database. Something like MongoDB that easily store the topic hierarchy and expanded metrics and expose them to clients through an API that can be accessed at the client’s leisure

Is any one else implementing this?

Does anyone else agree that this is a possible solution to the issues that have been pointed out?

It IS being adopted by quite a few vendors in the edge/SCADA/historian-space, but it doesn’t extend any beyond that space. Why would it? It’s designed for SCADA applications. If they did 3-4 things with sparkplug it would be even more useful for many more than it is now. 

But in a theoretical sense, protobuf is not the reason a vendor doesn’t implement sparkplug B support! Never has been. Can you even picture it?! “Ok.. let’s see here. Topic namespace check, metrics, timestamps, templates.. now what is this? Protobuf!!!! WTF!! No. No. NO! NEIN!”. 

Now I’m a practical dude, will using json instead of protobuf make it so that a non-compliant client can kind of consume the payload in spite of its non-compliance, yes. Ok, so it’s a nice additiinal option to have. Let’s include it. But there are valid reasons outside of compression to use protobuf as well, it’s a schema for one, and gives strong typing, I’ve heard.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
This is insightful.

Yeah, outside of some scenarios that the energy or utility industries would encounter, I don't understand the benefits of optimizing telemetry with compression.  It just seems like it sounds like a good idea to some in the way that a fast fieldbus is a good idea.  In isolation, it's efficient on the wire.  All things considered, it's inefficient to use.  

I especially question the merits for use cases involving the cloud, where compute is a real cost driver.  Add in the required transformations and parsing of overloaded metric payloads to make the data uasable, Sparkplug starts to look more inefficient than if it was not used at all.

A scenario where I've observed compression really pay off is moving data in bulk.  There tends to be more redundancies within the data sets.  If the destination system can natively handle compressed data or decompress them, it works out well.  The major cloud object storage services (e.g., Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage), for example, have decompression support.

When I think of most manufacturing, I think of the "edge" as a field switch in a panel.  Sure, the connectivity the PLCs may be anything from an ancient serial to a 100mbps ethernet field network.  But, beyond this, there will be "fast" or "gigabit" ethernet uplinks to an IDF with access switches and, from there, no practical limits on distribution to the core and any servers.  Going even further, the WAN or internet circuits may be slower, but these things are provisioned to handle web conferencing and browsing.  If there are going to be any type of knowledge workers on site, they're going to be expected to do normal office things like collaborate and research.  This is in addition to moving software updates, replication, backups, etc for infrastructure.  Why are people so concerned with optimizing transport in IIoT?  I would think optimizing data accessibility and usability would be more important.  

TLDR: "read" speed > "transmit" speed

And of course you can always GZIP/ZIP larger JSON payloads (not much benefit for smaller ones).

Author: jon.forbord
Content: Real time actually means «within the required deadline», and one often talk about hard/real time requirements, such that a missed deadline means the integrity is lost. Deterministic real time means a system that reliable keeps all given deadlines, ie there is no «give» or predictable jitter. An mqtt broker makes no guarantees that something is performed within a given deadline, ie it is non-deterministic real time and you should not use mqtt to Engineer a system with hard real time requirements, for instance closed loop Motion control or Process control. Point being, Real time has many meanings. MQTT can be perfectly real time, but it is non-deterministic real-time.

Author: mparris
Content:
Since in sparkplug, only one application or device can publish to a specific nodeID topic and topics underneath, I still recommend that "MES" be the nodeID.

Naming it MES clearly identifies who owns the namespace underneath (the one publishing to that namespace).  Naming it something generic not tied to the actual publisher may indicate to people that they can publish to that topic, too. And if they do, that will cause a conflict and trigger perpetual birth requests on the network until resolved.

The only reason to use the DDATA feature rather than putting all data into NDATA is if you want to reduce the granularity of what consumers can subscribe to, so they don't have to receive ALL. THE. DATA. from the MES node. 

Was this the purpose of you using DDATA, or is there some other reason?

Author: mparris
Content:
A common misconception is that the UNS must be strongly coupled to a specific protocol, information standard, etc.  This is not the true.

UNS should be defined outside of these things, and then be mapped to real products through technologies in a way that supports how the architecture will grow over the next five years.

Companies that tightly couple to specific technologies to build a UNS will hit a wall at some point when scaling out.

For example, forming a UNS strictly through MQTT topic paths or Sparkplug groupID/nodeID/deviceID schemes is equivalent to using IP Addresses or MAC Addresses when browsing the Internet.

Author: mparris
Content:
And to be fully transparent, I'm actually convinced that MQTT is not a good general interface between a consuming application and the IIoT Platform: (1) MQTT requires a-priori knowledge of the topic structure, (2) can only subscribe to data based on static topic paths rather than any number of other pieces of dynamic data/metadata, (3) requires publishing data to multiple MQTT topic structures resulting in duplicated data to account for all consumption patterns of consumers,  (4) it does not support queries, and (5) is not great for commands.

Thinking something as simple as HTTPS + Websockets would be best, to support subscriptions, queries, commands, etc?  GraphQL is an interesting idea so that the consumer can control how they will receive the data, rather than having a strict API and forcing all consumers to receive data in that way (doesn't seem scalable).

Not to say that the protocol used under-the-hood for the IIoT platform to move the data around isn't MQTT, but this is ultimately abstracted away from the producers and consumers, and the underlying IIoT Platfrom infrastructure can use whatever protocol or encoding is most efficient.

Author: dep05d
Content: This is more or less what we do. Sparkplug is the backbone of anything tag-centric at the edge (essentially for anything we wish to control), and we don't structure anything semantically here, outside of the asset groupings by site, area, system and asset type. The spB topic namespace is asset-oriented, so keep it that way and it won't seem so awkward.  For us, "assets" are any sort of device UDT, AOI, SCADA UDT, KPI function block, business system entity, or the classic one-off "pile of tags" that don't fit any model.  The naming convention for our group and edge node id's align with other non-sparkplug asset-based topic structures to align tag and business data.  We then historize all topics in these asset formats.  From this point, we are free to reference and re-use these core asset tags and events to mold and build as many UNS semantic layers, streaming topics, historical API's etc as we need.
