Content:
I would say
1) I do not use the UNS for 
     HMI to PLC comms, 
     PLC to PLC comms, 
    SCADA , not anything that is real time.  
   and nothing in a Safety Loop( report status nor problem but dont 'have the sensing or actuation depending on the UNS)
All of them can subscribe to data in the UNS,  for some comms, but I would not have a stop button on a SCADA linked via UNS .

But comms from any Level 3 or Level 4 nodes, I would communicate via the UNS. I ask myself , does the message need to be delivered in less than 1 minute?
No one will notice if the schedule is released 60 seconds later, but if you press a stop button, or change a temperature settings, 60s is probably too long

2) If you have Edge Devices, you could put a Broker on the Edge device, and then have that bridged to a Site Broker, that might help you accelerate you integrations 
( you could even have ignition Edge and a broker on each edge device)

3) I think the best way to scale is
      a) Team 1 Integrates the POC on one Cell in the Line, ( say OEE)
      b) Team 2 roll out the features to Line 1. Team 1 Develop new Features on the first Cell( Maybe Scheduling)
   c) Team 3 rollout the features to Line 2 then 3 ... Team 2 are rolling out the  Scheduling feature, and Team 1 are greeting a new feature

Team 1 are the superstars, Team 2 need to be good problem solvers too as they will come across lots of integration issues, and need to adapt the solution. Team 3 should have less problems  so are more focusing on rollout.

Team 4 start to take it to the next plant.

Back when I used to do Safety system, you might have an Estop and two channels are wired into to a safety really and then to a pair of contactors. I would take a auxiliary contact from the safety relay and put it into the Standard PLC.

Author: m_r_mccormick
Content:
I'm trying to figure out a workflow for handling flat MQTT (not Sparkplug) in JSON in ignition, which might cross over with what you're doing. The engine module allows you to consume flat MQTT into the 'MQTT Engine' tag provider via 1) JSON stored as strings in tags, or 2) deserialized json where the topic is a folder and a tag for each JSON field is created in that folder. The engine module also has a python function that allows you to publish flat MQTT, and is pretty straight forward to use. There is no bi-directional capability built in like there is for sparkplug (from what I can tell).

So, I tried making 'MQTT Engine' tags writable, and added a gateway-level tag change script to auto-publish any changes back to the broker at the same topic. If there wasn't a deadband for determining whether a tag changed, this would create a feedback loop, ping ponging data between the tags and the broker, since it's publishing back to the same topic that a change came from. However, the feedback loop gets stopped on the second loop back because the value coming from the broker matches the tag value, which is within the deadband. So, this works, but creates a bunch of additional network traffic for no reason, and you end up with the payload being duplicated with two different MQTT timestamps.

So, you have two situations:

A) User interacts with UI control binded to tag, tag change publishes to broker, broker subscription pushes to tag, new value matches old value (within deadband)

B) Value changes in broker, broker subscription pushes to tag, tag change publishes to broker, broker subscription pushes to tag, new value matches old value (within deadband)

Author: m_r_mccormick
Content:
To avoid the extra traffic, I tried using locks/semaphores in the tag change event. This doesn't seem to be a feasible solution because 1) tag change events occur after a synchronous write has completed, not during, so it doesn't actually block the publish (I haven't tried asynchronous writes but this might defy using locks/semaphores), and 2) It doesn't appear that you can distinguish between whether a user initiated a change from the UI vs a change coming from the broker (in a tag change event).

Before I dig deeper or devolve into writing a custom module, has anyone figured out a good workflow for this?

My desired end result is to have a tag provider that auto-populates tags to match the broker's topic structure, be able to drag an auto-populated tag onto the UI, and any UI modifications push back to the namespace without the excess network traffic.

Author: m_r_mccormick
Content:
I figured out a pattern I'm happy with using three tags and differentiating changes based on timestamp: ReadTag, UITag, and WriteTag.

ReadTag onValueChanged Script:
```python
def valueChanged(tag, tagPath, previousValue, currentValue, initialChange, missedEvents):
    # Read tag from MQTT Engine module
    system.tag.writeBlocking(["[~]UITag"], [currentValue])
```

UITag onValueChanged Script with Bi-Directional Bind to UI Element:
```python
def valueChanged(tag, tagPath, previousValue, currentValue, initialChange, missedEvents):
    read_tag_ts = system.tag.readBlocking(["[~]ReadTag"])[0].timestamp
    ui_tag_ts = system.tag.readBlocking(["[~]UITag"])[0].timestamp
    if read_tag_ts != ui_tag_ts:
        # UITag was modified by UI, not ReadTag
        system.tag.writeBlocking(["[~]WriteTag"], [currentValue])
```

WriteTag onValueChanged Script:
```python
def valueChanged(tag, tagPath, previousValue, currentValue, initialChange, missedEvents):
    # Write to MQTT Broker here. This is just to simulate a write to broker which induces change in ReadTag
    import time; time.sleep(1)    
    system.tag.writeBlocking(["[~]ReadTag"], [currentValue])
```

Author: m_r_mccormick
Content:
@Ted Garrison @RickBullotta  I think I need to add more detail to flush this out, because I can see a bunch of ways to skin this cat, each with tradeoffs.

Let's say I have a PLC with an actuator (single-acting pneumatic cylinder, boolean 'actuate') PLC variable1 (or register, pick your flavor) corresponding to MQTT topic1 (pub+sub), and a sensor (proximity at actuated position, boolean 'actuated') PLC variable2 corresponding to MQTT topic2 (publish only). So, to other nodes, variable1 is read/write via topic1, and variable2 is read only via topic2. The PLC can actuate by itself via on-board logic, and other nodes (not just Ignition) can command it to actuate.

This discretely separates the request (command) and response (status) across two distinct topics in theory. But, what if something is malfunctioning, I request for the cylinder to actuate, it doesn't move, so the prox doesn't update the other topic. It would make sense to me to want to know what variable1 actually is on the PLC via topic1, which requires you to consume status updates published by the PLC, as well as commands from other nodes.

So, when you say that you need two tags, one for the command and one for the status, are you saying?:

A) tag1 writes to topic1 which controls variable1 (actuation), and tag2 consumes topic2 which provides variable2 (prox sensor) status, or

B) tag1 writes to topic1 which controls variable1 (acutation), and tag2 consumes topic1 which provides variable1 (actuation) status. To distinguish between commands and status, you'd have to structure payloads differently? Along with this, the prox sensor would be checked via topic2 to ensure that it did actuate as intended.

C) Add a third topic+node to separate command, response, and status

Author: m_r_mccormick
Content:
The distinction I'm trying to make between A and B is whether command/response is piped through the same topic, and whether those are separate from status derived from a sensor.

From the UI perspective, both make sense to me when you have a UI with a input (text, drop down, toggle), with a button to send the command, and a read-only indicator of status. But, what if you bind an Ignition checkbox to a boolean tag like in this example? If you click on it, the UI element changes, tag changes, payload gets published, and that goes to the PLC. What if transmission fails or the PLC doesn't accept the change? Now you have a checkbox and tag in the wrong state.

Is binding to a checkbox a bad idea? Having an input+button+indicator seems excessive, like there has to be a better way.

Author: terrancesmith
Content: An mqtt facilitated UNS is centralized from certain perspectives like you pointed out. But it is also very decentralized at the same time. See, an MQTT broker has no schema enforcement. It is, without help, considered a dumb broker. The publishers are the ones in charge of what topics move through it. In that sense it is very decentralized. The edge nodes are in charge of what payloads move in and out because the broker just does what they say. You could never change the structure of an MQTT facilitated UNS by going to the broker. You have to adjust a publisher to do that.

Author: _dyland
Content:
Hence why I don't call it Test Driven Development. That said, I haven't reached a level in the PLC that it didn't work for. It is all iterative, as long as the smallest chunks are built and tested first, the rest of the code is just how they are combined. It helps that I organize the code into what I call "As close to object oriented as I can get in a PLC". Each object is tested before it is used to build a bigger object. That object is tested and so on and so forth. Those objects also help map to the UNS too.

My experience is that PLCs as we know them today and the logic under them is too custom to really put a generic framework around like TDD. I would like to see that change or be proven wrong. But more so than any modern software language, PLC guys tend to do their own thing in their own way and they are very resistant to change and collaboration.

Author: m_r_mccormick
Content: My preference would be to have a CI/CD pipeline drive infrastructure deployment, including delineating what services have read/write access at the broker level. Nothing can willy nilly write to the broker unless it receives permission to with traceability via version control. Then, at the service level, you can point to LDAP or some centralized management mechanism for granularity. Moreover, when a write occurs, include the service and user info in the 'command' payload, so that gets consumed by a historian. BAM! You have traceability back to who executed the change, and by what service, through the historian.

Author: m_r_mccormick
Content: I need to clarify: a command and status would not exist in the same instance of a payload, they would be distinct structures for separate payloads. On the PLC side, it publishes status payloads, and when consuming payloads, it only acts on payloads with a 'command' interface (JSON field). On the service (IIoT platform?) side, it publishes command payloads but not status payloads, and when consuming payloads, ignores command payloads (only consumes status payloads). This way, you still have a complete separation of concerns (CQRS), but it's based on interface (payload structure) rather than topic. I see this as having equivalent functionality to two topics in this regard. To address the order of received commands issue, yes it's a problem that multiple services could issue commands, but that also exists in the two-topic approach. A distinct advantage to the single topic approach is that you could add a unique identifier such as a `Sequence Number` to commands, and have a status (or response) include the sequence number when responding so you can identify what command the change is in response to. I don't think you can do do this with two topics easily, if at all.

Author: m_r_mccormick
Content:
I'm not married to the idea of one bi-directional topic. At this point I'm decomposing ideas and toying with them to figure out how to best assemble them for my use case. An argument I'd advance for having one topic is that it simplifies conveying design intent in a UNS, where a single topic correlates to a single edge device variable/register/meaning. Another advantages is that you don't have to keep adding more topics when you need to convey different information, like illustrated earlier distinguishing between a 'fault' and 'status', you just add another interface. This could simplify subscriptions as well, where you could consume commands, status, and faults via one topic.

I don't think `two-topic` and `payload interface` concepts are mutually exclusive, you could use both simultaneously. Your point about additional traffic is absolutely valid, and whether that's a big issue would depend on the use case. If data integrity is a concern, receiving the same payload back might be an advantage if you at least want to know that it made it to the broker. Also, you could see if someone else snuck in a command right before you published yours, or determine the order of payloads received by the broker.

What really interests me is what capabilities might be unlocked over the long term by getting away from the typical payload structure. I'll try not to beat a dead horse here as I've already tried to convey some ideas in section '5.5 Data Recommendations' (pg 29) here: http://dx.doi.org/10.13140/RG.2.2.31738.26565

Author: jon.forbord
Content: Birth messages contain both the metadata about all metrics AND the current state of all those metrics. This is such that all subsequent data messages only need to contain the changed metrics in order for the consumer to maintain an accurate representation of the current state of the node. Imagine that you have a box full of stuff that you can’t see. First you receive a list of all the items in the box (dbirth/nbirth), and all you receive after this, is notes about the changes to the content of the box (ddata/ndata). If one of those change notes gets lost or you lost consciousness for an hour, you can no longer be certain about the content of the box. So you have to ask for the list of all the content again, before you can proceed with just receiving the change notes. It doesn’t help if the broker can keep the original list (birth) for you, unless, unless the broker also maintains the cumulative current state of the box. In the sparkplug scenario, the broker does not keep this cummilative current state, so you have to ask the edge node for the rebirth. They are fixing this partly in the Sparkplug C, by separating metadata from the current state, such that the metadata can be kept as retain in the broker, and the current state is all you need to ask for.

Content:
Don't know which channel suits best for this question, but giving it a try here.

So me and my colleagues discussed around reason codes for e.g. assembly failed events or machine stopped etc.
In the first iteration (which isn't yet in production) we've simply set it up to be defined as a single integer.
The idea was to make it unique per cell giving us free hands to define whatever would be needed. One problem with this is that it's impossible to know what that number means for a human (data scientists looking for most common reason etc) without having that unique mapping at hand. But also other systems receiving the event needs to have some kind of mapping in case they want to make decisions based on the reason. And here's another problem, what if the same reasons are sent from many cells (as they use same torque wrench), then that code is actually unique per device and not cell.
So what about using string reason "codes" that can be self-explanatory? Is probably easier for humans to interpret, but can be hard to define in a sensible way.

Does anyone have any good ideas how do define these things and how to communicate their meanings to other systems/consumers?

Author: trentc
Content:
In the UNS, there should already be some context of where the code originated from. 
This could be from your ISA95 Site/Area/Line/Cell ....
or another topic on the MQTT broker for example Line1/Cell1/Device1....
or maybe inside of the payload On topic Site/Area/Line/Cell your payload might contain JSON  {"Device":"Device1", "Code": 1234}. 

These things give you where the code originated from, so you can have consistent codes for each /line/cell/device. 
Keeping codes consistent where reasonable will help keep technical debt down, and allow you to scale faster.

As far as making it human readable, you can either have the messages at the edge device/plc coded to be included in the message...for example in JSON {"Device":"Device1", "Code": 1234, "Message":"Code Explanation Message"} 
A better approach is the one that @Mark O'Donovan suggested and have a database where you can do an SQL query to get the human readable message based on where it originated from, and the code number.

If you only have the option to send a single integer. We have used larger INT like 32 bit Integers and if you have cell number 10, you could start your error codes at 10000 for example. where  the 10 identifies the device or cell and the remaining digits give you 0-999 for cell/device specific codes.

Anytime you are chosing to "encode" a meaning into a integer, it will be ambiguous to a human unless they are already familiar with the code value and meaning. So you will have to have a table somewhere to cross reference the code to the meaning.

Author: trentc
Content:
Codes are easier for using in applications, strings are better for human readability....so I try to include both where reasonably possible. 
I typically will have code definitions for the use case, for example "Production State" will have a table of codes that explains the production states. And it will be centrally stored where all devices and applications can access it. SQL DB is ideal....but most industrial devices don't have SQL capability built in, this is where the IIOT platform or architecture will have to have a service somewhere to look up the code and add the context in the UNS. 
Just a simple example, read a modbus register from a PLC representing production state using Node Red, then use Node-Red to query the DB, and package the code and meaning into an MQTT payload and publish it into the UNS.

Author: rickbullotta
Content: BTW, "it's not you".  It's just a general mythology and misinformation about what a UNS can and should be.  It's largely a byproduct of the technologies and architectural patterns that have been chosen for most implementations (MQTT and a pub/sub model).  Accessing data and functionality in external systems should not always require that the data be replicated in a UNS.  In fact, that's a really awful pattern for many scenarios.  The concept of a UNS needs to be expanded into a broader platform that allows nodes/entities to have "functions" or "services" that can query external systems.  I'm not suggesting that there aren't times where "caching" makes sense - e.g. publish slowly changing data to the UNS such as the current shift schedule from ERP - but it should not be a complete mirror of  "the whole business" IMO.  I can expose it, and make it accessible, but should not duplicate it.

Author: r.pop
Content: Multiple layers. We typically take a tiered approach to data. It's all about the persona accessing the information. Let's take plant folks, those we would typically consider Tier 1-2 (folks that need real-time data). The data layer at that level is within the 4 walls of the factory, typically managed from cloud, but physically on-prem. This gives us the granularity those folks expect, without having the cost of moving all data to "the cloud". Step up from that and you have a different persona that requires different information, Tier 3-4. This is typically where Snowflake comes into play. There's a sub-set of the factory data that gets rolled up, but less granular. This is more Shift/Day/Week/Month type information. We can manage the level of granularity here and this is the opportunity to sync our Enterprise and Business data to our factory data as well. Snowflake has the capability to access ERP data without moving it and without compromising it. --- This is the recommendation for most enterprise manufactures that are looking to step into this arena. We're agnostic to the technology used to accomplish this goal, as long as it can get the job done. Most of the time it's a combination of multiple technologies i.e Ignition, HiveMQ, Kafka, Snowflake, AWS Services, etc.

Author: m_r_mccormick
Content: Event driven systems/architecture and pub-sub are distinct concepts as well, which further complicates this. The `Observer Pattern` was established and utilized prior to but codified circa 1994 in the book `Design Patterns: Elements of Reusable Object-Oriented Software` and underpins `pub-sub`. There are a wide variety of ways to implement event driven systems, all with tradeoffs, and not all of which utilize the observer pattern (i.e., pub-sub). So, differentiating between a UNS and Event Driven Architecture/Pub-Sub may not provide the depth needed to drive satisfactory outcomes. It seems that manufacturing as a whole may benefit from deeper cross-disciplinary study.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
In specialized software, most APIs aren't really intent-based.  They're usually CRUD procedures that were designed for a front end to consume together.  At some point, someone wants to automate a transaction or process in the application.  The procedure gets exposed as a web service as-is or mildly refactored for external clients.  When an external client tries to interface with it, it doesn't have the same context as the application's front end.  The interface will have all these weird input dependencies (e.g., GUID, PK) the external client won't know about and these dependencies may span multiple endpoints.

This is the equivalent of someone writing a PLC program without any regard for another programmer, HMI, or SCADA interfacing with that program.  If the machine doesn't clearly expose its own state (e.g., availability, utilization), it means the external client will need to make a lot of assumptions or introduce logic to interpret the PLC and derive the state.  With PLCs, it's a bit easier because the data structures and the interfaces are basic (e.g., read a tag, write a tag), but it's still complexity nonetheless.

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: The best way to describe it is like this: ERP is a grouping of functions in a UNS.  Each function has its own functional namespace.  So — we may have a function that is BOM and another called Material Definition.  ./ERP/BOM and ./ERP/Material Definition  These are red functions and are essentially extendable classes (we will have many instances of these functions in the UNS).  BOM will have parameters that inform the function about which BOM we want in the namespace at any given time.  The BOM functional namespace will be inclusive of the ERP master data model for BOM (it will have all of the parameters, constants and result sets).  The ERP node will use the values of certain parameters to retrieve the BOM for a specific part (which has a material definition).  So — when BOM/Parameter changes, that event drives the publishing of BOM/Result with the current state of BOM.  🙏

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: UNS is structure, events, current state.  It is single source of truth not system of ownership.  UNS is not a data store or warehouse, functional nodes consume and produce to UNS.

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: We go into the details in Mastermind and Mentorship — the Namespace session of Mastermind is 4 hours long.  I am working on extracting a primer that will explain this fully.   But quickly — Functional Namespaces contain parameters and variables (including inputs, holding variables and outputs) that serve a business function.  An example of this is functional namespace would be OEE or Changeover or Work Order or Schedule.  Definitional Namespaces contain parameters and variables that define objects in the business or process.  Think metadata like in service date, serial number, model number, motor plate information.  Informative namespaces contain parameters and variables for information consumers — think Dashboards, Reports, REST Endpoints.  Ad-hoc namespaces are defined by developers — an example would be a one off namespace specific to one asset in an org.

Author: vatsalshah
Content:
Yep, we had a long internal discussion about it on both tech and business fronts. 

Some points: 
1. Branding was quite challenging between Litmus IDE / Litmus MQTT / Litmus UNS. We are doing more than MQTT broker (graphql / auth / hierarchy/governance), so  Litmus MQTT was out of the question from tech POV. It was a true sense Unified Namespace because of the core featuresets. Internally, we don't have to use MQTT, and users will never know the difference.

2. We wanted to keep Litmus Edge separate - already deployed 1000s of sites / Lots of OEMs / lots of credibility and we didn't want to touch the core sustainable business. Repurposing the internal NATS broker to an MQTT broker means replacing good stuff with a mediocre protocol. Touching that naming/tech/business was never up for debate. 

3. Our typical customer journey was "Collect -> Contextualize -> Analyze -> Integrate -> Scale". MQTT or UNS was 4th step in their journey (~80% of customers). So, it is right to launch a separate product that works standalone at the site or global level. 
Lastly, MQTT as an ingress protocol was a forced tech decision because customers started using MQTT clients in "data aggregators" on the plant floor that we were integrating. 

The screenshot is how we are implementing the customer journey.
With 400+ new users signed up since the UNS/MQTT broker announcement, we will have success stories in the next 6 months. There is a lot more to do, but current Litmus customers are super duper happy that we launched this UNS product.

My idea of it is to have 1 entry point into your plant data, 1 hub in a hub-spoke architecture from where all information can be queried.
The exposed interfaces can be MQTT (or another pub/sub protocol), web api's, whatever else is best suited.
The underlying data can be coming from different applications, PLC's, IIOT devices, databases, servers, you name it.
As long as there's 1 entry point, and 1 single source of truth for every piece of information.
This way it should (in theory) be easy to replace an application, and to expand.

When it comes to MES I'd argue starting from a solid and scalable data structure (ideally from a standard that a lot of thought went into already) is the way to go.

Author: sparkylarks
Content:
Considering the Universal Namespace (UNS) as a foundational layer—akin to a sheet of paper or a tablecloth—allows for a unique perspective. While the UNS itself isn't a broker, it can span across multiple brokerage systems. This thought experiment helps in conceptualizing and developing systems for enhanced connectivity and data management.

In the UNS, data may already be present but disconnected, with certain information restricted or prohibited from being shared or viewed across different nodes or brokers due to privacy or security reasons.

Current Human Resources (HR) systems often depend on disjointed Excel sheets, leading to inconsistent data. For example, one sheet might list Dylan as married with children, while another shows him as single. To address this, an AMQP broker was introduced to consolidate and synchronize data according to UNS guidelines, albeit with a unique data structure.

Simultaneously, Dylan and Jon are developing a UNS for manufacturing data, employing MQTT for communication. This project has identified a need to access specific information from the manufacturing floor, such as user activity on machines, within my UNS framework.

To facilitate this, data sharing between brokers could be permitted, allowing the HR UNS to access manufacturing data, while restricting the reverse flow. This is possible because the semantic hierarchies of HR and manufacturing data can be integrated into a single comprehensive framework without conflict. Such a unified structure enables the explanation and navigation of data architecture, despite the differences in mapping between HR and manufacturing domains

Author: _dyland
Content:
Not really. With the PLC example, a physical event triggers a sensor reading that is carried over a wire to a PLC Input, that input is pre process in the PLC (possibly used for a cascading series of events and control to outputs directly) We will say it ends up getting coerced into an early piece of information based on other inputs, now we have a machine state. That machine state is located in a data table or a tag (Some form of local memory in the PLC) That memory location is polled by a fieldbus to an OPC Server. An HMI and / or legacy SCADA platform uses that OPC Tag to display data and possibly log it to a historian or SQL database. Maybe that OPC Server is bridged to MQTT where it can finally be consumed by a UNS. And from there consumers of the UNS data.

The UNS can get aggregates of that OPC Tag from the SQL Database or Historian using a middleman, maybe a bridge to MQTT, maybe a separate application or dataops platform that can further process it and publish to the UNS. If we use that as a basis, there are a lot of steps to get to the UNS... I hope that Enterprise applications like ERP, HR, CRM, Marketing, etc dont also need to go through those hoops...

the non technical one is 
The UNS, is a Single source of truth where  all systems and people can obtain the data and information of the business, organised to match the structure of the business.

The Technical one is 
The UNS is the hub where the smart systems in your business communicate with each other, it presents a single source of truth by ensuring all systems access the same data to reveal the current state of the business, organised in a systematic hierarchy that matches the structure of the business, preventing the need to create point to point connections.

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: Ontological application works well in very strict, PLM driven environments — aerospace is a good example.  Ontology falls apart in discrete manufacturing for very much the same reason ERP driven architectures have gaps — there are deltas across even congruent processes and the deltas increase exponentially over time.  We apply ontological concepts with UNS with Semantic Hierarchy (structure that makes sense), context (relationships between namespaces) and functional or descriptive namespaces (the explanation of the relationship).  RE: Palantir — is monolithic.  I actually think it’s great tech for specific industries.  🙏

Author: trentc
Content:
1. My experience is that you will find more node-red use in industry than node.js....because it is easily accessible, flexible, capable, and "low code". The "low code" value in industry is that it allows to "meet in the middle" with OT and IT needs. It's familiar enough to IT focused disciplines, and OT individuals with IT comprehension to understand and use. It allows to quickly put together a solution without having to be a programmer. 

The limitations I see right now for node-red....
- Not all device communications are available, and you are largely relying on community developers. This is good and bad. I was using the sparkplugB nodes the other day and noticed the string functionality was missing, a ticket on github and it was fixed in 24hr. But this will not be the uniform experience.
- Not enough people understand how to use node-red effectively, this will come as it becomes stronger and more used in industry.
- Easy tools for configuration. With kepware you get tools to get directly to the value of the tool. You pick the driver, channel, point it to the device, browse or add tags....These tools aren't available in such a presentable way in node-red. You can still. handle all of this....some with development. For example, you will have to build your own list of tags/memory addresses to read...and potentially your own code to "scan" through them. Where as, kepware handles this for you and has been tested.

Author: trentc
Content: 2. Node red is free....kepware is not...but you can use kepware's resettable time-limited trial for testing. Also, node red runs on almost any OS, but kepware is windows only. I think if you want an industry proven solution with a huge library of device drivers....use kepware for this piece. However, I am of the stance that I like to use kepware when I can't easily do it in node-red. So I suggest spending some time trying node-red...and then do it with kepware using the trial....and see which one works best for your use case.

Author: trentc
Content:
3. Grafana is popular because it's freely available....but it has huge limitations when it comes to interacting with the data. It's good enough to create some dashboards that user's don't interact with much. And you will want to be comfortable with SQL to do it. 

Node-red is great here for being able to display data as well as interact with it, it's free, it's easy, and readily available. It's not too hard once you learn node-red. It is also fairly flexible and extensible. But you will be working within their architecture design, you don't get much control over the design and layouts. 

There are other industry focused rapid development applications that you can use....which involve more licensing cost.
You can download ignition and run it in a time-limited-resettable trial, python will be the language of choice here.
You could get a trial of Tatsoft FrameworX if you are comfortable with .NET/C#/Javascript
Note that both of the above have drivers to talk to devices....so kepware or node red may not be needed...this is dependent on your architecture choices. 

If you want to build your own web application, that's great, you will have the full design flexbility but you also will be spending a lof time developing all of the details of the function and form....depends on if you want to code and have flexibility, or if you want rapid development but work within a toolset. 
You won't find custom web development to be common at the OT level....maybe at the higher IT levels of an organization, however my experience is that custom web development isn't a common choice because of the cost, and effort to build, and TCO to modify and maintain.

I can agree with that node-red gets you quickly off the ground and is easier for non-coders to look into themselves. 
However, looking back on what we've learned in the IT sector the last 15y with DevOps, rigorous automated testing, better version control,  ticket systems etc. when developing semi-critical systems for IT, how can it suddenly be ok to cheat on these things when handling integration of a moneymaking machine that needs to run 24/7? Author: _dyland
Content:
I should clarify, I use Node Red for non critical systems. Sometimes collecting data from, but not interfering with, critical systems. And on a greenfield site, with no political restrictions on technology choice and an appropriate budget, I would probably not use Node-Red too often. Even then for a bootstrapped startup, some quick Node Red flows help the business scale to a revenue that affords them the use of better options. My ideal use case for Node Red would be for rapid prototypes. To be replaced with robust solutions after the concept has proven value.

Most of my Node-Red use cases were supplementing FactoryTalk SE capabilities. ex. PLC to SQL, FactoryTalk Historian Dashboards, or a machine status displays. These were kept small and distributed so that when that "second wave" comes they can be replaced as time and budget permits with minimal (hopefully no) effect on production.

That said, compared to the rest of the OT technology stack, Node Red is a lot closer to good. Try doing automated testing on the VBA scripts in iFix or FactoryTalk. Or working with some custom ActiveX components that some integrator installed in 2022 without any documentation. When you update the PLC code, how do you know it still works? You don't really, you trust the manufacturer. That's a much bigger issue than a few broken nodes in Node Red. As much as I want to see change, and push for it, Node-Red is way better than the vast majority of traditional OT tools.

On top of that, most uses of "Real Code" I have run into in manufacturing end up being custom compiled SCADA or MES products that are owned by some systems integrator... Want any changes better call that specific integrator... hopefully they still answer the phone. I have seen 10 year old desktops running critical batching systems on Windows XP service pack 1 because the software was never upgraded. Because of these experiences, managers spec big names like Rockwell because they believe that it will be better. That's much higher on my list of concerns.

Node-Red is far from perfect but it is a major step forward for OT. It is less about getting off the ground fast and more about getting off the ground at all. Someday OT will learn from IT rather than fight against them. We will all be way better learning from each other rather than fighting. But that culture shift is still a ways off. So while we work to change that culture, something needs to happen today to keep things moving forward. And sometime that is Node Red, as a bridge.

Author: _dyland
Content:
Personally, in the current culture and politics of the automation space, I am often choosing platforms over code more often than not. And I would say, ***NEVER *** accept compiled code solutions from Systems Integrators without access the source and the rights to modify. I have done multiple rip and replace jobs that should have been simple modifications because of black box solutions that a client was provided with in the past. Someday that may change. 

If you are a systems integrator I urge you to consider the maintainability, scalability, and usability for the end user. No one should ever feel trapped by an integrators solution.

That said, from the perspective of what to study, that depends on where you are starting. But personally I like to learn programming languages, Data Stores (Not Just SQL), Transport Mechanisms, Architecture patterns, and such to a basic proficiency. Cast a wide net to understand what is out there and then when a problem arises I can go deeper in whatever is needed at that time.

For your example of PLC -> Database there are many ways to make that work, but which to choose is dependent on many more factors.

Some platforms that make this simple are HiveMQ Edge, Coreflux, Node Red, and Ignition, among others. Throw Kepware in there and the options only increase.
If you are dead set on code, PLC4X is a very interesting project to watch. But for now, For Rockwell PLCs Python has `pycomm3` and `pyModbusTCP`, Node.js has `Node Ethernet/IP` and  `modbus-tcp` obviously there are other libraries too, these are the ones I know off off hand.

@thiagopvr some of my experiences. First off I used to work in automation in 80/90s.
I worked on i3.0 stack from AB PLC to SAP integration.  I now work with wireless IoT, node-red, MQTT etc.
I describe myself as a scripter not a software eng/dev.

BTW the first version of node-red came out during this development and it took me a few days to port.

Python easy to get started but most examples are "main looped"  look for event driven examples.
And look at the modules provided for platform/devices etc. 
See if they use call-backs and how they handle TCP connects/re-connects.
The Paho MQTT library is very good example of python event callback e.g. on_connect, on_message etc.

From what I've seen, OT mindset when it comes to development is about 20y behind IT. It's cowboy coding all day long. Don't get me wrong here, those PLC guys I've seen are very talented, but from my point of view they lack the thinking of traceability (who did what and why) and other best practices where IT has come a long way. E.g. we had supplier coming in to fix a bug on a PLC and when they left they fixed that bug but introduced an old one just because "he didn't use the latest version" 🫣. Version control anyone?

Author: sparkylarks
Content:
Are there no Cowboys in IT,?
I don't understand the need to constantly paint OT as backward.

I would ask why are you getting such bad OT suppliers? And are you investing the same amount into the traceability of OT systems.
I have worked with so many companies where there is a group IT and one or 2 on site IT and no onsite OT or group OT support.
no OTSM system. And then when outside OT support is used the cost is whittled down to about half what an similarly trained IT professional gets.

And if IT testing is so good, why are there so often issues when changes are rolled out. I had won where an IT update at the weekend stopped all Wifi in 3 locations, for 3 days.
or server rebooted and software not started,

Rant Over, if you want some constructive comments,  

if you want traceability and version control, 
 - use octaplant for version control . https://auvesy-mdt.com/en/octoplant
- Or AssetCenter if you have a lot of Rockwell. I am always amazed how many IT manufacturing people are shocked when I mention software like octaplant. These have been around for 20 years. CERN use VersionDog https://auvesy-mdt.com/en/case-studies/cern

That would solve most of your problems,

If you want better testing of changes,
 - Set up an OT Dev and Test Environment, make your supplier use this, you need to a few VM's and some spare PLC's 
 - Create simulation functionality in your UDT
- Force all supplier to do the same ( better still make them use your UDT for common components, Motor, Valve, Limit switch, ) 
missioned, major changes need commissioning too, 

It is important to have a common naming plan for variables, not sure about enforcing English, that seams very colonial of me :), but in practice it probably make sense.

Author: rutger_18900
Content:
My opinion is that this heterogeneity is wildly overstated/overestimated. Yes no two companies or industries are the same, but models like the ones in ISA88 and ISA95 are widely appropriate across manufacturing plants and can be a framework covering a great part of you operations.

I've worked on S88 (and to a lesser extent ISA95) implementations in many different verticals, some specific examples:
- biotech (monoclonal antibodies)
- other pharma (pills, literal sugar coating)
- Cookies
- Pastry fillings
- Chocolate paste
- Blending motor oils and additives
- Dairy (solid cheese wheels, milk, yoghurts)
- Rubber seals for pharma (vial caps, the rubber inside a syringe, ...)
- Animal feed
- Waste recycling
- Animal carcass processing (to fertilizer and biofuel)

I'm probably forgetting some.
The advantages outweighed the limitations by so much. 
Every engineer could work on any of those projects without knowing the process itself in detail.

This for different integrators, each having built their own libraries on top of (different!) products from major vendors, as well as custom solutions.
Now imagine this becoming standardized/shared outside of the single integrator (or end user when done in-house).

To an extent it was already the case, when going from integrator A using product X to integrator B using product Y, I had little trouble getting up to speed in record time since both were implementing these same standards.
And when I say limitations I mean mostly being "tied to" this general model, there was always room for custom logic and extensions, trying to aim for 80/20.

Whenever a customer asks me in what industry I have experience, my answer is it's all the same on an manufacturing operations level, at least for batch based processes. I don't have much experience with discrete and continuous but I see a lot of similarities.

Author: durinwinter
Content: Personally I have found the following to be true. ISA95 + S88 is hard to beat for structuring the relationships  between organization, site, area, and equipment. I think the batch stuff in S88 is undervalued for what it provides to an organization as it relates to "business specific temporal windows mapped to outcomes" that really does an incredible job in enabling guidance structures. I think the MTP data model overlay is the best way to think about how to model equipment down, since it's really just an extension of ISA95, no harm no foul. For the meta model I think a combination of some of the stuff from OPC-UA (information meta model and data access structures, please please nobody think I am talking about the transport layer or the XML stuff. But from an Ontology perspective Googles Digital Buildings Ontology with its concept of abstract model vs concrete model vs canonical model and how they compose their fields and subfields.

Author: durinwinter
Content: I also think thinking about a system as having a Process Orchestration Substrate including the command, state, and command enable channels present in MTP is necessary for enabling AI model orchestration. Because AI is very brittle one should think about them only running within certain system states. So if you have one VFD motor combo and one AI model is optimizing for energy savings. That's not something you want it to do if the underlying system is in a state where you want to run the motor full out such as during a system recovery phase. So you need the system to understand and know when to turn the AI off. This requires thinking about how you are wrapping all computations systemically.

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content:
A note in advance: If you buy off-the-shelf software, you are always dependent on a specific vendor. 

If you want to be locked in less to a vendor / cloud provider, it is helpful if you use software that uses open standards and/or is based on OpenSource (@Jermuk). In addition, the solution should not limit you in terms of where you can deploy the software. Let's take a look at Azure IoT Operations from this perspective:

- You can deploy AIO on any Arc-enabled Kubernetes cluster, no matter where it is located. It can be on bare metal at the edge, on Azure, on AWS or GCP, but the control plane always stays on Azure and you have to use Azure Arc. So that gives you some freedom, but still ties you to Azure. That was a conscious decision by Microsoft. Of course they want to tie you to Azure, but they also want to give you a consistent experience by using ARM. I think you should also be able to deploy AIO via Helm charts and configure it via Kubernetes CRDs (the latter is already possible, but not currently documented).

- AIO uses MQTT as an open standard in its core (Azure IoT MQ), so you can use a tool like Litmus Edge for Data Ops and simply use Azure IoT MQ as an MQTT broker, for example. As AIO also supports OPC UA as a data source, you can use other connectivity tools like Kepware with it. It also uses Kubernetes "standards" like CRDs and OpenTelemetry, which makes it integrate well with Kubernetes.

All in all, it makes you dependent on Azure, but it's still "normal software" running on Kubernetes, which gives you some flexibility. I guess if you're on Azure and already using Azure-specific things like Fabric for data analytics, I think you should consider AIO as an option when it becomes GA. Let's see how the product develops till then.

Content: So object storage itself is not very expensive. The problem are analytics tools like Synapse or Athena that have a pricing based on the amount of data being processed for a query. If people forget to use the partitioning key in their where clause, it becomes very expensive very quickly. We monitored this in one of our projects and it turns out that even data scientists almost always forget to use the partitioning and then complain that their queries take so long. So I would advise against letting regular end users directly use those tools. Smaller group of data scientists that know about data partioning might be fine. Otherwise you need your own frontend in front of those tools so you can get your hands in between the users and the tools to keep them from causing too much cost. For example, I think it's good for a random end user to be using the same drivers as a small brewery, fortune 100 oil & gas, cnc machine builder, system integrator, etc.  Each will push connectivity in a different way and solution provider will, as a result, "harden" the drivers based on their needs over time. Author: walker.reynolds
Content: Generally you have a JSON or array of n number of orders that all contain the metadata, then you have sister topics with the active work order parsed from the JSON or array.  So — if there are 7 key:value pairs per work order or 7 parameters in each row of the array, there are 7 topics for the current work order.

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: Most of the time, this is pushed from the node based on an event change in another topic of the namespace (like scanned word order id) that is coming from a barcode reader, for example.

Author: thunt.career
Content:
How much would this typically cascade for a single input in this example?

Barcode scan of work order id at node A initiates ERP node to publish WO details in same hierarchical level to relevant topics including manufactured item number back to UNS which triggers BOM node to publish its data for that item which triggers Master data node to publish descriptions and uom and conversions for those items.

Is this extreme or how it propagates in the real world?

Author: walker.reynolds
Content: There would be a functional namespace ‘WorkOrder’ with a sub namespace ‘CurrentWorkOrder’ that contains the parsed topics from the JSON or Array.  The JSON or Array is a sibling of ‘CurrentWorkOrder’.  In general, you want a single event in a functional namespace to drive the cascading events (avoid race conditions).  However, it’s flexible and up to the architect of the function.

Author: youri.regnaud
Content: It's important to decide in your architecture whether Tulip should persist data or simply call it up from applications via REST, for example. If you want to store data such as production orders, you need a solution that will subscribe to the UNS and then call the Tulip Table APIs to store the data. Tulip's Automation module is not far from being able to perform this kind of operation. If your strategy is not to store too much information in Tulip, which is our strategy, Tulip needs to be connected to a UNS node which will store data from UNS and expose it via REST protocols, GraphQL which Tulip can consume. We always come back to the question of how to consume UNS "Data at REST".

Author: zeratall
Content:
No point in arguing with Clemens. It’s very clear based on his post he doesn’t understand the problems of manufacturing and how the underlying philosophy around a UNS address those problems. Nor would I suspect him to, his role supports a variety of different industry’s. that being said, not sure why he’s speaking as if he is an expert in manufacturing. He says he understands the design pattern but it’s very clear he doesn’t. 

1) I don’t get the comparison of the UNS to “hierarchal database”. The area that Clemens is commenting on regarding the UNS is the semantic hierarchy, aka the structure. I would say the semantic hierarchy would be more akin to a data model than a data store, and a lot of data models are hierarchal in nature because of inheritance. 

2) No one is replicating databases with MQTT, where did he get that idea?

3) Graph is great when your data has lots of edges/relationships, and a hierarchal only model doesn’t make sense. That being said, graph isn’t suitable for all manufacturing data. Could you imagin storing all your streamed OT data into a graph, I couldn’t, your still going to want a TSDB to take advantage of compression techniques specific to TS data etc, in general, your always going to need other types of data stores in a manufacturing architecture, saying “throw everything in a graph, is just as idiotic imho”.

Author: pieterge
Content:
I'm a practical guy (electrical, automation, network infra), so the previous conceptual statements are normally not my cup of tea. Getting practical, and especially getting armed against armies of those major MES vendors who easily seduce our corporate & IT nitwits, I've built a quick test setup with open technology components suggested many times over the years on these channels:
1.    The PLC data is converted in OPC at the gateway (doesn't matter which). No immediate formatting (deliberately, reflecting reality).
2.    Highbyte is the DataOps converting the OPC to MQTT and ingesting the - well to hell with it - UNS. I've read articles about Highbyte not necessarily being the best place to build/house the entire asset model, but to provide the DataOps part to shape any required protocols and foremost data structures for nodes connecting to the UNS.
3.    HiveMQ is the broker where the UNS asset model is housed. Again, could be any suitable solution.
4.    Canary, advertised being the affordable PI, would be the self-aware historian for the UNS.
Now this is the part where it really gets interesting. In the video (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AjIgJ6sSrnU) some time ago Walker explains the self-aware Canary part, but as I currently experience starting from vanilla MQTT in HiveMQ, I'm pushed towards browse&parse scripting Canary side or HighByte side, also mentioned in the MQTT origin video. What is the latest status on this capability? Since HiveMQ and Canary advertise strong integration, maybe they offer something off the shelve? Or am I best of Highbyte side (which I was keeping mainly for in/out shaping)? And then there is querying the historian, if I'm not mistaken currently not available through the UNS (broker) in any related format (microservices wish list). Can I have the latest on this or is this the point where I'm risking of robbing talented people from making a living?

Author: sparkylarks
Content:
I am struggling to answer the "What is a UNS"
Funnily I know I can build one. but I feel a bit like a student who knows the answer that is being looked for.

I'm not seeking a definition per se, but rather, I'm curious about the category or class to which a UNS belongs.

A UNS is an omniscient, omnipresent, tablecloth?? 🤔 

For instance, a dog is an animal, and a car is a mode of transport. Similarly, what would we classify a UNS as? Is it an Architectural approach, an Architecture pattern, a Digital twin, a strategy, a data warehouse, a message Broker, or a broker with structured data or something else entirely?

At times, I ponder whether a UNS is essentially just a blueprint for a data warehouse, directing us where all the information is stored. If MTRs (Minimum Technical Requirements) are essential, and the first UNS didn't meet these requirements, I feel this could be a misleading argument.

There's a poignant line from the poet Yeats, "How can we know the dancer from the dance?" This makes me wonder if the UNS is the concept of what we build, and the outcome of that build is something else, yet we still refer to it as a UNS. 

So what class of a thing is a UNS?

Author: sparkylarks
Content:
@MParris Thinking on this a bit more.

   ** Book as Data and Information:** In this simplified system, I think of each book in the library as a set of data or information. The book is like our siloed service or system ,

    **Book Index/Namespace/Map:** A map or index at the beginning of each book that guides you to specific sections or chapters. This is similar a modbus Map, or Tag list in Device or System. But just like how index descriptions are not unique across books,( Introduction, Dedication), the namespace map will not be unique across silo namespaces.

**    UNS as the Library:**
        **Centralization**: The UNS acts like a grand library where all the books (data) are stored in one place. This makes it easier to manage because you can 'Publish' (bring in new books or data) and 'Subscribe' (take books or data out) in one centralized location.
        **Indexing System**: Like the Dewey Decimal System in libraries, which categorizes books into specific areas and topics, the UNS uses a similar indexing system to organize data. This system helps everyone know where to find what they need quickly and efficiently.

And just like a MQTT broker,  even though a book is in the catalog , it might not be visible to you when you visit. Though for different reasons

  **  Metadata as Index Cards:** In our library, the set of index cards represents the metadata. Each card provides a summary of what's in the book, such as the title, author, and a brief description of the contents—similar to metadata that gives you quick insights into what the data is about without having to look through it all.

    **Librarian as AI Assistant:** Lastly, the librarian in this system is like an AI assistant. Just as a librarian helps you find books you might like or need, the AI in a UNS helps by suggesting relevant data, offering insights, and guiding you through the database based on your needs and past activities.

Author: _dyland
Content:
I play devils advocate here on occasion. Sometimes I actually am the one criticizing it...

But I think the issue is that people largely don't understand what the UNS actually is. The messaging is not clear to most people I talk to outside this community, and most that I talk to are looking for a product or a single thing that is a UNS. That's why the MQTT=UNS mindset is so prevalent, it fits pre-existing expectations. It also puts a lot more responsibility on the end user, rightfully so, but a lot of end users I run into don't have the expertise to execute yet. Its a marketing problem above all else.

Author: zeratall
Content:
a UNS is a concept/design pattern and using Walkers Definition it is:
1) Event Driven (Event Orchestrator/Broker)
2) A structure for all your data and events (Data Model)
3) A single source of truth for all current state data and information from which all nodes of the architecture communicate through (Hub and Spoke Hybrid)

Author: zeratall

Author: zeratall

I think using MQTT as a implementation for the broker makes the governance less of an issue since the data model is now composable (aka pushing namespaces into other namespaces), but that can be hard to govern. aka all of the implement details for how you realize of a UNS have their own pro and con, but none of them are cons of a UNS unless the issue is with one of the underlying concepts of a UNS

Author: _dyland
Content:
I know we here are defining a concept. Something abstract, something ... bigger.
But a lot of people are still on clipboards and excel documents. We lose sight of that here. Everyone who finds themselves on this server is already biased by the marketing funnel that got them here.

To someone with a need of, "Eliminating Clipboards" they are fighting fires of Right Now. They lack a capacity to look ahead one year, let alone far enough out for real digital transformation. There are a lot of very big bold claims that scare them away.
A lot of the thoughts in this are from other perspectives, not necessarily what I myself think. Often the sentiment is that these business will die or these people** CANT BE HELPED**. I take pretty major issue with that sentiment.

-----

It is the structure of the business and **ALL **of the events. It is the Single Source of Truth. It is a hub through which things connect, and an architectural foundation for Industry 4.0 and Digital transformation.

-----

This section alone has 2 issues. 
1. It sounds like a daunting task. Connecting Everything! I just need this machine to store recipes... I don't need a hub for **EVERYTHING**! 
2. What if I already believe that Industry 4.0 or Digital transformation are marketing buzzwords? Maybe I was burned by a failed ERP implementation in the past that was sold as a "Digital Transformation"... Maybe the term Industry 4.0 is overused by sales team and has no more meaning to me? 

Then we get into Why we need it, this is good stuff but doesn't define the UNS... To use an example from this thread, The dictionary doesn't tell me **WHY **I need love... culture, society, and various other factors do. This needs to be tailored to the audience but doesn't belong in the pure definition. 

The section about HOW to implement has a similar issue to the WHY. But among other things, it references the Minimum Technical Requirements without defining what they are...

That is the bulk of it, ill cut it off here because this is starting to get to be too much of a rant... Sorry if it is incoherent.

Author: jon.forbord
Content:
Hmm.. some late night thoughts on how to simply explain the UNS to someone. 

Most people will be familiar to the concept of a single source of truth. And if they are not, it is fairly easy to explain how you can pull data from all your databases and applications and put it all into a data lake or some central repository from which everyone else can go to get to the data they need. Agreed? Well, this single source of truth is  usually updated in batches every week or day or some given interval, and contains all of the records or data from some past point in time. Like all the workorders from the last month or all stops with stop reasons from asset X over since 2010.. This SSoT can be used to give insights on what happened. But what about right now? In this very second? How do you know what the current state of the business is? For the most part, you have to go to the SCADA to known if all your machines are running, you have to go to the MES to see the current OEE, and the ERP to see the master schedule. Well.. 

Unified namespace at its core is «a shared single source of truth for the current state of your business». 

Now there are details on how you can achieve this in a scalable way (mtr/mqtt), and how you should structure the data (isa-95), and ... etc but at the core it’s a shared single source of truth of the current state of all the smart things and applications of the entire business.

Author: ravil1
Content:
Speaking of the "current state". With MQTT, there is no way for the subscriber to know, how "current", or how "fresh" the data value is. Of course, the expectation is that the value is reported by "exception", but, it is completely up to the Publisher, what is the "exception".
In OPC UA, the client knows what is sampling interval, what is the deadband, what frequency data is published at - that is when subscription is used. When the client reads data using Read service call, it sets MaxAge, which defines, how fresh the data value should be. When it is set to 0, it means, do not use cashed value, do read from the original data source now, so you get the most fresh, current value. And then, you have source timestamp, server timestamp, so all information is available - when a value was read, when it was received by the server, and you also know when it was received by the client. 
In most cases probably all this information is excessive and it is enough just to use client side timestamp. From other side, the client has ways to get only what is required to ket bandwidth on the wire low.
I think for some people such flexibility might be a problem, looks too complex, that is why OPC UA is perceived as something not complete and not specific. And that is fine, if your project does not require such flexibility, do not use OPC UA, simple.
The same about organizing data in UNS using ISA95 approach (Enterprise/Site/Area/Line/Cell, etc.). Comparing to OPC UA, it is simple and limited, but in most cases more than enough I guess. 

We just need to know what are the assumtions and limitations.
Simple UNS approach I think is applicable in most use cases, where it does not really matter, is your data really "real-time", or only "near real-time". Simplicity makes it easy to implement and deliver results quickly, and that is where the power of UNS is.

Author: zeratall
Content:
Now that I'm off work I can give a proper detailed reply, essentially what I’ve been observing from the nature of your replies @Mark O'Donovan is your essentially looking for a blue print on how you can deploy a UNS, and how you can address some of the implementation question that come up around deploying a UNS, you gave a few implementation question examples such as the use of OPC-UA, Snowflake, etc. 

However, there is a reason architects like myself design architecture in an abstract form before down selecting frameworks and technologies. That is because as soon as you down select and start working the implementation, it imposes constraints, often these constraints end up spinning up questions like the ones you mentioned above. A UNS as walker describes it, is really how we should be thinking about "good architecture for manufacturing". To give some examples, lets look at the typical definition Walker gives and breaks it down. 

**Edge-Driven:** Manufacturing network security controls are structured in a way that make most poll/response implementations hard, additionally most of the mfg devices are streams. Edge-Driven is not exclusive, that is to say a UNS should place high importance on optimizing for edge, resulting in mostly a pub/sub or event-driven architecture (EDA) type implementation. Edge Driven is not exclusive to EDA, but it does place a high priority on it. 

**A structure for all your data and events (Data Model):** A UNS should provide a structured approach to data and events rather than simply "dumping" data into a piece of software or datastore. This could be a semantic hierarchy or another type of data model. Walker often shows the use of a semantic hierarchy because it aligns with how most humans think about data. The key point of this part of the defintion is having a methodical way to structure data, which is an holistic approach to architecture, and improves the understanding of data, and reduces the burden for integration. 

**A single source of truth for all current state data and information (Hub and Spoke Hybrid):** All nodes of the architecture communicate through this single source. While a UNS isn't necessarily a single node (you can use techniques like bridging and clustered brokers for failover), it provides a single way to access data, easing integration. As @Rutger Van Aelst mentioned, this is more akin to a single access plane that all application nodes can communicate over.

These are general ways to think about data rather than an exact recipe. While Walker has shown various examples of how to implement a UNS, the core concept lies in the conceptual ideologies he has repeatedly discussed on this discord, as well as on his youtube channel. I do agree with you 100% we should always strive to understand how we can communicate more effectively, but I think the issue is most people are looking for a black and white definition of what a UNS is, or rather a blueprint on how to implement it. This is always going to prove difficult because a UNS is conceptual in nature, it can be implemented **MANY **ways as long as it addresses the conceptual ideologies that walker communicates.

Author: zack.scriven
Content:
I asked ChatGPT if it was aware of the unified namespace in the IIoT World and it replied:

Yes, the Unified Namespace (UNS) in the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) world is a significant concept that's gaining traction. It refers to a centralized, standardized data model and communication protocol that allows various devices, systems, and applications in an industrial environment to share and access data seamlessly.

Here are some key points about the Unified Namespace:

**Centralized Data Model:** The UNS acts as a centralized repository where all data from different sources (sensors, machines, systems) is collected. This data is stored in a uniform format, making it easier for different applications and systems to understand and use it.

**Standardization:** By standardizing data formats and communication protocols, the UNS helps reduce the complexity of integrating new devices and systems into the IIoT ecosystem. It simplifies the process of data exchange and interoperability.

**Real-time Data Access:** With a unified namespace, systems and applications can access real-time data from various sources. This is crucial for monitoring, control, and optimization processes in a smart factory or industrial setting.

**Scalability and Flexibility:** As new devices and technologies emerge, the UNS allows for easy scaling and adaptation. Since it provides a standardized way of data interaction, integrating new components becomes more manageable.

**Enhanced Collaboration:** By providing a common language and platform for data, the UNS fosters collaboration across different departments and stakeholders. This can lead to more innovative solutions and improvements in operational efficiency.

**Security and Reliability**: A well-implemented UNS can enhance the security and reliability of the IIoT network by ensuring that all data exchanges follow predefined protocols and are monitored centrally.

The Unified Namespace is an essential step towards achieving a more interconnected and intelligent industrial environment, aligning closely with the goals of Industry 4.0 and the transition towards Industry 5.0.

Sorry was a bit busy today with IRL work so didn't get to respond until now, but I would agree, design patterns, best practices, frameworks, etc all come and go in waves. This is because the surrounding environments those solutions interact with are dynamic, and are constantly changing. Good solutions are coupled to the surrounding ecosystems that those solutions interact with. 

A good example of this is compute/store, ~10 years ago there was a big push to move everything from local EDCs to the cloud because of the centralization/scale, and efficiencies gained by these large vendors like AWS, in addition to things like, managed services, and some of the cool cloud native design patterns (elastic scaling, etc). Now because of the big push around AI/ML, a lot of organizations are investing back into local hosting. 

I think this is why I'm really big on architecting around volatility and doing volatility based decomposition instead of functional decomposition, we should be designing architectures that are easy to change/refactor. Instead of architectures that might be good solutions today, but are hard to change/migrate as organization mature digital, or industry moves towards another direction.

Author: _dyland
Content:
I am not saying for sure that NATS.io can be the backbone of a UNS or not. Only that I am looking into it.

But no, NATS.io is not a formal standard and I fail to see how that is a problem. I don’t really care about what is standard, I care about what solves the problems.

The problem I see and hear from others is that with an MQTT based solution it lacks metadata, that it cannot be queried, and that it needs to allow for method and functions. NATS solves all 3 of these while maintaining interoperability with existing MQTT infrastructure. It also adds additional patterns like request / response and message ques. 

NATS is a messaging system that is lightweight, open source, and modular. It uses a lightweight text-based protocol using TCP/IP sockets.

Being open source and licensed under the Apache 2.0 license, anyone who wants to maintain the code could fork the entire repo and build their own service if they were so inclined. 

I really fail to see how this defies the concept of the Unified Namespace in any way. It does challenge existing implementations, but not the concept itself.

It Certainly meets the Minimum Technical Requirements..

1.    Edge-Driven
2.    Report by Exception
3.    Lightweight
4.    Open Architecture.

Author: aphexddb
Content:
An observation after lurking a bit is that a lack of constraints on structured data in automation leads to too many open questions, creating friction and the current state of things, vs questions of transport (which IMO is solved at this point thanks to open source, e.g. MQTT, Kafka, etc.). It's the wild west: all the data faucets in automation produce a different flavor. In a large distributed system, each service has it's own structured data, but everyone at this point has mostly aligned on open standards like OpenTelemetry, which impose constraints and let you handle 95% of your telemetry in the same way, over the wire, and during data processing. Another observation is vendors in automation seem to enjoy lock in with many walled gardens, which slows adoption of open standards. I include OPC UA as walled garden, it doesn't feel open at all ($$).

An example of constraints everyone is familiar with is SMS. You get 140 characters of payload, that's it. People came up with a million creative ways to use that constraint. From the outside, Sparkplug seems like a useful constraint, you have a common way to structure data that has a name (like sparkplug) and people can depend on that when they need to serialize data into it, or out of it. My current smooth brain understanding is that the data structure for Sparkplug doesn't work for all data use cases, and there is a "Open UNS Standard X'' that is yet to be defined that can articulate, with constraints (e.g. ISA-95, etc.), how structure data. This would make it easy to send data over the wire, and persist it across open systems.

Author: zack.scriven
Content:
Question: In relation to the above video, what is the difference in a functional, informative, and definitional namespace, and please show an example schema for each type, and within an ISA-95 part 2 schema

Answer from Google Gemini:
A functional namespace defines a group of related data elements that are used to perform a specific function within a system. It groups data together based on the function it serves, rather than its physical location or hierarchy.

An example of a functional namespace in the ISA-95 standard is the "Production Performance" namespace. This namespace would include data elements such as:

* Machine availability
* Production output
* Quality data
* Downtime reasons

A definitional namespace defines the meaning and structure of data elements within a system. It provides a dictionary of terms and their definitions, ensuring that everyone using the system understands the meaning of the data.

An example of a definitional namespace in the ISA-95 standard is the "Equipment" namespace. This namespace would include data elements such as:

* Equipment name
* Equipment type
* Equipment model
* Serial number

An informative namespace provides context and descriptive information about data elements within a system. It helps users understand the significance of the data and how it relates to other data elements.

An example of an informative namespace in the ISA-95 standard is the "Batch" namespace. This namespace would include data elements such as:

* Batch ID
* Product being produced
* Start time
* End time

Here is an example schema for each type of namespace within an ISA-95 part 2 schema:

*Functional Namespace: Production Performance*

```
ProductionPerformance
  - MachineAvailability (number)
  - ProductionOutput (number)
  - Quality (number)
  - DowntimeReason (string)
```

*Definitional Namespace: Equipment*

```
Equipment
  - Name (string)
  - Type (string)
  - Model (string)
  - SerialNumber (string)
```

*Informative Namespace: Batch*

```
Batch
  - ID (string)
  - Product (string)
  - StartTime (datetime)
  - EndTime (datetime)
```

Content:
I'm working on defining my company's standard semantic hierarchy for tags in our SCADA system, and I'm a bit miffed on the way Area is defined.

Currently we don't have a level in our hierarchy for Area as ISA 95 defines it.

So for example we have Enterprise>Site>Line>Cell>Equipment.

Author: _dyland
Content:
Hope this helps rather than confuses but a lot of the facilities I have worked at the example of Enterprise/Site/Area/Line/Cell didn't directly apply, especially with a lot of them being batch control.

For example on one site we could have (a real example just obfuscated a bit):

An area that receives and stores Raw Material.
- Enterprise/Site/Bulk Bins/Equipment/Asset/...

A Cleaning Area where the Raw Material is conditioned.
- Enterprise/Site/Cleaning House/Equipment/Asset/...

A couple Processing areas that processes and/or combine the materials in some way.
- Enterprise/Site/Process Area 1/Equipment/Asset/...
- Enterprise/Site/Process Area 2/Equipment/Asset/...

A bulk finished goods storage and distribution area.
- Enterprise/Site/Distribution/Equipment/Asset/...

And a Packaging area with multiple Packaging Lines.
- Enterprise/Site/Packaging/Line 1/Cell/...
- Enterprise/Site/Packaging/Line 2/Cell/...
- Enterprise/Site/Packaging/Line 3/Cell/...

Even a warehouse
- Enterprise/Site/Warehouse/Location/...

Each site is structured in different ways, the important part is to structure the hierarchy to model the reality.
Some sites don't really have areas, maybe the process is too intertwined or just not big enough to warrant it. In that case maybe it makes sense to omit it altogether or possibly organize it by function. Some sites might not have lines, or maybe there are so many sites that we need to add a level for region, or business unit. A warehouse wont have a Line or a Cell...

This is why standards are a good place to start but often need to be adapted to fit the needs.

Author: jon.forbord
Content:
There are two main types of technical objections. 

1. Limitations related to the most common implementation of UNS, MQTT. 
2. Criticism based on misunderstanding the concept. 

At its core UNS is the current state and events of a business, and a variant on event driven architecture, so I’d say it’s more about advantages and disadvantages as with any approach. 

Common criticisms:
“How secure is it?” (Hell if I’m connecting my X with my Y)
“How come we can’t use X?” (Usually some solution like OSI PI)
“MQTT can’t do X, Y and Z” (request response pattern - aka service oriented approach… )

Btw, I’d say there’s plenty of criticism in the community, but public blogs like what HiveMQ presents will usually be quite one-sided.

Author: jon.forbord
Content:
Most of the disadvantages Id say is more human in nature. 

1. It requires a shift in mindset that not everyone is ready for or motivated to do. 
2. Be prepared to meet resistance, unless UNS is already part of your digital transformation strategy. I’ve not met a single individual that has not met some form of resistance to adopt UNS as an approach or part of a digital transformation approach.
3. Some of the concepts taught with respect to governance and security  (red and blue, and open by default, make a case for closed) do somewhat break with a lot of established “best practices”. This does not fly easily into most organizations. 
4. Currently there are not a lot of integrators that actually knows how to implement a UNS, or has embedded the mindset and approach to solving problems that is part of the UNS. 
5. In above mentioned limited access to expertise, some companies will eventually try to take advantage of this and sell poorly executed solutions or services packaged as UNS, either because of their own ignorance or just being opportunistic.
