Author: jon.forbord
Content:
With QoS = 2 and the clean session flag set to false, in principle, a disconnected client should receive all messages since the disconnect. AFAIK. 

You have two options technically. 

1. The node keeps a copy of the «sub-UNS» (the part of the UNS the node subscribes to) i.e the current state maintained in memory or on disk at all times while connected to the UNS (Ignition does this for instance through its tag engine), and updates this as messages arrive through its subscriptions. Retain is there, so you can technically go back to the broker to get the last current state from the broker in case of disconnects. This is needed because of report by exception. 

2. The other option is to treat the broker as a key-value store, and disconnect between each time you need the data and use subscriptions to get the retained message once you need it.. this last one is probably not a great pattern. 

For the post-doc level: number 1 is why the UNS is omnipresent. All nodes will keep a part of the UNS at all times inside of the node, so the UNS is present in all the nodes, ie omnipresence!

Author: jon.forbord
Content:
Setting the retain flag to true, is one way to maintain an updated current state across nodes, because disconnected nodes will quickly have an outdated view of the current state as long as MQTT is used with report by exception. 

Sparkplug B uses births as the mechanism to maintain a correct current state (statefulness), and does not require (it actually mandates not to) the use of the retain-flag.

Author: jon.forbord
Content:
1. «And will increasing QoS …» no. It will add some overhead due to message ack-ing, but MQTT is still lightweight. Message ack-ing is unavoidable if you want delivery guarantees of at least once and at most once. Just a fact of life. 
2. «but saying…» no. Any other node who wants can connect to the broker and get the same information.  So it is not siloed. The copy is strictly only necessary if a node wants to keep a stateful picture of the part of the UNS it subscribes to. If the node will only Process the events in a fire and forget fashion, there is no need to keep the copy. 
3. «And we can…» I mean; you can always use Redis instead if you feel that way. Message brokers pass messages, and retain flag can reduce some of the overhead required to maintain a stateful overall system. The mqtt broker is designed to keep the last message on a topic if asked to do so. So it can sort of store information, but only the latest. This is the retain flag.

Author: oliver.m.
Content: I think truth, beauty (and goodness) are difficult to define if they're not considered objective standards. Taking the opposite view, claiming that "truth is subjective" is a bit of a paradox. If that statement is taken as an objective truth, it contradicts itself by making an objective claim that truth is subjective. On the other hand, if the statement is  taken as subjective, it undermines itself (e.g. "that's just your opinion). When it's considered objective, it becomes a lot easier to define but still just as impossible to achieve completely, i.e. it's "true enough". The strongest counterargument to that is the observer effect, where subjectivity seems to be intrinsic to truth. I haven't seen any good answers to that.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
It would be nice to see more standard pricing.  Perhaps it would be easier if there were some stipulations or assumptions on what it's scoped for.

Years ago, I remember submitting RFQs on a big project.  One of the quotes from a vendor came back with astronomically high pricing.  Because of the tag counts, they were under the impression that the plant it was for was 10-15x larger than it actually was.  The plant was greenfield with very advanced automation.  Almost every asset had motion control and very high tag counts.  The vendor was accustomed to selling to other verticals where there was less sophisticated automation and more resource intensive implementations.  Their pricing modeling was way off and assumed significant onboarding costs.

I think what makes it challenging is when solution is sold into different industry verticals with varying cost of sales and support.  For example, there are MES/ERP software companies that have completely different pricing models for regulated industries like life sciences, aerospace & defense, utilities, etc than their other customers.  Life sciences buyers, for example, are accustomed to a white glove process that can go on for many months or years.  What it might take a couple weeks for a self-sufficient Jon Forbord, it could take six months of professional services and formal project management at other orgs with less competent team members.

PLC hardware and SCADA software are known entities.  For most buyers and in most cases, it's a predictable market.  It doesn't require involving as nearly as many people and as much of their time as say an MES or ERP.  When solutions are more specialized and vary in implementations, it requires more consultation pre-sales and post-sales.

Author: jon.forbord
Content:
Only the changed metrics will be published with Sparkplug B, ie it is truly report by exception. I think @Mark O'Donovan is talking about something else or is misunderstanding something. 

All metrics are published at birth, which is part of the STATEFULNESS of SpB. Since SpB only publishes changes in the payloads, any consuming node that misses one or more payloads will have an incorrect representation of the STATE of the edge node. To correct this, when missed payloads are detected, the consuming node will send a command to the edge node to publish a birth (rebirth). The edge node will publish a birth with ALL metrics (ie its STATE), and the consuming node again knows the current state and can keep track of that with only the changes to the state reported from each subsequent payload from the edge node. 

TLDR; in sparkplug B, birth messages will contain ALL metrics precisely BECAUSE sparkplug B is Report By Exception and a missed payload means you don’t know what the current state of the node is.

Author: stephenbryant_89711
Content:
Hi Ravi!
The same terms have been used for slightly different things.  This happens often.

When people talk about deterministic or hard real time, they mean that the amount of time something takes is very well defined; this is required for example for precise machine operation.  This is the meaning used by experts in the hardware domain.  A "real time operating system" makes deterministic behaviour possible, so you know that a certain operation will always take the same amount of time.  A PLC is a real time device, using this definition of the term.

The UNS is about how data is structured and made available.  It does not define how long it takes between when an event happens (or data is published) and when a subscriber receives that.  When Walker talks about data being made available in real time, he just means it's low latency - but what that actually is varies.  UNS is not deterministic when it comes to timing of messages going in and out; the same is true of MQTT.

It looks like you are also using the term "deterministic" in relation to how (not when) results are obtained from data.  This is a different context of "deterministic" than the others were using.  Such a difference of understanding is very common between IT and OT people.  You seem more "IT" whereas many (most?) here are more "OT".

Did that help?

Author: stephenbryant_89711
Content:
Regular ethernet is not deterministic, as you never know in advance how you'll be affected by other traffic.  This is why things like EtherCAT exist.  ProfiNet and Ethernet/IP are ostensibly ethernet compatible but are, in my opinion, just hacks on top of ethernet where all nodes agree to behave deterministically... but plugging your laptop in can still upset things.

I'm not aware of a real time implementation of an MQTT broker.  If one exists, it would need to run on a real time OS and be accessed only via a deterministic real time network.

TSN adds determinism to ethernet - providing you have TSN capable routers.   A sensor can communicate deterministically with a PLC (eg: using IEC/IEEE 60802) in one VLAN, can post to MQTT in another VLAN, and can download an update from the Internet in a third VLAN.  All of this is over a single ethernet cable, and each VLAN with appropriate priority and bandwidth settings.  If it uses PoE too, it's a true single cable solution.

Part of the problem with deterministic timing over networks is that different devices don't have the exact same time.  If you use NTP, you can sync to within around 1ms on a LAN in ideal conditions.  At the last TSN plugfest I was at (quarter of a year ago), TSN's time synchronisation (using PTP) was always within 100ns no matter the network load.  That is literally one million times more accurate.  This was over a gigabit TSN network across routers from 7 manufacturers too.

Now consider that you could sync an entire factory - or probably an entire site with that accuracy.  Now your AI and other algorithms can truly see all the machines as parts of the whole.  I guess you can see why that's useful, right?

Author: stephenbryant_89711
Content:
To your question about inter controller communication: do you need deterministic real time for your case?  If you do, you require that they be linked via a real time network.  Plain ethernet will not do.  Your exact choice depends on your PLCs.

I've been looking at control use cases outside of the real time domain, and I see plenty of scope for using MQTT and UNS exactly for this.  As individual systems become more intelligent, they handle the real time constraints internally and can be given higher level commands.  For example, we had a project where a self-driving cart needed positioning more accurately.  Instead of real time motor start and stop command, and instead of a really expensive positioning system, we put a QR code on the cart and used a camera to tell the cart to move a certain amount left or right - over MQTT.  The cart maintains its status in MQTT too, so we know when it's finished moving.  This is an ideal UNS use case.  Control is possible, and deterministic real time is not required.  Low latency is necessary though, so I wouldn't use a cloud MQTT broker.

Content:
the message is the speed of light but the data is not used until the next scan.

@Ravi.S I think the phrase deterministic , is used to mean, that the data is received in the order it is sent.

at the start of OT/IT convergence, real time communications was often used to describe PLC to PLC traffic.
the idea being that at the bottom of the perdu model, a loss of communication would cause issues immediately (or almost immediately to a  human observer)
and while this is a useful concept to differentiate it from a lot of IT traffic, as you move up the stack a loss of comms to the MES may not be noticed for an hour and certainly you  could run production without the MES for a short time.
As you move to general IT, email, sharepoint, Service now you get a much larger time where you can manage a disturbance.

VOIP and meeting videos are often considered to be more real time and given the appropriate QoS and other priorities by IT.
I have many many time had to forcibly explain to IT that the priority has to be " Production Data" VOIP, Video, all your other stuff.

but Real-Time only covers part of the story for the Production Data, it is vital for a machine that the start and stop commands come in the correct order, and withing a predefined time. So deterministic is a more appropriate phrase, to cover those two requirements, especially at the control layer, but also as you travel up the stack to SCADA and some parts of MES. but there is likely to be less of an issue, if the messages to an ERP about the completion of jobs is received in an incorrect order.

To me if we are timestamping the data and using the timestamp to sort order it is because it is not deterministic

Author: sparkylarks
Content:
My understanding of this was ,I think that because MQTT does not have any controls to make it deterministic any UNS based on MQTT would not be deterministic. That is part of why sparkplug was defined to allow MQTT to be used in the lower levels, and solve that Stop then Start <> Start then Stop

If there is a protocol that was deterministic, and you build an UNS based on that, then you might in theory have a deterministic UNS.
but  I would question a need for that. Certainly in how a UNS is used to day in a manufacturing plant.

It is designed to allow us to "Spot Patterns and Solve Problems" and we use the timestamp to organise the data in whatever platform we are using.
the UNS is the mechanism of getting data to that platform. And if one node transmits nearly instantaneously and the other due to a comms problem, does not transmit for 20 minutes, buffers the data, and retransmits it all later, that is generally no problem the data is received by the platform and model may be rerun or whatever is needed.

I am not sure what I woudl want to happen in a deterministic system when the data from the node is not recieved. I know in ProfiSafe I want to stop my machine and put it in a safe state.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
MQTT relies on TCP for transport.  TCP is helpful because of the acknowledgments, retries, transport security, etc.  The QoS feature in MQTT is more about how to handle messaging between clients.  It's different than the QoS used in general networking (e.g., 801.1p DSCP).

MQTT was designed to be stateful, specifically over less reliable or constrained IP networks.  Having a client "fire-and-forget" to a broker would be a problem.  It needs to know it's connected and publishing.  UDP is not suitable for this.  Also, when the protocol was invented, I don't believe there were transport security for UDP (e.g., DTLS).

I think you're referring to probabilistic determinism.  On a provisioned process control network in a plant, it's possible to use UDP for many control applications.  This is what EtherNet/IP does for exchanging I/O.  It's not complete hard real time, but it's good enough.  Because it's on a planned network, the likelihood that traffic arrives in a timely and orderly manner is high.  There are limits to this, of course.  That's why there are things like PTP, TSN, etc as well as the more "pure" layer-2 oriented field protocols like PROFINET, EtherCAT, etc.

Content:
To complete your exchanges and propose an alternative solution to MQTT for distributed and real-time applications *(Maybe off topic)*.
In robotics we use RTPS (Real-time Publish-Subscribe Protocol) with DDS (Data Distribution Service).
DDS is a "data-centric connectivity framework" based on the publish-subscribe paradigm like MQTT. 
It provides its users with advanced data-management features, including a comprehensive type system, multiple communication patterns and different types of Quality of Service, which simplify the task of building distributed (real-time) systems.
ROS2 relies on this protocol.

Then it is possible to make a ROS2 to MQTT gateway for example to return to the USN world

Author: jon.forbord
Content:
To my understanding this is not why SpB was introduced. 

SpB uses QoS=0 to avoid the problem of messages arriving too late (which can happen with QoS=1/2). Either the message arrives now, or never. You don’t want a pump turning on three hours after the operator gave the command to start the pump. In order messaging I’m not quite sure about. SpB has sequence numbers on messages to detect missing messages, and to allow some handling of message ordering. I’m not sure how it’s meant to handle the start then stop problem. Probably ask for a rebirth.. but I’m not sure. 

SpB introduced improvements to the statefullness of mqtt (since been rendered pretty much redundant with mqtt 5.0), autodiscovery of the entire namespace (births) as opposed to waiting for a value change to be notified of a topics existence, and a standardized schema for metrics, properties and templates (in short).

Author: sparkylarks
Content:
I take everything that is said about the Semantic Hierarchy as guidelines not rules.
So ignore everything and ask yourself, what structure will help you solve problems.

when I do that I  normal have a UNS with the following.
**- my contextualised namespace-** this is the ISA-95 structure it forms the spine UNS really. Most of the nodes in the eco system will subscribe here and a lot will also publish directly.
but sometimes it is not enough and because the world is not ideal I also have 
**- A raw namespace**: this is where I publish data straight from the Edge. It is not contextualised, and often can be essentially a big dump of information. my Data ops Platform will take this data and Normalise it, contextualise it and publish it into my Contextualised namespace. Sometimes I have a "Raw" topic at the same level as Plant or Area. Or sometimes i have a Raw topic down at a machine level. I am leaning more towards keeping the contextualised and Raw namespaces apart.
**- Special namespaces. **Theses are namespaces where I publish data, often already in the contextualised name space to be used for functional reasons, but more often for dashboarding, It is just a bit easier a dashboard looks at one topic and finds all the data. I have also had a historical namspace where I publish all the data I want historised, but I tend to not do that so much any more

Author: jon.forbord
Content:
I’m curious how other people in here feel about a topic. It takes a bit of setup, so bear with me. 

When I see blog posts or article from a vendor about «how we enable UNS» (such as this one: https://blog.palantir.com/industry-ai-8cd003a81be1 )
It almost always falls short of how I want that type of piece to read:
«We can plug into YOUR ecosystem using these technologies, and here’s how you can easily share insights and send data back into YOUR ecosystem. We will be the node that can do best in class x and y… ».

No instead Its almost always «we can BE your UNS» or «hey we can do X with your data and btw we have heard of mqtt, and here’s a misunderstood definition of UNS that kind of fits well with our world view». 

 I mean, should not a vendor that has REALLY understood the UNS be very aware that the UNS-savvy customer wants (or at least should want) vendors that act as nodes in the customer’s ecosystem? So when they present themselves as «we will BE your ecosystem», it pretty much fails the basic snifftest. Even Litmus calling it Litmus UNS?! I know they mean well, but it just feels like it goes against some of the very principles of UNS!! (For the record, I think other than the to me blunder of marketing as «Litmus UNS», they’re doing a lot right)

Am I way off, or how do the rest of you feel? One of the cornerstones of UNS are the «nodes in an ecosystem», but it seems almost zero vendors that are jumping on the bandwagon these days that seem to understand this?

Author: _dyland

Its not just UNS marketing or even tech I have issues with this for most advertisements. I often ask myself, am I really the target for this add, for this campaign, or this product?

In the case of the UNS, I don't think they are targeting the Tech Savvy Customer. The Tech Savvy are a much smaller demographic and much harder to appeal to with traditional methods. I feel like the target audience is the demographic responsible for the final decision, likely an individual or group a few people removed from any real tech savvy. The ones who will actually purchase the product. At the end of the day, it is about generating profit. You want the campaign to appeal to as broad a group as possible for as cheap as possible.

They may or may not understand the UNS, but it is certinaly a hot topic. And regardless of their understanding, they need to sell the product and everything they do will be in service of that.

Really why would a company like Palantir care to market to people who truly understand the UNS when they can market to a much larger much less skeptical audience that actually makes purchasing decisions?

Author: sparkylarks
Content:
On one had it is marketing. and for marketing a lot of that is taking something that is standard and saying it is amazing.
Watch any advert for a soft drink and it promises a religious experience level of refreshment.

And Unlike general marketing, Technical marketing is actually people who don't really understand the topic telling others who don't understand the topic that you need to buy this stuff.

That article is a bit to like that in places like "Connecting to PLC's or having JDBC Connectors" WOW!!!!!!! and to a lot of people that sounds really far out there. 

I thin @Dylan DuFresne 's Tech Savvy Customer is not the intended audience, and a bit like a physicist watching Star Trek you have to not really worry about all the thing that they get wrong.

So on one hand I think theses sorts of article will help the Tech Savvy Customer get buy-in at a corporate level when then pitch migrating towards a UNS based Architecture.

But I do think there is a worry trend, where lots of companies are saying we can be your UNS. Companies will have 4 or 5 applications each with their own name space, and they may even be connected, they may even all form part of the same semantic hierarchy, but there is not single a source of truth. And we end up with lots of MQTT brokers in lots of application and point to point connection between those brokers.

Author: rickbullotta
Content: The irony is that sometimes these approaches *INCREASE* the number of connections to make.  Let's envision a scenario where most of my integrations are actually point to point.  I could just write a single adapter between two systems, but if I want to use the OPMQXYZ protocol or the SAI9500 standard, I need to write two adapters to convert to/from those for each system.  In some cases that's better in the long run, in others it's a waste of time and resources.  "It depends".

Author: vikanchira
Content:
As a follow up. Here is my MVP of the following requirements:

**1. Visualization:**
- **Operator Interface**: Needs to include input forms, action buttons, and process flow SCADA visual.
- **War Room Dashboard**: Comprehensive dashboard for monitoring.
- **Business Analytics Dashboard**: Transactional data analytics per day, month, hour, work order.
- **Operation Analytics Dashboard**: Time-series data analytics for troubleshooting assets and machine attributes.
- **PDF & Excel Reports**: Capability to generate and automate PDF and Excel reports.
- **Video HLS Stream Player**: Integration of a video player to view the site's surveillance camera streams.
- **Display Compatibility**: Views should be compatible with PC screens, large war room displays, site kiosk control rooms, and mobile devices (not tablets).

**2. DataOps:**
- **Data Ingestion**: Collection of data from OPC-UA servers and MQTT brokers.
- **Data Modelling**: Structure data in the Unified Namespace and ISA-95 Part 2 format.
- **Snowflake Connector**: Ingest data to Snowflake and use Snowflake as the analytics data source.
- **Historian (Time-Series Database)**: Store time-series data for analysis and troubleshooting.
- **Aggregate Data**: Aggregate data into transactional records and larger time buckets (e.g., 15 mins and hourly) and store them in a relational database such as PostgreSQL.
- **Send Aggregated Data to Snowflake**: Send the aggregated data to the Snowflake data platform (since time-series data storage in the data platform will be costly and wasteful).

**3. Data Sources:**
- **OPC-UA Server**: 12 sites with 8k - 10k tags per site
- **MQTT Broker**: 60k tags
- **Assets**: 320 - 380 assets under management

Author: jon.forbord
Content:
Noone? Ok, I would not say its a trivial question, given noone has responded yet, that should be a clear indication. 
TLDR:
1. and 2. «it depends»


1. You generally want to consider that all data MAY be useful some day in the future, so collect more than you need. Collect it all if you can, I/O, calculated values, state variables, alarms, drive
data.. but if you can’t, you have to prioritize. What to prioritize will be dependent on your Process and machine. Hard to give any advice on this in general. If its a brown field, the MINIMUM, should be what is on the HMI/SCADA from before. 

There is no hard rule to store everything in a data lake. It is quite common to do so, but it is also common to also have a historian. 

Remember UNS is not a hard set of rules, its guidelines and principles. Often budget, cost and technology can limit what you’re actually able to do. Ideal, collect all, and store everything forever. This is likely not possible, due to cost, technology or both.

2. see above. It depends, and cost eventually plays a role.

Author: markm._00001
Content:
Your comment seems to overlook the true value proposition that Palantir brings to the table, which is centered on its powerful ontology framework rather than simply a Unified Namespace (UNS). While it's true that Palantir uses the terminology of a UNS, it’s important to recognize that this is just one component of their broader solution.

A Unified Namespace serves as a method to aggregate data sources, but it doesn’t inherently solve the complexities of data integration, contextualization, or real-time decision-making. This is where Palantir’s ontology truly shines. The ontology is not just about connecting data; it's about modeling, contextualizing, and operationalizing it across an organization. 

The ontology allows users to define and enforce relationships, create data-driven workflows, and apply AI/ML models in a way that a simple UNS cannot achieve. In short, the ontology is the engine that drives meaningful insights and actions, while the UNS is simply a part of this larger ecosystem.

Palantir may use UNS terminology because it resonates with current trends, but once you delve into their ontology, you’ll understand that the real power lies in its ability to unify, contextualize, and activate data in ways that go far beyond the scope of a typical UNS. It’s not about trying to be a fix-all product; it’s about offering a robust framework that addresses the complexities of modern data challenges.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
A main difference is the imbalance between ingress and egress.  These solutions are "net consumers" in the architecture.  Yes, they offer "exhaust" APIs for external consumers, but that's more of a special case or secondary function.  Their primary mission is to ingress, persist, construct ontologies, analyze, visualize data for itself.  It's not about virtualizing or distributing data for many consumers.  They're more of a projection of a UNS.  They're just a very sophisticated consumer of data.  It's not necessarily a bad thing.  It's solving a different type of problem.  It's solving analysis problems as opposed to integration problems.

An MES company would not predicate its integration strategy with ERP, LIMS, EAM, CMMS, etc solutions with one of these platforms.  They would seek more "neutral" architectural components to facilitate interoperability.  These platforms are more likely to need an MES partner than the other way around.  To them, MES is another valuable data source to consume for itself and provide greater analysis value.

An airline or automaker would not run fleet management or connected services through one of these platforms.  They would probably start with some sort of message brokering.  If one of these platforms were present, they would be an advanced "spoke" for analysis.  They would not be a "hub" for all the disparate systems that might need to consume the fleet data.

A manufacturer would probably not center its integration strategy spanning (and within) OT networks, site networks, corporate data centers, multi-region private cloud, SaaS apps, etc through one of these platforms.  These platforms would sit very high in the architecture as a destination for data rather than as an intermediary.

Author: rickbullotta
Content:
Nats won't solve it either.  We need a comprehensive IIoT platform that embraces the realities that:

- Data doesn't always come from devices in the way we want it
- Historical data is as important as live data
- Metadata is as important as data
- The entire name and data space needs to be queryable
- We need a combination of on-demand queries and pub/sub, not just pub/sub
- Blending metadata and data in queries is of massive value
- What works fine in POC does not often scale well, particularly when you have thousands or millions of entities

TBH we solved many of these with ThingWorx, but some of those capabilities were removed from the product after I left.  Will never understand why.  Totally illogical.

Author: b.goode
Content:
I'd like some criticism on a UNS structure, if anyone's willing. I'm wanting to track generic "health" metrics on a broad range of assets, including servers, significant software processes, and other things. Each individual asset could have its own unique set of metrics. Example: all servers might track the last time they restarted, but a particular server might track whether, idk, it can currently ping a certain IP address. Each category of asset would have its own topic namespace, like below:

`Enterprise/Site/Area/AssetType/AssetName`, or
`Enterprise/Site/Area/Line/AssetType/AssetName`

for the server example, i could subscribe to all servers with `+/+/+/Servers/+`. If a particular server `123` was tracking any metrics, it would describe them with a retained message at `+/+/+/Servers/123/Metrics`. Data for those metrics (value + timestamp) would be found below: `+/+/+/Servers/123/Metrics/ABC` for metric `ABC`.

so, i have two particular points in mind:

1. My use of retained/not-retained messages:

These two topics would be retained:
`+/+/+/Servers/+`, `+/+/+/Servers/+/Metrics`. These are retained because they declare that an asset and its metrics exist. that allows a web app to dynamically build its navigation of these assets. as soon as i publish an asset, it's automatically available in the dashboards, without updating any code - the different asset teams (there are many) don't need to coordinate with the web app team other than to understand the expected UNS structure. ("Hey, who do i talk to, to get this asset's health graphed in the dashboards?")

Individual metrics (e.g., `+/+/+/Servers/123/Metrics/ABC` would *not* be retained, and these are just raw data (timestamp + value). For the dashboard application of this data, a service is subscribing to these and inserting them in a time series database to provide the historical values.

2. The AssetType (Servers in my example above) is under an ISA part II Area in this case, but could also be under a Line (the way MES, ERP are typically seen), and maybe other places? Because Area teams generally manage their own servers here, it seems more logical to publish their data under an Area, but other types of assets might exist under a Line.

anything problematic or missing? has anyone seen or done anything remotely similar?

Author: zack.scriven
Content:
**
Topic Synopsis: Intellectual Property, Terminology, and Gatekeeping in Industry 4.0**

In a recent discussion, members of the community explored the balance between protecting intellectual property (IP) and fostering open collaboration within Industry 4.0 concepts like the "Digital Transformation Maturity Assessment" (DTMA) and the "Unified Namespace" (UNS). The debate raised important questions around ownership, influence, and terminology in a growing field.

**Key Points:**

**Defending IP and Terminology: **Zack Scriven highlighted the importance of protecting terms like DTMA, which refers to a specific process developed by 4.0 Solutions, and ensuring consistency in how it's applied across the industry. He emphasized that while many people now use DTMA, it originally referred to 4.0 Solutions’ methodology. Trademarking such terms was also discussed, though UNS, being an architecture rather than a product, couldn't be trademarked.

**Organic Evolution of Terms:** Some members, like Rutger Van Aelst, questioned the extent to which defending terminology might appear as gatekeeping, potentially alienating others. They suggested that terms might evolve naturally as more people adopt and adapt them, contributing their own interpretations. Rutger proposed focusing on promoting the 4.0 Solutions version of DTMA as the best implementation, rather than strictly controlling its use.

**Missionaries vs. Mercenaries: **Scriven introduced the idea of “missionaries” and “mercenaries” within the industry: those who evangelize and spread the methodology versus those who take concepts without attribution. He acknowledged the discomfort of seeing ideas used without credit but suggested that this is a common challenge for creators.

**Educating vs. Alienating: **Many participants, including Dylan DuFresne, stressed the need to focus on education over alienation. The consensus leaned toward a more inclusive approach—educating the community on best practices, while still maintaining recognition of original work.

The discussion underscored the tension between guarding intellectual contributions and promoting open knowledge sharing, with an emphasis on fostering positive growth for the Industry 4.0 community.

Author: markpitout
Content:
UNS is based on report by exception. It is therefore up to the edge application to determine when data becomes exceptional.
Eg. An analog measurement: 
1. Has the measured value deviated beyond a preset deadband?
2. Is there significant rate of  change in the value (over time)?
3. Has the value crossed some preset threshold (eg. traditional high / low limits)?
4. Has the value become stale (No change at all over time)?
5. Do I send periodic updates regardless of value changes?

Neither the UNS or the subscribers determine a rate at which data must be published. Only the publisher determines when data is exceptional enough to warrant transmission.

Author: youri.regnaud
Content: At my company, we consider the RHIZE solution as an IoT Data Hub. Our definition combines a headless MES/MOM, decoupling the backend from the frontend, and acting as a Data Hub (aka Digital integration Hub definition from Gartner) where data from various systems can be replicated and contextualized in a single platform that ease consumption with GraphQL and Pub/Sub. This platform aligns production, quality, and maintenance domains while also serving as a time-series historian, contextualizing data within production environments. One key advantage of RHIZE is its 100% compliance with the ISA 95 standard, avoiding the need for custom models, though it requires a high level of maturity to fully leverage the ISA 95 framework. In summary, RHIZE is a headless MES/MOM, a Data Hub, and a historian built on time-series database technology with a strong ISA-95 ontology

Author: galileo86
Content: Thanks. Then I have a followup question 🙂 whats the issue with sending it like that? Or spreading it out in different sub-topics?

Author: _dyland
Content:
Like that is very verbose, not every consumer wants all that metadata. You cannot subscribe to all of a specific "sensorType".

Over different topics is going to mean that the data is sent asynchronous. The subscribing application would need to keep the metadata for each topic in cache, and know what to subscribe to in order to get it.

Depending on the application, either option, or both, could work. It just depends.

Author: stephenbryant_89711
Content:
> whats the issue with sending it like that?
The meta data is the same each time - sending unchanged data lots of times is not "report by exception".  It wastes bandwidth and recipient CPU, and thus doesn't scale well.
For this reason, it's better to separate it out.  You can have it in its own topic (or topics), or - with MQTT5 - you can attach it as user properties on the topic of the actual data you're sending.

I'd love to see MQTT extended with something like XPath, so I could then subscribe to topics which have certain user props, ie `enterprise/site/area/line/#[@sensorType=temperature]`

Author: stevenledoux_19961
Content:
Hello,

Let's say our data scientist starts a machine learning project and accesses the historical database (data lake, lakehouse, time series, etc.), which is a subscriber to our unified namespace. The data scientist needs periodic data, for example, the temperature, speed, pressure, and state (e.g., failure) from a machine every 5 minutes , in order to train a model. If we only have events in the historical data, it brings some complexity for the data scientist to convert this into periodic data.

Up to now, I have configured my kepware to recieve OPC/UA tag-changing data combined with polling the tags at least once per hour. From a data engineering or data science point of view, there is now a guarantee that our historical database for each hour has the latest state of the data (e.g., speed). This allows us to convert hourly data into 5-minute interval data without having to search back in time for the changing event (never knowing where that data is).

In 4.0 solutions, report-by-exception is mentioned along with normalization. In a YouTube video 'UNS and the Data Historians Role' by @Zack Scriven  , normalization is discussed at 5:57. It is mentioned: “Every event in your business passes through a single UNS, ... the timestamps are aligned, ... this plays into machine learning, ... if the timestamps are not lined up, it does you almost no good for root cause analysis.”

I am trying to understand normalization, to see if it can address my problem of preventing polling. My question is: does normalization mean that you end up saving periodic data into your historian, like Canary? If so, how do you achieve this, do you use an external function that connects to the MQTT broker (each 5 minutes in my case), and receives the latest state of the data (using MQTT retained messages), in order to store it into our historian? If not, can you explain normalization, what do you mean in the video with "align the timestamps and plays into machine learning"? 

Thx

Author: stevenledoux_19961
Content:
Thx for the responses on my question. 

At first, indeed i would also say that data on the UNS should always have a timestamp, so you now when it occurred. 
 
Let's say an event occurred one hour ago and since then it's state is unchanged (so no new events are send out = report by exception), when you view the broker 
(ex. with MQTT explorer) you see it's state for the current time. So the broker aligns all events to the current state and time of you business regardless when
the event occurred. I think that is what the mean in 4.0 solutions with normalization. The question is how you translate it to the historian?

why? For machine learning you need the state for all your model input data, at a certain frequency for a certain period. Ex. for 2 years we have each minute
the state of these 50 inputs + output. So if you only save the report by exception data into a historian, the data scientist needs to convert it to periodic data 
(search back in time to get the input / output data for each minute). Ex. for the minute 10:10 we have these 50 input states + output, for 10:11 these, for 10:12 ... 
And so it will be complex for a data scientist to iterate fast due to complexity or dependency on other people like a data engineer.

As a solution i could follow Jeff, who said that you can take a snapshot of the UNS each minute and save it into the historian resulting in periodic datapoints 
and so making the data scientist happy. But then can i assume that we need MQTT retained messages for normalization? (could be heavy for the broker performance 
if you do it for each message). Or do i need to implement the logic into a external function (saving the latest state), or is there another correct implementation?  

Would be great if an expert can (dis)confirm this, and give more feedback on the implementation.
There is a new video on 4.0 solutions where they mention briefly normalization in the context of machine learning and what needs to be in the historian.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
So, to answer your question, yes. All that work involved organizing UNS, normalizing data structures, reshaping data for cloud data services, etc is what HighByte focuses on and, arguably, does best.
>
(reusing a response from a few days ago)
>
It sometimes concerns me how much focus there is on solution comparison over problem solving. It’s best to inquire about merits of different solutions in the context of the types of problems one seeks to solve. Otherwise, one risks comparing apples to oranges (“fruit”), conveyors to robots (“material handling”), hack saws to CNC machines (“material cutting”), etc. At the end of the day, if a solution is solving one’s problems well, there is nothing wrong with that solution. What works for others may work for you or not work for you. There is nothing wrong with people building different architectures composed of different solutions. Digital transformation is not a law or prescriptive standard.
>
Ignition is not a DataOps platform. It can facilitate integrations, but it does not facilitate DataOps. Integration features ≠ DataOps. Ignition is a SCADA and IoT platform and sometimes an MES. At its core, it’s an application platform that has a lot of useful connectors and facilities to consume data from them. It’s (arguably the best) full stack solution, but not specialized middleware. DataOps is not about storing, visualizing, or analyzing data. DataOps goes beyond converting protocols, organizing tags, and ad-hoc scripting. It’s about engineering data pipelines to transform data between many external producers and consumers of data. It’s unbiased about how data is produced and consumed as well as its type (telemetry, transactional, historical). DataOps is a discipline for cross-functional teams to engineer interoperability, govern it, and drive down the cost of making changes towards zero. This is, in my opinion, is what scale is all about.
>

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
Sometimes, the Industrial DataOps problem space is difficult for industrial control system professionals to grasp. Their worldview of data of predicated on their experiences of programming PLCs, SCADA/HMI, and historians. They are accustomed to having end-to-end control of data within the process control domain. They think of data as data points, tags, or collection of tags. They programmed the tags in the PLC and they programmed their consumption in the SCADA or historian. Their coworkers working in other departments (e.g., process engineering, quality, maintenance, supply chain, operations, accounting) will have a very different view of data. They will need data derived from process control data, enriched with other data sources, and then tailored to their access patterns and destination apps/services. They will often need the ability to easily construct relationships with other datasets for unplanned purposes long after the data was collected. Walker’s recent video on failed ML initiatives covered this well. Digital transformation outcomes require a competency in being able to not just move data, but shape and curate it to the evolving needs of data consumers.
>

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
Having some very large Ignition shops as customers, here are some observations in their journeys. At first, users are enamored with the awesome licensing model and “overbuild” gateways. It leads to monoliths that are fragile, difficult to maintain, and upgrade. This is not a fault of Ignition as a platform, but organizations learning to not architect operations technology like they have done in the past. Over time, gateways get broken up into separate roles that align with functional ownership and requirements. This typically means separate gateways for SCADA, IoT Platform, MES, etc. In terms of additional solutions, they’ll often start with replacing the embedded SQLite with a full RDBMS. If it’s process/batch industry with a time series data strategy, third-party historians like PI System or Canary Labs are present with Seeq for analysis. Device connectivity will get offloaded to Kepware for more features, performance, and broader protocol support. If there is an enterprise data strategy, reporting and analytics will rely on platforms like Snowflake or Databricks. If MQTT plays a big role in the architecture, HiveMQ will get adopted for brokering with all its scaling, security, and observability features. If an Ignition gateway is deployed as a SCADA, HighByte will facilitate the northbound interoperability to UNS, MES, cloud, etc. If a gateway is deployed as an IoT platform, HighByte can drive the gateway’s tag providers with ready-to-use, contextualized datasets spanning telemetry, transactional, timeseries, and file-based data sources. If a gateway is a running the Sepasoft MES modules, HighByte can pick up new events and modified historical records from many sites, remediate schema variation, and then optimally package them for use in an enterprise data lake.
>

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342

If this is all confusing, don’t worry and don’t buy any software yet. Create labs with tools like Node-RED and build solutions for actual end-to-end use cases. Author: marco_moiron
Content:
In the last workshop, I think Walker mentioned (or at least this is how I understood it) that when normalizing variables—such as temperature, updating once a minute, and a machine running signal, updating once an hour—the normalization would involve publishing both at the rate of the fastest-changing variable.

I have a few concerns with this approach, especially in real-world scenarios:

- Some variables (e.g., process pressures) update every second, temperatures every minute, and running signals might change once every few days. Normalizing to the fastest rate could mean tens of thousands of events per second per site, overloading brokers and the historian with unnecessary data.

- Interpolating values to fill gaps is often used but not well-accepted in statistical studies, as these values didn’t actually occur.

- Assuming a "shortest update rate" implies polling, which contradicts the UNS principle of reporting by exception. If a source publishes on exception at 1 ms, should all variables be resampled or interpolated at that rate?

- To preserve the extra sampled data, historian compression would need to be disabled, reducing storage efficiency.

While I see the benefits of having normalized data ready for AI without preprocessing, I’m struggling to see how this scales in real-world applications.

Thoughts or alternative approaches?

Author: t.vesa
Content: I've thought about this a lot recently, and it has kept me awake for a few nights. RBE is not interpolation: When using RBE, the system only reports when there is an actual change in the data value, no matter the measuring frequency. It doesn't assume anything between reports—if no new value is reported, it’s because the value hasn’t changed. Therefore, there’s no need for interpolation, as the system accurately reflects the current state at all times, avoiding the risk of introducing false data. But on the other hand if and when there's any deadbanding for filtering out small variations that don’t meet the reporting threshold, I guess it could be argued as interpolation so go figure. 🤷

Author: sparkylarks
Content:
Interpolation is the process of using known data to estimate values at unknown locations.

And we normally think of it a a linear approach where we draw a straight line between two known points. 


But there are many approaches
And within that you can break it down to adaptive and non-adaptive techniques.

You can use cubic or quadratic interpolation, Excel does that 

Perhaps what I am talking about is an adaptive approach, where the interpolated data adapts to where there is a change.

But I prefer to think of it not as interpolation.

If I have three values reporting by RBE. All are polled by modbus at 1 s and then published if they change.

My temp transmitter publishes most seconds.
My state publishes a few times a year 
My Firmware version publishes once every 3 years at that 

If I normalize the Firmware over three years to have a value every second I am not interpolating. I know the Firmware version has not changed.

If I take the temperature sensor and wat to have an entry for every millisecond, I would need to interpolate and essentially invent data in-between my know points

Author: rickbullotta
Content:
MQTT issues

- Decision to use 4 bits for message type. Short sighted and now a major limitation
- Multi-publish is essential (publish more than one topic in a single message)
- Topics should have durable metadata (could be passed as headers in publish or as its own message type)
- Payloads should have a data type (mime type) to enable parsing/processing by subscribers or intermediaries
- Topic binding should be a built-in broker feature (like a symlink) - topic aliases are not this
- The lack of a capability to query topics is a huge flaw/gap. Ideally these queries should be able to include metadata filters as well
- MQTT's subscription patterns are hopeless limiting. They should support richer match expressions and also metadata filters
- MQTT should officially support a REST binding for request/response query/publish/read/subscribe/unsubscribe
- Handling of large payloads (e.g. file uploads, video content, firmware/software updates, method responses) needs a lot of work to improve reliability
- Handling of RPC/method invocations remains an awful hack. This MUST be addressed.

Author: rickbullotta
Content:
Sparkplug issues:

- The rigid Node/Device format does not fit real world models. Do away with one of them and allow more flexible topic hiearchies.
- The handling of *BIRTH messages and the intermingling of data and metadata in them is a poor design
- The process for requesting *BIRTH messages is terribly inefficient. Metadata should be retained, not requested each time by each client.
- There should be *METADATA messages to deal with metadata
- The opaque/multi-value nature of *DATA messages makes it impossible for client(s) to subscribe to individual metrics. Huge issue.
- The "primary client" stuff is unnecessary and should be removed
- Any device commands/methods should be fully declared (inputs and outputs fully typed)
- Naming of metrics/commands needs to be locked down to a more restricted character set
- Add a few more top level data types (Location, BLOB (w/mime type), 
- Support other encodings besides Protobuf (e.g. plain JSON, zipped JSON, BSON, etc.)
- Millisecond resolution for timestamps is inadequate for modern systems where accurate event sequence is critical (e.g. power grid)

When I first read "metric fuck ton", I thought you were about to refer to the Sparkplug payloads. But yeah, I agree it's elegant for transmitting data over constrained networks.

The problem is, in practice, usually all those devices are placed behind a single Ignition gateway.  They're not lots of individual or groups of devices publishing. It's one massive thing publishing. UDTs are over defined, not governed, and don't align with access patterns. They'll point to a root in the tag provider and send it over Sparkplug. The topic payloads are tens of thousands of lines long.

Without significant downstream data engineering and operational domain expertise, the data is not likely easy for line of business users to use. It was efficiently moved from the edge though. For whatever the reason, this technology tends to induce design patterns that don't involve "working back" from the end user experience. Perhaps it's less of a problem if the person who programmed the device or its data acquisiton is the same person who is consuming its data.

You know if the Machine is in Fault, and probably the nature of the fault, i.e. blocked output, no product at infeed, jam.

you know of there is an order active on the machine.

you should know if the machine is in Changeover, when you start an order i would start the changeover timer, and then automatically finish when you start producing at x speed. or after x units.

you know the shift start and finish and break times.

you know if it a safety interruption

and normally you are looking at downtime reasons over a month and one or two incorrect reasons don't really change the charts.

Someone logged lunch instead of a safety meeting, I don't think it is worth that.

Of course it depends and your case my be different, I just think way too much effort is put into change OEE figures, and when there is it is because someone does not like the numbers.


But if you need to , I think you should never change values in a historian historian, that is a record of what was reported.


change it in the applications and the tables in the applications should be able to adjust and recalculate any reports that you need.
and publish the values back to UNS, Line\Downtime Modification\ { WO: Initial Even{No: ,time:, reason:} Modified Event{No: ,time:, reason:} republish the A Q & P too if you need to. That allows any applications creating reports to adjust their records too.

- privately owned, so no need for formal organization
- growth through acquisition, where each acquired business was considered a separate business unit and usually referred to as a 'region'

Author: brianpribe
Content: I am starting to believe that a UNS does not require query functionality. To query, you must have one schema and that schema must fully govern every model in the namespace. I don't think this is practical. If you have a schema (S95) that you want to create an API from to query, then pipe the events from the UNS into it, but a query-able UNS is outside of its scope.

Author: _dyland
Content:
I would argue that without a known schema, the benefits of a UNS are severely limited. 

If the Schema isn't standardized, than its like everyone is talking a different language. Requiring translators in the middle of every conversation.

If the information is in an accessible namespace but a node cannot find or make sense of it than its not doing any real good. 

That said, the answer has to lie somewhere in the middle because the Schema has to be flexible enough to represent the constantly changing state of the real world.

At some point, governance becomes a necessity. The question than becomes how big is the scope of that government?

Author: mparris
Content:
Thoughts on some UNS interface standardizing on the following:

•    BROWSE – returns structure of data/metadata/methods (NOTE: metadata IS data 😊)
•    QUERY/READ – returns previous values using parameters EndTime, StartTime, or HistoricalCount, which defaults to EndTime=“now” and HistoricalCount = 1 for latest values.  Different combinations of parameters facilitate historical retrieval
•    SUBSCRIBE – returns latest value and all future values
•    WRITE/PUBLISH/MUTATE – modifies the current value
•    COMMAND – calls a method with defined parameters, where a return value is expected

Author: rickbullotta
Content: With you except I'd separate current and historical on-demand API reads/queries.

Author: mparris
Content:
Can you explain more on separating current and historical FUNCTIONS?

I haven't gone far down that road to consider if overloading QUERY/READ function with historical parameters would over-burden the "currentValue" function?

Keeping them together as one function, where parameter defaults would treat the QUERY function as asking for "currentValue", would help communicate to OEMs that some amount of historical capability would also be expected.

Author: mparris
Content:
For example:

`QUERY value=/plant/line/cell/temperature` 

would return  the current value, and

`QUERY value=/plant/line/cell/temperature HistoricalCount=2`

would return the current value and the value just before that, and 

`QUERY value=/plant/line/cell/temperature EndTime=2024-10-16-00-00-00 HistoricalCount=100`
would return the last one hundred values before Oct 16, and

`QUERY value=/plant/line/cell/temperature EndTime=2024-10-16-00-00-00 StartTime=2024-10-14-00-00-00`
would return all values from Oct 14 and Oct 15, and 

`QUERY value=/plant/line/cell/temperature EndTime=2024-10-16-00-00-00 StartTime=2024-10-14-00-00-00 HistoricalCount=100`
would return the most recent 100 values from Oct 14 and Oct 15

Author: stephenbryant_89711
Content:
> I think the "Unified" part in the popular nowadays term "UNS" might be misleading. You might think it is unified in the scope of whole industries, but I think in fact the scope is a specific company or even maybe different components like ERP or MES. In other words, each company has its own "standard", the common part is only idea.

The unit of "unified" is not one company.  I recently had different parts of a well-known large auto parts supplier tell me they needed different things from MQTT.  One section had to have Sparkplug, another said Sparkplug wouldn't do at all and needed this and that, and a third wanted something else again.

I'm guessing they don't have a digital strategy... but perhaps they have multiple digital strategies.  Yeah, like that'll work well.  🙂

The unit is simply the ecosystem itself: one namespace per ecosystem.  For digital supply chain, this can and should extend across the companies that use the same ecosystem. At some point there needs to be agreement about how things are structured in the UNS, particularly lower down.  There are no formal rules for the details, but I often see best practices being discussed here.

Some people prefer externally defined formal structures, and perhaps that's why they're so drawn to things like OPC UA.  To my mind that comes at the cost of flexibility, and speed - you can generally get stuff actually publishing into UNS faster than mapping the physical world correctly to the formal model, especially when it's complex or volatile.

It might sometimes take a bit of time to understand their ERD, but once we do, we use HighByte to connect to their tables\views and map the data to the UNS. HighByte provides the tooling to be able to integrate from their database to a structure in the UNS. It's some times necessary to standardise, validate and map their data to more descriptive values (e.g. they have status 1, 2, 3, 4 and it maps to Operation, Idle, Down, Standby ) and al this we also do in HighByte. 
Once the data is published (onchange) to the UNS, consumers can subscribe to these topics, to raise maintenance requests. If the consumer can't directly subscribe, then we also use HighByte as the intelligence gateway to subscribe to the topics, build the json structures or whatever the target systems API requires and call the target system endpoint with the fields it needs to be able to raise the maintenance ticket. 🇿🇦

Author: karltbraun
Content:
For starters, explaining the cost benefit of a UNS vs. P2P connections is easily done with a diagram and/or math (connections grow exponentially with P2P: (n**2 - n) / 2.  But of course you have to account for the cost of converting the P2P connections to using the UNS appropriately, and you have to decide what is published back to the UNS from each of the nodes to avoid excessive subsequent P2P connections.

I think (but don't know because I haven't done it) you can do the same with the other data ops tools.  It reduces the connections from ~n**2 to a few P2P connections to the data ops platforms.

Just a thought - hopefully others with more experience will chime in.

Author: milanhurban
Content:
I can talk about Siemens Industrial Edge as I am very familiar with it. Obviously I am not here to speak for a company of over 300.000 people, and especially not about product strategy or proprietary IP. I'm here for myself and anyways will only share stuff you can already easily find online.

At its core, Industrial Edge is a system to deploy containerized software (apps) and firmware updates to edge devices (IPCs or VMs) with a central management system (on-prem or cloud). Somewhat in contrast to products of the past, it is a very open system using familiar IT technologies like Linux, Docker and Kubernetes. The central management is also the only part that has to come from Siemens, the edge devices and apps can also be third-party (through the Industrial Edge Marketplace) or your own compatible hardware and Docker containers. I want to stress this part, if you're unhappy with the selection of Siemens or third-party apps, you can just write your own Docker (Compose) apps and deploy those at no extra cost.

That said, Siemens offers apps for things like connectivity (protocol converters), dashboarding, AI + simulation model runtimes, and so on. The most common way for the various apps to share data among themselves is through the Databus, which is an internal MQTT broker. So all the data you read from the PLCs is already natively available in a standardized format in MQTT and if you're happy with that, you can just publish it (e.g. using Node-RED, but there are other options) to your UNS.

Author: milanhurban
Content:
There is also something called the Industrial Information Hub (IIH), I think that's what @Jermuk  couldn't remember in the comments below the video. This is a collection of apps that offers functionalities on top of basic connectivity. It allows you to build a data model, perform aggregations and transformations on your data, save historical data locally, publish your data model on an OPC UA server, and use GraphQL or a REST API to access it. It also allows synchronization of your data model to another MQTT broker in a customizable format (e.g. your data model hierarchy can automatically become the topic structure).

While it has definitely become easier over time, integrating Industrial Edge into a UNS was possible since the first release over 4 years ago. I would say the marketing only reflects the rising popularity of UNS. After all, the reason I am here is ultimately because a customer mentioned Walker's videos to me a couple years back.

How long does a good UI for this data take? How long to work with the consumers and learn what the UI should be? $17,500 or less might be feasible after the initial cost of architecting the solution is complete, assuming you know the user base and have some frameworks in place.

Author: brianpribe
Content:
Highbytes market is for the large to medium sized manufacturers who need a dataops tool that can scale to the pace of deploying to multiple sites in one project (level3 and up). That $17,000 justifies itself there. Where it won't have an impact on is the 90% of other small to medium sized manufacturers that need dataops, but not at the scale or pace HighByte gets used for. 

You may chuckle that the labor and resources spent on developing these applications are not free, but if you want to compare what the average spend is on education, health care, and social assistance for US manufacturing as a whole, it's only $500M. Compare that to US manufacturing GDP of $2.4T, it's less than 0.0%. The US spends around 3.5% of GDP on R&D, and the manufacturing industry represents 2/3 of that total.

Manufacturer also don't educate their workforce. Plain and simple. We purchase machinery to increase our output and spend most of our man hours on R&D to make it work. What you end up with is an industry that relies not on it's own workforce, but the workforce of another to develop the production operations (production lines, MES, LIMS). And we wonder why the large manufacturers are as productive as they are and smaller manufacturers will be the first on the chopping block to go. It's a conglomeration of multiple enterprises that have specialized themselves into a specific niches, to which none of that knowledge or experience gets pasted down to the smaller enterprises.

Author: patrickeritchie
Content:
I'm currently working on an open source project to address this type of issue. My approach is to have a common API for applications to interface with and use routing on the backend to route requests to the 'appropriate' database/broker/etc. Each client/application can specify which router to use for each request. There are a few compromises but for the majority of applications it seems to be a good fit. I would love to hear feedback on this and what requirements users are looking for.

Demo: https://www.trakhound.com/demo/_admin/configuration/routing
GitHub: https://github.com/TrakHound/TrakHound

Author: mparris
Content: Is it right to summarize your project as a "Reverse Proxy for Data Sources"?

Author: patrickeritchie
Content: It could be, I typically describe it as an API that normalizes requests and creates an abstraction layer between applications and infrastructure. Similar to an Operating System, an application should not need to directly interact with hardware (ex. database/broker/etc.). This allows applications to be portable and for functionality like caching, redirects, etc. to be handled by the framework and not the application.

Content:
...and the ARC AGI test is not it.  Even  the guy who created the original benchmark says so.  From their blog:

"So is it AGI?

ARC-AGI serves as a critical benchmark for detecting such breakthroughs, highlighting generalization power in a way that saturated or less demanding benchmarks cannot. However, it is important to note that ARC-AGI is not an acid test for AGI – as we've repeated dozens of times this year. It's a research tool designed to focus attention on the most challenging unsolved problems in AI, a role it has fulfilled well over the past five years.

Passing ARC-AGI does not equate to achieving AGI, and, as a matter of fact, I don't think o3 is AGI yet. o3 still fails on some very easy tasks, indicating fundamental differences with human intelligence.

Furthermore, early data points suggest that the upcoming ARC-AGI-2 benchmark will still pose a significant challenge to o3, potentially reducing its score to under 30% even at high compute (while a smart human would still be able to score over 95% with no training). This demonstrates the continued possibility of creating challenging, unsaturated benchmarks without having to rely on expert domain knowledge. You'll know AGI is here when the exercise of creating tasks that are easy for regular humans but hard for AI becomes simply impossible."

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
I don't think it's necessarily a bad idea. If the core platform is in AWS and running native services, it can make a lot of sense to use Kinesis.

Kinesis might seem exotic and proprietary, but it has a lot of seamless integrations to the core services in AWS that your customer may already be using. I think of it as an event stream like Kafka, but with way less complexity. It doesn't have the unlimited scale and ecosystem, but much of this is probably not relevant most industrial use cases. If you have a lot of different consumers and processing logic, it might make sense to explore MSK in lieu of Kinesis. In terms of native processing (Kinesis Data Analytics, Flink) and service interoperability, they are pretty interchangeable.

If there is already a competency around using Kinesis and associated native services, there is limited upside to reinveinting the wheelelsewhere. Utilizing the core, managed services can reduce the need for optimization and more involved infrastructure management with other approaches. Also, consider transit costs (ingress, egress, inter-az, inter-vpc) as the more native options can be economical.

There are some HighByte users utilizing Kinesis. I would say that the most common scenario is if they already have existing workloads in AWS with ingestion pattern and they want an easy way to "plumb in" data pipelines to meet the pattern. Alternatively, some elect to do the stream processing on the edge and go direct to destination service (e.g., S3, Redshift).

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
Another approach to consider is IoT Core. While it's an essentially an MQTT Broker, there are broader platform features for edge, security, and integration. Because there are external entities involved, having security integrated into the IAM framework might be preferable from a maintenance and automation perspective. This can be packaged into Greengrass clients for publishing at the edge. Also, the "IoT Rules" features has a lot of turn-key integrations to other services like Kinesis, Lamda, etc. IoT Core could be a decent "front door" approach to aggregate the ingestion.

Because this is a "customer asset fleet" style use case, I would put less stock into the typical UNS approach with big fan-out namespace of topics/shards. This makes more sense in a manufacturing enterprise where there might be lots of different/decentralized teams than need to use real time data streams to solve their own use cases. If you're building a multi-tenant solution of data products for customers or supporting customers, it's best to think of the "UNS" as a conduit (to stream/process data in motion) and a store (a semantic projection of the data at rest). The actual consumption is probably best done within application (IoT platform) or API abstracted from the data store. Why? Think about the access patterns. Beyond a few scenarios of monitoring state in near real time, most consumption will involve calculations or transformations of historical data. And because its multi-tenant (e.g., customers, service providers), there will be a great deal of segmentation, filtering, and grouping in queries. Having batch procedures that can periodically process this data might make more sense than doing it on disparate event streams from many customer nodes.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content: Another consideration should be around the customer interface points. How do they want to get data in and out. It's not common to expose their Kafka or Kinesis clusters to external entities. They're usually abstracted as well-scoped API service. This puts some "guard rails" to simplify integration including payload and security. Kinesis or Kafka could work, but only as like a northbound interface in like a turn-key edge gateway provided to users. Otherwise, MQTT or HTTP would make sense for streaming the ingestion. HTTP is probably best for egress as users will probably need simple endpoints and to pass in query parameters.

Author: geoffnunan
Content:
Benefits of SSE (Server-Sent Events)
Simplicity and Ease of Use:

SSE is simpler to implement than WebSockets, especially when the requirement is to send data in one direction (server-to-client). There’s no need for complex protocols or low-level message handling, which makes SSE a great option for simple real-time communication.
Leverages Existing HTTP Infrastructure:

Since SSE operates over HTTP/2 (or HTTP/1.x), it benefits from HTTP/2’s multiplexing and header compression, which improves performance. You don’t need to manage a separate protocol or deal with connection management complexity.
Built-in Reconnection Logic:

SSE includes automatic reconnection mechanisms in case the connection drops, with the client automatically attempting to reconnect after a timeout. This makes it resilient to network instability without needing to manually handle reconnections.
Efficient for Unidirectional Updates:

SSE is particularly well-suited for applications that only need unidirectional communication (e.g., live news feeds, notifications). It’s optimized for scenarios where the server pushes updates to the client at regular intervals.
Works Well in Proxy and Firewall Environments:

SSE, being based on HTTP, works smoothly with existing web infrastructure like proxies, firewalls, and load balancers. WebSocket connections might require special handling in some network environments, but SSE is generally more “firewall-friendly.”
Low Overhead for Continuous Streams:

When continuously sending data from the server to the client (e.g., live updates, stock ticker), SSE maintains a persistent HTTP connection with minimal overhead, unlike polling or other traditional methods.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
In terms of data ingestion, Databricks is generally a client that pulls in data rather than an endpoint one pushes data to. Over simplifying things, Databricks is not necessarily like a data warehouse (e.g., BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift) with its own storage and primary ingestion endpoint. It's basically compute that sits on top of storage that a user provides from their own cloud. Instead of delivering data into Databricks, data is provided to an intermediary for Databricks to use. There do exist some APIs to insert data, but they're abstracted interfaces and require additional warehouse/cluster resources to host. They incur more latency and are better suited to niche scenarios. Alternatively, the client interfaces are more efficient and purpose-built for ingestion.

The most common ingestion approaches are using the Auto Loader or Structured Streaming. Auto Loader involves monitoring and retrieving data from an object storage service (e.g., Azure Blob Storage). Structured Streaming involves pulling in data through a streaming service (e.g., Azure Event Hub, Kafka).

If you're trying to ingest telemetry event data (e.g., frequent publishes from MQTT), Structured Streaming through Event Hub is probably the way to go. Spark can reshape the events to be efficiently stored. It won't flood the storage with small files and negatively impact query performance. The auto loader method with storage is more conducive to processing the data in larger batches.

Interesting. Are you using the internal file system ("DBFS") instead of external storage (e.g., Blob, ADLS Gen2)? I see the latter recommended and adopted more often.

If you're trying to replicate SQL to Databricks, look into Fivetran. It has turn-key functionality to do this. It's a "partner connect" integration that streamlines much of the setup. It has CDC for SQL and can connect to directly to the cluster/warehouse in Databricks. It can publish through storage or through an endpoint. Alternatively, if you have broader set of industrial data sources and variability, look into HighByte. Among other things, it supports CDC and can publish directly to storage in optimal form for Databricks. SQL CDC + Pipeline (model, buffer, parquet format, gzip compression) + Object Storage is a popular solution pattern.

And for the cloud, Hive

Author: geoffnunan
Content:
ISA95 is a precise language to describe manufacturing concepts.
It is an information architecture for representing how things are defined, how orders are received, how work is sequenced, how actuals are captured, and how quality tests are recorded.
If your factory makes stuff, with things, and captures the record of that against some form of order, conceptually you are doing what ISA95 describes.
I've not come across any other standard that provides a language for manufacturing like this.

Author: geoffnunan

Author: zeratall
Content:
I promised myself I would stay out of the ISA95 debate this time around, but I can’t help myself. 

One thing that is important to note is that ISA95 isn’t **just **a data model, it’s a domain model, a function model, an interaction model, and then a data model. The data model itself is pretty flexible, and it includes concepts like resource relationships that naturally form graph-like structures. One thing to remember is the data model is built upon assumptions embedded in the other three models, assumptions about how processes are organized, which functions interact with each other, and how information flows from one layer to another. These underlying models assume that factories share similar operations, imho this is the crux of the problem with ISA95 (and **any **universal data model): it’s trying to standardize a language where the real world behavior isn’t actually standard.

Data models are meant to support the flow of information and the interactions between different parts of a factory. Let me ask an honest question: how many times have we visited a site where the operations were what we’d call “standard”? I can’t think of any. It’s always a spectrum. Some sites are pretty similar, though not exactly the same, to me these are the sites where adopting ISA95 makes a lot of sense and can save a lot of time, but on the other hand  there are other factories that are completely nuanced and not following convention. When you have that much variety, you have to abstract things to a very high degree. But you will find that when you abstract to a high degree, the model can become useless, be bloated, have added complexity, where it becomes much slower to work with, where you "might" have been better off creating your own data model.

I understand the need and desire for a standard data model because there are huge benefits, but because factories do not have standard operations, I think it's an effort that's dead on arrival.

Author: geoffnunan
Content:
ISA95 is a domain model, built and refined over 30 years with input from hundreds of engineers across hundreds of different factories.
It's not at all opinionated about what your factory looks like, or how you operate your equipment. My team have proven that with implementations in Pharma, Discrete, Batch, and Steel Making, and it has wide adoption in Mining.
The value of the standard is not evident in the first use-case that you implement, and for many people, that first use-case is where you learn the standard.
The value of the standard is that it allows you to move on to the second, third, fourth ... use case without tripping over the data model and needing to start again.
My team had a long discussion about this just last week. For many engineers, all they can see is the immediate need of the first use-case. Future use-cases are unknown unknowns, and not relevant to them. For these engineers, it can seem more viable to design their own schema.
Once you move past that and onto the next use-case, and the next, and you find that you need to change the data model to support a new requirement, you are stuck. ISA95 saves you from that.
