Author: zeratall
Content:
I agree, education is definitely a problem (as you highlighted), it's something that needs to be addressed, and certainly is a factor with adoption and the public opinion/evaluation of the standard. I also love that end users are getting value from rhize and the implementation of ISA95 regardless of the approach, at the end of the day that's all that matters!  Going through the Socratic Method regarding your comment above: 

> "ISA95 is a domain model" 
> "It's not at all opinionated about what your factory looks like, or how you operate your equipment"

How can both of these statements be true at the same time? 

I understand and recognize that ISA95 is a highly abstract, conceptual model. However, with abstract models, the shape of the abstractions are informed by the variation in implementations. In other words, a domain model can’t truly capture its domain unless it reflects the entities, actors, functions, and interactions that define manufacturing operations, even when these elements are abstracted to a high level. This is precisely my concerns with ISA95. For some sites that abstraction becomes too unrepresentative from the practical nuances of a factory, it risks introducing unnecessary complexity or “bloat” where a simpler, more manageable model might be preferable.

I agree that standards have value, I agree that ISA95 is probably a huge time saver for most sites, I agree most sites probably don't have individuals that have expertise in data modeling and could go down a dead end. Where I disagree is the indiscriminate recommendation for ISA95. Just as with architecture, every site should evaluate what their data needs are based off architecture, functions, interactions, etc. and evaluate if the standard is appropriate or not.  Surely we can both agree on that?

Author: r.pop
Content:
Ok, lot to unpack here so I'll try my best to answer all your questions.

I will preface this with giving some background on the type of projects we typically take on. We are not a typical systems integrator. Our team is built for Digital Transformation initiatives. If you're looking for a vendor to deploy an MES system, that's not what we do. If you're looking for a partner to help you build a define a digital strategy that will scale across 100+ facilities and leverage modern OT/IT technologies to do it, that's our expertise. We are creating digital strategies at scale encompassing things like data warehouses, AI/ML, infrastructure as code, change management, policy deployment, business outcomes, etc.

So as part of that, we have to build a dynamic data model that can incorporate data from a multitude of different systems. ERP, MES, SCADA, HR, MRP, CRM, WMS, etc. I can share some more details on the approach we take to this, but I;ve mentioned it a few times in conversations in this community. It's a tiered approach to deliver information to those at different levels of the organization, i.e. an operator needs a different set of data than a quality tech, than a maintenance tech, than the CFO. In my view, the goal of industry 4.0 is "To connect assets in a factory, and assets can be anything from people, to sensors, to software systems, for the purpose of delivering information to those that can act upon it the fastest." 

We define modles based off the outcomes we are trying to achieve, not on a heirarchy of assets, because at the end of the day, the asset structure changes from plant to plant, from machine to machine, from region to region. When we focus on the outcome we are trying to achieve, the model is can be focused on value.

Author: r.pop
Content:
Do you link the ERP directly to PLC?
     ---Quite rarely, but there has been times in the past where we have created transactions to backflush inventory directly from the PLC. Again, quite rare, but it can happen.
Do you call the same equipment objects in the SCADS MES and ERP?
     ---Tough to say again because we don't build SCADA, MES, or ERP solutions. Most customers already have these things in place and we have to build a framework around leveraging all of these existing systems. Good luck telling a manufacturing                       customer that you want to change their master data models in SAP becuase they don't match what you have in the MES or SCADA system.
 Have business logic operating at the PLC level, Do you not follow request response?
     ---Typically not at the PLC level, but if you lok at what Ford is doing, they are creating a Common Data Model infrastructure where the PLC's are pushing data models directly into an MQTT broker via Rockwells MQTT AOI.
Do you put all of the machine cells into a flat not hierarchical structure.
     ---Sometimes we don't have machine cells. Again, depends on the goals we are trying to achieve from the customer. But at a high level, it's similar to the UNS concept, Enterprise -> Site -> Line -> Machine (though this varies greatly depending on                 the customer/factory)
Do you segregate Production from Quality From maintenance data in your MES?
     ---Again, we don't deploy MES systems, and I think the idea of what an MES system is, is changing greatly, though that's another topic of discussion.

Author: r.pop
Content:
Easy, use Highbyte, and create an OEE data model.
 
You can stitch all those different systems together in Highbyte and store them in your DB to calculate OEE as if they all came from the same place. @js can tell you all about it.

This is the point of my word vomit above. Create your models based off the problem you're trying to solve, and it will be way easier for you. OEE is the KPI you're trying to measure, build a model that is defined for you on how you want to calculate/measure/view it. This way you aren't bound by heirarchies. That OEE data model you create will be applicable to machines, lines, cells, etc.

Author: rutger_18900
Content:
I'll give an example that's even closer to home for me, having worked 90% in batch based manufacturing as an SI, doing mostly PLC/DCS/SCADA/MES (earlier on more PLC, lately more MES).

ISA88.

It has allowed me to walk into a lot of plants, looking at the software, and being able to understand it and make changes in no time.
Around the world, in tons of sectors. 

Chocolate spread? Monoclonal antibodies? Jam filled cookies? Performance motor oil blends? API coated sugar pills? Injectable liquids? Yoghurt? Cheese? Fertilizer? Animal feed? Bio fuel? UHT milk? Windshield wiper fluid?  Natural and synthetic rubbers for pharma and automotive use cases?
All examples of things I've worked on, off the top of my head, I'm sure there's more.

Guess what it's all similar processes, and mapping to ISA88 makes the structure easy to understand and the resource pool (both engineers and software) giant. 
I often get the question "what sector do you have experience in" and my anser is -at least for batch based mfg- it doesn't matter, they're all the same.

Latest project I've been working on is a biopharma line for viral reduction in blood plasma. Guess what, same.
We use our resources to perform operations in order to create products we can ship to customers.
ISA88+ISA95.

Same as with ISA95, ISA88 allows you to drop stuff you don't need, and add extra stuff you need.
I've often seen the EM level dropped completely for example, just units that run phases that control CM's.
Just try to not reorganize stuff, mix up terminology, and use what is useful.

Do you need a stopping state? no, never? drop it. Use what is useful.
You only have a running and an idle state? Great, I can still read that!
Ideally pick software that supports the full model, or write your own in a way that you can easily update later on when you realize you do need it on that other line for that one use case 🙂

Author: geoffnunan
Content:
The intent of the ISA95 standard is to reduce the effort of integrating ERP and MES. The implementation of the standard for this purpose is B2MML. 
I started to look into ISA95 as the data model for Manufacturing in 2020, and created an implementation of the standard in GraphQL that suits the purpose of being a data model, rather than a canonical message model.
The result is that we can, and do, take university graduates and train them as productive Manufacturing Systems Engineers in about 4 to 6 months.
That is possible because of the simplicity of our tech stack AND the extensive documentation in the ISA95 standard.
Prior to this, I had just accepted that becoming a good Manufacturing Systems Engineer takes at least a decade of experience

Author: geoffnunan
Content:
I completely agree with that.
I think the intent of the standard, which was to reduce the integration effort between MES and ERP, has demonstrably failed.
The standard has succeeded in creating a rich and very precise language that is perfect for a manufacturing ontology which has use-cases that could not have been imagined over 30 years ago when the standard was first created.
The GraphQL implementation of ISA95 an implementation of the standard that is designed to be an ontology.
B2MML is an implementation of ISA95 that is designed to be a canonical message model.
They are 2 different implementations with different purposes.
The beauty in the ISA95 standard is that it is a conceptual standard that leaves room for implementation specifics.

Author: nickn5549
Content: ISA-95 is intended for the integration between MES and ERP systems (typically Levels 3 and 4 in the automation stack). Using it at the PLC/SCADA level (Levels 0-2) disrupts the intended layered architecture, leading to inefficiencies. PLCs/SCADA systems prioritise real-time control and reliability. ISA-95 emphasises data integration and information management, which are not primary concerns at these lower levels. PLCs are designed for real-time control with limited processing power and storage, making them ill-suited for handling the extensive data and hierarchical structures proposed by ISA-95.

Author: uwe1774
Content: Hi! I have a question about UNS and schemas: (1) How does a publisher register schema per topic and (2) how do consumers over time deal with schema changes on topics from producers?

Author: durinwinter
Content:
Hi @uwe  this is my answer but I am not a certified practitioner so am prepared to be corrected here. UNS is pretty flexible and doesn't as a rule mandate a specific schema, the manufacturer might choose their own methodology for this. The specific functionality that enables your question though is actually the Sparkplug standard, which was an optional way to publish and subscribe at the ProveIt conference we just had. 

The structure of a UNS topic using Sparkplug B is primarily defined by the NBIRTH and NDEATH messages. These messages indicate the schema being used. Each time a new NBIRTH message is received, it signifies the introduction of a new schema.

Author: codepoet80
Content:
I'll share my/CESMII's opinion...

MQTT doesn't by itself have a place to register a schema. I agree with @Durin's Bane  (and Arlen Nipper) that a NBIRTH (or DBIRTH) explicitly identifies a schema, but our guidance is to store the authoritative schema definitions *separate* from the live data. There's a few reasons for this:
- Not everything speaks Sparkplug/B (hopefully that changes in the future)
- Historical data is stored separate from the Broker, but should share the same schema as the live data (by version)
- Consumers need a mechanism to know the schema before it comes to life (instantiates) on the broker

We really need two things:
1) a transport independent mechanism of expressing a schema (aka data template, profile)
2) a standard endpoint for looking up these schemas

Fortunately, industry standards exist for both -- and they're free to use.
- OPCUA Part 5 (which can be used independent of the other parts -- so *does **not** require you to use OPC for comms*) provides a transport/data source/end-point independent language for expressing schemas. A number of big players have begun adding support for this "nodeset" format as the schema language (@Travis Cox demonstrated Ignition support this week at ProveIt)
- The CESMII CloudLibrary (an open source, open spec JWG that included all three Cloud vendors) provides a free to use, and free to host endpoint definition for looking up schemas

Content:
There is more to this question in my opinion.
Let's take an example to help the thought process:
Imagine we have a factory that contains hundreds or even thousands of machines. In a UNS, where is the meta-data model for what each of those machines are? That meta-model will likely be the source of the schema for the information that needs to be published.
Let's imagine we have a meta-model for Pumps. where are the attributes ( machine provided, calculated, and statically defined) of a pump defined?
When that meta-model changes, how are those changes deployed to all the nodes that are publishing to the UNS?
Imagine I add a requirement for sending `amps` as part of the pump data, Amps is now part of the schema.
Imagine I can do this at a group level. I have a user-defined type for pump that I add `amps` to, and now hundreds of pumps are expected to start sending amps data to my UNS.

The schema are not fixed, they are model dependent.

Content: I work in a battery manufacturing company where we cake telemetry, traceability, state, alerts, commands from all machine and run them through our own iot proxies, which basically acts as a mapper from any standard on the PLC to our own company standard. Author: uwe1774
Content:
Now we have started to look into UNS, as we have build quite some point-to-point integrations between PLM, ERP, QMS, MES, and other systems. What we struggle to understand are a few things: 
1. How would we handle schema management, _dynamically_ over time. It's easy to either use a central registry, but how do you inform a subscriber that there will be a new schema version published soon? Do you publish to a different topic? The same and just allow eventual understanding of the schema? (not talking about the syntax - if it's a meta field, URN, RDF, we can figure that out and pick our poison).
2. Relying on SparkplugB as the enterprise UNS format feels tricky - I can't see convincing our PLM or ERP owners to comply to a quite sensory/machine integration protocol. 
3. We model our state changes mainly in events, not state changes. Sure for telemetry data state changes to certain values makes sense, by I struggle to see us move away from events for traceability data ("machine x has finished process y on material z with measurements m"). Would we have to give up events and convert to purely state changes? What is a state change look like not for assets (machines, lines, etc.) but materials / products? ("coated roll r was cut into n sheets")
4. Walker Reynolds mentioned during the Tulip firecamp roundtable (?) that larger data volumes are actually only virtually published, by publishing e.g. REST addresses and parameters. I wonder how that would look like and what a "state change" for large volume data set would be.
5. If namespaces can be overlayed, as I believe to understand it from the recently announced HiveMQ Pulse dashboard, I wonder if each namespace follow their own semantic hierarchy and syntax on topics? Would that "break" the initial UNS idea to have _one_ semantic hierarchy?

So there are a lot of UNS specific question I have to fully grasp the general concept and the specific architecture choices to be made for certain aspects I am thinking through.

Author: marc.jaeckle
Content:
Ad 1) The schemas describe the interface contract between a specific system/machine/sensor and the UNS so typically both sides should be involved in changing it. In cases in which it is not possible to do so you have to make sure that your schema is backwards compatible, meaning you can add things and make them optional but shouldn’t change existing things.
Ad 2) SparkplugB is not suitable as the basis for your UNS. You can find an article in this LinkedIn post of mine on this topic: https://www.linkedin.com/posts/activity-7171866197477449728-9VYR
Ad 3) Use events and state information (current state) in your UNS. 
Ad 4) I assume he meant something like files, images etc. and not larger volumes of machine data for example.
Ad 5) not sure what you mean. 

To better understand the UNS concept I suggest the blog posts on the HiveMQ website on the topic. Just make sure that you ignore the older Sparkplug ones.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
Lots of good comments. 

I will say one fact finding mission (or dare I say... opposition research) is to understand what motivates these concerns. It may not necessarily be nefarious or due to the sunk cost of a particular system.

If I had to levy criticism of those that criticize IT is that they, often OT folks (e.g., PLC/SCADA owners), fail to understand the broader operational business processes that depend on systems they don't own. If one is accustomed to putting out their own fires all day, it can be really challenging to find time to learn this. It's super important to fluent in the problems of others. There could be concerns over how this might impact managing inventory, cost accounting, taking orders, scheduling the plant, managing supply chain, etc. The "opposing" team might also be under resourced and under pressure to support other initiatives. For a variety of reasons, it can be simply easier to just say no. Priorities, management directives, and resources can influence turf wars. It's not always strictly a motive to consolidate power and influence. It's not always because they don't like the ideas of others.

I would advise meeting outside of formal channels to collaborate with counterparts. In other words, if you're asking for access to APIs or databases or unusual stuff over a help desk ticket, you're destined to fail. Those channels are meant to fix Excel and reset passwords. IT business analysts are not necessarily tooled up for digital transformation. For industrial companies that don't have a significant customer-facing digital presence (e.g., e-commerce, digital marketing), the IT departments can be less resourced than perceived. At labor-intensive manufacturers, it's not uncommon for IT spend to sit at less than 1% of revenue. In other words, their ability to support the business may not be much more than keeping the lights on. They may only have enough resources to lifecycle what is getting old / not secure and basic support of end users.

Author: koios6274
Content:
Which MES system are you referring to? UNS handles real-time state and events, not historical data. If you're talking about tracking past downtime reasons, you could send transactional information through UNS, but it wouldn't store historical records.

For example, if a machine goes down at 10:00 AM, that state change would be logged in MES with a unique event*ID. Later, an operator could select that downtime event and enter a reason code. You could then publish a message to the UNS topic /area/line/machine1/downtimetracking/reasoncodes, including details like the operator’s name, the selected event ID, and the downtime cause. MES could then consume this data.

There are multiple ways to handle this, but UNS is designed for current state and real-time events, not long-term historical storage.

Author: koios6274
Content: One other note - transactional data through UNS is tricky, how do you verify / validate messages are picked up etc.  Typically I see in whatever MES you are using/build/customize for this exact purpose the operators would be able to add a downtime reason which would interact directly with the MES system and not pass transaction data through UNS

Author: .killnine
Content:
Yes, that's an excellent point. 

However, a common two mantras that often get thrown out are "single source of truth" when discussing a UNS. 

A historian is taking this stream of real-time data and persisting it for future reference, but how do we knit together things we capture in real time (machine speed) and things we can't always know about from our machines (machine state?) and have it available in a single location (the historian)?

1. Perhaps this premise is flawed. The historian is just going to get what it can get from the event stream and it's up to some sort of higher-level system to knit together historian data with more transactional data (event records from something like the MES) to compose a more comprehensive view of the machine in the past.

2. Perhaps "single source of truth" is missing a bit. Instead, maybe it's "single source of truth for the machine context for which we have an actual stream of data". If it's something that happens after the fact, then it's probably not a good fit for UNS. 

I just wanted to make sure I wasn't missing some design pattern or implementation concept. But I think I have a better understanding now

Author: brianpribe
Content:
ERP tends to be a couple of steps ahead. Most UNS deployments start with just getting metrics on their machine and operations. A sales order and asset ID tends to be the first things end-users integrate with a UNS. Difficult to plan exactly how ERP will be integrated, because of what the business needs. If you need a sales order to automatically get planned for your machines to produce, there are a tonnn of steps that you have to take before you can get to that point. 

Also, are you trying to do transactions between your ERP and machines via UNS like sales orders for example? Are you just trying to track your machines performance via UNS like machine state? These are two very different things. Transactions are natives to ERP systems (RPC, REST), because they have expected outcomes (200,400,500). If I tell a machine to produce a products for a sales order, I expect a specific set of responses back for confirmation. In MQTT, this is difficult. There is nothing built into MQTT to make transactions a feature. You have to do it yourself. This is where an API would come in, but now all of your assets have to communicate with this API (point-to-point), which creates the overhead that UNS is trying to solve. If you are just tracking metrics (what had happened) like machine status, then UNS is a no-brainer.

Content:
I can't speak for others, but I'd say 'tags' is too low-level a concept for the MES or ERP. Im sure "it depends" on each organizations actual system, but we try and abstract that away from the MES and ERP because PLC tags is just too low-level a concern for those systems.

Instead, we model our equipment to have standard interfaces (all equipment have a 'line speed'. Presses have 'oven temps', 'deck statuses', etc.) and how those fields are mapped to PLC tags is a concern for the OT software (Ignition, Litmus, whatever). The MES and ERP only care about the 'what' (data points they need to ingest) not the 'how' of it.

From a practical level, our equipment is so disparately designed at the PLC level, it would be almost impossible to standardized the tag organization within the PLC itself. However, at previous organizations, I have worked with vendors to agree on a 'standard interface' that they provide to us for reading variables from, so it's not unheard of. But it definitely requires an organization to be ahead of the game and is hard to do after the equipment is deployed.

We’ve seen that when organizations establish a clear data model early on, it significantly improves scalability and interoperability across different equipment and vendors. Of course, standardization is always a challenge, but having the right architecture in place makes a huge difference.

Author: .killnine
Content:
Including UoM is such a valuable thing, for sure. Allowing your systems to self-configure with metadata like that is clutch.

Where I am going with this is that I have two prototypes stood up:

1. System A: It connects to our PLC and retrieves a half-dozen individual signals. Machine speed, some temperatures, status of print decks, like I said in the conversation above. Each signal comes in on a different sub-topic.
2. System B: This uses a vendor's 'Modeling' feature to wrap up a PLCs data points from all these different locations into a single JSON object and send that off to MQTT in one fell swoop.

Our system is based in C# with an MQTT client  watching a topic related to that piece of equipment's raw data. It's much easier to configure the system to deserialize a known object type that matches the model than to set up all these handlers for every single sub-topic. The additional benefit I see is that all the data comes in as one immutable snapshot at that point in time.

Perhaps if I was integrating with a different system I would feel differently but System B seems like a better way to go for us in this regard.

Author: .killnine
Content:
Thanks for that link. I missed that discussion but it's very informative. 

For our system, it really is beneficial to ingest it in one unit. However, I do get concern over that same structure being really hard to reuse for other consumers, which defeats some of the goals of UNS.

I guess where I may land is putting this structure in its own namespace (topic). And then also shooting out the individual fields as well for other folks to consume ad hoc (not doing that yet but would be open to it if we had consumers for it). Having the same data in two places raises its own risks (if its all getting historized you're using 2x space, people may be confused as what the source of a system's data actually is). However, they're both being populated from the same thing so I see it as more 'choose your own adventure' and less 'pick your poison' 😄

Let me say this... there is nothing ambiguous about the definition of UNS.  Everyone here can recite my definition.  

It is current state
It is semantically organized like your business
It is single source of truth
It where current values for all data and information lives (one must know the difference between data and information for this to be meaningful)
It is an architecture
It is how orgs manifest their digital strategy
It is the hub through which smart nodes communicate
It is how orgs connect to a digital supply chain
It is where context and normalization of data and information starts
It is built on open, edge driven and report by exception tech

It is valuable because it mitigates the three reasons orgs fail when it comes to DT -- Wrong Strategy, Wrong Tech, Wrong Partners

It is valuable to the business because it addresses

Scalability
Normalization
Time to Value
Security
Agility

That is not ambiguous.

Author: r.pop
Content:
As an integrator/partner for manufacturing customers for the last couple of years, I've talked a lot about how I used to have to sell WHY companies need to digitally transform. Thanks to Covid and the general state of manufacturing, I don't have to sell the WHY any more. Now I sell the HOW.

And this conversation has also changed drastically since the popularity of UNS has sky rocketed. In almost every single conversation I have with a new customer and even existing customers, the topic is, "Can you explain what a UNS is and why I should care about it?" So I've gotten pretty good at describing it in terms most people understand.

Depending on the audience, we'll talk about the technical details of it, and we've even built some wild visual versions of some customers UNS', and for a lot of that I bring up what @Walker Reynolds mentioned above.

But for simplicity sake, I tend to refer to it like this of which I'll credit Tony Huffman for the term:

People understand the idea of Data Lake. It is a storage mechanism for the entire wealth of data of your business. But how does a data get to the data lake in a way that allows us to build business cases? Well, through a Data River of course. This is the UNS, it is the current state flow of information from all corners of your business on it's way to a resting location. We can take data out of the river, we can put data into the river, but it is always flowing and never at rest. For those things, we need the data lake. A river can feed many lakes, and can even be tied to ponds, but the most important thing you have to remember about the river, is that it always flows better when it's clean. And the more time you spend on maintaining your river, the better it will feed your lake.

This explanation allows me to get through to a lot of customers in a way they understand extremely well. I've found it to be a great analogy.

Author: walker.reynolds
Content:
The answer about the historical component for UNS is, ‘it depends, but…’

When I architect history in three layers with UNS.  

Layer 1 - edge historical node, often times this is influxdb and/or Canary.  Canary for high speed sensor events over fieldbus and influx for high speed events over telegraf in the edge broker.

Layer 2 is the plant layer - this is almost always Canary over sparkplug with Flow for analytics and Axiom for TS Dashboarding.

Layer 3 - this is generally one of two things - Kafka stream from the L5 broker to a lake OR its Google MDE / Highbyte into BigQuery, Table or Snowflake.

History is best layered but from a common infrastructure.  🙏

Author: walker.reynolds
Content:
I choose Snowflake for commoditizing data and for data that I won’t commonly process on (so much cheaper here).  I use Google for native integration of all their GCS tools and for data I will process on frequently.

I’m really not using anything but GCS or Snowflake right now, except to test.

Author: _dyland
Content:
The answer depends on too many factors. There are at least a dozen different ways to accomplish that with Ignition. It also depends on how the project was structured, how the tags are structured, if UDTs were used, if you want SparkplugB or Flat MQTT, how you want the payload to be packaged, if you want to debounce the signal or validate the value or quality, to name a few... 

Assuming that UDTs are being used (which is typically best practice) and the tag you want to publish is in an instance of that UDT, then it would take you however long it would take to write the python scripts that one time. If you already have a gateway script set up to handle it then it should take 15 seconds. If you are starting from a brownfield site that hasn't used MQTT before and you are writing the script for the first time it will take longer... If you are still learning MQTT or Python then it will take longer yet. 

There is no one answer to this question.

Author: _dyland
Content:
If I wanted to do this today it would likely take me just a few minutes. Opening up the software and my examples being the most time consuming part...

Because I already have UDTs structured composable and modular. I already have it written these scripts in a way that I can copy into a new gateway (and have published on the ignition exchange for everyone to use). The first time I wrote it, it took a few hours.

That said, I don't usually do it that fast because identifying HOW we need it in a specific application is the most time consuming part. Writing a script is quick... Figuring out what to write, where, and why takes time.

Author: singhnitish.disc
Content:
We’re just getting started with a Unified Namespace (UNS) implementation for our high-mix, low-volume manufacturing environment, and I’d love to get some feedback or tips from folks who’ve been down this road before.

Here’s what we’ve got so far:
    •    Our machines (PLCs) publish to their own MQTT broker using a vendor-defined namespace.
    •    We’re using Node-RED to subscribe to that, process some logic (e.g., determining if a machine is “active”), and then publish to a Mosquitto broker that serves as our UNS.
    •    Our topic structure is modeled after ISA-95:

Enterprise/Site/Area/Line/Cell

For now, we’re just tracking machine availability. The payload is pretty simple:

{
  "availabilityMachine": "active"
}

We store the data in InfluxDB and visualize it in Grafana.

This is a very basic setup, just to get the UNS framework going. Eventually we’ll expand to include performance, quality, and other metrics.

What I’m hoping to learn:
    1.    Namespace structure:
    •    Does this topic hierarchy seem solid for the long run?
    •    Should we be including things like event types or timestamps in the topic? Or any other best practices (I hear informational/functional/descriptive namespace structure but not sure how to push into a namespace for that)
    2.    Payload structure:
    •    Is a simple JSON like the one above good enough, or should we add more context (e.g., timestamp, units, source, etc.)?
    3.    Best practices or lessons learned:
    •    Anything you wish you’d done differently when you first set up your UNS?
    •    Tips for keeping the namespace clean and scalable as things grow?

Would really appreciate any thoughts, gotchas, or examples you’re willing to share.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
Transforming data != DataOps. 

This is like saying a Windows Installer Package or Group Policy Object is DevOps. A seasoned DevOps engineer would not consider WinServer/SystemCenter/AD/GPM a DevOps platform. These are another OS or set of admin configuration utilities they might need to orchestrate. Sure, both deploy applications, but the similarities end there quickly.

DataOps is a collaborative methodology for teams to reach/sustain interoperability objectives, adapt to evolving requirements, and drive down the resource burden of doing so. Orchestration, observability, governance, and quality are at the heart of this. Converting a protocol or organizing/normalizing tags is an ad-hoc task. It's not data engineering.

There is nothing wrong with using Node-RED, Ignition, or FactoryStudio to publish on behalf of industrial data sources into an MQTT broker. They're great platforms. My focus here is not on platforms, but practice. When we casually broaden the use of technology terms, we risk losing meaning and precision. It makes it harder to define what something is and what it is not. Obviously, I'm biased in my perspective, but I say this out of concern. I've seen a lot of manufacturers in a difficult situations lately because they conflated IoT Platform, iPaaS, edge gateway, digital twin, contextualization, UNS, data strategy, DataOps, etc as all the same thing. In general, they spend a lot of time connecting things, but fail to accomplish what they set out to do. At the end of the day, it's normal for definitions to evolve. Hopefully the term "DataOps" evolves with more clarity.

DataOps is not a product, but a methodology of people, process, and technology. Author: fuzzyo3
Content:
Hello everyone,
We have been working with the UNS for some time now, but we still haven't found the final answers to two questions about the semantic hierarchy.

1. individual machine vs. line
In some areas we simply have individual machines. In others we have lines. We often consider whether we should use a kind of fake line so that the actual machines are at the same hierarchy level (cell), making it easier to subscribe, publish and aggregate data.
What is your opinion? Is there a best practice for this?

2. area vs. department
We understand the area (ISA-95 Part 2) as an actual production area, e.g. drilling, assembly, ... . So actually they are not areas but departments. The actual area is the production. And both departments belong to it.
Because further down the line, other areas and departments are also added. Logistics, Shipping, Quality, Engineering, ... We imagine that it could be practical to bundle the departments into their own areas. Here too, to make it easier to subscribe, publish and restrict authorisations. But there could also be cases in which every department has to report the same KPI. Without additional nesting, it would not be so easy to compare the entire areas and, above all, it would be questionable where the results are published.

Author: scrapper7161
Content:
Thanks @Dylan DuFresne for the mention — and @RickBullotta , I completely agree with your point: this should live inside the broker.
That’s exactly the direction we’re going with Coreflux. We’re building what we call the Language of Things (LOT) — not as another layer, but as logic embedded directly into the MQTT broker. The goal isn’t to add components — it’s to remove them.
Our vision is simple:
If MQTT is the backbone of your architecture, then it should be capable of more than just transport.
It should understand, route, and act — without pushing logic upstream or sideways.
We’re doing this to:
 - Accelerate how UNS (Unified Namespace) architectures are built
- Let developers and integrators define models, actions, and routes natively
- Reduce friction across OT/IT without creating new moving parts

We’re not building an “Uber broker” — but definitely an MQTT+, where structure, flexibility, and reaction live in one place.

Appreciate all the insights in this thread — it’s exactly the pain we’re trying to solve. Happy to share more if anyone’s curious.

Content: Anyone got an easy definition of the Funtional, Informative and Definitional namespace? How would you put it on a reference document?

Author: sparkylarks
Content:
Probably the best I have seen 
https://www.hivemq.com/blog/practical-applications-unified-namespace-uns-iiot-usecases/

https://www.linkedin.com/posts/walkerdreynolds_unifiednamespace-digitaltransformation-iiot-activity-7178425450698797056-_KBS?utm_source=share&utm_medium=member_desktop&rcm=ACoAAAFcK9sB7oawUPTfk9Eg2-vCbi-E6kJQIQY


My own take is somewhat simpler 
**1. Definitional Namespace (The Backbone)**

    Published once, retained forever.

    Defines the structure of the business: Enterprise / Site / Area / Line / Machine.

    Payloads hold metadata:

        Enterprise: minimal

        Site: address, facility type, etc.

        Area/Line/Machine: descriptive text, basic attributes

This forms the "map of the business" and is foundational for structuring the UNS.
I am working on an Excel file I can use Node red to import. I'll share once I finish

**2. Functional Namespaces **

    This is the beating heart of the UNS ,These are what the various nodes publish and consume during operation.

    Examples:
        MachineStatus
        CycleCount
        Temperature

    Often start as raw data, which I treat as somewhere between a Functional namesapce and an Ad-hoc namespace or a kind of fourth type.
    Raw data typically comes first and gets contextualised by nodes and published bavk into Functional namesapces

3. Informational Namespace (Curated Data)
    Built for consumption, typically by dashboards or downstream systems.
    Examples:
        Dashboard/Area1/OEE
        MES/Scheduler/DailyWorkOrders
    Payloads are often aggregated, contextualized, or pre-processed.
    If someone asks “Can you expose that for consumption by X?”, the answer is usually: “Sure, we’ll publish it to the informational namespace.”

But  I don't know if there is a massive benefit in obsessing too much about which type of namespace is where , its more important to have structure match the business

Invalid argument type supplied to setValue.` Some addition to the message, or a disclaimer in the documentation, (or both!) would be helpful.

for the particular situation that surfaced this error, my understanding is that a collection of dotnet class instances are being serialized to an array of JSON objects (using Newtonsoft), and sometimes those instances are null. this causes pipeline failures in highbyte because of the `null` element. example:

  },

]

^ will cause the `Expression engine failed ...` error. we had a lot of fun chasing this down, because we knew we had valid JSON, we knew we had valid JavaScript,  - even GraalJS's `JSON.parse()` worked fine with our data, when highbyte's JSONParser stage doesn't - and yet highbyte failed over and over, and we're just thinking ... why? and this serialized class example is particularly difficult to eyeball IMO because it's subtler than something like `[1, 2, false]`.

if we do actually want support for mixed arrays, I'll certainly submit a support ticket. the critical thing here was discovering the issue and confirming it is intentional and just lacking documentation - so thank you!

Author: _dyland
Content:
Somewhere between $100 and $100,000,000.
As there is no "Average" Unified Namespace to measure a cost to. 

It depends on what you mean by "UNS". What you are looking to get out of it, what scale is required, and what the current state looks like. 

A better question would be "What is the average cost of solving [Problem] with and without a UNS" and "How does using a UNS affect the cost of solving future problems like ...?".

I can say that in my experience a typical Plant MES / SCADA / IIoT implementation using UNS principles is usually $100,000 to $200,000 for the first go around once licensing, infrastructure, and integration services are accounted for. Once that infrastructure and licensing is in place, additions can often be cheaper smaller agile sprints. 

Anything less almost guarantees technical debt. Though, sometimes that is the cost of getting started. 

That said, a silo'd single site approach is not something I recommend for larger multi-site enterprises.

Either way, the first project is expensive, whether you pay now or pay  interest on the technical debt later. Once the foundation is built, it can be built upon for less over time.

Content:
I like to pull data from the UNS, It means I don't have to worry about polling rates, or the interval that I call the DB Query.
Especially compounding of query intervals i.e. system 1 polls the ERP every 15 minutes, and writes the orders to a DB.

It also means that In the future if the ERP is upgraded , or the classic DB table, I know I do not have to worry about the operators screen  . I just worry about publishing the data back into the same Topic.

It also reduces concerns about scalling. i.e. when you have 5000 operator screens can the DB handle them all independently querying the DB?

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
You might find this case study presentation useful - particularly if you already work with AWS services:
https://youtu.be/GMTlqvsbYSs

UNS architectures and solutions become more intuitive when there is a strategy and desired outcomes defined. The downstream apps/services or data products (ideally aligned with high value use cases) that are consuming the UNS are arguably the most important. Working backwards from these to the tech helps prioritize what you may need. Otherwise, it can be daunting working from a blank slate and figuring out what to build towards. By working backward, you'll start to observe some patterns of how data is going to be consumed and how it needs to be managed. Don't worry too much about getting it perfect the first pass or over committing to something. Change and experimentation is healthy.

The most important and significant cost is not software, but your time. Technologists in industry are usually in short supply and anything they do have high opportunity costs in terms of other initiatives they could be working on. Setup lab environments. Use open source or free trial licenses. Being able to understand business problems, gather requirements, build out solutions with the tech, and evolve them as you learn more is important. Think of this as the people and process part of UNS. If there isn't a plan for this, the technology won't go anywhere.

Content:
This week, I noted three thought provoking posts about UNS on LinkedIn . As someone WITHOUT practical experience implementing UNS in Industry,  I want to air these posts out a bit further here.

1st up, @Mark O'Donovan posted this:
https://www.linkedin.com/posts/mark-o-donovan-8777847_unifiednamespace-mqtt-digitalmanufacturing-activity-7339227231962980353-3mLZ?utm_source=share&utm_medium=member_desktop&rcm=ACoAAAtzbAgBkrAZFO7DdeiNjpEtTeEsLw04vAI
and 2nd @Dylan DuFresne posted this:
https://www.linkedin.com/posts/dylan-dufresne-solutions_digitaltransformation-iiot-uns-activity-7339322938086539265-7JUR?utm_source=share&utm_medium=member_desktop&rcm=ACoAAAtzbAgBkrAZFO7DdeiNjpEtTeEsLw04vAI
My takeaway from both is this: Simply spinning up an MQTT broker and making some devices or apps dump some data into it is not UNS. To truly call something a UNS, more is needed:
1. Good-practice engineering to structure and contextualize the data so that it is useful to other apps in the enterprise.
2. The UNS must be transformational to the business - ie. it must enable things that were difficult to achieve before.
3. The people who will use the UNS and their goals are important, so creating a UNS is a consultative activity.
4. The UNS must serve some established business goal, not just be used to dashboard some data.

On the other hand, I found this post by @Freek Bos:
https://www.linkedin.com/posts/freek-bos-19084a4_i-saw-a-post-from-hivemq-asking-if-you-and-activity-7334225553874436096-JNUG?utm_source=share&utm_medium=member_desktop&rcm=ACoAAAtzbAgBkrAZFO7DdeiNjpEtTeEsLw04vAI
Freek advocates that starting with building a UNS, should not scare anyone - essentially: "put on your Nike's and Just Do It!". This approach leans more towards learning by doing. My take away is that you might not have everything figured out up front, but once you get started, you will learn what works and what doesn't. The value of having a UNS could be discovered along the way.

Author: markpitout
Content:
So I guess I am asking: What's in a name?
Beyond the definition for UNS given by @Walker Reynolds :
1. Edge-Driven
2. Light-weight
3. Report By Exception
there is no standardized or universally agreed upon definition of what is or isn't a UNS.

That means it is easy for a company to jump on the hype train, co-opt the term UNS and make a sales pitch out of it. Inexperienced customers who are just starting to learn about UNS will have a difficult time distinguishing between snake oil salespersons and engineers bringing real value.

The UNS of customer A could be very different from the UNS of customer B, because their businesses and tech stacks are different. So, is it even possible to pin down a concrete definition of what UNS is? 

My inexperience is probably shining through here, but I would like to hear from this community: What is your complete and all encompassing description of what is (and what isn't) a UNS?
Is this even a reasonable question to ask?

Author: vaughnturner
Content:
The Unified Namespace (UNS) is the single source of truth for all business and industrial data in an organization. It is the structure through which all events and states across the enterprise are published and consumed in real time.

Key elements of UNS:

Real-time, event-driven architecture: Every change in state or event across people, processes, assets, and systems is published to the UNS as it happens.

Single, centralized namespace: Instead of siloed data across disparate systems, the UNS aggregates and organizes all data hierarchically (often modeled on the ISA-95 standard) and makes it available to all consumers.

Technology agnostic, typically broker-based: Walker emphasizes that the UNS is not a specific product or platform; it’s an architecture. MQTT is the preferred protocol because it naturally supports UNS principles (lightweight, publish/subscribe, report-by-exception), but it can be other protocols as well.

Author: _dyland
Content:
First takeaway, the UNS will almost always be different from Customer A to Customer B. 

A common criticism is that a couple sites (even within the same company) that start with concurrent UNS pilots in isolation are very likely to develop two architectures that are not easily compatible. Even if all the same tools are used, say Ignition - Highbyte - Flow - MQTT. The topic paths, schemas, UDTs and Models may all be very different from each other. They likely picked different brokers too...

Starting truly "Bottom Up" will rarely scale past the site it was initially designed for. More realistically, it will rarely scale past the domain on the single site it was built for. This is where conversations about champions and executive buy in become a part of the equation. Eventually, the CIO, CTO, COO, CFO, and CEO all need to be bought in.

Author: _dyland
Content:
But that gets to the fine line of what is a UNS. And I'll probably get some pushback on this but it is not an Architecture. 

It's the concept of an architecture. It's the rules, strategy, and philosophy that you use to design and build your architecture. 

More importantly, it's the definition of what is often called the "Holy Grail". It's not necessarily something that anyone would build on a brownfield site. Not exactly as described anyways. 

As there is no chance of eliminating all of the existing stovepipes. Especially not overnight. Bridging the stovepipes, yeah. Connecting disparate assets to a common infrastructure, yeah. Ripping out the entire DCS because it doesn't meet the requirements, no...

This is why there is no single diagram of what a UNS is.

Author: _dyland
Content:
It's also why I will never sell a "Unified Namespace". As the UNS is just the tool.

When I am asked for a UNS my first question is "Why?". The answer is often, "Because we need a single source of truth."

A few more rounds of the 5 Whys gets me to the fact that they saw it on YouTube, LinkedIn, or at a conference. Or maybe their buddy at another plant built one and they want in on it. 

To reiterate, the UNS is just a tool. Don't deploy it unless you know what problem it is going to solve.

Author: _dyland
Content:
For the more hopeful point. Don't let this intimidate you from starting to build something. Pilots, demos, MVPs are all important. They are easy, quick ways to solve Immediate problems. They are also the best way to learn. 

But don't confuse a one off pilot with a strategy. Don't expect that MVP to scale.

Technical Debt is inevitable. And these small wins have a way of piling it on. What looks cheaper and easier today is probably going to incur debt that will be paid with interest tomorrow.

Author: _dyland
Content:
Sorry for the novel here... In short. 

Strive for the ideals laid out in the definition @Vaughn Turner laid out above. But the reality is a lot messier than that. 

All three of the posts you linked are accurate. 

The balance is unique, but it is somewhere between the poles of:

Move fast, get the quick wins, and start with the low hanging fruit... And sitting down in a conference room with a dedicated team to map out and plan every schema, every topic, and every step. 

It shouldn't be scary, but the scope of it should be respected.

Author: _dyland
Content: More simply put. It's a tool. Never lead with the tool. Always start with a problem. Work the solution back from the problem. Then pick the tools required.

Author: markpitout
Content:
My take-away from this post:
If engineers at Site 1 and Site 2 have each started their own independent UNS pilots, that end up being incompatible, then what was  created are two Namespaces (not UNIFIED). The only true way to end on a UNIFIED Namespace is if both sites follow the same standard for structuring the data hierarchy, which later on enables the two Namespaces to be joined into a single namespace. Hence the need for a top-down approach involving CIO, CTO, COO, CFO, and CEO, etc.

May I then conclude that your main objection to what so many call UNS, is that it does not regard the whole enterprise. Or more crudely, simply chucking some sensor data in a broker and then popping it on a dashboard does not make a UNIFIED Namespace - it is just a simple Namespace of some subset of the enterprise.

Author: _dyland
Content:
You don't like my answer on the starting point. But the combination of Ignition, Highbyte, and Flow make a toolbox that can solve probably 70% of the plant floor "Low Hanging Fruit". 

If that is too expensive, it's either a cannot or will not afford it situation. In the rare case it is a cannot, then the UNS is not your solution.

If it is a will not, you have two options.
1. Start at the top-down, affect change in the culture and align the solution to the business needs. 

2. Build pilots and MVPs that just become more stovepipes. Even if we pretend that we are building a UNS...

From there.

The first thing it depends on is what the brownfield situation looks like. After that, the next steps depend on both the roadmap and the immediate need identified. 

Typically, if we are actually doing a UNS implementation, this is building a controls / OT network. If that is already in place, it is modeling the machines / equipment / assets we care about for this first use case. If we are starting with business processes, it's likely not a UNS we are building. 

So, with the "Starter" stack above, this is probably reverse engineering machines, PLC Logic, DCS, etc and making an asset / item model for each using UDTs in Ignition. 

If allowed, and safe to do so, this may also be changes to the PLC logic to add count buffers or state enumeration. 

Once we have the machines connected, the data identified, and the models built. We can "Wire" these UDTs to the actual tags/registers in the controllers. This is the "Connect, Collect" part. Add in a Historian (Probably TimeBase at the edge) and we have "Connect, Collect, Store" though with the cost to install and configure network switches and the labor to reverse engineer the models, the licensing of the software looks incredibly cheap. 

Once we have Connect, Collect, Store down for, let's say a single line, (or whatever we needed for the PoC) we can do the next steps. "Analyze, Visualize" this is where Flow comes in alongside Ignition. Connect the existing stovepipes and databases to the models we built in Ignition. Building further contextualized models and calculating KPIs to drive dashboards. Along with the Ad-Hoc trending enabled by the historian. 

Now, after some time working with the operators, maintenance team, and management, we should have a pretty good user story to build the UX of the dashboard.

Once we have made the interface. 

We have "Connect, Collect, Store, Analyze, Visualize".

Or phase 1 of the UNS. 

Now, we face another fork. Do we take the foundation we built and keep building on that or do we connect more machines. 

Once we get the plant floor exposed. We can start connecting it to the Enterprise. This is where Highbyte shines. Connecting the UNS to the enterprise apps, data lake, and traditional IT world. 

- This was written on my phone, so excuse any typos or odd formatting... Also, as always this is over generalized and may or may not apply in a given situation. 

The key is, of anyone is asking for a UNS they are asking the wrong question. First is what is the need. Then it's what tool do we use to solve it. 

A UNS is a big lift. Depending on the need, the culture, and the risk assessment, it may or may not be the right answer for a given manufacturers problems.

Author: _dyland
Content:
It depends and personally, I’m usually of the opinion: no, don’t buy it yet.

If the team is aligned and there's a clear strategy, I generally say buy the modules when you actually need them. But I admit... that’s a bit idealistic.

There are valid reasons to move earlier:
Is the budget approved today, but might not be tomorrow?
Do you know you’ll need MQTT later? How much later?
If you wait, how much technical debt will pile up?  Will it lead to rework?

As an integrator, I usually didn’t push too hard for it early, because the budget just wasn’t there, and clients didn’t want to pay for “what-ifs.” 
Unless we wrapped it as part of a broader strategic roadmap.

But we’d often push the what we started with to its breaking point. The client would see what we had working “well enough,” and despite our warnings, we’d hit predictable, unplanned downtime before they finally approved the modules. And by then, the debt was too much so even with the right licenses, nobody wants to pay for the cleanup.

So, it’s always a balance... Especially when you have been there before and know what to expect...

I once spent literally two years telling a site that they needed more than one Ignition Gateway, they kept saying it wasn't in the budget, eventually - the gateway crashed and I worked with them for 16 Hours overnight remotely spinning up a second gateway and hastily splitting the projects and tags between them to get them back into production... years after that and they are still slowly digging out of the same technical debt we warned them about.

All that said though, there are plenty of reasons to wait too - maybe you decide down the road that you would rather use Highbyte or Flow Software to connect to Ignition and Model the data before publishing it, so maybe you don't need the transmission at all. Maybe you want to do the same with incoming messages, or the existing infrastructure would work better with the transactions over the WebDev module. 

Maybe it will only ever be a traditional SCADA and the client doesn't want a UNS...

Maybe there is already a separate corporate initiative that is putting pressure on the plant manager to do things a certain way - or another integrator that is working with them on a UNS.

My answer to Integrators is to do what you can with what you are given to provide the best possible outcome to the clients - So, that would mean educate, recommend, and concede when they know the risk and accept it. 

To end-users, plant level, it would be to make sure you have a roadmap and a strategy and to make the decision based on where you are on that journey as well as accounting for where the politics are likely to lead.

TL;DR: If there’s no consumer and no roadmap, it’s probably premature. But there are real-world reasons to move early - just know why you’re doing it.

Author: codepoet80
Content:
I think what keeps getting missed  in this conversation is that information modeling doesn’t in itself have much value. The purpose of modeling the information is so that you can bind applications to the data — applications include visualizations (dashboards), analytics (reports and predictions) and AI use-cases (chatting with your data hopefully not being the only one).

Without a common API, we’re at risk of moving the protocol problem (and without broader Unification, the mapping problem) up a few layers.

The API effort hasn’t yet chosen an API *style* (eg: graphql or RESt) but it is on-track to defining common API primitives (methods). The goal is that applications (the part that extracts value from information) can be written once, and run against any middleware that implements the common API signature.

It’s not intended to be implemented in multiple places in each stack — it’s explicitly an API for *contextual* information platforms. Anything that an imposes a UNS on one or more data sources is contextual, but the API will be most useful where multiple sources are aggregated, and where the middleware can provide more than just current values, but also history, hierarchical relationships, and non-hierarchical (graph-style) relationships.

Author: codepoet80
Content:
I’ve given up believing there will be one ontological model to rule all of OT. I still hold out hope that common elements will exist in a wide variety of OT information models — in the same way there are classes of USB devices, and common electrical interfaces, we can and should arrive at reusable and common building blocks found in many (ideally all) “namespaces.”

If we then have a common way to query for, and bind to those things programmatically, *then* we can have commonly used,  collaboratively developed, and actually portable applications.

So Requirements have a type (User Requirements, System Requirements, Subsystem Requirements, etc) , the other part aka  Functional Requirements, are requirement subtypes(constraints, functional, performance, etc). 

1) User Requirements tell you what the user needs.
2) System Requirements tell you the super high level things that the system needs to be able to satisfy but dont tell you the implementation details (or shouldn't).
3) Subsystem Requirements tell you the lower level implementation details that the designed systems need to satisfy. 

1) Functional Requirements: Tell you the Behaviors of the System.
2) Performance Requirements: Tell you the performance thresholds you must meet. 
3) Constraint Requirements: Tell you the constraints that are not design parameters.
4) etc

The answer will be “it depends”…. 
Your application tolerates greater than 1min state changes…. Where my automotive assembly line has a 16s cycle time so if i only monitor state every 1 min…. I will miss state changes… counts would be fine as long as I don’t need more granularity in my count samples.

Author: bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
MQTT is not a durable and queryable data store. It's not a database. It's largely a technology for efficiently distributing telemetry data.

I would recommend mapping out the business process and interactions between MES and the industrial automation in a technology-agnostic way. Author: sparkylarks
bright_hummingbird_31342
Content:
If someone is married to the whole MQTT-based UNS thing, they can still publish the results of a transaction in parallel for secondary consumers (e.g., dashboards) in parallel.

Where it gets wonky is the tunneling of recipe transactions through an MQTT broker and trying to use it as a document database of sorts with retained messages. Backfilling historical data is another bad pattern I've seen lately. Also, holding open an HTTP connection to wait to relay requests, verify request received, listen for response, verify, etc through MQTT messages before responding is just nuts. If all the integration patterns are 1:1, it's time to reevaluate. And particularly it's absurd when it's just one node pub/sub'ing to itself.

UNS is about unifying namespaces and making data accessible. It's not about forcing MQTT onto every single problem. Start with the access patterns of the data consumers and stay focused on this. 

Not everything is an L1 or L2 telemetry node that produces and consumes tag data. Those accountable for an operation don't care about tags. They need 2nd, 3rd, 4th, etc order information derived from it (among other stuff) to schedule, staff, supply, maintain, budget, etc the plant. They don't conceptualize data like an industrial controls engineer does.

Author: _dyland
Content:
First - I don't think we disagree on anything here. I am in full agreement with what Aron wrote there too. 

Then...
Getting technical is dangerous here - it often gets into semantic debates that go nowhere - First question is "Is a Unified Namespace" using the word Namespace in the same way  that "Most other environments do". 
Then we need to define what a "Single Source of Truth" is and how it is scoped. 

The definition of a "Semantic Hierarchy" - and more so, the difference between a "Hierarchy", a "Taxonomy", and an "Ontology".

At some point we need to come to a common meaning of "Report by Exception" and "Event Driven" in the context of a Unified Namespace.
While also addressing what was (or is) intended when it is stated that a Unified Namespace is "Omniscient and Omnipotent"... in a way that doesn't offend.

Then we need to define the lines between "Concept", "Architecture", "Pattern", and "Implementation".
Which one (or more) the (or a) Unified Namespace is categorized under.

Assuming many, what is the distinction between the Concept, the Architecture, the Pattern, and an Implementation.
From there, when discussing implementation patterns, we need to understand on if we are talking about the same thing or not.

Are we talking about an MQTT Broker with a semantic hierarchy?
Are we talking about a Node Based Ecosystem? A traditional hub and spoke? Maybe A Full Mesh or a Partial Mesh?

All this is before even talking about what happens at each node... or where we store data... or how we access it.

My two cents, Even the UNS is a tool - too many here put the tool before the business case.

Author: mparris
Content:
@Brian McCarver hello Brian!

The goal of a common entry point for consumers is laudable, and I believe most in this Discord would agree with pursuing that goal.

It gets interesting real quick answering the next question: what protocol should be used for the common interface being served up by the Information Broker?

Some may think that an MQTT broker could fulfill the role of Information Broker. Lack of a request/response (such as read latest value) should be a red flag whether an MQTT broker can serve as an Information Broker. Also, HiveMQ has signaled that an MQTT broker is not sufficient for an Information Broker with the announcement of their new product Pulse.

MQTT brokers are great as infrastructure for an application, where its data needs to get fanned in/fanned out and the application controls the data format on both ends. SparkplugB took it to another level so it’s possible to integrate applications/devices from different vendors. Still, request/response (such as read latest value) is missing.

Because MQTT is inherently a point-to-point connection, Information Brokers can offer MQTT endpoints (like an MQTT Broker) so devices can publish data and the Information Broker can immediately consume the MQTT topics and map them to its internal informational model for others to then consume…even other MQTT clients! Won’t be as light weight as existing MQTT Brokers, and not as easy to swap one Information Broker for another, but in this space, you will need to select a partner with someone to build out the infrastructure.

Back to the original question: what protocol should be used for the central endpoint of an Information Broker?  I’m with @Jonathan Wise… I3X interface will be the best option for layer2 and  layer3 applications 😀

Content:
Don't have a ton of experience with issues, but currently I don't worry about 'harmonizing' my tag structure according to things that change at the same rate. 

My goal with the UNS has been to group topics by their meaningful area within the model. For example, we have a printing press with a print section, a dryer section, a waxing section. Within the waxing section are temperature and humidity readings that are common across all our waxing cells so we modeled the structure based on that. 

For some lines, all the temp/humidity readings come from a single Banner DXMR90 pushing data to the broker. For other lines, it's a bunch of disparate sensors doing it on their own. So the 'shape' of the data is common but we don't make guarantees on the order or timeliness of the data, for the most part.

It hasn't been an issue for us (so far) but I do know that folks often talk about resampling to ensure for any point in time all the signals have a value. I thought this was more a function of the historian than anything...

Even in the best case scenario of super-duper advanced modeling, a lower-level device/application will never know the full context of its relation within the UNS. The information must be additive as you move up the stack.

IMHO, the best to hope for regarding  smart devices with models is to announce itself to an Information Broker, where it may recognize the object type and the broker can then use known properties from the defined object template to automatically insert the new object instance within the UNS where other metadata and relationships can be layered on top.

Author: codepoet80
Content: unless you're designing (or 3D modeling) the mechanical behavior of the equipment, relationships within it can reliably be modeled hierarchically -- and the context for a single device is, by definition, self-contained. Its over-kill to implement a rich, context oriented API on a device that already has a common language.

Author: codepoet80
Content: i3X is far more concerned about external relationships. where is the device physically located? what utilities are supplying resources to that equipment (WAGES)? what are the direct and indirect interactions with that equipment and other objects (people, material, other equipment)? are there ambient (or transient) variables that may impact the performance (speed, reliability, output) of that equipment?

Author: codepoet80
Content: I'd say for a "contextual information platform" (pure examples: Flow, Rhyze, ThinkIQ), a data ops platform (eg: HighByte) or a SCADA platform (see you at ICC next week?), the most basic unit we're generally interested in is the equipment model itself (although I wouldn't rule out a component model).

Author: codepoet80
Content: So, the Modbus device should be an instance Object, of a class. But the actual connectivity to the device is a solved problem -- there are plenty of connectivity/driver/server/adapter solutions out there. There are only a few "contextual information platforms", and each has its own API.

Author: codepoet80
Content: If a contextual information platform has its own drivers/adapters, that's great -- but its not the core value prop here.

Author: codepoet80
Content:
The core value is understanding the device in the context of the manufacturing operation. questions like:
- is the device executing a job?
- is the job part of a customer order?
- will the equipment produce more waste than expected?
- if so, what is the reason for that waste? are there correlations with material? operator? other equipment failures?
- will the job be completed on time and at the expected quality?
- if not, can we predict a cause (or at least correlate potential causes)?

Author: codepoet80
Content: The device itself is a critical node in that graph, but the focus of i3x is giving weight to the graph itself -- and ensuring it is accessible programmatically.
